News.title: Russian sailor threatens to shoot dead crewmate after warship crashes into refuelling vessel off Kent coast
News.content:
KILL THREAT Russian sailor threatens to shoot dead crewmate after warship crashes into refuelling vessel off Kent coast







Next

A RUSSIAN sailor threatened to shoot dead his crewmate after their warship crashed into a refuelling vessel off the Kent coast.

The heavily-armed Neustrashimy smashed into the Valentin Rykov while attempting to secure itself to it in rough seas between October 21 and October 23.

Radio transmissions revealed after an engineer delayed the operation over an issue with paperwork, one crew member fumed: “We need to bring him out onto the helipad and execute him there in front of everyone.”

Another crew said: “F***, this is an absolute nightmare, I’m getting really worked up.”





They added: “We’ve just been waiting around for this f***ing ridiculous wind and current.”

The operation was later abandoned and both crews the headed to shorelines off eastern Scotland where they managed to refuel, The Times reports.

A defence source described the collision as a “shambolic and reckless” display of seamanship that risked spilling oil into British waters and probably left the vessels with damage to their hulls and upper decks.

The warship only had two days worth of fuel left during its botched attempt to raft together with the vessel.



Earlier this year sanctioned Russian vessels were still sailing through the English Channel at a rate of almost one a day – with experts warning Andy Burnham must act now to stop tyrant Vladimir Putin.

A Sun investigation revealed that at least 28 ‘banned’ boats were caught on radar transiting the channel since June 19.

It included many flying under a false flag, like Gabon, Panama or Comoros, which are part of Putin’s illegal “shadow fleet” of tankers.

Our probe tracked more than 600 Foreign Office-sanctioned boats around the world using open-source radar tracking data.

News.title: Paedo Gary Glitter’s outrageous jail demands – from poster of HIMSELF to luxury watches… and he’s not the only one
News.content:
YOU WANT WHAT? Paedo Gary Glitter’s outrageous jail demands – from poster of HIMSELF to luxury watches… and he’s not the only one







Next

HIGH-profile jailbirds think they can demand the world while inside.

And paedo Gary Glitter – who the Sun revealed has won a new parole hearing – is no different.



This hearing could be the pervert’s last chance at freedom before he dies.

Glitter, a glam-rock star of the 1970s, was first jailed in 1997 after being caught with 4,000 child abuse images.



He was released from prison in 2023 after serving half his 16-year sentence.

But he was recalled within weeks after the The Sun obtained footage of him at a halfway house hostel discussing net browsers and the dark web.

In a bid to make his second stint in jail more cushy, Glitter is said to have made a long list of outrageous demands.

Glitter, real name Paul Gadd, is understood to have had his designer clothes, Bluetooth headphones, an XBox and an expensive Longines watch delivered to his jail.

He also requested a copy of his own autobiography Leader, and a poster of himself in his glam-rock heyday, which is said to be plastered

on his cell wall.

Speaking out at the time, an insider told the Mirror: “It’s a disgrace this was allowed. He was recalled for utterly vile behaviour and is the most hated pervert in Britain.



“He’s a serial child abuser and this should not be happening.

“His poor victims would rather the belongings be burnt than transported at a cost to the taxpayer just in case he gets bored.”

Glitter is understood to spend his time locked up watching Freeview TV and DVDs that have been deemed suitable by jail censors.

And he is believed to be “on his last legs” as his health woes pile up with the prisoner often using a wheelchair to move around his Category C jail.

And he’s not the only one… Here we break down all the outrageous jail demands made by Britain’s most high-profile lags.



Russell Brand

The Sun this week revealed Russell Brand has been begging prison guards to let him use his specialist shampoos and hair loss pills over fears his trademark long locks will fall out behind bars.

The vain rapist pleaded with warders to let him have Alpecin caffeine shampoo and Propecia tablets, a prescription drug used to treat male pattern baldness.

Both were confiscated when he entered category A prison HMP Wandsworth at the start of his 10 and a half year sentence. He’s now in HMP Littlehey.

One insider told The Sun : “He was kicking off because he’s worried he’s going to lose his hair. He takes Propecia pills for his hair, but he had them confiscated inside.



“He isn’t allowed to take them because they’re not essential. They’re considered cosmetic.”

Finasteride, the drug in Propecia, is not available on the NHS for hair loss because baldness is classed as a cosmetic problem instead of a medical one.

Former comic Brand has already been shipped out to cushy category C prison HMP Littlehey in Cambridgeshire.

Experts say those who stop taking the daily pill can expect hair loss problems to return within six to 12 months.



Ronnie Kray

Twin brothers Ronnie and Reggie Kray ran a gangland empire in London during the 1950s and 60s and were sent to prison for 30 years for murder.

Ronnie spent 16 years in Broadmoor Hospital after being judged to be criminally insane before dying in 1995.

During his time in the high-security psychiatric hospital, Ronnie was allowed a few home comforts.

After his death, Ronnie’s second ex-wife Kate spoke out as some of the late screws’ possessions went up for auction.

She told the Mirror: “Ron did probably have nights out with Diana Dors and Barbara Windsor in the dinner jacket with velvet lapels, but he wore the green Lester Bowden sports jacket, in Broadmoor.



“Because it’s a hospital not a prison, inmates wear their own clothes. And Ron took advantage of this privilege.

“He had his tailors go in to measure him up for Italian-cut suits. I’d get them dry-cleaned but he got inmates to iron his shirts and polish his shoes. I gave him a Giorgio Armani tie.

“He sent me to Russell & Bromley to get crocodile shoes. He’d say: ‘Don’t worry if the size isn’t quite right, I’ve hardly got far to walk’.”

Ronnie also kept a framed portrait of Kate by his bed alongside a clock with a canary in a cage, as well as watches, including one sent to him from twin brother Reggie and gold cufflinks.



Charles Bronson

One of the most demanding prisoners living at taxpayers’ expense is also one of the country’s most notorious – Charles Bronson.

Now in his 70s, his weekly menu requests include an astonishing 18 bacon rolls, whole goose and chicken, 10 Pot Noodles, a big tub of ice cream, curry, steak and chips.

He also wanted ‘liquid Wednesdays’ featuring three pints of Guinness, and gallons of tea, coffee, water and squash



But he won’t get any of that inside, instead directing his requests to his then wife and former Coronation Street actress Paula Williamson.

The ‘Salvador diet’ was his dream should he ever get

released.

Bronson was convicted of armed robbery in 1974 and has earned a reputation as a violent and dangerous inmate.

He has held 11 hostages in nine different sieges – including governors, doctors, staff and, on one occasion, his solicitor.

In one chilling siege, Bronson ambushed a jail librarian, demanding an inflatable doll, a helicopter and a cup of tea.



Robert Maudsley

Serial killer Robert Maudsley tried his luck by writing directly to a newspaper for his prison cell demands.

Quadruple killer – who was given the name Hannibal the Cannibal – killed a fellow inmate by jamming a plastic spoon in their ear after taking them hostage and torturing them.

He’s spent most of his time inside in solitary confinement.

In 2000 he wrote a series of letters to The Times asking why he couldn’t have a pet budgie, promising to love it and “not eat it”.



He also questioned why he couldn’t have a TV to “see the world” as well as classical music tapes and pictures. He wrote: “Why can’t I have a budgie instead of the flies and cockroaches and spiders I currently have? I promise to love it and not eat it.”

In another, he wrote: “If the prison service says no then I ask for a simple cyanide capsule which I shall willingly take and the problem of Robert John Maudsley can easily and swiftly be resolved.”

… and it’s not just famous faces

This summer, we reported how prisoners are flaunting their cells on social media – complete with TVs, games consoles and cupboards crammed with food.

A Sun investigation unearthed dozens of videos posted online which show lags bragging about their set-up, which also include rows of trainers, laptops, and impressive speaker systems.

All of the footage appeared to have been filmed on illicit mobile phones and posted online, despite handsets and internet access being prohibited across all UK prisons.



The behind-bars videos are a far cry from the bleak image many Brits associate with prison life and raises questions about the standards of security and access to contraband.

Vanessa Frake, former prison governor of Wormwood Scrubs said: “The broadcast of recent “Jail Tok” footage from within His Majesty’s Prison Service represents an appalling and absolute breakdown of institutional control that will deeply shock the public and veteran prison professionals alike.

“I find the images entirely unbelievable and deeply offensive to the standards of our profession.”

Andrea Coomber, Chief Executive at the Howard League for Penal Reform, said: “People in prisons should not be filming videos on banned mobile phones and sharing them online. However, the ability to earn privileges encourages good behaviour, and access to equipment and extra food forms a key motivating factor for those who are locked up.

“Ultimately, many problems in prison are exacerbated by the poor regimes across our system. Week after week, we see inspection reports showing that men are spending up to 23 hours a day locked in their cells with nothing to do.



RECOMMENDED STORIES

“Overcrowded and overstretched prisons are not able to provide the work, education and training that ought to be getting men out of their cells and into more productive pursuits, and the result is not just boredom but adverse impacts on mental health, violence and rehabilitation.”

News.title: Preschool teachers ‘gave four-year-olds sleep gummies during naptime’ that ‘left child knocked out and slobbering’
News.content:
Next

PRESCHOOL teachers allegedly gave four-year-olds sleep gummies during nap time that left one child “knocked out” and “slobbering”.

Two California mums are suing the Kiddie Academy of Orange daycare claiming staff gave their children melatonin without their permission.



The lawsuit accuses employees of negligence, battery, emotional distress and negligent hiring, according to KTLA.

Cassandra Sandoval and Priscilla Ayala claim their children were given “sleeping gummies” between May and September.



Sandoval enrolled her four-year-old and two-year-old at the facility after it offered a livestream service allowing her to monitor them.

She told ABC 7: “It helped me know if my child was eating, if they had a tough time for the day or if they were making friends.”

Sandoval claims she started noticing changes in her son’s sleeping patterns in August, according to the complaint.

She claimed that in September he asked her for sleeping gummies that he had taken during nap time at the daycare.

When she asked him about the alleged gummies, her son said he did not get them from any friends, but instead the school “in my bed”.

“I was shocked. How am I supposed to trust anyone?” she told CBS.



“These women were so kind to me and to my face. They were kind to my children.”

Sandoval bypassed speaking with the staff and instead filed a complaint with the California Department of Social Services, who launched a probe.

“I wanted to make sure this was done right,” she said.

“I don’t wanna just have an accusation like that without actual evidence.”

She said she started to closely monitor the livestreams while her children took naps.



She told the outlet: “I wanted to make sure this was done right. I don’t wanna just have an accusation like that without actual evidence.”

Footage taken on September 11 allegedly captured a member of staff receiving gummies from another employee.

The lawsuit claims that they then placed an unidentified substance into the mouth of Sandoval’s son while he was under a blanket.

Sandoval said: “I was so angry. Why’d I send him back?

“I left work immediately, ran into the daycare, grabbed one child and he was knocked out. That was my child who was given the sleeping gummy.



“He was slobbering. It was really sad.”

Sandoval said she immediately removed her children from the daycare and filed a police report.

Police have reported that the allegations do not constitute a criminal offense, according to CBS.

Kimberly Degonia, Sandoval’s lawyer, said she argued with the assessment and said the allegations could constitute battery.

Degonia is also representing Ayala, who claimed that a staff member asked for permission to give her daughter melatonin.



A Kiddie Academy of Orange spokesperson told ABC 7: “As an independently owned and operated Kiddie Academy franchise, we care deeply about the children, families and community we serve.

“Because this matter involves children and an ongoing review, we’re limited in what we can share publicly.

“We have been made aware of an allegation involving an employee who is reported to have provided an over-the-counter non-prescription dietary supplement to an enrolled child.

“The franchisee is cooperating fully with the ongoing investigation.”

They added that the staff member responsible was placed on administrative leave while the investigation remained ongoing.



Sandoval said she hopes the lawsuit will lead the daycare to take accountability.

RECOMMENDED STORIES

“They need to be held responsible because how many other parents has this happened to and they just weren’t able to navigate it this way, you know,” she said.

The Sun has reached out to the Kiddie Academy of Orange for comment.

News.title: Inside jet-set life of jailed ‘organ harvesting king’ who said he was doing ‘God’s work’ by selling body parts for £150k
News.content:
BLOOD MONEY Inside jet-set life of jailed ‘organ harvesting king’ who said he was doing ‘God’s work’ by selling body parts for £150k







Next

WITH his sprawling penthouse, exotic five-star holidays and business-class flights, Boris Wolfman lived a life of wealth and luxury.

But behind the glitzy Instagram-worthy facade lay a macabre underworld trade – and now a 12-year stretch in a bleak Russian prison.



The dual Israeli-Ukrainian citizen, 42, was the ruthless kingpin of a sickening organ-trafficking gang that preyed on the poor to harvest healthy human kidneys for the super-rich.

Claiming his black-market transplant business was doing “God’s work”, Wolfman banked a fortune while desperate donors were lured under the knife – with some even cheated out of the tiny sums of cash they were promised.



Before his downfall, he owned a luxury Istanbul flat and prime Mediterranean real estate, enjoying lavish getaways at exclusive resorts with his glamorous Ukrainian wife Yuli Guralnik.

Photographs showed the jet-setting couple flying business class, relaxing in tropical paradises and dining in high-end restaurants.

Yet Wolfman now faces more than a decade behind bars in a strict-regime penal colony after a Moscow court convicted him of human trafficking for organ removal and deliberately causing grievous bodily harm as part of an organised group.

The case exposed a gruesome international racket in which poverty-stricken victims from Russia and other former Soviet republics were recruited to supply kidneys to wealthy patients willing to pay over the top for a transplant.



At the centre of the grisly scandal was the notorious Medicus clinic in Kosovo, where prosecutors revealed patients were flown in from across the globe.

Its dark secrets were blown open in November 2008 when 23-year-old Turkish donor Yilmas Altun fainted while waiting for a flight home.

Customs officials discovered a fresh surgical scar across his abdomen, leading them to discover how he had just had a kidney removed at the clinic after being promised a substantial payday by an organ broker in Turkey.



His collapse sparked a police probe that exposed an international trafficking ring.

When officers raided Medicus the next day, they found Israeli recipient Bezalel Shafran, 74, who had coughed up £76,000 for the new kidney he desperately needed.

In a chilling twist, the impoverished Turkish donor and elderly Israeli patient had been placed on operating tables next to each other.



They even exchanged glances before being put under anaesthetic.

Around 30 suspected victims were identified at Medicus over just eight months in 2008 in one of Europe’s worst-ever organ trafficking scandals.

While Wolfman was not named as Altun’s Turkey-based recruiter, the clinic was central to the crimes for which he has now been jailed in Moscow.

Russian prosecutors said Wolfman was a member of a transnational criminal gang operating between 2006 and 2008 that targeted people in desperate financial straits with adverts offering cash for kidneys.

Donors were assured the operations were safe and legal before being trafficked abroad for surgery.



Wolfman – whose trial heard evidence involving three Russian victims, according to reports – negotiated with prospective donors, helped arrange travel and met them at airports in Istanbul or Tel Aviv.

He would then accompany them to Kosovo, prosecutors said.

Once surgeons at Medicus removed their kidney, Wolfman organised their flights home.

Each dodgy surgery was valued at no less than £67,000 – but donors were only offered between £6,670 and £12,550, with some never even paid in full.

The Medicus scandal also exposed Turkish transplant surgeon Yusuf Ercin Sonmez, dubbed “Doctor Vulture”, who carried out illicit kidney transplants for years while dodging authorities across multiple countries.



He was identified as the surgeon involved in the operation connecting Altun and Shafran, becoming the subject of an international manhunt.

Among the victims caught up in the grim trade were a Russian mum and daughter who sold their kidneys at the same clinic just 25 days apart.

Vera Shvedko, then 50, was living in Israel and struggling financially after her younger daughter suffered a serious head injury.

Promised £5,000 for a kidney, she was flown to Medicus via Istanbul in July 2008.

She recalled meeting Wolfman, describing him as a handsome, blue-eyed young man who spoke perfect Russian.



Recalling her fear before surgery, Vera said: “I was just afraid that they might cut something else out as well.”

She suffered months of agonising pain following her surgery before her divorced elder daughter Anna Firsova – a mum-of-two desperate for money – also went under the knife.

Anna’s recipient paid £61,000 for her organ, though how much she actually received remains unclear.

Both women’s cases were examined during Wolfman’s Moscow trial, where he denied any wrongdoing.

Sonmez had previously been exposed by undercover Turkish TV journalists posing as donors in 1998 and was barred from Turkey’s public health sector.



However, his name continued to crop up in illegal transplant probes – including an investigation in Azerbaijan in 2010.

Authorities also pursued Israeli broker Moshe Harel, before finally arresting him in Cyprus in 2018 after years on the run.

Prosecutors revealed donors travelled from Turkey, Moldova, Russia and Kazakhstan to sell kidneys to buyers from Israel, Germany, Canada, Poland and more.

They often left Kosovo with little or none of the sum of money they were promised.

Medicus boss Lutfi Dervishi, a prominent Kosovo urologist, was convicted of human trafficking in May 2018 following a retrial and jailed for seven-and-a-half years, while anaesthetist Sokol Hajdini was handed a one-year sentence.



Judges discovered at least seven donors were recruited through internet adverts, while prosecutors uncovered at least 23 “dodgy” transplants in 2008 alone.

Recipients paid between £59,000 and £92,000, while donors were typically promised around £8,400 to £10,000 a go.

Away from the clinic, Wolfman and his wife were linked to five-star resorts in tourist hotspots Marmaris and Bodrum, as he snapped up valuable Turkish property and built business interests in international trade and medical tourism.

His transplant firm was named Leshem Shamain – meaning “In the Name of Heaven” – with Wolfman insisting his work merely helped desperately ill patients find treatment.

He claimed: “In our company, we don’t have any contact with the organ.”



RECOMMENDED STORIES

Wolfman, who has always denied wrongdoing, claimed he once personally donated a kidney to a sick friend and bone marrow to his son, who suffered from blood cancer.

He was finally detained in Turkey in 2025 and extradited to Russia to face justice over the long-running investigation.

News.title: US security chiefs warn airlines over Al-Qaeda hijack and terror attack threats – weeks after Flydubai horror
News.content:
‘TERROR’ WARNING US security chiefs warn airlines over Al-Qaeda hijack and terror attack threats – weeks after Flydubai horror







Next

US security chiefs have sounded the alarm over chilling Al-Qaeda hijacking plots after the horrifying Flydubai terror attack attempt.

The horror incident occurred when an axe-wielding co-pilot attempted to take control of a Tel Aviv-bound jetliner carrying 174 people.



Brave passengers helped pilot Smit Machchhar fend off would-be terrorist Hamam al-Hammami, 29, and wrestle back control of the plane.

In the wake of the terrifying incident, security bosses warned of threats against “perceived US, Israeli and Jewish interests”.



The alert comes ahead of Thanksgiving, which is routinely the busiest travel week of the year in the US.

Airlines and industry counterparts were sent the report by Department of Homeland Security (DHS) and Transportation Security Administration (TSA) officials.



The report, obtained by CNN, warned that Al-Qaeda and its supporters have praised the attempted Flydubai hijacking and encouraged similar attacks.

The terror group’s messaging “reiterates longstanding AQ narratives that encourage supporters to exploit aviation access, evade security measures, and conduct attacks using commercial aircraft,” the report said.

There are no known credible threats underway and sharing of information is standard practice, a law enforcement source told the network.

However, a series of possible red flags for people who may be planning an attack was sent to aviation officials.



They included individuals seeking detailed information about flight information security procedures without a legitimate business reason, and those expressing “a strong desire to handle specific items of luggage”.

The unexplained loss of items like airline radios, access badges, and uniforms were also highlighted as possible red flags.

Al-Hammami launched his attack on the Tel Aviv-bound plane around two hours after taking off from Dubai International Airport on September 30.



The plane dropped 14,000ft in just 29 seconds as the Omani co-pilot slashed open the captain’s head with a crash axe.

The would-be terrorist confessed to plotting the terrifying 9/11-style attack before he was even accepted as a Flydubai pilot, Israeli sources said.

They also claim that he admitted he “tried to get hired” at several other airlines during his interrogation.

“The dream was to crash into Ben-Gurion Airport,” he added, a source told The Jerusalem Post.

Al-Hammami is said to have been frequenting the Tel Aviv airport during his time as a pilot.



One of his last visits to Israel took place around July and was allegedly used to gather intelligence in preparation for the attack.

He is believed to have intended to carry out the plot days later, but aborted the effort when he realised a crew member he was friends with was on board.

Al-Hammami is understood to have been a student at one of the UK’s biggest flight schools between 2018 and 2019.

RECOMMENDED STORIES

Hero captain Smit Machchhar was left with horror scars on the back of his head and later awarded the United Arab Emirates’ First Class Order of Zayed II.

The award, presented by UAE president Mohamed bin Zayed Al Nahyan, honoured his bravery in thwarting the suspected terror plot.

News.title: Sick unseen messages from Holly Willoughby’s kidnap plot revealed as undercover cop who stopped psycho speaks out
News.content:
Next

THE undercover cop who foiled Holly Willoughby’s kidnap has relived the moment he realised her life was in grave danger.

Investigator David Nelson says he raised the alarm after online sicko Gavin Plumb described to him a plot to snatch and kill the TV host.



He tells a new Channel 4 documentary how the ex-security guard sent him hundreds of messages detailing plans to overpower Holly at her home with chloroform, sexually assault her and dump her body.

US-based Nelson alerted the FBI after Plumb forwarded him footage of his “restraint kit”, containing a ball gag, ankle and hand shackles, ropes, metal cable ties and two sets of handcuffs.



Recalling the moment he received the recording, which features in tomorrow’s show, Nelson says: “I see a lot of messed-up stuff working in cyberspace.

“But for someone to have all those materials collected and spread out on the bed like a trophy shot, it was extremely disturbing.

“When I saw that video, I knew this was gonna be something we were going to have to move with real quick or things were going to get real bad.”

US crimebusters relayed Plumb’s plot to the UK’s National Crime Agency and cops nailed the fiend following a 2023 swoop on his home in Harlow, Essex.

The role Nelson played in the case features in documentary The Plot To Kidnap Holly Willoughby, which airs tomorrow night.

It looks at how clueless Plumb, 39 — now serving at least 16 years for soliciting murder, incitement to kidnap and incitement to rape — had no idea he was talking to an undercover cop when he shared his heinous blueprint.



He had tried to recruit an accomplice to help him execute his chilling plans through online forum, Abduct Lovers.

Nelson, whose name is an alias, recalled how Plumb said he had “wanted to rape” Holly for three years and bragged about knowing where she lived and how her security operated.

He went on to share in private messages that after the attack, he planned to dump her body in water.



Nelson told how he even had to discourage Plumb from staging a practice run targeting a woman he referred to as “my fit-a** neighbour”.

The officer, who is based in Owatonna, Minnesota, admitted he no idea who Holly Willoughby was when Plumb posted a series of snaps of the star on the Abduct Lovers page, which he says regularly has over 100 users engaging with content.

He revealed he decided to send Plumb a private message questioning why he had uploaded the photos, only to receive the response: “Why do you think?”

Nelson messaged Plumb, who used the name Big Bear on the site, on October 3, 2023, saying: “Alright, I’ll bite. Who’s the hottie?”

He told how Plumb initially seemed guarded, but opened up after the pair swapped live video messages of each other reading out the date and their agreed code word, “Holly”.



Within hours, the pair had swapped hundreds of messages in which Plumb laid out his vile plans, describing Holly as “the one in the public eye I want”.

Unaware he was incriminating himself, he bragged that he had “a s**tload of info on her” and later added: “Yeah, got everything to hold her and chloroform.”

When the cop said: “Stfu (shut the f*** up). You serious?”, Plumb responded with a photo of a bottle of the chemical.



The officer tells the documentary: “He wanted to recruit someone to come with him to carry out his ultimate fantasy . . . to conduct a home invasion, put her in a vehicle, drive her to an unknown space, sexually assault her. And then we’re going to leave her body in a body of water.”

As the pair continued swapping messages, Nelson asked when he should travel and Plumb offered to pick him up from the airport, suggesting he was trying to recruit a third accomplice “who can drive”.

Asked if he had weapons, he replied with a photo of a menacing-looking knife.

But with every snippet of information Plumb shared, the net was closing.

Nelson went on: “He started to share more information that really helped me narrow down where I needed to go and who I needed to work with.



“He shared that he was from Essex and that he was a security guard for a pharmaceutical company. He constantly shared images during the conversation.

“We would be in the middle of a topic and he may just drop four or five images of Holly. His excitement just continued to go up and up and up.

“He wanted to do a trial run so then he began sharing additional photographs of another woman.



“I can’t have two intended targets. It’s very difficult to mitigate two different threats to two different victims at the same time from one suspect. His criminal history frankly scared the s**t out of me.

“At that point I reached out to the Federal Bureau of Investigation, who then made contact with the National Crime Agency in the United Kingdom.

“I had learned from the Essex Police department that this individual was Gavin Plumb. The stakes were extremely high. Ms Willoughby was in extreme danger.”



In October 2023, with an arrest pending, the officer continued to speak to Plumb so that his device would be open and searchable by cops who swooped at his home in Harlow.

When the responses abruptly stopped, Nelson says he knew Plumb had been nicked.

He revealed: “I would have paid for my own ticket to fly over just so I could put the handcuffs on him myself.”

Plumb would later claim that his plan was purely a “fantasy” that he had no intention of acting on.

But Chelmsford crown court heard that, in August 2006, Plumb had tried to abduct two air hostesses from a Stansted Express train using a threatening note, three lengths of rope, and an imitation firearm. He got a 12-month suspended prison sentence.



Jurors were also told that in December 2008, Plumb attacked and attempted to tie up two 16-year-old girls in the stockroom of the Woolworths store where he worked. He was sentenced to 32 months behind bars.

RECOMMENDED STORIES

Last month, an attempt by Plumb to appeal his sentence for the Holly plot was rejected.

The Plot To Kidnap Holly Willoughby airs on Channel 4 tomorrow at 9pm.

News.title: Streeting calls Putin a 'cold-blooded killer' as he meets Zelensky in Kyiv
News.content:
UK Defence Secretary Wes Streeting has met with Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky following continued Russian attacks on Ukraine on Friday evening and overnight.

Zelensky has justified Ukraine's repeated attacks on a critical bridge linking Russia to occupied Crimea, describing it as a "fair response" to 109 separate Russian attacks on bridges in Ukraine.

He rejected a claim from Russia that the bridge, which links Russia to the peninsular it illegally annexed from Ukraine, was "exclusively civilian" in use.

Streeting and Zelensky hugged upon meeting and the British defence secretary explained he had come to Kyiv to see what support Ukraine needs for winter.

The BBC's Sarah Rainsford reports from Kyiv.

Read more on this story.

News.title: Catherine talks openly about how cancer changed her in documentary on BBC
News.content:
The Princess of Wales has spoken about how "cancer does change you," in a forthcoming documentary called Heal to be shown on the BBC.

"It changes your body, it changes you physically - but there is a much, much deeper part to what a cancer diagnosis shifts in you," says Catherine in the first glimpses from the documentary, which features her private thoughts on her illness and recovery.

The highly personal film, to be screened on BBC One on 29 November, will see Catherine share her experiences of cancer, saying: "Healing is a journey."

It includes new footage of her completing the Three Peaks Challenge earlier this year, which involved climbing the highest peaks in England, Scotland and Wales over a day.

"It's clear we're not meant to carry life's challenges alone," says Catherine's voice-over, accompanied by images of other cancer patients and the princess hugging her own family, including Prince William.

"It is often through pain that we realise there is a greater beauty that lies beyond that," she says, once again reflecting the sense of change from her cancer experience.

News.title: 'We're not meant to carry life's challenges alone', Catherine says in first clip
News.content:
The Princess of Wales' cancer journey is set to be depicted in a new BBC documentary "Heal" that will air next weekend.

It follows Catherine announcing in January 2025 that she was in remission after having revealed her diagnosis less than a year prior.

She has since spoken openly about her illness and treatment although has never disclosed publicly what type of cancer she faced.

The new documentary will include footage of her completing the Three Peaks Challenge earlier this year.

"It changes your body, it changes you physically - but there is a much, much deeper part to what a cancer diagnosis shifts in you," she says.

More on this story.

News.title: Spitting Image co-creator Peter Fluck dies aged 85
News.content:
Peter Fluck, co-creator of award-winning satirical puppet show Spitting Image, has died aged 85.

His family said he died in the early hours of Saturday at home in Cornwall, following a recent illness.

Spitting Image was immensely popular and sometimes controversial, running from 1984-1996 across 18 seasons, and featured puppet caricatures of celebrities, politicians and royals, including former Prime Minister Margaret Thatcher and Queen Elizabeth the Queen Mother.

"The spirit that Spitting Image brought to the country was epoch defining," a family statement said.

"With Roger Law ('Luck and Flaw'), he brought a unique cutting edge to caricaturing that later evolved into a production company that created the TV series Spitting Image," it added.

"Peter's creative life continued after the series for many years from his studio in Cornwall. He was a private man who eschewed fame and attention."

The show won several awards, including one Bafta TV award and two Emmys and at its peak drew an audience of 15 million.

Fluck was born in Cambridge in 1941, and created the show alongside childhood friend Roger Law, who he met while studying at Cambridge School of Art.

Following school, both Fluck and Law moved to London and set up as freelance illustrators, and in 1976 set up their partnership 'Luck and Flaw' back in Cambridge.

News.title: Australia hold on for narrow win against Wales
News.content:
Nations Championship

Wales (7) 26

Tries: Lake 2, Murray, Elias Cons: Costelow 3

Australia (12) 29

Tries: Tupou, Paenga-Amosa, Jorgensen, Ikitau Cons: Lonergan 2, Gordon Pens: Gordon

Wales could not emulate their famous victory against New Zealand as Australia claimed the Nations Championship spoils in Cardiff.

The Wallabies ended a four-match losing run thanks to tries from hooker Brandon Paenga-Amosa, prop Taniela Tupou, wing Max Jorgensen and centre Len Ikitau, while fly-half Carter Gordon kicked a late penalty.

Wales captain Dewi Lake scored two tries, while full-back Blair Murray also crossed following a superb assist by wing Louis Rees-Zammit.

Replacement hooker Ryan Elias grabbed a late try but Australia held on for victory as Wales paid the price for not capitalising on attacking chances.

Wales finished fifth in the northern hemisphere section and will play Japan at the Allianz Stadium in Twickenham on Saturday (13:10 GMT).

Australia finished third in the southern hemisphere table and play Ireland on Friday (20:10 GMT).

News.title: How a teen gamer and his mother helped rescue a missing girl
News.content:
The Colorado mother knew things were serious when she read the missing persons articles. Jenny knew she was in Oregon and gave the name of a city, but she didn't know where she was being held exactly. Khristina knew she needed more. She told Jenny to find a piece of mail or another document in the house that had a full name on it, which the girl did.

"That's when I went to work," Khristina says, delving into tax and property records.

Khristina narrowed down addresses, then searched them on a real estate site to find pictures. She showed the photos to Jenny, who confirmed that the second one was where she was being held.

The "next thing she asked me was to please not tell anyone until [her captor] was gone - that he did have weapons in the house and she was very scared," Khristina said.

Jenny promised Khristina she'd call her back through the game platform when he left the next morning, and in the meantime Khristina began looking for the law enforcement agency that had been assigned to the missing teen's case. She contacted Jenny's mother on social media, spoke briefly to her on the phone and then got a call from an FBI agent.

"Have you seen her alive?'" the agent asked Khristina.

"And I said: 'I have; I video chatted with her, I've seen her, and she goes 'Oh my God, I cannot believe any of this'," Khristina recalled.

When Jenny called Khristina back after her alleged captor left home, the FBI monitored their conversation. According to the criminal complaint's record of the conversation, Jenny explained how she'd met Adam Hunter Harmel on social media in May 2025.

He'd told her he was disabled and his hips were "messed up," offering Jenny money if she'd help get him to Oregon.

After he picked her up in Utah, however, Harmel threw her phone into a river, drove her to Oregon and kept her in the basement. He forced her to sleep against the wall in his bed, with a knife under his pillow, to prevent her from escaping. He gave Jenny a cell phone with no ability to make calls, but it could connect to wifi, which is how she played the online game.

The 39-year-old "would become violent and aggressive", the document says, which included hitting her and sexually assaulting her.

He also allegedly forced Jenny to remove her braces with pliers so she wouldn't be identifiable.

News.title: Why Nicola Coughlan's new drama might leave viewers uncomfortable
News.content:
Filming the series without a script meant the actors were fully immersed in their characters, making them real not just for viewers but for themselves too.

"I'm not playing myself, but there's far less, let's say 'character' here than anything else I've ever done because a lot of this is about just reacting," Coughlan says.

She and Cole would film long takes, some lasting about an hour and often with heated exchanges, which might need to be shot multiple times.

Coughlan describes I Am Helen as "the most challenging thing in terms of material that I've ever worked on", adding for the first time in a role she needed counselling.

"You literally would be physically and mentally quite exhausted," she says.

"There were times that I said to Dominic [Savage] if he wanted to do a third take for example - and I've never said this before on set - but I actually don't think I have that in me because you hit a wall.

"It's a lot to keep going."

Cole agrees that "it was tough".

"When you're given that freedom, things happen and I think you can get some really interesting and also quite shocking stuff," he says.

For him, that came when he damaged a fridge on set with a punch.

But it's that authenticity of emotion which, while difficult for the actors, is what Coughlan thinks makes the series so engaging.

"When people watch the 'I Ams', they feel quite truthful," she says.

"I think that's a big reason as to why, to be honest."

News.title: Employers are being asked to give interview feedback - here's what applicants want
News.content:
Have you ever applied for a job or attended an interview, only to hear absolutely nothing back from the employer?

So-called "job ghosting" has become a big problem for jobseekers in the UK, leaving them "demoralised", denting their confidence and undermining their hopes of finding work.

It's an issue that was mentioned in former minister Alan Milburn's major review into young people who are not in employment, education or training - those dubbed as Neets - this week.

Among his recommendations - aimed at reducing the proportion of Neets from 13% to about 5% by 2036 - Milburn proposed that large employers should give all unsuccessful job applicants under 25 "meaningful feedback".

The report's proposals relate mostly to England, with a recommendation that Scotland, Wales and Northern Ireland adapt the principles to suit their own systems.

But is feedback for all applicants realistic, given the vast number of applications these firms receive? And what can people do to improve their chances in such a tough job market?

Yugraj Samrai, 23, from Coventry is currently unemployed and says he has submitted hundreds of job applications since he graduated from his marketing degree in July.

But 30 to 40% of the time he hears nothing back at all, which can make him "feel like a statistic, not a person".

He tells the BBC: "I understand there are very few graduate jobs available, but at least give me a response to say whether I'll progress onto the next stage or not.

"I've spent all that time and energy submitting my application but got nothing in return."

News.title: England run up record win over New Zealand in rugby union's Nations Championship
News.content:
England (19) 37

Tries: Slade, Van Poortvliet, Earl, Chessum, Atkinson Cons: F Smith (2), M Smith Pens: M Smith (2)

New Zealand (5) 12

Tries: De Groot, B Barrett Cons: McKenzie

England's revival roared up a gear as they beat New Zealand by a record margin after former captain Lewis Moody led the hosts' response to the haka.

Moody, who was diagnosed with motor neurone disease last year, stood at the centre of a flying V formation that England had adopted for their victories over the same opponents last year and in the 2019 Rugby World Cup semi-final.

In terms of margin, this win trumped both - and the other seven England victories in the teams' 121-year rivalry.

And the hosts were full value for it. They dominated the All Blacks from the start.

Henry Slade crossed for the opening try in the fourth minute and only England's own mistakes prevented them taking a bigger lead than their 19-5 advantage into the break.

Beauden Barrett marked his 150th Test appearance by rounding off a coast-to-coast Kiwi try to cut England's advantage to 24-12. But his team never really threatened to reel in Steve Borthwick's men.

England introduced five forwards off the bench in the immediate aftermath of that 55th-minute score and, with Ellis Genge in fearsome carrying form, they had more than enough to see out victory in comfort.

Seb Atkinson took a delayed pop pass from Marcus Smith to stroll in for England's fifth try just after the hour.

The hosts finished the game camped down in the New Zealand 22m in search of a sixth score while choruses of Swing Low rolled around the stands.

For New Zealand, who suffered a shock defeat by Wales last weekend, it is a result that suggests a long Test season, which included four Tests against South Africa, may be catching up with them.

By contrast England, who could still end up in next weekend's Nations Championship grand final depending on results, are riding a wave of confidence.

News.title: UK should only rejoin EU if it innovates on technology, Blair warns
News.content:
Former prime minister Sir Tony Blair has said Britain should only rejoin the European Union if it reforms - and allows more innovation on technology.

Speaking to The Sunday Times, external, Sir Tony said: "I was painted as saying Britain should just go back and rejoin - I'm not saying that - it's heavily conditioned."

Sir Tony was a prominent opponent of leaving the EU, and told the paper: "I do think Brexit was a real mistake."

But he added the debate was different now than it was in 2016.

Referencing the need for technology innovation, he said Europe could and "probably are" moving in the wrong direction.

He said: "The problem if we go back and join Europe is that; I can't say that the technology revolution is the single biggest thing, and then if Europe moves in the wrong direction on technology innovation, which they might do and presently probably are doing, that it's a good idea for Britain to rejoin. That's what's changed in this last ten years."

He argued Britain should have an ambition to reform the EU.

But he added that we have to be "prepared to walk away from that negotiation" and need to make our own economy and tech sector strong.

Prime Minister Andy Burnham this week agreed what he called a "win-win" deal with the EU.

The agreement covered British food exports, emissions trading and a youth experience scheme.

European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen also announced that the trading bloc and the UK are launching a digital partnership, including areas like artificial intelligence (AI) and quantum technology.

The EU and Britain "have enormous potential to innovate together", she added.

News.title: Village votes to 'leave UK' over migrant plan
News.content:
Villagers vowed "this is only the beginning" after voting overwhelmingly to "leave the UK" in protest at plans to house migrants at a former airbase.

Residents in Barnham, Suffolk, held a symbolic poll on Saturday to decide whether or not to declare independence.

The referendum was called after RAF Barnham, near Bury St Edmunds, Suffolk and Thetford, in Norfolk, was earmarked by the government as a site to house up to 931 male asylum seekers.

Two-hundred-and-fifty-seven people - 94% of those who took part â voted in favour of leaving, 16 voted against and one vote was spoiled.

Following the result, which is not legally binding, residents unveiled a flag - a Stone-curlew against a Suffolk blue background - to celebrate the village's newfound "independence".

Barnham is the second village to hold a symbolic poll over migrant housing plans, after residents of Piddington in Oxfordshire voted to leave the UK in September.

John Bauer, chair of the parish council, has said the Suffolk village will now declare itself the Bailiwick of Barnham.

News.title: Man charged with attempted murder after Bradford councillor stabbed
News.content:
A man has appeared in court charged with attempted murder after a Bradford councillor was seriously injured in a stabbing.

Councillor Ibrar Ali was attacked at about 11:00 GMT on Thursday on Thornbury Avenue, before being driven to nearby Manse Street, according to West Yorkshire Police.

Arfan Ali, 32, of Thornbury Avenue, is also charged with assault and possession of an offensive weapon in a public place. At Leeds Magistrates' Court earlier, he was remanded into custody until he appears at Bradford Crown Court on 21 December.

Councillor Ali remains in hospital in a serious but stable condition, police said.

Councillor Ali is a Your Bradford Independent Group representative for Bradford Moor ward and was first elected in May.

He works as a community development manager at charity The Leap, and was one of the founders of Leeds Road Festival.

Speaking after Thursday's incident, his family thanked police, paramedics and members of the public who "courageously provided first aid and assistance at the scene" and asked people to "keep him and his family in your duas [prayers]".

News.title: Staff gagging clauses lifted ahead of probe into culture at data watchdog
News.content:
Non-disclosure agreements (NDAs) signed by staff at the UK's information watchdog will be lifted to allow them to speak out about its culture, the government has confirmed.

Ministers are expected to publish the details of how an independent review of the working environment at the Information Commission will be carried out next week.

It follows the departure of the watchdog's boss five months ago amid allegations of sexually inappropriate behaviour.

A government spokesperson confirmed that NDAs, known as "gagging clauses", would not be enforced by the Information Commission, saying the regulator "will not use the terms of any agreement to prevent people from participating in the review".

The government "will set out further details on the review, including its terms of reference and the independent reviewer, shortly", they added.

The Information Commission is one of the UK's most high-profile regulators charged with the crucial task of regulating AI, data protection and Freedom of Information requests.

It recently won a court battle with TikTok after it fined the social media platform Â£12.7m for misusing children's data, and has penalised bodies including the Ministry of Defence after an email blunder exposed the details of interpreters fleeing Afghanistan.

But it has been without permanent leadership since Information Commissioner John Edwards resigned earlier this year.

It came after an independent investigation found a "case to answer" over reports of alleged inappropriate behaviour towards staff including claims of sexual harassment.

The Information Commission said the investigation found Edwards' behaviour "fell short of the conduct expected from a public official".

In a resignation statement posted on his LinkedIn page in June, Edwards said he disagreed with how the investigation had been carried out but accepted his position had "become untenable".

The statement continued: "I have accepted that there have been occasions where I exercised poor judgement and made attempts at humour that were inappropriate and caused offence."

Freedom of Information requests have found that since the start of Edwards' tenure in 2022 to the present, 16 current and former employees have signed non-disclosure or confidentiality clauses costing more than Â£354,000.

Nine of those , externalincluded a "non-derogatory clause" which legally prevents employees from making negative comments publicly.

While this is a small proportion of the more than 1,000 staff employed by the commissioner, government advice stipulates that public bodies should only use confidentiality clauses "when necessary" and that they should "not seek to stifle or discourage staff from raising concerns".

Since 2025, new laws also mean they cannot be used to silence employees subjected to harassment or abuse.

After Edwards' departure, the government announced a review, external into the Commission's culture and governance, with the then-Secretary of State for Science, Innovation and Technology Liz Kendall telling a committee of MPs she was "absolutely appalled at what the independent investigator found - sexual harassment and bullying".

Five months later, the investigation has not begun.

In recent weeks, the two major civil service unions, the PCS and FDA, have pushed for an external examination of the events leading up to Edwards' resignation in meetings with government officials.

The unions have also asked for those who signed non-disclosure agreements with the ICO to be released from them so they can contribute to the review.

The PCS union says other concerns had previously been raised with them about Edwards, including a bullying complaint, which was investigated at the time.

An internal staff survey, published in August and released under FOI, external points towards wider issues at the Commission, with 14% of all employees reporting they had either personally experienced bullying, harassment and discrimination.

Multiple current and former employees have also told the BBC of experiencing or witnessing incidents of bullying or harassment.

PCS General Secretary Fran Heathcote said the union's members at the Commission "have been failed for too long by a toxic leadership culture that has allowed bullying and harassment to persist, leaving many staff fearful of speaking out".

Heathcote said she welcomed the "positive engagement" the union had received in recent weeks from the Commission and officials at the Department for Culture Media and Sport (DCMS), which oversees it.

But she added: "For the review to command the confidence of staff, it must be genuinely independent, robust in its approach, and prepared to identify where accountability lies."

Conservative MP Caroline Dinenage, who chairs the DCMS select committee, said the Commission "needed a firm new direction" after the departure of its former boss.

"Instead, a leadership vacuum has compounded what went before at a rudderless organisation where it seems the worst behaviours in the workplace are not being challenged," she added.

She said it was "vital" the government brought in "someone who can set a new tone and is dedicated to changing attitudes and protecting staff" to head up the Commission.

A spokesperson for the Information Commission said its commitment to an independent review reflected its "ongoing commitment to listening and learning from the events of the past year and those leading up to it".

"Our new Board, appointed this summer, has been working exceptionally hard to provide fresh leadership, ushering in a new governance structure and a new strategy," they added.

"It is committed to listening carefully to the review's findings and recommendations, and building on the positive work on our culture already taking place across the organisation."

News.title: Former journalist and Lost Lives author David McKittrick dies
News.content:
The renowned journalist and author David McKittrick has died at the age of 77.

McKittrick was best known for his work during the Troubles, and the book Lost Lives.

The book detailed the people who died as a result of the Troubles.

It was first published in 1999 after several years of research by McKittrick and co-authors Seamus Kelters, Brian Feeney and Chris Thornton.

Lost Lives won the Ewart-Biggs Memorial Prize for the promotion of peace and understanding in 2000.

At a later stage, David McVea joined the project.

A death notice for McKittrick said he was the "beloved husband of Pat, much loved father of Julie and Kerry, cherished grandfather of Daniel and Emma and the dear brother of Arlene and Freda".

"He will be sorely missed by all his extended family and friends," it added.

Social Democratic and Labour Party (SDLP) leader Claire Hanna MP paid tribute to McKittrick, describing him as an "outstanding journalist".

"David McKittrick was the outstanding journalist reporting in Northern Ireland throughout the Troubles," she said.

"Calm, empathetic and rigorous, he combined exceptional integrity with an unrivalled network of contacts.

"Throughout decades of conflict, he preserved his humanity and remained true to his moral compass."

Hanna added that her "thoughts are with David's family, friends and former colleagues at this sad time".

News.title: Scouts say they face £1m tourist tax cost for overnight trips
News.content:
Scout groups are warning they could face an additional annual bill of Â£1m as a result of the government's proposed tourist tax for England.

The overnight levy would allow councils and regional authorities to charge visitors an additional fee for their accommodation, including campsites, raising money to be spent on local services.

The increased cost from the Visitors Levy could price some young people out of joining Scout camps and other trips, the group said.

Dwayne Fields, the UK's Chief Scout, has called for youth groups to be exempted and said the charity - which sees more than 1.4m overnight stays a year - would be "firmly opposed to any proposal that would see local mayors tax Scouts and other voluntary youth organisations".

The Ministry of Housing, Communities & Local Government told the BBC that local leaders who introduce the levy "will have the option to exempt certain types of accommodation in their areas, including accommodation which is often used for trips by youth groups like Scouts and Girl Guides - such as camping pitches".

They added money raised from the levy will "stay local and be invested in the visitor experience and local growth including in high streets, parks and events".

Labour mayors have indicated they would cap the levy at 5% but the legislation contains no maximum limit.

In a statement, the Scout Association said the tax, if set at 5% across the country, could cost the charity Â£1.04m a year and force volunteers to deal with onerous paperwork.

They worked this out by assuming the levy would be set at 5% for all the 1,423,344 annual overnight stays across Squirrels, Beavers, Cubs, Scouts, Explorers and volunteers.

Girlguiding would also be subject to the levy.

In a statement, Fields said: "We strongly support investment being made available to strengthen local communities. Well-crafted legislation can unlock that opportunity.

"But we are firmly opposed to any proposal that would see local mayors tax Scouts and other voluntary youth organisations for camping trips that equip young people with skills for life, while burdening volunteers with the role of unpaid government tax collectors."

News.title: Bad Girls star Helen Fraser dies aged 84
News.content:
British television, theatre and film star Helen Fraser, who was perhaps best known for her role in the hit prison drama Bad Girls, has died.

The actress, who also appeared in episodes of Coronation Street and The Royle Family, reportedly died on 10 November at Yaxley House Care Home, in Eye, Suffolk. She was 84.

Born in Oldham, Greater Manchester, she had lived in Wickham Skeith, in Suffolk, with her late husband Peter Handford.

From 2004 until 2019, she was also an ambassador for East Anglia's Children's Hospices (EACH). The charity said it was "deeply saddened" by her death and would "remember her with enormous fondness and gratitude".

"Helen was very special to us and a wonderful ambassador, supporter and friend who worked tirelessly to champion our cause," a spokesperson said.

"Whether fundraising, attending events, opening our shops or rallying our volunteers, Helen brought incredible warmth, empathy and joy.

"She had a wonderful way with people and made a lasting impression on all those fortunate enough to spend time in her company."

The actress first trained at the Royal Academy of Dramatic Art in London before making her breakthrough in the 1963 film Billy Liar.

But it was her role as the tough prison officer Sylvia Hollamby in the long-running ITV show Bad Girls that made her a household name among British audiences.

Fraser appeared in more than 90 episodes across all eight series, from 1999 to 2006, and later reprised the role in the West End stage version of Bad Girls: The Musical.

Fraser's funeral will be held at West Suffolk Crematorium on 4 December at 13:30 GMT, according to a death notice published by the East Anglian Daily Times, external.

Attendees are asked to make donations in her honour to East Anglia's Children's Hospices charity.

"We feel truly honoured that EACH will benefit from donations made in her memory at her funeral," the charity's spokesperson added.

News.title: CFP bubble drama builds in Week 12 as BYU survives and Ohio State, UCLA, Indiana stumble
News.content:
Become an Independent member to bookmark this article Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today. Already a member? Log in

In the first regular-season week of college football in three years with no AP Top 25-ranked teams pitted against each other, there has been no shortage of excitement.

And much of that came from the Big Ten, where the top-two ranked teams — No. 4 UCLA and No. 6 Indiana — both lost in overtime.

Michigan handed UCLA its first loss of the season — an 18-16 triple-overtime defeat — after quarterback Ty Dieffenbach was carted off the field with an injury in overtime. Madden Iamaleava struggled under difficult circumstances, failing to complete a pass and losing a yard on two carries.

In Seattle, Indiana came up short when a game-tying 37-yard field goal attempt was blocked by Washington's Drew Azzopardi, carrying the Huskies to a 27-24 overtime win. Grant Wilson started the game at quarterback for the Hoosiers and threw a 74-yard touchdown pass on his first snap, before Curt Cignetti turned to Josh Hoover in the third quarter.

There was more. Former front-runner Ohio State fell 31-28 to Nebraska on the road and dropped to 7-4 just days after surging six spots to No. 14 in the latest CFP rankings. The Buckeyes had been clinging to a glimmer of hope with three losses, but a fourth slams that door shut.

It was Nebraska’s first Top 25 win in more than 10 years, ending a 31-game losing streak against ranked opponents.

And Penn State, playing with only pride on the line, fell to Rutgers 25-24 after giving up a touchdown and subsequent 2-point conversion in the final seconds.

Overtime wasn’t all bad news

BYU may not feel like a winner after narrowly dodging a playoff-shattering loss to Kansas, but it was the only ranked team to escape overtime with a success story on Saturday afternoon.

The Cougars had nearly fumbled away their playoff chances, but they won the turnover battle when it mattered most. BYU turned a forced fumble into a two-point conversion to improve to 9-2 with a 31-29 triple-overtime win and stay in the thick of the playoff race.

Elsewhere in the Big 12, Houston narrowly beat West Virginia, and Texas Tech, the first team out in the most recent playoff picture, outscored Baylor 20-10.

Over in the SEC

No. 9 Tennessee stayed alive in the playoff race with a 27-13 win against LSU — an effort that required both quarterbacks.

Tennessee quarterbacks Faizon Brandon and George MacIntyre split time in the win. MacIntyre completed 12 of 21 passes for 79 yards and a touchdown. Brandon had the more unusual stat line, completing 1 of 6 passes for six yards, an interception and a lost fumble, while carrying the ball 9 times for 90 yards and two scores.

Texas and Alabama both put up more than 40 points against Week 12 opponents. The Longhorns routed Arkansas 45-3, and Alabama beat Chattanooga 47-0 under a strong performance from backup quarterback Austin Mack.

News.title: Little Mercury gets its first visitor in years as a pair of spacecraft loop into orbit
News.content:
Become an Independent member to bookmark this article Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today. Already a member? Log in

A pair of spacecraft slipped into orbit around Mercury on Saturday after an eight-year cruise through the inner solar system to unravel our littlest planet's mountain of mysteries.

The linked robotic explorers — one European, the other Japanese — will separate from one another next month in order to map and study the scorching little planet from different altitudes. The $2 billion (1.7 billion euros) mission is known collectively as BepiColombo.

The European Space Agency announced BepiColombo's arrival via social media. A series of thruster firings slowed the spacecraft enough to be captured by the planet's weak gravity. But it took several anxious hours before flight controllers in Germany — 94 million miles (152 million kilometers) away — could confirm that BepiColombo had achieved orbit. Teams pored over the data streaming back; additional information was not immediately available.

BepiColombo is only the third spacecraft to visit Mercury — the sun's closest planet and barely bigger than our moon — and the first in more than a decade.

NASA's Mariner 10 flew past Mercury three times in the mid-1970s. The team included the late Italian mathematician Giuseppe “Bepi” Colombo, for whom this latest mission is named. NASA's Messenger spacecraft entered orbit around Mercury in 2011 and, after running out of fuel, crashed into the planet in 2015.

Launched in 2018, BepiColombo took a slower, more roundabout route to get to Mercury, flying once past Earth, twice past Venus and six times past Mercury for gravity-guiding assists. All those loop-de-loops put more than 6 billion miles (10 billion kilometers) on the odometer. The conjoined spacecraft shed their mother ship in September for the final leg of the journey.

Lead project scientist Geraint Jones said he and others can’t wait for all the new data to start streaming down in the spring. The mission will provide the ability to compare “unprecedented measurements taken by two spacecraft at the planet at the same time,” he noted.

Once orbiting separately, the European Space Agency's satellite and the Japan Aerospace Exploration Agency’s smaller craft will study Mercury’s dense interior and exterior magnetic field, as well as everything in between: impact craters, volcanic plains, mountain ridges and peaks jutting as high as 3 miles (4 1/2 kilometers).

The mercury at Mercury can hit more than 800 degrees (427 degrees Celsius), adding strain to electronic and engineering systems. Space agency officials want to keep the mission going for at least one Earth year — or the equivalent of four Mercury years.

“The spacecraft and its instruments need to be kept as cool as possible, which is a huge technical challenge in itself,” Jones said in an email.

Despite its relative proximity to Earth, Mercury is one of the solar system’s least explored planets. Only outer planets Uranus and Neptune have had fewer visitors — a lone Voyager 2 back in the 1980s.
