Sports.title: Chris Eubank Jr in talks to fight Kell Brook in first bout since Conor Benn loss - with 'Special K' to come out of retirement
Sports.content:
Chris Eubank Jr in talks to fight Kell Brook in first bout since Conor Benn loss - with 'Special K' to come out of retirement

Chris Eubank Jr is in talks to fight Kell Brook in his return to the ring.

Brook, 40, has not fought since beating Amir Khan in 2022, but has emerged as a potential option to fight Eubank in his first fight since losing to Conor Benn late last year.

According to Elliott Amoakoh, the executive director of Eubank Jr's management team, Nova Sport LLC, any agreement is still a way away.

He told Sky Sports: 'Talks are ongoing but the date, purse and location are yet to be confirmed.'

Ben Shalom, however, who has represented both fighters in the past, told talkSPORT: 'It's a fight that we have been trying to make for a couple of months.

'They have pretty much agreed terms on both sides, there is just some final bits to go. It is one of the biggest fights in British boxing. I think you are right on February and in Manchester.'

Chris Eubank Jr (pictured) is in talks with Kell Brook to face off in his return to the ring

Brook (pictured) hasn't fought since 2022 and retired after beating long-term rival Amir Khan

Brook retired after beating long-time rival Khan in Manchester, having been linked with a fight with Eubank in the aftermath.

Brook has seemed almost certain to return to the ring, having revealed his return fight would be 'announced soon'.

He retired with 40 wins from 43 fights, and is a former International Boxing Federation welterweight champion.

Having debuted as a professional in 2004, he didn't lose until September 2016, when he was stopped in the fifth round by Gennady Golovkin.

Eubank Jr, meanwhile, had faced questions over retirement following his defeat by Benn but has refused to call it quits on his 15-year career.

He had claimed to have major fights scheduled for 2026, but has taken a whole year out of action.

Sports.title: English boxer, 18, banned from World Championships after extraordinary sex test mix-up: 'Broken' teenager reveals how his dream was shattered after team forgot to prove he was a man
Sports.content:
English boxer, 18, banned from World Championships after extraordinary sex test mix-up: 'Broken' teenager reveals how his dream was shattered after team forgot to prove he was a man

A teenage English boxer has said they have been left 'broken' after being denied the chance to compete at the World Championships due to officials failing to organise a sex verification test to prove he is male.

George Francis, 18, had been due to represent England at the Under-19 World Championships in Budva, Montenegro last month.

Francis was withdrawn from competition on the eve of the event after an administration error by England Boxing, with the governing body having failed to arrange the necessary sex verification test.

'They got me in a room and told me that I couldn't box because they didn't know if I was a boy or a girl, basically,' Francis told the BBC.

'The explanation was that they couldn't provide a blood sample for me in time. Everyone else was able to provide a blood sample, but they just forgot me.

'Somehow I wasn't on the system.

George Francis, 18, missed out on competing at the Under-19 World Championships after England Boxing failed to arrange a necessary sex verification test. Source: Instagram/georgefrancis_07

'It was the worst news I've ever had in my life.

'I wouldn't wish it on anyone, to be honest. I was just broken. They were speaking to me and I couldn't even really hear. I was devastated.

'I couldn't really talk. I literally couldn't feel anything. There was a hole left there.'

Francis's situation, first reported by The Times, followed the mandatory introduction of sex verification tests by the sport's governing body World Boxing.

World Boxing announced the move last year, with genetic sex testing initially introduced for female competitors aged 18 and above. The governing body stated the move was due to a 'duty of care to deliver safety and competitiveness fairness'.

It followed controversy at the Paris 2024 Olympic Games, where boxers Imane Khelif and Lin Yu-ting won gold.

Khelif and Lin had been disqualified from the previous year's World Championships, with boxing's former governing body – the International Boxing Association – claiming the pair had failed sex eligibility tests.

Earlier this year, Lin was cleared to compete in women's events following a review of her sex eligibility.

World Boxing's mandatory tests were extended to include male boxers earlier this year.

Francis had been required to undergo a test due to turning 18 four days before travelling to the World Championships.

Francis, a multiple national champion, had been required to undergo a mandatory test after turning 18 days before the World Championships. Source: Instagram/georgefrancis_07

World Boxing introduced sex testing last year amid the controversy surrounding Algerian boxer Imane Khelif's participation at the Paris 2024 Olympic Games

The multiple national and GB champion has claimed he is considering turning professional following the mix-up.

England Boxing reportedly contacted Francis's father to apologise for the 'administrative oversight', with the governing body stressing it will 'strengthen processes' to avoid a repeat incident.

'We maintained open communication with George and his family throughout, despite this, a resolution was not possible,' an England Boxing statement read.

'George remained a valued member of the England team, including representing the squad as flag bearer.

'England Boxing has no greater priority than the health and wellbeing of athletes on its performance pathway and are committed to learning from this experience and strengthening our processes to prevent a recurrence.'

World Boxing's policy requires boxers to undergo a once-in-a-lifetime PCR (polymerase chain reaction) test to determine their sex and their eligibility to compete in either the male or female category.

The PCR test is a laboratory technique used to detect specific genetic material, in this case the SRY gene, which reveals the presence of the Y chromosome that is an indicator of male biological sex.

A dozen boxers, representing five nations, were last year blocked from competing at the World Championships in Liverpool because deadlines for their sex tests were missed.

Under World Boxing rules, national federations are responsible for testing and will be required to confirm the sex of their athletes when entering them into World Boxing competitions

Sports.title: Viddal Riley opens up on why he stuck with his dad instead of moving to Las Vegas to train with a Mayweather as he eyes fighting Oleksandr Usyk
Sports.content:
Derrick Riley almost never speaks publicly. Ahead of his son's European title defence against Seydi Coupe at Wembley on Saturday, father and son sat down together to talk about trust, tough love, Joe and Enzo Calzaghe, and why Oleksandr Usyk returning to cruiserweight is 'a little bit greedy'.

But to understand where Viddal is going, you first have to understand the man in his corner.

Derrick Riley has been watching his son get punched since he was a little boy. He still can't put into words what it does to him.

'It's strange,' he exclusively tells Daily Mail Sport. 'I've been doing it for a long time. But you have to try and separate it. You have to shut off the emotion and the sentiment. If you let that sentiment in, I think that's a bad thing. That's your boy in there. He's getting hit and he's getting hurt. I would say it's not easy, and some people can't separate it.'

It's rare to hear Derrick say anything at all. He stays out of the spotlight, and he leaves the talking to his son. Sitting beside Viddal days before the biggest night of his career, when the unbeaten Londoner headlines OVO Arena Wembley against Frenchman Coupe, you quickly see how their relationship works.

'Only my dad would be able to speak to me the way he does,' Viddal says. 'But it comes from a place of genuine care. It's not a job. Someone can only care so much when it's a job. It's like being an employee at a company and having your own business. It's a completely different mentality. This is my business, so he cares and I care.'

WATCH THE EXCLUSIVE INTERVIEW ON THE DAILY MAIL BOXING YOUTUBE CHANNEL

Derrick Riley (R), the father and trainer of son Viddal Riley (L), almost never speaks publicly

Viddal is set to take on Seydi Coupe at Wembley on Saturday evening, headlining the event

Derrick added: 'Part of caring too is the fact it's the same brain you've got now that you're going to need after boxing. You can't go to the shop and buy a new one, so you need to protect it. That's why it's difficult to separate the two.'

Viddal grins and says: 'It's the same brain I need for the grandkids.'

The partnership was not always a given. At 21, Viddal went looking for something of his own.

'I was at a stage where I was trying to find some independence. That's the truth,' he says. 'I was presented with the opportunity to go to Vegas, train with a Mayweather and work with Jeff Mayweather. I was thinking, "Yeah, I'm doing this my way. I'm doing things differently."

'But the truth is, I knew my ceiling was getting lower. And I knew the only person who could push that ceiling higher, and continue to do so, was my dad.

'So when I came back to the UK, I said, "Dad, can you train me?" He was like, "Nah, I'm alright. I'm not doing it." And I was like, "Nah, I need you to do it, because that's the only way this dream we've been talking about is going to be fulfilled."

Derrick's refusal was not stubbornness. It was self-preservation.

When asked why he initially said no, Derrick admitted: 'I know what the game is about. I know what boxing involves, and I thought to myself, do I want that in my life? It's a good question when you're in your 50s. I've lived life. There are no rose-coloured glasses. I know what boxing is. But I had to think about it.'

Derrick Riley has been watching his son get punched since Viddal was a little boy

The irony was that he was already qualified for the job. 'By this point I already had a British Boxing Board of Control licence, because I was in the corner with Viddal in Dubai,' he laughs. 'So, funnily enough, I already had the licence.

'He looked at me with those puppy-dog eyes, and I thought, you know what? We've got to do this. But I did say to him, "It's not going to be easy, son. We're going to have to do this properly. You're going to get no ranking belts, no intercontinental belt, nothing like that. You're going to have to do it the old-school way, with the British, Commonwealth, European, and it's going to be hard." And we've done it, man.'

The record backs him up. Viddal is 14-0 with seven knockouts. He won the European title in April with a wide points win over the vastly experienced Pole Mateusz Masternak at The O2, a fight that also served as an IBF world title eliminator. Saturday is his first defence, and it's a mandatory one against a challenger who is also unbeaten in 14.

For a template of what father and son can achieve together, Derrick points to Wales.

'I appreciate Enzo [Calzaghe] more now than I did before,' he says. 'I've always appreciated him, but I appreciate him even more now because I'm doing it myself. People have no idea what it takes, and for him to do what he did with Joe was absolutely amazing. I take my hat off to him.

'Don't get me wrong, I had a boxing background. I wasn't great, I wasn't pulling up trees, but I had a boxing background. Enzo had no boxing background whatsoever, yet he managed to do what he did with Joe. That is amazing.

'It's funny. During the fight with Bernard Hopkins, I think Enzo was saying something to Joe, and Joe gave Enzo a look. I know that look. I give Viddal that same look.'

Viddal and his father have become a force to be reckoned with but they've faced criticism

Joe Calzaghe has described his own brief split from his father, and how he came back because he realised he wanted those highs to be shared with Enzo. Viddal sees the same story in his own.

'We relate to that story because we were severely doubted,' he says. 'It wasn't celebrated. The partnership is only now starting to get some recognition, with people acknowledging that it works. It wasn't like that at the beginning.

'It's been suggested to me that my dad shouldn't train me and that there are people better suited to the job. That's what we walked into. It wasn't accepted as, "Oh yeah, this is a nice family dynamic, let's get it going." It was challenged. The aim was to separate us.

'When we're up against it, we just keep proving ourselves, time and time again. That's what I take from Enzo and Joe. It wasn't celebrated either. They had to keep doing what they were doing, and he turned his son into a 46-0 fighter and one of the best to have ever done it.'

Fathers who train their sons are often accused of living through them. John Fury, so often more visible than Tyson, is the obvious example. Derrick, a former boxer himself, rejects the comparison.

'I don't live vicariously through Viddal. I don't want that,' he says. 'I'm not hogging the camera. It's not about me. It's about Viddal. He asked me to help him, and I'll help him.'

Viddal is just as clear about who he fights for. 'I do it primarily, first and foremost, for me,' he says. 'And very quickly after that, it's for everyone around me that's put work into me achieving it, because it couldn't be done by myself.

Derrick has said he resonates with Enzo (pictured right) and Joe Calzaghe (pictured left)

'When I became British champion, it made me give my dad the belt. We sat down at home for years watching people pick up the Lonsdale belt and hold the Lonsdale belt. So I heard the announcement, "British champion", and I'm like, "Dad, hold this." That's something he's always deserved.'

By rights, Viddal should already have fought for a world title. When Jai Opetaia was stripped of the IBF belt after signing with Zuffa Boxing, the Masternak win put Viddal in line for a shot at the vacant title against New Zealand's David Nyika. Then Opetaia sued the IBF, the governing body held off sanctioning the fight, and Viddal was left waiting.

At the same time, the division has been turned upside down. Opetaia is moving up to heavyweight to face Deontay Wilder on the Tyson Fury vs Anthony Joshua card in Cardiff on December 11. David Benavidez holds the WBA and WBO belts and faces WBC champion Michal Cieslak next month. And now Oleksandr Usyk wants to come back down.

'As I have been saying, it's messy, but I'm trying to get in the mess,' Viddal says. 'I don't want to be on the outskirts of that mess. I'm trying to be in it.

'Right now, I'm just on the outside of the door. I can hear the music in the club, I can hear the bassline. I know there's a vibe in there. I've been seeing the people getting in the door, walking past me. I want to get in there. And Coupe this weekend is another step towards that.'

The most famous person trying to get through that door is Usyk. The Ukrainian became undisputed at cruiserweight, moved up to become undisputed twice at heavyweight, and his team says he now plans to return to 200lbs to chase Benavidez and become undisputed at cruiserweight again. He hasn't fought at the weight since knocking out Tony Bellew in November 2018, and he turns 40 in January.

Viddal admires him. But he isn't convinced.

'It's a bit greedy. It's a little bit greedy,' he says. 'He's completed the level here. He's gone up, he's completed it there, and I think he's just needing that challenge. He's a guy you can tell lives for challenge. All he does is take challenges. "If I'm fighting for a world title, I'm going to go to your country and I'll beat you there." He's that character. That's what makes him a GOAT. That's what makes him a legend.

Viddal has said Oleksandr Usyk is 'greedy' for returning to the cruiserweight division

'But it's dangerous too. Forty years old, dropping all that weight. He hasn't been a cruiserweight since 2018. If I'm in his circle, I'm saying, "Bro, you ain't got to do this. Why? There's no need to." It's not going to be financial. It's just that craving for a challenge.'

Regardless, Viddal is happy with where he is at.

'What I like is that if I'd done this interview four or five years ago, everyone would have asked me, "Do you want to fight Tommy Fury or Jake Paul?" he says. 'Now people ask me, "Would I fight Usyk?"

'Clearly, I'm doing something right.'

Sports.title: Antonelli and Russell set for Mercedes talks over Las Vegas GP qualifying mix-up
Sports.content:
George Russell and Kimi Antonelli will discuss the fallout from Formula 1’s Las Vegas Grand Prix qualifying “offline” following confusion over team orders and track position.

Traffic played a significant role in qualifying on Friday night with drivers reluctant to go first, considering the advantage of a tow is huge around the low-downforce street circuit.

There was the added complexity of five drivers taking a grid penalty, so their primary role was to help their team-mate like Haas’ Oliver Bearman giving Rafael Camara a tow in Q1.

Antonelli was another one of those, taking a five-place drop for a new engine, so the plan was to give Russell the slipstream in the fight for pole but it quickly unravelled.

That was because the Mercedes duo got caught in a pack with both Alpine and Racing Bulls cars ahead of the final lap, at times going three-wide despite trying to find space.

Antonelli eventually backed off at Turn 5 while Russell reluctantly went first of the pack and the 2026 world champion was fastest in qualifying with his team-mate 0.331s off in third.

So when asked afterwards if he was hoping for assistance from Antonelli, Russell replied: “It's still important, if you've got a grid penalty, to start as high up the order as possible.

“But we'll take it offline and we can talk about it. I think tomorrow is going to be very close between everybody, similar to Monza - it'll be very challenging to pull away from the pack.

“I would have liked to have been on pole, but I think anywhere in the top seven positions and you're in the fight.”

The situation caused Mercedes boss Toto Wolff to express disbelief at how Antonelli was quickest, particularly because Russell didn’t receive his request of leaving the pits second.

“It's very high risk,” added Russell, who will share the front row with Red Bull’s Max Verstappen due to Antonelli’s penalty.

“Kimi got the pole, but if he started the lap a second later, he wouldn't have got the lap in.

Max Verstappen, Red Bull Racing, George Russell, Mercedes Photo by: Patrick T. Fallon / AFP via Getty Images

“It's very difficult to orchestrate because everybody's going for it, and also the fact that half the cars were doing prep laps and half the cars were not also made it difficult.

“If you could choose, you would be at the back of a pack of nine cars with around a three-second gap, if you could perfectly choose.

“But that's what everyone's chasing, so it's kind of like Monza 2019."

Although Antonelli eventually backing off gave him the space needed to set his fastest lap, a 1m33.893s, it could have cost him as he only just crossed the line in time to start his final tour.

“As George said, we will talk about it because we've been sent out at the front in qualifying always,” said Antonelli.

“About Turn 5, it was fully on me. Like I said, we were three-wide, first of all, and I just said, "You know what? I'm just going to back off’."

George Russell, Mercedes Photo by: Clive Rose / Formula 1 via Getty Images

“It was tricky because, first of all, I almost missed the flag. Yes, I did get a big tow, but I was also so close that getting around the corner was actually difficult with the dirty air and so on.

“We're already on a lower-downforce package, so you do feel even more the loss when following.

“But overall, it was just one of those times where you think you're screwed, but actually it works out.

“On Turn 5, I just decided to back off. I didn't really know how tight I was with the timing. I probably would have done it differently, but in hindsight, it still worked out.”

Sports.title: Verstappen reveals mysterious Red Bull F1 car issue that cannot be fixed in Las Vegas
Sports.content:
Thanks to Kimi Antonelli 's grid penalty, Max Verstappen will start Formula 1's Las Vegas Grand Prix from pole position, but that is not necessarily a reason for the Dutch driver to be satisfied.

Yes, Red Bull has made significant progress with its power unit on energy-poor circuits and, following the balance problems during free practice, the team also managed to make effective set-up changes, but the feeling behind the wheel was still not what Verstappen believes it should be.

"Already since Brazil I have some weird issues in the car and that continued this weekend. I'm just trying to get my head around how to deal with that for the remainder of the weekend," Verstappen said.

"That didn't make things easy in FP3, but I think in qualifying we managed to make it work."

When Verstappen was asked during the press conference whether he could elaborate on those "weird issues", he responded firmly: "No."

Nevertheless, the subject naturally came up again during his subsequent Dutch media session in the paddock. Verstappen was still unable to go into detail, but did shed a little more light on the situation.

Max Verstappen, Red Bull Racing Photo by: Jordan McKean / Formula 1 / Getty Images

"It's not a balance problem, I can tell you that. There's simply something wrong with the car, but we can't fix it right now," the Red Bull driver said, when asked about the issue by Autosport.

"We know where the problem is coming from, but we can't solve it. It's now the second weekend in a row that it's been like this, but I can't say too much about it."

On the face of it, the issue appeared to emerge during the race in Brazil. After all, Verstappen reported that the car felt very different during the second and third stints compared to the opening stint, but the Dutchman clarified that the problem had actually been troubling him for longer.

"It suddenly appeared in Brazil, yes, but that was already before the race. I had problems there throughout the entire weekend," he said.

The four-time world champion clarified that it is different from the 'car degradation' he complained about at circuits including Monza. Back then, the car would deteriorate over the course of a session, whereas this time the issue is more fundamental. According to Verstappen, it is mainly related to the feeling through the steering wheel.

"It's something completely different from car degradation, but the feeling is simply not how I want it to be," he said. "I can't say much more about it, because otherwise I'll start explaining things that I don't want to give away."

Following the introduction of Red Bull's Baku upgrade, Verstappen said he had gained more confidence in the car and could therefore attack the corners more aggressively, but that has become more difficult because of this issue.

Max Verstappen, Red Bull Racing Photo by: James Sutton / LAT Images via Getty Images

He added: "In certain places that's less the case now, yes. It doesn't matter what type of corner it is, either. The problem is simply there everywhere. I just have to try to adapt, but that's not easy."

Finally, Verstappen made it clear that team-mate Isack Hadjar is not experiencing the same problem: "No, apparently it's only on my side. It's not dangerous, but it's just not pleasant for me to drive. We just have to try to solve it. It had been working well for a very long time, but suddenly it wasn't in Brazil, and it isn't here either."

Sports.title: Verstappen responds to Russell after Las Vegas GP practice clash over 'gentleman's agreement'
Sports.content:
During the final practice session for the Formula 1 Las Vegas Grand Prix, Max Verstappen and George Russell crossed paths once again. The Dutchman overtook the Mercedes driver, but then slowed down in front of him and, according to the stewards, changed direction several times.

Russell subsequently went down the inside of the four-time world champion, leading to contact between the two at Turn 14. It earned both rivals a trip to the stewards, although they ultimately dealt with the incident by issuing a warning to Verstappen. Unlike a reprimand, a warning carries no consequences at all.

When Verstappen was asked about the incident during the press conference after qualifying, the Dutchman had little interest in discussing it. Asked what had happened, he simply replied: "Nothing. Nothing happened."

Russell, however, subsequently launched an attack on the Red Bull driver in the media pen. Speaking to Sky Sports Italy, Russell said: "I’m not just going to accept somebody to screw me over like this and walk around like they’re bigger and better than everyone else. Somebody has got to stand up to that guy."

Verstappen was largely unmoved. When Autosport asked him about the clash during the Dutch media session that followed in the Las Vegas paddock, he replied: "I don't even want to waste my time on that. It's not worth it to me at all."

Max Verstappen, Red Bull Racing Photo by: Jim Watson / AFP via Getty Images

When it was pointed out that the stewards had referred in the FIA document to a gentlemen's agreement during preparation laps, under which drivers are expected to maintain their positions and avoid interfering with one another before starting a flying lap, Verstappen responded: "I've never seen such an agreement in my life."

The stewards also made clear that they had attached little weight to the gentlemen's agreement mentioned by Russell in reaching their decision, instead focusing on the actions of both drivers.

"The Stewards noted these explanations but considered that such informal understandings were of limited relevance to the assessment of the incident. The decisive considerations were the actual movements of both cars and their relative positions."

It is particularly notable that the two drivers will share the front row of the grid in Vegas on Saturday night following Kimi Antonelli's grid penalty, but Verstappen insists the clash has not given him any extra motivation to keep Russell behind: "No, that's definitely not where I get my motivation from."

Sports.title: Floor damage, deployment down to Hamilton's Las Vegas GP Q2 exit
Sports.content:
Lewis Hamilton put Ferrari's Q2 exit in qualifying for the Las Vegas Grand Prix down to energy deployment and floor damage, as the seven-time Formula 1 world champion felt he'd rallied from difficulties with overall tyre grip.

The Briton struggled throughout FP3 under braking, as the front tyres proved particularly lock-up prone and resulted in Hamilton enduring multiple excursions into the run-off.

Hamilton landed in Q2 despite suffering floor damage in the opening stage of qualifying, but neither he nor Charles Leclerc were able to make their way into the top-10 shootout for pole.

Hamilton appeared generally happy with his runs in Q2, which demonstrated few of the lock-ups characteristic of his lead-up to qualifying, but the Ferrari power unit's energy deployment seemed to hit its maximum sooner than the Mercedes and Red Bull-powered cars and inhibited straightline speed and performance.

Ferrari has been down on power versus those two manufacturers, and the long acceleration zone along the Strip exposed this deficit throughout the session.

"We lost a piece of the floor on the first or second lap of Q1 and the car balance shifted, and we lost I think it was like three or four tenths of downforce we lost," Hamilton stated.

"And then after that we were struggling more so with sliding, but it was basically from the get-go.

Lewis Hamilton, Ferrari Photo by: Mark Sutton / Formula 1 via Getty Images

"And then my last lap was really good at the end, but I did the best I could with what I had. But then we lost something like six tenths just on deployment. So I think with that we would have been in Q3, but otherwise I was happy with my lap.

"We knew long straights and stuff was going to be challenging. The gap seems to be a little bit more than I anticipated in a straight line. It's not insignificant. It's a big chunk on the straights."

There had been a pervading sense that Ferrari would struggle in the low-temperature conditions in Las Vegas, as the team has struggled throughout 2026 to maintain tyre temperature through a qualifying lap.

Hamilton agreed that the car was difficult to work with amid frequent sliding through the low-speed corners, especially after losing a chunk of floor, and only hopes that Ferrari can move forward in the Saturday night race as it aims to lock out second in the constructors' championship.

"Just grip-wise, it just didn't feel like we had a ton of grip. We were struggling to get the tyres working and we were just kind of nowhere," he added.

"These tyres have been very, very difficult this year to get working, even on hot surfaces. So it's definitely been difficult. I don't have any expectations [for the race]. Just trying to see if I can move forward."

Sports.title: Russell slams Verstappen after Las Vegas GP practice clash: ‘He walks around like he’s bigger and better than everyone’
Sports.content:
George Russell has hit out at Max Verstappen after they collided in Free Practice 3 at Formula 1’s Las Vegas Grand Prix.

Verstappen overtook the Mercedes ahead of Turn 14 in a quest for free air, but Russell moved to get back ahead, with the Dutchman unsuccessfully closing the door. Russell eventually muscled his rival out of the way, with the Red Bull racer later giving him the middle finger.

Russell was indignant at Verstappen’s driving, which earned him a warning from the stewards.

“I think a warning was fine but, you know... There's nothing in the rules to say you cannot overtake someone who is starting the lap, but when you do this, you are screwing this person over,” the Briton told Sky Sport Italy.

“He does this week in week out with many drivers and everybody accepts it, and I'm not just going to accept somebody to screw me over like this and walk around like they're bigger and better than everyone else. Somebody's got to stand up to that guy.”

Meanwhile, Verstappen’s assessment of the situation in the post-qualifying press conference was straightforward: “Nothing happened.”

A warning is largely inconsequential as, unlike a reprimand, it cannot lead to a bigger penalty in the event of a repeat offence.

Why stewards gave Verstappen a warning

Max Verstappen, Red Bull Racing Photo by: Patrick T. Fallon / AFP via Getty Images

Still, Verstappen was found responsible for the incident, and here is how the stewards viewed it.

“Both cars were approaching Turn 14, with Car 3 ahead of Car 63,” the stewards’ report read. “Car 3 braked earlier than expected and changed direction under braking. Car 63, approaching from behind, moved to the left and attempted to overtake on the inside. During the manoeuvre, the front axle of Car 63 was ahead of the mirror of Car 3. The two cars subsequently made contact.

“During the hearing, the drivers also discussed the informal gentlemen’s agreements concerning the preparation for a flying lap and the conduct expected between drivers in such situations. The Stewards noted these explanations but considered that such informal understandings were of limited relevance to the assessment of the incident. The decisive considerations were the actual movements of both cars and their relative positions.

“The Stewards therefore examined the braking and change of direction of Car 3, the evasive manoeuvre and positioning of Car 63 and taking into account the applicable Driving Standards Guidelines.

“The Stewards considered that Car 3’s change of direction under braking was unpredictable and contributed to the situation in which Car 63 had to move to the inside to avoid contact. While the Stewards did not consider the manoeuvre sufficiently serious to warrant a more severe penalty, they concluded that changing direction under braking in these circumstances fell below the standard of driving expected.

“Taking into account the circumstances of the incident, the Stewards determined that a Driver Warning was appropriate.”

Verstappen and Russell will share the front row in Saturday’s Las Vegas GP, having qualified respectively second and third with pacesetter Kimi Antonelli taking a five-place grid penalty.

Sports.title: F1 Las Vegas GP: Antonelli tops qualifying but Verstappen gets pole
Sports.content:
Max Verstappen will start on pole at the Formula 1 Las Vegas Grand Prix despite Kimi Antonelli going fastest - while Charles Leclerc and Lewis Hamilton both failed to make Q3.

The 2026 world champion beat the Red Bull driver by 0.258s, but is set for a five-place grid drop due to a new internal combustion engine on his Mercedes.

It came after Verstappen took provisional pole with a 1m34.151s while Antonelli was down in sixth, but he failed to improve on his final lap allowing others the chance of beating him.

Yet only Antonelli managed to topple the Dutchman, setting a 1m33.893s at the chequered flag, for the eighth time he has gone quickest in qualifying this year - first since Austin.

But because of the grid penalty, Verstappen will be joined on the front row by Mercedes’ George Russell who hoped for a tow from his team-mate but traffic denied that opportunity.

Russell set a 1m34.224s, two tenths quicker than his opening lap, and was just 0.020s ahead of McLaren’s Lando Norris who will therefore complete the top three on Saturday night’s grid.

Max Verstappen, Red Bull Racing Photo by: Jim Watson / AFP via Getty Images

Verstappen’s team-mate Isack Hadjar was fifth quickest in Q3, 0.699s off the pace, with sixth going to impressive rookie Arvid Lindblad a week after Racing Bulls confirmed him for 2027.

Oscar Piastri took seventh, but is one of five drivers set for a grid penalty, his being 10 places for an engine change, while eighth went to Lindblad’s team-mate Liam Lawson.

Alpine duo Pierre Gasly and Franco Colapinto respectively completed the top 10, 1.212s and 1.421s off Antonelli, but the biggest talking point came in the second session as Ferrari suffered its first double Q2 exit since Imola last year.

The Italian outfit occupied row six after what was a really messy Q2 for Ferrari, highlighted by Leclerc aborting a lap midway through due to a Turn 7 lock-up.

The Monegasque subsequently failed to make the line to start a lap at the end, so Leclerc dropped to 11th ahead of 12th-placed Hamilton who failed to improve on his final tour.

“Unbelievable,” reacted Leclerc, whose team-mate would have knocked out Antonelli had he improved at the chequered flag with the 2026 world champion surviving the drop by 0.111s.

Three tenths behind Hamilton was Audi’s Nico Hulkenberg in 13th with 14th going to Williams man Carlos Sainz, who is set to serve a 10-place drop for a new turbocharger.

Andrea Kimi Antonelli, Mercedes, Max Verstappen, Red Bull Racing Photo by: Clive Rose / Formula 1 via Getty Images

So Hulkenberg’s team-mate Gabriel Bortoleto will jump up from 15th, while 16th went to Alex Albon for Williams’ first double Q2 appearance of the 2026 season.

Rafael Camara, who suffered a spin at the opening corner early on, looked set to profit from a significant tow by team-mate Oliver Bearman until Bortoleto dropped him into the Q1 elimination zone at the chequered flag.

So the Haas newbie missed out on Q2 by just 0.071s to take 17th, with a 1.163s gap to Cadillac’s Sergio Perez in 18th and 1.180s advantage over 19th-placed Fernando Alonso.

Alonso’s Aston Martin stablemate Lance Stroll took 20th, but is set to serve a 10-place penalty for a new energy store and new control electronics being fitted on his AMR26.

That will therefore bump up Valtteri Bottas from 21st, who was slowest in the Q1 representative times just two days after Cadillac announced the 10-time grand prix winner for 2027.

Bearman was therefore the only driver not to complete a proper lap, as his 35-place grid drop for a complete engine change meant his main role in Q1 was to assist Camara.

Sports.title: F1 Las Vegas GP: Russell fastest in final practice after Verstappen collision
Sports.content:
George Russell collided with Max Verstappen in a tense third practice session at the Las Vegas Grand Prix as the Mercedes Formula 1 driver topped the timesheets.

After both of Thursday's practice sessions had been derailed by rain, the Las Vegas Strip was buzzing with activity at dusk on Friday. The sole remaining practice session became crucial as it presented the only dry running heading into qualifying and the race, as all 22 cars sprinted out of the pitlane in short order.

Amid chilly 14C temperatures, the Thursday rainfall only made the 6.2km circuit around the Las Vegas Strip even more difficult to drive, with surface grip extremely limited.

Verstappen survived a sideways scare and steering rack issues to lead the early running with a 1m35.675s on soft tyres, by far the most popular tyre in cold conditions as it was easier to fire up to temperature.

Just after the halfway mark Russell took over top spot with a 1m35.124s, the Briton aiming to finish the season on a high as he declined a Mercedes turbo upgrade to avoid a grid penalty. Russell further lowered his own benchmark to a 1m34.805s lap, before becoming one of several cars to find the runoff area on the slippery circuit.

The urgency to get plenty of clean laps in was on full display with Verstappen and Franco Colapinto almost coming to blows in their quest for clean air. Verstappen's Red Bull team-mate Isack Hadjar also lobbied for a penalty for Williams' Alex Albon.

Max Verstappen, Red Bull Racing Photo by: Guido De Bortoli / LAT Images via Getty Images

Annoyed by Verstappen forcing his way past, Lando Norris couldn't hide his glee when the four-time world champion subsequently locked up and sailed into the runoff area. "Instant karma, amazing," he said over team radio.

The biggest clash followed right at the end of the session, again involving Verstappen, as he tried a similar move on Russell on the straight. Undeterred, Russell sent his Mercedes down the inside of Turn 14 to re-pass the Red Bull, making side-on contact as he muscled Verstappen off the track. The incident will be investigated by the FIA’s stewards. "Fun and games," Russell described the incident on the radio.

Norris initially came closest to overhauling Russell in the closing minutes of the session, settling for second with a 1m35.060s lap. Russell found late improvements too, though, to pull out a massive seven-tenth lead on Norris at the top of the timesheets with laps of 1m34.306s and 1m34.041s.

Read Also: Formula 1 F1 set for V8 return from 2030

Norris was demoted to third by his world championship heir Kimi Antonelli, while Charles Leclerc skated his way to fourth after sampling several escape areas.

Ahead of Verstappen, Colapinto was fifth for Alpine on a circuit that should suit the Enstone team's slippery car, as evidenced by the Pierre Gasly's shock pole back in Monza.

Racing Bulls driver Liam Lawson was seventh, followed by Lewis Hamilton, Gasly and Arvid Lindblad.

Sports.title: F1 set for V8 return from 2030
Sports.content:
Formula 1 has moved closer to a return to V8 engines from the 2030 season as the FIA announced that a unanimous agreement has been reached between the governing body, F1 management and the power unit manufacturers.

F1 has long worked towards cheaper and simpler engines for the next regulation cycle, which starts in 2031, having recognised the current formula is too complex and physically heavy, and a relic of a different direction in the road car industry.

The FIA could have set the series’ future power-unit regulations for 2031, when the current cycle ends, but there has been broad alignment within the sport to bring that timeline forward by one year, driven by both president Mohammed Ben Sulayem and F1 CEO Stefano Domenicali.

So following recent gatherings by the F1 Commission and power unit advisory committee, where key aspects like the formula, timelines and costs were discussed, there had been broad support to bring forward the next generation of engine regulations by one year and curtail the current formula. The consensus is for F1 to move to a 2.1-litre turbocharged V8 engine with a smaller electric component of 200kW, half of which will be ringfenced for overtake-mode use.

The 2.1-litre capacity is derived from the current 1.6-litre V6 formula as a starting point, with two additional cylinders intended to reduce development costs.

After an aborted announcement on Tuesday, the FIA has now officially confirmed there is unanimous support among its stakeholders about bringing that move forward to 2030.

"The FIA presented F1 Power Unit regulations for introduction from 2030 with a 2.1 litre turbocharged V8 as the power unit of choice carrying over some geometrical specifics," the governing body said on Friday.

"The overriding objective is to deliver a power unit which is a lot less complex, lighter and cheaper than the current power units. It will feature limited hybridisation, relevant and sustainable technology with the aim of enhancing attack-oriented racing and a sound which resonates with fans.

"Additionally, the plan is to marry the V8 power unit to a chassis which will also be lighter, more agile and placing greater emphasis on driver skill and close racing. "

F1 and FIA Photo by: Benjamin Vinel

Ben Sulayem added: "This agreement marks a significant milestone in shaping the future of Formula 1.

“From the outset I have been clear in my ambition to deliver a sport that is more competitive and more exciting for our fans, while remaining at the forefront of innovation and sustainability.

"The return of V8 engines represents an opportunity to reconnect with the DNA of this championship, bringing back the sound, emotion and pure racing that is loved worldwide.

“Our vision is clear, lighter, simpler and more affordable cars that put driver skill at the heart of the competition."

The 2030 power unit rules still need to be formally voted through by the World Motor Sport Council and by the power unit manufacturers, with a number of finer details, including the exact level of the power-unit cost cap, still to be agreed.

Sports.title: Pirelli’s F1 tyres still can’t cope with Losail: Maximum stint lengths imposed again | Formula 1
Sports.content:
Formula 1 will return to Losail International Circuit for the fifth time this weekend and once again its official tyre supplier is concerned about potential failures.

For the third time in the race’s history, and the second year in a row, Pirelli has announced drivers must obey a maximum stint length at Losail.

This year Pirelli has set the limit at 27 laps. This is more than last year’s limit of 25, but as the race is 57 laps long, it will again force drivers to make two pit stops.

Pirelli imposed an 18-lap limit for the 2023 event. That required drivers to make three pit stops.

Once again, Pirelli has decided the limit is needed despite having selected its most durable tyres for the event: the C1, C2 and C3.

F1’s official tyre supplier has struggled to create a product which can withstand the demands of Losail’s track since the series first visited the venue in 2021. On that occasion no limit was applied but McLaren’s Lando Norris, Mercedes’ Valtteri Bottas and the Williams drivers all suffered tyre failures. Pirelli blamed the combination of the high loads placed on its tyres and the configuration of its kerbs.

By the time F1 returned in 2023, the series had switched to a new 18-inch tyre format. The Losail circuit was also extensively refurbished, with new kerbs installed.

Advert | Become a RaceFans supporter and go ad-free

But during practice on Friday, Pirelli discovered problems with its tyres. In addition to imposing stint limits, the track limits were redrawn to force drivers to avoid kerbs and an extra 10-minute practice session was scheduled. “It is embarrassing because this is not where we should be,” remarked one team principal.

Pirelli did not set stint lengths during the 2024 race. But after inspecting the tyres used during the race it decided a maximum limit was needed again for 2025.

F1 changed its tyre format again this year as it introduced new chassis regulations. It also extended Pirelli’s contract to remain its official tyre supplier until the end of 2028 at least.

Pirelli says the reduction in downforce this year is partly why it has permitted a slight increase in the maximum stint length for next weekend’s race. “The maximum number of laps permitted per set is slightly higher than last year, when the limit was fixed at 25 laps,” it said in a statement.

“The increase has been made possible by the lower load levels recorded so far on the current generation of cars and by a further reinforcement of the tyre construction.”

However the fact remains that at every other circuit on the calendar F1 teams are free to run their tyres as long as they choose. By imposing stint limits for the third time in five Qatar grands prix, Pirelli increasingly appears incapable of producing a tyre which is up to the job at this track.

It confirmed the latest restrictions in a press release issued on Friday during the Las Vegas Grand Prix weekend. Shortly afterwards Pirelli issued a corrected version, admitting it had accidentally included part of its similar 2025 announcement in its latest statement.

What are the chances they’ll need it again next year?

Sports.title: On This Day: McLaren hire Zak Brown to lead team after ousting Ron Dennis | Brief
Sports.content:
McLaren made a major change to its leadership 10 years ago today, putting it on course to rebound from a series of poor seasons. The team finished ninth in 2015, its first season with Honda power units, and improved only to sixth in 2016.

Having already ousted long-term leader Ron Dennis, McLaren hired Zak Brown initially as an executive director. Brown eventually took greater control of the team and set about rebuilding it.

Within five years the team had ended its grand prix victory drought and in 2024 it won the first of two back-to-back constructors’ championship titles.

Brown marked his 10 years at McLaren by taking a photograph with the team in Las Vegas ahead of this weekend’s race. He said the team “was a pretty grim place when I joined at the end of 2016.”

“It’s been remarkable, the turnaround. A few championships since then, we’ve won 24-plus races, having a lot of fun, which I think is very important. The culture, the energy of the racing team has been outstanding. It’s great to be back at the front on a regular basis, and now we’ve found it’s kind of just as hard to stay at the front.”

Sports.title: Drivers expect Monza-style race at Las Vegas with “extreme” slipstream | Formula 1
Sports.content:
The powerful slipstream effect at the Las Vegas Strip Circuit will shape this weekend’s race, say drivers.

Andrea Kimi Antonelli surprisingly topped qualifying thanks partly to the power of the slipstream he gained from running behind a queue of cars.

Max Verstappen, who will start from pole position due to Antonelli’s penalty, said running closely behind another car was worth a significant amount of lap time.

“The tow around here is crazy,” said the Red Bull driver. “I was actually close to getting knocked out in Q2. Then I went out on my final lap, and I was four or four and a half seconds behind the car, and I gained like seven or eight tenths on the lap while not actually gaining that much in the corners. That just tells you how much you actually gain around the lap if you have a decent tow.

“That’s what I then did again in my first run in Q3. It was a solid lap, as good as I think it can be, with also the car in front, because you have a bit of dirty air in the corners. But it’s just insane how much you gain on the straights.”

The power of the slipstream effect has risen since F1 reduced the energy harvesting limit of its power units to prevent some of the high closing speed differences seen earlier in the season.

“When they reduced the harvest limit, it doesn’t make it as bad,” said George Russell. “I guess a lot of people are confused about why the slipstream is so powerful.

Advert | Become a RaceFans supporter and go ad-free

“I’m still not exactly sure whether it’s purely because of the [Straight Mode] and that creates some strange disturbance, or whether it’s also having an impact on the energy, because if you deploy that a little bit longer, you’re on a power offset for half of the straight.

“So it’s a bit complex to explain, but the slipstreams are more extreme than I think we’ve ever experienced in any category, to be honest.”

The benefit of running behind another car will be amplified in the race when drivers are able to use Overtake Mode, which allows them to deploy extra power when running within a second of another car.

Antonelli expects to see a race similar to the Italian Grand Prix, where the leader is unable to break free of the pursuing pack.

“Tomorrow is going to be a race where we will all be super-close to each other because the tow is so strong, and it’s going to be really hard to pull away,” he said. “If Monza was difficult, here it’s probably going to be impossible.

“It’s going to be interesting because, yes, by staying close, you do lose a lot in the corners, a lot of downforce, but because the tow is so big, you catch it back and even more.

Advert | Become a RaceFans supporter and go ad-free

“The car has been feeling good in the long run. I’ve been struggling a lot on a single lap, but the long run felt good, so I think tomorrow there will be plenty of opportunities to move.”

Having won the Italian Grand Prix from 19th on the grid, Antonelli is positive about his chances in Las Vegas, where he lines up sixth. “It’s not [like] I’m starting nowhere,” he said.

“The tow is so strong that it’s probably going to be easy to stay close and make a move. But it’s going to be a race where you have to be very smart as well with how you attack and defend and with everything.”

Sports.title: Antonelli says he made the decision to run at the back of the field in qualifying | Formula 1
Sports.content:
Andrea Kimi Antonelli beat the entire field in qualifying but admitted he was not happy with his car’s balance.

The Mercedes driver set the best time in Q3 partly because he was perfectly positioned to benefit from a slipstream from rival drivers on the final lap. He said he had struggled for grip prior to then.

“It was such a weird qualifying for me,” said Antonelli. “I had zero feeling with the car and the tyres.”

Antonelli dropped to the back of a group of cars before beginning his final run. Although this allowed him to gain a useful tow on the straight it also put him at risk of not starting his lap in time and running too close to other cars through the corners.

“That last lap, because I was going to miss the flag, I had to push through,” he said. “First of all, I backed off because we were all fighting, but then that last lap I started probably 1.5 seconds from the car in front, and I had low tyre temperature as well.

“I just tried to do the lap, but because the tow is so strong here, I managed to put it on pole, but only thanks to the final sector.

“To be fair, I’m not really happy at all because it’s one of those qualifying sessions where it’s just so weird and you didn’t even know how you’re on top. But I guess I’m going to enjoy it tonight and then be ready for tomorrow.”

Advert | Become a RaceFans supporter and go ad-free

The new world champion said the session reminded him “how it was back then in Mini Karts and just [trying to] replicate it.”

Antonelli said the decision to drop to the back of the queue was “fully on me” and he might not have done it had he realised it would put him in such a difficult position.

“We were three-wide, first of all, and I just said, ‘You know what? I’m just going to back off.’ It was tricky because, first of all, I almost missed the flag. Yes, I did get a big tow, but I was also so close that getting around the corner was actually difficult with the dirty air and so on.

“We’re already on a lower-downforce package, so you do feel even more the loss when following. But overall, it was just one of those times where you think you’re screwed, but actually it works out.

“At turn five, I just decided to back off. I didn’t really know how tight I was with the timing. I probably would have done it differently, but in hindsight, it still worked out.”

Antonelli’s team mate George Russell confirmed they did not make an arrangement about giving each other a slipstream. “No, obviously, it’s still important, if you’ve got a grid penalty, to start as high up the order as possible,” he said.

Sports.title: Norris fears passing will be impossible due to “insane” straight-line speed deficit | Formula 1
Sports.content:
Lando Norris doubts he will be able to gain many places in the Las Vegas Grand Prix due to his lack of straight-line speed.

McLaren are at a disadvantage on the Las Vegas Strip Circuit’s long straights due to its aerodynamics, said Norris after qualifying.

“It felt pretty good, honestly, I’m very happy with my lap,” said Norris, who will start the race from third on the grid. “I really couldn’t get much more out of it.

“We just struggled a lot here in the straights, like an insane amount. There’s not much more we can do, but I think we made the most of it with the slipstreams and things. We just have a deficit at the moment.”

McLaren introduced a new floor upgrade this weekend but chose not to run it on the first day of practice due to the wet conditions. Norris said the team “didn’t learn much” from practice and he is doubtful they will be able to attack Max Verstappen and George Russell ahead of them.

“We have to just see how tomorrow goes,” he said. “The pace in the car is not bad, the car is performing well, but our straight-line speed is so far off that we’re not going to even be able to overtake someone, so I think it’s going to be a tough day.”

Oscar Piastri qualified seventh but will start near the back of the grid as he has a 10-place penalty. He said “getting back into the points is definitely the biggest aim” for him.

“We’ll have to try our best. I think qualifying showed that with slipstreams and stuff, a lot of people are at a very similar pace, so I’m not sure how easy it’s going to be tomorrow, but we’ll try.”

Sports.title: “Somebody’s got to stand up to that guy” says Russell after latest Verstappen clash | Formula 1
Sports.content:
George Russell said it was important to show Max Verstappen he won’t be pushed around on-track following the latest clash between the pair.

The stewards gave Verstappen an official warning after he and Russell collided at turn 14 during final practice.

Verstappen passed Russell as they drove towards the corner. Russell then moved to re-pass the Red Bull driver, but the stewards ruled Verstappen “braked earlier than expected and changed direction under braking” at turn 14. The pair made contact as Russell passed Verstappen.

Russell said he thought “a warning was fine” and said he passed Verstappen to avoid being delayed by his rival.

“There’s nothing in the rules to say you cannot overtake someone who is starting the lap,” Russell told Sky. “But when you do this, you are screwing this person over, and he does this week in, week out with many drivers, and everybody accepts it.

“I’m not just going to accept somebody to screw me over like this and walk around like they’re bigger and better than everyone else. Somebody’s got to stand up to that guy.”

The pair did not elaborate on the incident when asked about it during the press conference after qualifying.

This was the second time in three weekends Verstappen has been involved in an incident with a rival during practice. He and Liam Lawson were given one-place grid drops for colliding after Verstappen tried to overtake his rival in Mexico.

Verstappen and Russell have a history of collisions and incidents. Verstappen called Russell a “dickhead” after the pair clashed during a sprint race at Baku in 2023. The following year Russell accused Verstappen of threatening to deliberately crash into him in Qatar.

Last year Verstappen made contact with Russell during the Spanish Grand Prix, collecting a penalty which ultimately cost him the world championship.

This week the FIA confirmed it will appoint a group of up to 15 full-time stewards to work at races beginning next year. Russell said the change is “absolutely the right decision”.

Sports.title: Hamilton reveals car damage, Leclerc “very angry” as Ferrari pair fail to reach Q3 | Formula 1
Sports.content:
Lewis Hamilton said he experienced multiple problems in his Ferrari as he and team mate Charles Leclerc both failed to reach Q3.

The Ferrari drivers struggled with a lack of straight-line speed at the Las Vegas Strip Circuit . However Hamilton revealed he was also grappling with other problems in his car.

“I didn’t really know where we were going to be today,” he told Sky. “We knew we would struggle a little bit with these long straights, but I was optimistic going in and I thought the car would be okay.

“But on the first or second lap we took a hit of something on the floor, some debris or something, and damaged the floor. We lost a bunch of downforce with it, a few tenths.”

Hamilton said he also suffered on his final lap because he wasn’t close enough to another car to gain the benefit of a slipstream, which he particularly needed due to Ferrari’s weakness on the straights.

“I was giving it everything, my lap was as good as it could be at the end, but I didn’t have anyone ahead of me,” he said. “Then we lost – we had a lack of deployment at the end and I lost like six tenths [of a second] just on deployment.

“So, when it rains, it pours, and you know that’s one of those days.”

Advert | Become a RaceFans supporter and go ad-free

However he admitted that even without his problems it would have been difficult for him to reach Q3. “We were scrapping to just get into Q3,” he said.

“I think without the deployment loss [and] without the downforce loss, I think I could have got into Q3, but it would have still been tough. I think my lap was good enough in order to put me there if we weren’t losing so much on the straight there.

“But it is what it is. It’s over and it’s definitely not a nice feeling for the team, but we’ll try and move forward tomorrow.”

Ferrari team principal Frederic Vasseur said Hamilton “damaged the floor in Q1 which affected the performance of his car.”

“We tried to repair it, but were only partially able to,” he added.

Leclerc also believes he could have reached Q3. He made a mistake at turn seven on what turned out to be his final run in Q2 as he did not reach the finishing line in time to start another run.

“We didn’t do a good job,” he said. “I did the mistake, the only lap I was given basically and at the same time the execution has been very poor.

“I don’t know, we’ll review it. I’m very angry now so I would rather not speak too much but I think there were plenty of things we could have done much better.”

Sports.title: Antonelli fastest but Verstappen takes pole for Las Vegas Grand Prix | 2026 Las Vegas GP qualifying report
Sports.content:
Andrea Kimi Antonelli exploited the power of the slipstream on the Las Vegas Strip to set the fastest time in qualifying.

However Max Verstappen will start from pole position due to the Mercedes driver’s penalty.

Straight-line speed dominated the shoot-out for pole position at the Las Vegas Strip Circuit. Q3 was contested solely by drivers using Mercedes and Red Bull-Ford power units as both Ferrari drivers were eliminated in Q2.

Antonelli began his final run in Q3 perfectly positioned behind the queue of cars, crossing the line just a second before the chequered flag came out. As the cars hammered towards turn 14 Antonelli gained around 16kph compared to his team mate further ahead in the queue.

That proved enough for Antonelli to snatch the fastest time away from Verstappen by more than a tenth of a second. However his five-place grid penalty for changing his engine means he will start sixth.

Verstappen therefore inherited his third pole position of the season. George Russell, who headed Q1 and also looked in contention for pole position, will start alongside him in second place. The pair already had their first clash of the weekend during final practice.

Lando Norris will move up to third on the grid ahead of Isack Hadjar. Arvid Lindblad took an excellent fifth on the grid but faces an investigation after his Racing Bulls team waved him out of his garage in front of Alexander Albon.

Advert | Become a RaceFans supporter and go ad-free

Ferrari suffered a double blow in Q2 as neither driver made it through to the final round. Lewis Hamilton looked under threat from the moment the session began but Charles Leclerc’s elimination was more of a surprise.

“I just don’t have any grip for some reason” Hamilton remarked as his early effort left him half a second shy of Leclerc’s best. He then ran wide at turn one. Although Hamilton managed to get a final run in, he was not well-positioned to benefit from the slipstream of any other cars, and his last lap left him outside by just under two tenths of a second.

Leclerc, meanwhile, appeared on course to progress early on. However he ran wide at turn seven late in the session, and the subsequent loss of time meant he did not reach the line in time to start his final lap. “Unbelievable,” he remarked as the Ferrari pair joined the Audi and Williams drivers in failing to progress beyond Q2.

With Oliver Bearman carrying a 35-place grid penalty, Haas told him to give a tow to team mate Rafael Camara. He did, but the rookie only rose to 16th before Gabriel Bortoleto knocked him out. The Aston Martin pair succeeded only in beating Bearman and the Cadillac of Valtteri Bottas.
