Technology could help digitise application processing, document verification, inspection scheduling, permit tracking and regulatory records.

A properly integrated platform would improve transparency, reduce administrative delays and make compliance easier to monitor.

Governments could also benefit from better urban development data and more efficient building control.

AI-powered construction education and workforce development: Africa cannot build the infrastructure it needs without a skilled construction workforce. There is an opportunity to develop digital learning platforms for artisans, technicians, junior engineers, quantity surveyors, project managers and other construction professionals.

Artificial intelligence could personalise learning, provide technical explanations in accessible language and support practical training.

Local language support, including Yoruba, Hausa, Igbo and Pidgin, could make technical education more accessible to workers who may not benefit from conventional English-language training alone.

Land intelligence and title verification: Land ownership and title verification remain significant challenges in many African property markets. Technology platforms could integrate land registry records, survey information, ownership documentation, encumbrance checks and geographic information systems.

Where government data access and legal frameworks permit, secure verification APIs could help professionals, developers, investors and financial institutions conduct more reliable due diligence.

This could reduce information asymmetry and improve confidence in property transactions.

Digital estate and infrastructure planning: Housing developments require more than individual buildings. They require roads, drainage, electricity, water supply, waste management and other essential infrastructure.

Digital planning tools could integrate land surveys, topographical data, engineering designs, utility networks and development requirements to support more efficient estate planning.

AI-assisted design could help professionals evaluate alternative layouts, estimate infrastructure costs and identify potential planning constraints.

Integrated construction collaboration platforms: Perhaps one of the most important opportunities is the creation of a shared digital workspace for the entire construction value chain. Architects, engineers, quantity surveyors, contractors, developers, suppliers and clients need to work with the same project information.

A centralised collaboration platform could connect drawings, revisions, bills of quantities, procurement, contracts, schedules, budgets, site reports, payments and project performance.

Think of it as the digital operating system for a construction project.

Rather than managing every activity through disconnected applications, stakeholders could operate within a coordinated environment.

Why this opportunity is bigger than another startup trend

There is a temptation to approach construction technology as another opportunity to build an application, raise venture capital and pursue rapid user acquisition. That would be a mistake.

Construction technology requires a deeper understanding of the industry. A product that works in a conventional consumer technology environment may fail on a construction site if it does not account for procurement practices, professional responsibilities, contractual relationships, payment structures, regulatory requirements and the realities of field operations.

The most successful founders will not necessarily be those who write the best code. They will be those who understand the problems deeply enough to build technology that people are willing to use repeatedly.

This requires collaboration between technology founders and construction professionals. Software engineers need to understand construction workflows. Construction professionals need to become more comfortable with data, automation and digital systems. Investors need to understand that some construction technology products require longer adoption cycles but can eventually become deeply embedded in the industry.

There is also a need to build for Africa’s realities rather than simply importing solutions designed for different markets. Products must account for fragmented supply chains, mobile-first users, varying levels of digital literacy, unreliable connectivity in some locations, local payment systems, regulatory differences and the informal economy. Technology must simplify the industry, not make it more complicated.

The investment opportunity: from individual applications to industry infrastructure

The most interesting opportunities may not necessarily be standalone applications. They may be the platforms that become essential infrastructure for how the industry operates.

A material marketplace that becomes the primary procurement channel for thousands of contractors. A financial technology platform that manages construction savings, project financing and milestone payments. A project management system that becomes the standard operating environment for developers and contractors. A labour marketplace that connects millions of skilled workers with verified opportunities. An AI-powered construction intelligence platform that becomes an essential tool for estimating, planning and monitoring projects.

Each of these businesses could develop substantial commercial value if it achieves product-market fit, trusted distribution and sustainable unit economics.

They also create opportunities for interconnected ecosystems. For example, a construction cost platform can connect to a material marketplace. The marketplace can connect to financing. Financing can connect to project monitoring. Project monitoring can connect to procurement and payment verification.

This is how technology can move beyond isolated applications and become an operating layer for an entire industry.

The role of governments and institutional investors

The transformation of construction cannot be left to startups alone. Governments control important parts of the enabling environment, including land administration, building regulations, public procurement, infrastructure investment and access to official records.

They should create opportunities for responsible technology companies to participate in digitising these systems. Public agencies can support interoperable data standards, transparent procurement processes, digital building approval systems and reliable property information infrastructure.

Financial institutions and institutional investors also have a role to play. Construction technology companies may require patient capital, industry partnerships and access to real project environments to validate their solutions.

Venture capital firms should look beyond the familiar consumer technology categories and examine businesses that improve productivity across construction, infrastructure and industrial supply chains.

The OECD’s infrastructure investment analysis makes clear that Africa’s development ambitions require substantial capital mobilisation. Technology will be essential in improving how that capital is translated into productive assets.

Africa needs builders who understand both code and concrete

I believe we are approaching an important moment in the evolution of African technology. The continent has demonstrated that it can develop financial technology platforms, digital marketplaces and innovative consumer products.

The next opportunity is to apply that same entrepreneurial energy to the industries that underpin economic development. Construction is one of them. The opportunity is not simply to digitise paperwork or replace manual processes with mobile applications. It is to redesign how projects are financed, planned, procured, executed and managed.

It is to make construction more transparent, more productive, more predictable and more accessible. It is to use technology to reduce waste, improve project delivery, expand access to housing and accelerate infrastructure development.

This is also the thinking behind what we are developing with Ladaar: a connected construction technology ecosystem bringing together construction finance, professional services, procurement, project intelligence and workflow automation.

But the opportunity extends far beyond one company or one platform. Africa needs many more innovators willing to understand this industry and build solutions around its real problems.

The next generation of technology leaders should look beyond the sectors that have already attracted the most attention. They should look at the industries where inefficiencies are deepest, where the economic stakes are highest and where technology can produce tangible improvements in people’s lives.

Africa does not just need more technology companies. It needs technology companies that can help build Africa.

The next great African technology opportunity may not be another application for transferring money, ordering food or booking a ride. It may be the technology that helps us build a million homes, deliver infrastructure more efficiently, connect construction professionals, finance projects responsibly and create better cities.

The future of African technology will not be written by code alone. It will also be built with concrete, steel, data and innovation. And it is time the technology ecosystem paid attention.

Razaq is a construction and project management professional

World.title: The future of automobile technology: Embracing AI for business growth in Nigeria
World.content:
By Moses Stowe

The growing importance of technological innovation, professional development and sustainable business growth in Nigeria’s automobile industry took centre stage at the 2026 Nigeria Automobile Technicians Association (NATA), Lagos State Council Day, where Intercontinental Distillers Limited (IDL), makers of Action Bitters, participated in an initiative recognising and supporting the contributions of automobile technicians to the nation’s economy.

Held under the theme, “Harnessing Artificial Intelligence (AI) to Transform and Develop the Business of Auto Technicians in Nigeria,” this year’s celebration provided an important platform for industry stakeholders, automobile professionals, corporate organisations and association leaders to examine emerging opportunities in the automotive sector and the need to equip technicians with the knowledge, skills and resources required to remain competitive in an increasingly technology-driven industry.

A major highlight of IDL’s participation was its support for the empowerment of automobile technicians through the provision of automobile tools. The initiative underscored the importance of practical support in strengthening the capacity of technicians, improving their operational efficiency and helping them deliver better services to customers. Beyond the recognition of their professional contributions, the gesture reflected the importance of providing tangible resources that can support the growth and sustainability of small businesses within the automobile value chain.

Speaking on the significance of the occasion, Celestine Anyanwu, Brand Manager, Wine and Bitters, IDL, acknowledged the invaluable contributions of automobile technicians to the nation’s economic and industrial development. He noted that their expertise, dedication and entrepreneurial spirit remain essential to the effective functioning of the transportation and automobile sectors.

He emphasised the importance of initiatives that recognise the efforts of professionals whose daily activities contribute to keeping businesses, individuals and transportation systems running. According to him, supporting the NATA community through the provision of relevant automobile tools represents a meaningful contribution towards professional development, business improvement and the advancement of the automobile servicing industry.

He further acknowledged the relevance of this year’s theme, noting that Artificial Intelligence presents emerging opportunities for automobile technicians to improve diagnostic processes, embrace modern automotive technologies and develop more efficient approaches to business operations. He encouraged industry stakeholders to continue supporting platforms that promote innovation, practical empowerment and sustainable professional growth.

One of the major highlights of the event was the presentation of the grand prize, a complete set of automobile tool kits, to Kazeem Oladeji, one of the beneficiaries of the empowerment initiative.

Expressing his appreciation, Oladeji described the award as a significant boost to his profession and business, noting that access to the right tools is essential to delivering quality automobile services. He commended Action Bitters and Intercontinental Distillers Limited for recognising the efforts of automobile technicians and extending support beyond mere celebration to practical empowerment.

In the address of the Chairman of NATA, Lagos State Council, Morufu Egberongbe, described the celebration as a significant milestone in the association’s collective journey towards the growth, recognition, empowerment and professional development of automobile technicians across Lagos State and Nigeria.

He reaffirmed the association’s commitment to promoting professionalism, unity, excellence and sustainable business development among its members, who operate across different segments of the automotive value chain. These include auto mechanics, auto electricians, panel beaters, spray painters, vulcanisers, auto air-conditioning technicians, diagnostic specialists, spare parts dealers and other related professionals.

Egberongbe explained that the choice of this year’s theme reflected NATA’s determination to embrace innovation and adequately prepare its members for the future of the automotive industry. He noted that Artificial Intelligence and other emerging technologies are creating new possibilities for vehicle diagnostics, maintenance, customer service and business management, making continuous learning and adaptation increasingly important.

The NATA chairman also expressed appreciation to corporate partners, sponsors and exhibitors for recognising the importance of the automobile technician community and supporting initiatives that promote innovation, capacity development and business growth. He described their contributions as investments in the future of the automotive industry and the thousands of businesses sustained by the sector.

He equally acknowledged government institutions, industry leaders, association executives, the planning committee and other stakeholders whose contributions helped make the celebration a success.

For IDL, its participation in the 2026 NATA Lagos State Council Day provided an opportunity to recognise a professional community whose contributions extend beyond automobile repairs to entrepreneurship, employment generation, technical expertise and economic development.

The provision of automobile tools also highlighted an important dimension of corporate engagement: the need to support professional communities with resources that address practical business needs. For automobile technicians, access to appropriate tools is essential to improving service delivery, adapting to changing vehicle technologies and maintaining the confidence of customers.

As Nigeria’s automotive landscape continues to evolve, the integration of Artificial Intelligence, digital diagnostic systems and modern vehicle maintenance solutions will increasingly shape the industry’s future. Platforms such as the NATA Lagos State Council Day therefore remain important in encouraging collaboration, knowledge exchange and stronger partnerships between professional associations and corporate stakeholders.

Ultimately, the 2026 celebration reinforced a shared vision of an automobile industry built on technical competence, innovation, professional recognition and economic empowerment. Through its participation and support for the initiative, IDL joined other stakeholders in recognising the importance of strengthening the capabilities of automobile technicians and creating opportunities for the continued development of their businesses.

The message was clear: the future of Nigeria’s automobile industry depends not only on technological advancement but also on empowering the skilled professionals who make the sector work.

World.title: Oando’s rising fortunes: How Wale Tinubu is rewriting growth story
World.content:
By Adebayo Adeoye

Jubril Adewale Tinubu, CON, is not one to be easily satisfied with yesterday’s accomplishments. For the Oando Group Chief Executive, every milestone appears to present another opportunity to raise the bar, test new possibilities and push the boundaries of what an indigenous energy company can achieve. That restless ambition is once again finding expression in Oando’s improving fortunes.

At Oando, the story has never been one of an overnight success. Rather, it is a tale of calculated risks, corporate reinvention and an unwavering belief in the possibilities of indigenous enterprise. Over the years, Tinubu has remained at the centre of the company’s evolution, steering its affairs through difficult economic seasons, industry uncertainties and the complex demands of a rapidly changing energy landscape.

Today, the signs of another promising chapter are becoming increasingly visible, as the indigenous energy company continues to record encouraging improvements in its operations, strengthening its position in an industry where survival and relevance are often determined by the ability to anticipate change and respond decisively. For Tinubu, who has spent considerable years building Oando into a recognisable name in Africa’s energy industry, the latest developments represent more than a corporate milestone. They reflect an enduring ambition to build an indigenous institution capable of competing beyond Nigeria’s shores and holding its own among established players in the global energy market.

One of the most encouraging aspects of Oando’s recent performance is the improvement in its operational efficiency. The company has continued to strengthen its production capacity, improve asset utilisation and address some of the operational challenges that have historically confronted the oil and gas industry. Its improving production profile suggests that the investments and management decisions taken over time are beginning to yield meaningful results.

But beyond increased production, the company’s efforts to reduce operating costs and improve facility reliability have equally attracted attention. In an industry where operational disruptions can quickly erode profitability, efficiency remains a critical ingredient for sustainable growth. Oando’s renewed focus on operational discipline therefore speaks to a management philosophy that recognises the importance of building a business on solid foundations rather than merely pursuing expansion for its own sake.

Indeed, Tinubu’s corporate journey has been defined by an appetite for ambitious decisions. His leadership at Oando has seen the company navigate major transitions, expand its interests and deepen its participation in Nigeria’s energy value chain.

The acquisition of additional upstream assets further underscored his belief that indigenous companies should not remain spectators in an industry that has for decades been dominated by international oil companies.

That ambition, however, comes with its own demands. The acquisition and development of oil and gas assets require substantial capital, careful financial management and the ability to balance immediate obligations with long-term business objectives. Oando is not insulated from these pressures, particularly as it continues to manage the financial commitments associated with its expansion strategy.

Nevertheless, the company’s improving operating performance offers reasons for optimism. Its ability to generate cash from operations while maintaining investments in drilling and other production-related activities demonstrates a determination to sustain its growth trajectory. Equally important is the company’s continuing effort to strengthen its financial position and manage its borrowing obligations.

For Tinubu, the task is clearly not simply to preserve what has already been built but to ensure that Oando remains relevant in an industry undergoing profound transformation. The global conversation around energy security, cleaner energy sources and sustainable development is changing the rules of engagement. Indigenous energy companies must therefore demonstrate not only financial resilience but also the capacity to adapt to emerging realities.

This is where the Oando story becomes particularly interesting. Tinubu has consistently projected the ambition of an African entrepreneur who believes that local businesses can rise above structural limitations and compete on a much bigger stage. His approach has been characterised by bold corporate moves, strategic partnerships and an understanding that the future belongs to companies willing to evolve.

Yet, beyond the boardroom calculations and corporate announcements, there is also the question of legacy. Building a successful company is one thing; establishing an institution that can withstand changing leadership, economic cycles and industry disruptions is another. It is a challenge that every ambitious business leader must eventually confront.

For now, Oando appears determined to keep its place in the unfolding energy narrative. Its improving operational fortunes provide fresh momentum, while Tinubu’s leadership continues to attract attention as the company pursues its broader ambitions.

Clearly, the Oando story is far from finished. And if the current momentum is anything to go by, Wale Tinubu is not ready to take his foot off the accelerator. In the competitive race for relevance in Africa’s energy industry, he appears determined to ensure that Oando is not merely present at the table but has a voice in deciding where the industry goes.

Adeoye Adebayo writes in from Lagos.

World.title: 2027: Imperative of Peter Mbah’s second term in Enugu
World.content:
By Willy Eya

Politics apart, Enugu State Governor, Dr Peter Mbah deserves a second term in office. That is not contestable. Certainly, the governor’s achievements since assumption of office in 2023 will campaign for him ahead of the 2027 general elections. One good turn, they say, deserves another.

Mbah came in as an accomplished technocrat determined to reshape the public sector using his private sector background.He approaches governance with a structured blueprint rather than the usual, impromptu trial-and-error tactics by regular Nigerian politicians.

Every step the governor takes is intentional, hence, he links infrastructure directly to economic growth. His idea for instance is that fixing roads or investing heavily in security isn’t just for safety but a targeted prerequisite to open up the state for tourism, agriculture, and private sector investments.

He deliberately avoided slow, conventional governance steps and pushed instead for immediate macro-level structural adjustments from Day One.Mbah’s strength lies in translating private-sector efficiency into public-sector execution.This quality is evidenced by his courage to dismantle slow legacy systems—such as implementing the fully digitized Enugu Geographic Information Service (ENGIS) to fast-track land administration and heavily relying on data to drive executive decisions.

Unlike career politicians who rely on political patronage, the governor is largely a corporate technocrat whose leadership is rooted in rigorous planning.

From inception after his inauguration, he was clear in his road-map to radically change the story of Enugu State. His first major challenge was to end the Monday Sit-at-Home disruptions. For years, the illegal “sit-at-home” orders crippled the economy of the Southeast and his immediate and uncompromising ban on the orders from his first week in office is frequently cited as a defining test of his leadership.Despite initial hiccups, the administration restored normal business and economic activities on Mondays and Enugu State is better for it today.

In his cabinet appointments, Mbah consciously shifted the political culture of Enugu State by actively recruiting top-tier professionals from academia and the global private sector. He believes in inclusive and merit-based governance, hence, prioritized competence over partisan rewards. For him, governance is a serious business of service delivery, thus, he established a culture of accountability across state ministries.

Knowing the importance of security to his set goals, he was quick to establish the Command and Control Centre which deployed modern surveillance and security infrastructure, including an ultramodern command and control center, to improve safety across the state.

His administration has focused on a multi-faceted development framework aimed at growing the state’s economy from $4.4 billion to $30 billion. For many observers including this writer, that was a tall dream considering that hitherto, Enugu was largely a civil service state. He has proved pundits wrong as internal updates reveal a stark upward trajectory in the state’s fiscal performance, rising from ₦26 billion in 2022 to ₦181 billion in 2024, reaching ₦460 billion in 2025, and carrying an estimated projection of ₦871 billion for the 2026 fiscal year.

So, the imperative of a second term for the governor, is strengthened by his administration’s documented performance, structural transformation and repositioning of the state since 2023. As the 2027 general elections approach, the voters would not forget the need to institutionalize ongoing economic reforms, finalize massive infrastructure projects, and sustain human capital developments that have redefined Enugu’s developmental trajectory.

Across the state including the rural areas, there are visible projects and evidence of the administration’s commitment to improve public services. Governor Mbah’s ambitious vision to expand Enugu State’s economy from $4.4 billion to $30 billion and his obvious dogged determination to reposition Enugu State are his unique selling points.

Part of the projects that would speak for Governor Mbah’s second term include 260 Smart Green Schools, 260 primary healthcare centres, an international hospital intended to reduce medical tourism and the establishment of Enugu Air which has already commenced international flights. The State’s fiscal architecture had undergone significant reform through revenue automation, reforms at the Enugu State Internal Revenue Service, improved financial management, the Treasury Single Account, enterprise resource planning and broader institutional restructuring.

The administration has also ensured the sustenance of investments in youth empowerment, women development, technology, skills acquisition, social protection, tourism, environmental sustainability and community development.

So,most critical observers agree that Enugu is on an aggressive path to development, and disrupting the upward momentum in 2027 would stall the state’s economic trajectory.

It is then preposterous to imagine that people of the state will abandon Governor Mbah for a gamble with the opposition forces in next governorship election.

Though opponents and paid social media activists point to economic hardships and taxes as issues in the coming election but objective and critical observers agree that the revolutionary reforms by the Enugu State government are laying a foundation for enduring progress and development of the state.

It is not surprising that the governor’s supporters have moved away from the traditional political culture of treating a second term as an automatic entitlement but readily flaunt a data-backed scorecard to justify governance continuity.

On September 6, 2026, Governor Mbah unveiled a compendium of more than 10,000 milestones recorded in the first term of his administration. Among others, the compendium records over 1,521 kilometres of constructed and reconstructed roads, over 7,000 classrooms, 260 Type-2 Primary Healthcare Centres, Enugu Air, the New Enugu Smart City, and the revamp of moribund assets.

In an official manifesto performance review presented on October 29, 2026, Governor Mbah had noted that a second term is vital to deepen ongoing structural reforms and maximize completed projects rather than letting momentum stall. There is no doubt that re-electing him in the 2027 general elections would allow his administration to consolidate ongoing development projects, strengthen federal-state alignment, and expand economic opportunities.

Willy is a member, Public Communication, Enugu State APC Campaign Council

World.title: PSHAN, WHO urge increased private investment to rescue Nigeria’s healthcare system
World.content:
By Matthew Johnson

The Private Sector Health Alliance of Nigeria (PSHAN) and the World Health Organisation (WHO) have called for increased private sector investment and stronger public-private partnerships to address persistent challenges confronting Nigeria’s healthcare system.

The organisations said government alone could not shoulder the responsibility of transforming the health sector, stressing that sustained private sector investment was critical to improving healthcare delivery, strengthening infrastructure and achieving universal health coverage.

The call was made at the 2026 PSHAN Annual Gala and Awards Night held in Lagos on November 20, with the theme, “Legacy Builders: Honouring the Visionaries of the Nigerian Healthcare System.”

Speaking at the event, Managing Director and Chief Executive Officer of PSHAN, Dr. Tinuola Akinbolagbe, said the alliance was working to position the private sector at the centre of Nigeria’s health development through strategic partnerships, investment, innovation and institutional strengthening.

She said PSHAN was seeking to move beyond fragmented private sector interventions towards coordinated investments capable of strengthening health systems and delivering measurable and sustainable outcomes.

According to her, meaningful progress in healthcare requires shared responsibility and collaboration across different sectors.

“As we look towards 2027 and beyond, our ambition is to move from fragmented contributions by the private sector to coordinated investment, from isolated interventions to stronger health systems, and from good intentions to measurable, sustainable outcomes,” she said.

Akinbolagbe explained that the theme of the event was designed to celebrate individuals, institutions and organisations whose courage, leadership, innovation and commitment had contributed to shaping the future of healthcare in Nigeria.

In his keynote address, former President of the African Development Bank Group and Executive Chairman of the Global Africa Investment Summit, Dr. Akinwumi Adesina, described healthcare as an investment in human capital and essential economic infrastructure rather than merely social sector expenditure.

Speaking on the theme, “Health as Wealth: Mobilising African Leadership and Capital to Build Sustainable Health Systems,” Adesina said a healthy population was fundamental to productivity, innovation, economic competitiveness and national prosperity.

He maintained that no country could achieve sustainable wealth without a healthy population, insisting that investment in healthcare was essential to building a productive workforce and inclusive economy.

Adesina called for stronger partnerships between government and the private sector, noting that government alone could not finance and deliver the transformation required in the country’s healthcare system.

He urged businesses to move beyond philanthropy and corporate social responsibility initiatives to embrace healthcare as a strategic investment priority.

“I urge businesses to move beyond philanthropy and corporate social responsibility initiatives to regard healthcare as a strategic investment priority.

“Investments should be directed towards strengthening primary healthcare, training and supporting health workers, local production of essential medicines and vaccines, digital healthcare infrastructure, reliable diagnostics and sustainable health financing,” he said.

The former AfDB president said Nigeria must build a healthcare system where women did not die during childbirth because of lack of access to quality medical services and families were not pushed into poverty by illness.

He urged stakeholders to prioritise women, children and vulnerable communities, stressing that access to quality healthcare should not depend on an individual’s income or circumstances.

“Nigeria must reduce its dependence on imported essential medicines, vaccines and diagnostic products by strengthening local manufacturing, promoting health innovation and developing resilient healthcare supply chains,” he added.

Also speaking, Dr. Pavel Ursu, representing the World Health Organisation, warned that Nigeria and other African countries risked losing the benefits of their growing youthful populations without deliberate investments in healthcare.

He identified high maternal and child mortality, inadequate healthcare funding, shortages of health workers and poor infrastructure as major challenges undermining the continent’s healthcare ambitions.

Ursu stressed that healthcare facilities required essential infrastructure, including reliable electricity and water supply, to deliver quality services.

He cited Nigeria’s Universal Health Coverage Compact, signed in December 2023 and expanded in 2025 to include the private sector, as an example of the importance of involving businesses in health policy development and implementation.

He also identified the incorporation of the private sector into the implementation of the Basic Health Care Provision Fund as an opportunity to strengthen collaboration.

“Government policies must encourage private sector participation. The responsibility of developing the health sector cannot be left to government alone,” he said.

Ursu maintained that Africa’s demographic advantage could translate into a productive workforce and economic growth only if governments and other stakeholders took practical steps to improve health outcomes.

Similarly, the Special Adviser to the President on Health, Dr. Salma Ibrahim-Anas, said the Federal Government had urged the organised private sector to deepen collaboration with public health institutions to translate national health policies into measurable improvements in the lives of Nigerians.

She outlined six priority areas for private sector alignment under the Nigerian Health Sector Renewal Investment Initiative. These include primary healthcare revitalisation, expansion of national health insurance enrolment, domestic manufacturing of pharmaceuticals and medical equipment, digital health deployment in underserved communities, maternal and child survival, and health workforce training.

Citing 2026 Federal Ministry of Health statistics, Ibrahim-Anas disclosed that the private sector already contributed over N5 trillion to healthcare delivery, owned 82 per cent of secondary health facilities and had revamped more than 5,400 primary healthcare centres.

She called on corporate organisations to move beyond isolated corporate social responsibility projects towards integrated investments aligned with state and local government priorities under the sector-wide approach.

She warned against abandoned and poorly equipped healthcare projects, stressing that renovated facilities must be adequately staffed and supplied with essential medicines, electricity and water.

“Private sector healthcare spending should be viewed as a strategic investment in human capital, workforce productivity and national economic growth rather than mere charity,” she said.

The United Nations Under-Secretary-General and Special Adviser on Africa, Dr. Ahunna Eziakonwa, also urged private sector leaders and policymakers to move beyond isolated health interventions and build enduring partnerships capable of strengthening public healthcare delivery for future generations.

Eziakonwa said the theme, “Legacy Builders: Honouring the Visionaries of Nigerian Healthcare,” represented the importance of building sustainable institutions that continuously improve lives rather than measuring legacies merely by physical structures or accumulated wealth.

She noted that governments had the primary responsibility of setting standards, financing public services and protecting equity, but maintained that private sector capital, technology and operational expertise could achieve greater impact when aligned with national, state and local health priorities.

“Cross-sector partnerships remain critical to Africa’s broader economic transformation, food security and climate resilience. Corporate and public leaders must sustain long-term alliances that deliver quality healthcare across generations,” she said.

The awards ceremony featured 125 public nominations across five major categories and 25 subcategories, which were subsequently reduced to 75 through public voting.

The organisers said the awards were designed to celebrate excellence across Nigeria’s healthcare ecosystem while encouraging greater commitment to sustainable healthcare development.

World.title: Who wants Odegbami dead? By Segun Odegbami
World.content:
Patrick Omorodion

The Bible told us that the Jebusites were descendants of Canaan, the son of Ham. An ancient Canaanite tribe who inhabited the hill country and fortified stronghold of Jebus, later known as Jerusalem.

They were among the peoples inhabiting the land God promised to Abraham’s descendants and Moses. They derive their name from a Hebrew root meaning “thresher,” “to trample down,” or “to tread on”.

Breaking this further down spiritually, “the name denotes a force that “stomps” or grinds down others, attempting to minimize, humiliate, or crush a person’s potential and authority”.

I have used the above to explain the situation we have in the administration of football in Nigeria since a certain group of human hyenas took control of the running of the game by ‘forcefully’ truncating the second term of one of Nigeria’s renowned sports administrators, Alhaji Ibrahim Galadima in 2006.

Alhaji Galadima, now late, wanted a reform of the Nigeria Football Association’s (NFA ) laws that excluded the majority of football’s key stakeholders.

After successfully getting the Kano-born administrator out of their way, the football ‘Jebusites’ changed NFA into NFF (Nigeria Football Federation) and manipulated the statutes to give more voting powers to the State FA Chairmen.

One stakeholder who would not rest until a proper reform was carried out for an inclusive Congress that would allow other stakeholders an opportunity to help change the face of football in Nigeria is Chief Segun Odegbami.

He used his weekly Column syndicated in some Nigerian newspapers for the campaign. He made speeches at seminars and sports workshops to spread his message for the reform of the NFF to no avail.

Nigerians carried on as if all was well with our football. A handful of Nigerians, sports journalists and passionate fans, joined in the crusade but their ‘cries’ seemed not to make any impact as the football Jebusites who seemed to enjoy the support of the government carried on.

Still Odegbami would not be deterred. His campaign intensified and went wide when he established a radio station, Eagle7 FM based in his little rustic town of Mosimi in Ogun State of Nigeria.

He talked about the rot in football and assembled analysts regularly to talk about why a reform is desirable before it causes Nigeria’s football to go into the ICU- Intensive Care Unit.

Odegbami is not a prophet of doom like Jeremiah and Ezekiel in the Bible who predicted gloom for Israel if the leaders didn’t do the right things, but his fears for football eventually came to pass.

Nigeria’s football prospects declined and all her teams, from ‘top to bottom’, apologies late President Muhammad Buhari, began to crash, surprisingly against minnows of yesterday.

Despite this, the Jebusites were climbing on both CAF and FIFA profile ladders and smiling.

At this stage, Odegbami’s campaign began to make sense to Nigerian fans who depended on the success of our football teams to console themselves in the midst of the unending economic crunch that had put them under physical and emotional stress.

And at last the government thought it was high time it looked into the simmering crisis in football and how it could be stemmed.

When the Jebusites saw the stand of the government, they talked to themselves and step aside. Although some people still believe that they were forced to throw in the towel.

Their mass resignation led to the decision by CAF and FIFA to step in and today a 5-man Normalisation Committee has been appointed to start the process of repositioning football with a reform that would allow a level playing field for all stakeholders.

With the Committee in place, it has become clear to the Jebusites that the end to their vice-grip on football has come to an end and that the era of deciding who could be elected into the NFF Board and become the president has gone.

Not quite a week after FIFA announced the Normalisation Committee, armed men invaded the Abeokuta home of the champion for the reform process in football, Chief Odegbami and nearly snuffed life out of him.

I don’t want to believe that those who are not happy that they lost their juicy positions in the NFF because of Odegbami’s consistent campaigns are behind this dastardly act.

An African adage which says, ‘the witch cried last night and the child died today’ that has kept me thinking since the news of the attack on Odegbami broke.

Odegbami has been a very easy going man, living for his former teammates, creating opportunities for them whenever he has a sports or football project to carry out for the good of the country.

They were involved in the Shell Cup for secondary schools he coordinated with the support of Shell Petroleum and Development Company as sponsor and the Nigeria School Sports Federation, NSSF as the organising body.

He still involves them to run his Segun Odegbami International College & Sports Academy (SOCA). They are among analysts he features frequently on the Eagle7 FM radio to dissect the problems of sports and proffer solutions that could make Nigerian athletes excel.

Would anyone say that the man, who uses his money and connections to assist his colleagues and help make things work for the progress of our athletes, hates Nigeria?

That is why I ask today, who wants Odegbami dead? The police must get to the root of the assassination attempt on him, fish out the culprits and bring them to justice.

A man like Odegbami who has had sleepless nights thinking of how the Super Eagles could be great again with a proper running of the NFF should not be the target of wicked people and must be protected by the country.

Chief Odegbami, here is wishing you a quick recovery from that deadly machete cut which could have snuffed life out of you.

World.title: Pedro Clinches 2026 TotalEnergies Charity Golf Trophy
World.content:
Follow THISDAYLIVE on Google Add us as a preferred source to see more of our stories in Google 

Blessing Ibunge in Port Harcourt

Abiye Pedro has emerged overall winner of the 2026 TotalEnergies Charity Golf Tournament held at the Port Harcourt Club 1928, Rivers State, scoring 45 points to claim the top prize.

The tournament, which brought together golfers, business leaders, TotalEnergies executives and other stakeholders, was organised not only to promote sporting excellence but also to raise support for two charitable organisations: the Rosalie Home Rehabilitation Centre in Ogale, Eleme, Rivers State, and the Little Sisters of the Poor Home for the Elderly in Enugu.

In the men’s category, Moses Amadasun won with 43 points, while Jones Okorie and Emmanuel Chiejina finished first and second runners-up respectively, both recording 41 points on countback.

Susan Cole-Kotas emerged winner in the ladies’ category with 40 points. Juliet Okoro placed first runner-up with 38 points, while Chinyelu Komori finished second runner-up with 37 points.

Among staff participants, Sung Yuh won the men’s category with 40 points, while Stella Eze emerged winner in the ladies’ category with 32 points.

Other subsidiary category winners were Tari Dickson and Tobe Eze, who won the Nearest to the Pin awards, while Cole-Kotas and Benjamin Briere claimed the Longest Drive prizes.

Speaking at the event, Country Chair and Managing Director of TotalEnergies EP Nigeria, Matthieu Bouyer, said the tournament was about more than golf, stressing its humanitarian objective.

“Today is about more than golf. It is about supporting two organisations whose work deserves our attention,” Bouyer said.

He disclosed that TotalEnergies would supplement proceeds from the tournament to support the two beneficiary organisations, with each home allocated N5 million.

Bouyer said the company’s intervention was aimed at supporting institutions providing care to vulnerable people, adding that “the real winners are the people and communities whose lives will be improved by what we achieve together.”

The Rosalie Home Rehabilitation Centre provides care and rehabilitation for homeless and abandoned women living with severe mental health conditions, while the Little Sisters of the Poor Home for the Elderly provides care for elderly people in difficult circumstances.

A representative of Rosalie Home, Sr. Bibiana Dura, expressed appreciation to TotalEnergies, describing the company as a consistent supporter of the centre.

“Since I arrived seven years ago, they have never failed, even for one year,” she said, adding that the support had helped care for women living with mental health conditions and those who were destitute.

World.title: Farida Waziri: From Childhood to Combating Corruption
World.content:
Follow THISDAYLIVE on Google Add us as a preferred source to see more of our stories in Google 

The former Chairman of the Economic and Financial Crimes Commission, Farida Waziri, never planned a career in the police, but found in it a calling to serve. In a recent encounter, she tells Vanessa Obioha about growing up in a convent, her journey through law enforcement and the defining moments of her tenure at the EFCC.

Sometimes, Farida Waziri wonders how her life might have turned out if she had become a reverend sister. Would it have been different from the career she eventually built? Would she have found the same fulfilment?

Growing up in Gboko, Benue State, she spent considerable time at a convent, introduced to its life through an uncle. It was a formative experience. She learnt discipline, order and a sense of purpose. She also acquired a deep appreciation for service, understanding early that character was built in small, unglamorous routines and that “you owe something to people who have less than you,” she told me during a recent encounter.

There was music, reading and flower arrangement, too. During school holidays, she sometimes stayed back to help the reverend sisters. With so much of her childhood shaped by the convent, the thought of becoming one of them seemed almost inevitable.

But life had other plans. Waziri never became a reverend sister, although she insisted she never entirely abandoned the calling. She loved the convent life and believes she would have been content had she followed that path.

“I only changed the uniform. Whether in a habit or in a police uniform, the task is to protect the vulnerable and stand for what is right. I have no regrets, only gratitude for how the path unfolded.”

Interestingly, policing was not even her first career choice. Medicine was. The idea of wearing a white coat and stethoscope appealed to her until an encounter with a dead body and an explanation of the autopsy process changed her mind.

Then came law. Having read books about Perry Mason, the fictional California lawyer who seemed to win every case, Waziri thought she could make a good lawyer, too. She eventually studied law, but it was in the Nigeria Police Force and later the Economic and Financial Crimes Commission (EFCC) that she would make her most defining mark.

The police force, however, was far removed from the quiet, orderly world she had known. It did not help that her perception of a police officer was that of a distant and rather stern figure.

“I saw the police as a male, rough-edged profession, very far from the quiet world I grew up in. I did not see it as a place for someone like me.”

So, when the opportunity came for her to join the force after her secondary school education, she was initially reluctant. It took the persuasion of her uncle, who was an instructor at the police academy, to get her to enlist in the Nigeria Police Force.

Her love for the job did not happen overnight. It came gradually. At first, she was simply doing her job. But when she saw what a well-handled case could do for a person, when a victim got justice or a wrongly accused person was cleared, she knew she would love to be in a position to make such a difference.

“What I discovered was a profession that, at its best, stands between ordinary people and harm, and that changed my view completely,” she said. “Once you have seen the difference honest policing makes in someone’s life, it stops being just a job.”

That conviction would become an important part of her professional identity. Working in a male-dominated institution came with its assumptions about what women could achieve, but Waziri relied on competence to challenge them.

This was reflected in her career, in which she blazed several trails. She was the pioneer Commissioner of Police in charge of the Special Fraud Unit, where she recorded the first conviction in an advance fee fraud case in Nigeria.

“I’m grateful to God that I’m the first Police Woman AIG from the North,” she added.

She also held the positions of Assistant Commissioner of Police (Operations), Screening and Selection, and Assistant/Deputy Commissioner of Police, Force Criminal Investigation Department (CID), Alagbon, Lagos.

But it was her appointment as the first and, so far, only female Executive Chairman of the EFCC that brought her into the national spotlight. Appointed by the late President Umaru Musa Yar’Adua in 2008, Waziri took charge of an institution whose mandate placed it in direct confrontation with some of the country’s most powerful people. She had already spent 35 years in the police force, including three years building the Special Fraud Unit from scratch between 1994 and 1997, with a focus on financial crimes, particularly Advance Fee Fraud. At the EFCC, however, she would confront corruption on a much larger scale, including cases involving Politically Exposed Persons (PEPs), such as politicians, ministers, commissioners and other public office holders.

“Graft is very big in this country,” she said. “More than you could imagine. Sometimes the scale of the offence is humongous; at other times, the modus operandi is so despicable that it leaves you wondering whether the perpetrators are in the right frame of mind.

“But I would also add that those who are charged with the task of leading the fight against graft are themselves exposed to harm, which includes physical harm and character assassination.”

Waziri experienced the latter in different ways. Threats came through telephone calls, letters and intermediaries who sometimes approached her under the guise of friendship.

“When you do this work, you accept that you will make enemies.” Her resilience came from faith, family, “and from the conviction that I was doing something worthwhile. I also learned not to dwell on fear, because if you let it, it governs every decision.”

Despite the allegations that trailed her removal, Waziri insisted that she recorded modest achievements that remain significant in the agency’s history.

“For starters, I was accused of having a low conviction rate, but the question is: How many convictions were recorded before my time? How many after my time? Who were the big PEPs convicted? In the five years before my time, the EFCC only managed plea bargains, not a trial conviction. In the real sense of the word conviction, Chief Bode George was the EFCC’s first. We took a complete case file to the High Court and the Court of Appeal, where judgment was upheld.

“Although the Supreme Court overturned the judgment, that was after he had served his jail sentence. We also got convictions against Oceanic Bank’s managing director and chief executive, Cecilia Ibru, and former Edo State governor, Lucky Igbinedion. I inherited 10 high-profile cases in 2008, and I took 65 high-profile cases to court,” she recounted.

She added that the commission recorded over 400 convictions, representing two-thirds of all convictions secured since its establishment in 2003. “This was the case when I left office in 2011.”

Waziri also rejected allegations that the EFCC under her leadership was selective in its arrests and prosecutions.

“We simply went for anyone against whom we had ample evidence for prosecution. And there was nothing personal between me and any of the high-profile citizens we arraigned for graft, including two former Ministers of Aviation and the then Speaker of the House of Representatives.”

Other achievements included the restructuring of the commission.

“We used to have offices scattered all over Abuja, in about four different locations. We developed the plan to build a corporate headquarters, got the parcel of land and had the ground-breaking ceremony performed in 2011 by Vice President Namadi Sambo. That building was completed seven years later, in 2018.”

The commission also deployed EagleClaw and Go-Case software to improve the tracking of electronic fraud and transparency in prosecutions.

During her three-year tenure, Waziri said, the EFCC recovered over $9 billion.

“We upgraded our academy to a world-class standard; we built a proper interrogation room; we prioritised training and changed the working etiquette; we did a whole lot of things, all in a bid to improve the efficiency of the EFCC operatives. More importantly, we were able to reposition EFCC as an independent anti-graft agency and not necessarily the attack dog of the government to harass perceived political foes.”

Still, there were things she wished had turned out differently. Many of the high-profile cases were still in court when she left office, and the slow pace of corruption trials remained a concern. She would have liked to see stronger reforms to ensure that painstaking investigations did not lose their value to judicial delays.

If anything, dealing with high-profile cases at the EFCC taught her something instructive about powerful people.

“They rarely believe the law applies to them, and will mobilise every resource to prove otherwise: lawyers, politicians, the press, sometimes threats. It taught me that corruption is a network, not a person, and that institutions need to be stronger than individuals. It also taught me that an investigator’s only real protection is a clean file and a clear conscience.”

Today, Waziri holds no grudges against those who may have hurt her along the way. At 80, and no longer in active service, she has entered a different chapter of life that keeps her away from the demands of public office to allow more time for herself.

The concerns that occupied much of her professional life, however, have not entirely receded. She remains particularly troubled by the evolution of Advance Fee Fraud into the more sophisticated world of cybercrime. The methods may have changed from letters and faxes to the internet, she argued, but the underlying principles remain the same.

“Fraudsters exploit greed, trust and weak systems,” she said.

To tackle this menace, she proposed modern forensic and digital capacity in law enforcement agencies, continuous training, deeper international cooperation “because these crimes are borderless,” and faster prosecution and real consequences, “since a slow justice system tells young people crime pays.” She also called for attention to youth unemployment and a culture that celebrates sudden wealth without asking where it came from.

“Parents, schools, religious leaders and the media all have a role.”

If there is anything policing taught her, it is this: “People are rarely what they first appear to be. The educated can be capable of terrible deceit, and the poor can show remarkable integrity. I learned that most wrongdoing begins with opportunity and rationalisation, a small compromise that nobody challenges. I also learned that people respond to fairness and firmness together. Pure harshness breeds resentment, and pure leniency breeds contempt.”

Perhaps the most interesting thing about Waziri’s journey is that she never entirely lost the girl who once imagined life in a convent. The little girl is every inch proud of the woman who never planned a career in the police but went on to serve with integrity and was not broken by the journey.

“If my legacy is that other Nigerian women see what is possible and that young officers see that honesty is not naive, then that is enough.”

World.title: Desayo Adesina’s World of Timeless Designs
World.content:
Follow THISDAYLIVE on Google Add us as a preferred source to see more of our stories in Google 

For her debut collection, fashion designer and creative consultant, Desayo Adesina, is inviting guests into an enchanted forest, where she will unveil timeless and elegant pieces for brides and contemporary women. Vanessa Obioha writes.

Today, November 22, fashion designer and creative consultant Desayo Adesina will host guests to an enchanting showcase of her debut collection, Sylvan Rarity in her new atelier shop.

Inspired by the idea of unearthing precious gemstones within a forest setting. The 13-piece collection reflects this through its colours, including emerald green, ruby and turquoise. A mix of imported and locally sourced fabrics was used, with velvet selected for its rich, light-absorbing texture.

The forest inspiration also finds expression in the details of the designs. Twisting, twig-like embellishments reminiscent of branches winding around leaves, alongside patterns inspired by foliage, bring the concept to life. The collection further incorporates storytelling, with designs bearing names associated with forest goddesses and vegetation, creating a deeper connection between the garments and their wearers.

The collection marks a new chapter for her fashion brand, Sayo Silver, with a renewed focus on brides and the sophisticated contemporary woman.

Adesina started out as a designer catering to a wide spectrum of clients, from children to women. She also ventured into ready-to-wear, working from her home in Apapa, while running a training school alongside. But over the years, she realised the need to scale the business and give it a clearer direction.

“Along the line, I felt as if my energy was pretty much everywhere. My energy was dispersed everywhere. It felt like I was not focusing on one particular type of dressing for women,” she said in a recent encounter.

That realisation led to the revamped Sayo Silver, now occupying a spacious compound in the heart of Ikeja GRA, off Isaac John Street.

Here, Adesina focuses on creating timeless and elegant designs for brides and contemporary women, ranging from bridal wear to cocktail dresses and couture.

Her preference for luxurious fabrics has also influenced the direction of the brand.

“I love working with delicate fabrics. I love the shine and the lustre that comes with those fabrics, evening wear, party dresses, couture, embellishment, surface decoration fabrics, manipulation. I love fabric manipulation,” she said.

Her interest in bridal wear, however, dates back to her university days, when trips to Lagos exposed her to a particular bridal store on Herbert Macaulay Road in Yaba. She was captivated by its beautiful designs and imagined returning there one day to pick out her wedding dress.

It was not until about a decade ago that Adesina made her first bridal dress, for her sister-in-law. She had chosen a wedding dress by Justin Alexander, which she wanted Adesina to reproduce. Before proceeding with the actual garment, Adesina made a toile, a prototype using cheaper fabric, usually calico, to test the fit and make necessary adjustments.

“It’s something that most designers don’t do here in Nigeria. They just go straight to sewing, but you need to do the toile so that you can correct errors,” she said.

The experience also exposed her to some of the challenges facing the fashion industry, particularly the shortage of competent and skilled workers. She called for more investment in training to bridge the gap.

Although it was her first attempt at making a bridal dress, Adesina was pleased with the outcome.

Adesina’s love for fashion designing can be traced back to her childhood. Born in Ibadan, Adesina was introduced to the world of fashion at an early age. Her mother was both a teacher and a fashion designer, and it was from her that she learnt the craft of needle and thread.

“I could make clothes as early as five or six years old. I could sew from the sewing machine as well as with needle and thread with my hand,” she recalled.

“And I had dolls, so I would make clothes for them, and I would give them to my mum. I remember we used to read a lot of comics, and there was this female comic for girls called Bunty. Bunty had these back-page paper dolls. I remember telling my mum to make those dresses for me and I was always so happy when she made them. It was the same when we watched ‘The Sound of Music.’ As a child, I don’t think they ever bought me a dress. All my dresses were made by her.”

With such an early fascination with dressmaking, studying fashion design might have seemed like the natural next step. But Adesina took a different academic route, earning a degree in social studies and a master’s in educational administration. It was only after marriage and childbirth that she pursued formal training in fashion design, attending the London College of Fashion and Central Saint Martins. She also undertook further fashion training in Nigeria.

After starting her business in Apapa, she relocated to Surulere, partly because of the traffic situation. But it was in Ikeja GRA that she began to visualise the kind of clientele she wanted to serve.

“When I came to Ikeja GRA two years ago, I felt that the area would actually work for luxury designs, for the more upscale dresses and clothes because of the people that live around here, the environment, then the space, the atmosphere, the ambience. I knew this is what I wanted to do here,” she said.

Sylvan Rarity is an expression of that vision and her desire to create pieces that endure beyond seasonal trends.

“I like to do things that are unexpected. We do not follow trends. Ten years down the line, you would be able to look at our creation and still marvel because of its timelessness,” she said.

World.title: Aisha Rimi: Celebrating a Leader Championing Nigeria’s Investment Growth
World.content:
Follow THISDAYLIVE on Google Add us as a preferred source to see more of our stories in Google 

Few birthdays arrive with a scoreboard. Aisha Rimi’s does. In 2025, the Nigerian Investment Promotion Commission (NIPC), where Rimi is Executive Secretary and CEO, tracked more than $10 billion in investment commitments across manufacturing, ICT, agro-processing, and renewable energy, and generated 5,432 direct jobs in two quarters.

Rimi was appointed in October 2023 and took office in December, bringing more than 30 years in international commercial law and project finance to an agency that had mostly advocated policy, tracked announcements, and digitised its Single Window Investors’ Portal. She turned it into a deal desk.

The commission now structures transactions, handles regulatory compliance, curates deal rooms and a Deals Book matching public-private projects with foreign capital, engages development finance institutions, and looks after investors once they arrive.

Flagship work includes a $2.5 billion livestock investment interest from JBS, the $1 billion Green Imperative agricultural mechanisation programme, and about $50 million from negotiations in the African Continental Free Trade Area deal room.

At the front door, NIPC facilitated nearly 100 company incorporations, approved 186 expatriate quotas, and granted Pioneer Status tax incentives to 17 companies in 2025, before moving the framework to the Economic Development Tax Incentive scheme in January 2026.

And why does this matter? Because total capital importation rose from $3.91 billion in 2023 to $12.32 billion in 2024 and $23.22 billion in 2025, and economists credit mostly exchange rate unification and high interest rates, which drew short-term portfolio money, for 85 per cent of 2025 inflows.

Direct investment, the long-term kind NIPC courts, was about 4 per cent of 2025 inflows, yet it rose 36.8 per cent, from $674.71 million to $923.01 million. That is the slice where an agency’s hands-on work is meant to show.

The $10 billion is commitments, which take several years to convert into investment that the National Bureau of Statistics records. All this because an Amazon like Rimi is in charge.

World.title: Tony Elumelu, Idris Elba Cross Paths in Sierra Leone
World.content:
Follow THISDAYLIVE on Google Add us as a preferred source to see more of our stories in Google 

Tony Elumelu’s role at the West Africa Integration and Investment Summit in Freetown has brought him into the same room as Idris Elba, the British actor whose family roots and development interests extend to Sierra Leone. Their recent meeting brings two different routes into Africa’s development debate into focus.

Elumelu, chairman of Heirs Holdings, led private-sector mobilisation at the inaugural summit, which ran from November 16 to 18. Convened under Sierra Leonean President Julius Maada Bio, the gathering brought governments, investors, and development institutions together around regional projects and cross-border investment.

Elba brings a global entertainment profile and a personal connection to the country. Of Sierra Leonean and Ghanaian heritage, he has advocated attracting diaspora private capital to African projects. He has also been associated with plans to develop Sherbro Island into an eco-focused urban and tourism destination.

The connection between the two men lies in a question facing the summit: how can Africa convert international attention into productive investment? Elumelu’s approach centres on businesses, entrepreneurs, and long-term private capital. His Africapitalism philosophy argues that African businesses can generate financial returns while contributing to social development.

Elba’s work draws on cultural reach and diaspora networks. His projects have included advocacy around sustainable energy, agriculture, and opportunities for young people. The proposed Sherbro Island development gives that agenda a physical focus, although its success will depend on financing, infrastructure, and implementation.

Their meeting follows a year in which both they and their significant other were named among the 2026 TIME 100 Philanthropy honourees. Tony and Awele Elumelu were recognised for the Tony Elumelu Foundation’s entrepreneurship work, while Idris and Sabrina Elba were recognised for development initiatives.

The summit provides a practical setting for these overlapping interests. Organisers list an investment pipeline exceeding $180 billion across West Africa. The challenge is to turn project discussions and private-sector interest into funded ventures, jobs, and operating businesses.

World.title: Tompolo Emerges as a Major Financier of Tinubu’s 2027 Re-election Bid
World.content:
Follow THISDAYLIVE on Google Add us as a preferred source to see more of our stories in Google 

The donation of 25 campaign vehicles in Ebonyi has added another state to Tompolo’s expanding political mobilisation network for President Bola Ahmed Tinubu’s 2027 re-election campaign. The vehicles are one visible part of an operation built around the PBAT Door-to-Door Movement.

Government Ekpemupolo, popularly known as Tompolo, is the movement’s convener and grand patron. At the Ebonyi chapter’s inauguration on November 16, he was represented by Kestin Pondi, MD of Tantita Security Services. The vehicles carry public-address equipment and generators.

The scale is larger than the Ebonyi handover suggests.

The movement says it has distributed more than 500 vehicles and taken its activities to about 20 states. Its plan is to build coordinators from state level down to local government areas and wards, taking the President’s message to communities.

That structure gives Tompolo a role beyond endorsements. Campaign vehicles, local organisers, and communication equipment provide the means to sustain political activity between rallies. The movement says it is promoting Tinubu’s economic reforms, infrastructure projects, student loans, and local government autonomy.

Tompolo’s reach also has a commercial dimension. He chairs Tantita Security Services, which holds a federal contract for surveillance of oil pipelines in the Niger Delta. Supporters describe the campaign effort as a personal commitment to Tinubu’s second-term bid.

The overlap between a federal contractor and a campaign organiser will place questions of disclosure and political finance in public view.

The Electoral Act 2026 sets presidential campaign expenditure at N10 billion and limits donations to a candidate by an individual or entity to N500 million. The treatment of support-group spending depends on how donations, in-kind assistance and coordination with a candidate’s campaign are classified and reported.

The 25 vehicles in Ebonyi do not establish Tompolo’s total contribution, but they do show the movement’s effort to build a national ground operation beyond the Niger Delta. As the campaign develops, the network’s funding and reporting will attract attention alongside its political reach.

Babajimi Benson: A Representative Who Stays True to His Word

Babajimi Benson’s record in Ikorodu rests on a political claim: that representatives should remain answerable for campaign promises. The House of Representatives member chairs the Defence Committee. Since entering the National Assembly in 2015, he has pursued projects in roads, electricity, healthcare, education, and business support.

The most visible evidence is physical. Reports document more than 65 roads built or rehabilitated across the constituency. His Light Up Ikorodu programme has supplied transformers, solar streetlights and household solar systems. Health projects include an 80-bed Mother and Child Hospital in Imota and four primary healthcare centres.

Other facilities serve wider community needs. They include IKD 106.1 FM, a community radio station, and a town hall in Ibeshe. His office also lists classroom blocks and ICT centres. One six-classroom building at IsawoJunior High School was commissioned in April 2026.

Benson’s legislative work extends beyond Ikorodu. He sponsored constitutional amendments allowing states to generate, transmit, and distribute electricity, and participate in railway development. He backed a law requiring power generators to allocate five per cent of operating expenditure to host communities. Other laws cover defence industry and military research.

His October 2026 empowerment programme added a substantial economic component. Eight hundred entrepreneurs received N225 million in grants, in which 700 got N250,000 each, while 100 received N500,000. Vehicles, laptops, solar systems, and vocational equipment accompanied the cash support.

These figures show the reach of the programme, although distribution alone cannot establish lasting impact. A grant is celebrated when it helps a trader expand a business; the same is true for equipment when recipients can maintain and use it. That requires follow-up beyond the launch event.

Benson has announced further plans, including a bridge at Majidun-Ogolonto, completion of the Pacific-Igbe road, and equipment for hospital diagnostic and trauma centres. Those commitments remain outstanding. His claim to consistency will continue to be judged against what Ikorodu residents can see, use and sustain.

World.title: Bayo Ojulari’s Major Headache
World.content:
Follow THISDAYLIVE on Google Add us as a preferred source to see more of our stories in Google 

Bayo Ojulari has spent a year at NNPC trying to make the national oil company perform more like a commercial business. Project Delta now threatens to test how well that ambition survives the politics surrounding Nigeria’s strategic assets.

The sale of the oil blocks has returned to the agenda after repeated postponements. Africa Intelligence reported that Phase Two concluded on October 30, 2026, involving individuals linked to Ojulari and British financial institution Standard Chartered. The renewed activity gives NNPC another chance to advance the transaction, while placing its handling under scrutiny.

Oil blocks carry claims on future production and revenue. Their sale requires credible valuation, financing, due diligence and regulatory oversight. Investors need confidence in a clear process. Nigerians have an equally strong interest in whether the country receives fair value for strategic petroleum assets.

That burden falls on Ojulari, who became Group Chief Executive of NNPC Limited on April 2, 2025. His record gives him grounds to present the company as undergoing a commercial reset. National crude production reached a five-year high of 1.71 million barrels per day, while NNPC’s exploration and production subsidiary peaked at 365,000 barrels per day.

NNPC reported a 2025 profit after tax of N5.76 trillion and revenue of N19.04 trillion in the first half of 2026. Ojulari ended legacy crude-for-fuel swap agreements, introduced performance-based refinery maintenance partnerships and restored monthly financial disclosures. Project Delta sits awkwardly beside that reform agenda. Repeated delays can unsettle investors, particularly when interests around a transaction attract attention. The reported involvement of people linked to the NNPC chief makes transparency especially important. The account does not establish wrongdoing by him or the bank.

For Ojulari, completing the sale would count for little if the process damaged confidence in NNPC. The company must show how the blocks were valued, how bidders were treated, and what Nigeria stands to gain. Project Delta is a test of whether commercial reform can withstand public scrutiny.

World.title: Davido, Anu Dispute Takes a New Turn
World.content:
Follow THISDAYLIVE on Google Add us as a preferred source to see more of our stories in Google 

The dispute over whether Afrobeats star David Adeleke, known as Davido, is the father of 12-year-old Anu Adeleke has acquired a new complication: allegations that the girl’s mother and grandmother have been held by police in Ibadan since August.

Journalist Kemi Olunloyo made the claim on social media on November 18. She alleged that Ayo Labinjoh and her mother, Ropo, remained at the State Criminal Investigation Department in Iyaganku after Anu was released. Olunloyo also claimed the women had been charged with conspiracy, paternity fraud, cyberbullying, and cyberstalking.

Police and public court records have not confirmed the claims. A March 23 invitation letter asks the family to report to the SCID for an interview over allegations including conspiracy and cyberstalking. It does not establish that charges were filed or that anyone remains in custody.

The claims have reopened a dispute that returned to public attention in January, when Anu appealed to Davido for another DNA test. She said the unresolved question had exposed her to bullying.

Davido says five DNA tests returned negative results. His father, businessman Deji Adeleke, told a Lagos press conference on January 21 that tests, including analyses in South Africa, showed a zero per cent probability of paternity. He said he had supported Anu’s schooling and upkeep.

Labinjoh disputes that account. She says only one test was conducted in 2014 and alleges its procedure and result were compromised. She has called for a fresh, independent test. The Adeleke family maintains that the existing results settle the question.

The disagreement spans the child’s appeal, competing accounts of the DNA process and police allegations. Each raises a separate issue.

The latest allegations add a police dimension without resolving the central question. The Oyo police have yet to confirm the reported detention or court charges, while the two sides remain divided over whether another DNA test is necessary.

World.title: ‘The system wants the people to be beggars’: Pensioners’ anger runs deeper than grant reviews
World.content:
Frustration over SASSA’s grant reviews has opened up a wider conversation about how far the grant actually goes.

Petro Snyders shared her view on The South African’s Facebook page, in a thread about SASSA’s bank account checks.

‘While the can just take’

Snyders accused the system of keeping people dependent.



“The system want the people to be beggers while the can just take!!!” she wrote.

Linda Arran shared that suspicion: “They are using any excuse to cut your grant.”

Their comments reflect a feeling among many pensioners that the grant barely covers the basics, and that reviews now threaten even that.

A grant stretched thin

The Older Person’s Grant reaches most older South Africans. Nearly three in four older people in South Africa receive an old-age grant.

Researchers say it carries a heavy load. The grant has helped reduce poverty among older people, but rising living costs and growing care needs are stretching it to its limits. The grant has kept pace with inflation, but only just.

In many homes, the pension supports grandchildren and unemployed adult children as well as the grant holder, which leaves little room when food, electricity and transport prices rise.



Fewer recipients ahead

Government expects the number of grant recipients to shrink. Treasury expects tighter controls to result in fewer people receiving grants. It expects stronger verification measures to save R13.1 billion over three years.

Pensioners also face other pressures on their grants. GroundUp reported that pensioners complained to the minister about deductions from their grants.

For Snyders, Arran, and many others, the reviews feel like one more burden on a grant that already struggles to stretch to month-end. That explains why their anger runs deeper than any single bank account check.

World.title: Leon Schuster plays another epic prank [video]
World.content:
Leon Schuster has done it again with another one of his silly pranks, this time on his best friend, Alfred Ntombela.

The veteran comedian is known for his popular candid camera movies, like You Must Be Joking, Millennium Menace and Oh Schucks!

Earlier this month, Schuster pranked SABC media personality Leanne Manas during an interview. He also reflected on his scariest filming experience.



LEON SCHUSTER PRANKS PAL

In a video posted on Facebook, actor Alfred Ntombela revealed how Leon Schuster had pranked him yet again.
