World.title: At least four injured after rapper OsamaSon’s New York show
World.content:
At least four people were injured following rapper OsamaSon’s concert in New York City on Thursday evening, police said.

Just before 11:30 p.m., police responded to the Terminal 5 concert venue in the Hell’s Kitchen neighborhood and found a “disorderly crowd” exiting the space, the New York City police department said.

Four people had minor injuries, officials said.

Two were transported to local hospitals in stable condition and the other two refused medical attention at the scene.

Video circulating on social media shows the halls of the venue packed with people and a whistle blaring in the background.

No arrests have been made, police said.

The New York Fire Department said it received a call for a reported alarm activation due to overcrowding. Firefighters arrived to evacuate the venue.

Terminal 5 did not immediately respond to a request for comment Saturday.

OsamaSon is a 23-year-old American rapper whose real name is Amari Deshawn Adham Middleton. He rose to fame with the singles “Cts-V” and “Troops.”

World.title: Princeton neuroscientist detained by ICE at D.C. airport after leaving conference
World.content:
U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement arrested a Princeton University Ph.D. student at Ronald Reagan Washington National Airport on Thursday as she was preparing to fly back to New Jersey after presenting her research at a conference, her adviser said.

Eva Yi Xie, a third-year neuroscience student from China, has had an asylum application pending for 10 years after her family came to the U.S. when she was 14, according to her attorney, Kerry Doyle. The Department of Homeland Security said Xie was in the country illegally, which Doyle disputed, saying she had permission to live, work and study in the country while her case was pending.

“Her arrest and detention is without legal basis as ICE and DHS are fully aware,” Doyle told NBC News.

DHS said in a statement about her arrest that Xie was admitted to the United States temporarily in March 2016 and was required to leave by Sept. 15 of that year. The agency said she stayed past that date.

“Xie has NEVER held valid authorization to study in the United States,” the statement said. “To be clear, a pending application does not confer legal status in the United States.”

Xie, 24, was being held at the Caroline Detention Facility in Bowling Green, Virginia, according to a detainee search on ICE’s website.

Doyle filed a habeas corpus petition in federal court in Virginia challenging the legality of Xie’s arrest. She argued that ICE had no grounds to arrest Xie without a warrant because Xie was not a flight risk or a danger to the community.

Doyle said people with pending asylum cases “have permission to be here” while their cases are decided.

“It’s their over-the-top enforcement used as a way to scare people,” Doyle said. She called Xie’s arrest “an incredible waste of time and resources — to what end?”

Ronald Reagan Washington National Airport in Arlington, Va., on July 30. Kevin Carter / Getty Images file

The Trump administration has detained asylum-seekers and others with pending immigration applications as part of its broader immigration crackdown.

In its statement on Xie’s arrest, DHS repeated a warning it issued in recent press releases, saying it was working to prevent people it considered to be in the country illegally from flying domestically.

Xie’s adviser, Carlos Brody, described the research she presented at the conference in an emailed statement.

“There, Eva described her work discovering and researching an unexpected link between how brains make decisions and how they navigate through space,” Brody said.

Brody said Xie mentors undergraduates and sent messages to colleagues from the detention center “to make sure that her experiments could move forward and the grant applications she is part of could be submitted.”

“Eva is a gentle, kind, caring person who is contributing enormously to the United States,” Brody added. “She belongs back home in Princeton, doing the science that she loves, and helping our country excel and grow.”

Princeton’s graduate school dean, Rodney D. Priestley, said that Eva’s arrest “is distressing for me and many members of the Princeton University community.”

“The University has arranged for Eva to be represented by legal counsel, and we will remain in contact with her legal team, her family, and colleagues to provide support,” Priestley said in a statement. “We hope Eva will soon be able to resume her studies at Princeton.”

Xie’s attorney did not immediately respond to requests for comment on Saturday.

According to Xie’s professional biography page, she graduated from the Massachusetts Institute of Technology in 2024 with degrees in computer science and mathematics. She was helping to plan a cognitive computational neuroscience conference in the U.K. in 2027, according to the page.

World.title: Athlete swims Strait of Hormuz to highlight Iran war's wildlife toll
World.content:
British endurance swimmer Lewis Pugh has swum in the North Pole and Antarctica to draw attention to environmental causes. But battling freezing waters and extreme conditions hasn't prepared him for his latest challenge: swimming the Strait of Hormuz while tankers are attacked and blown up nearby.

Pugh, who is a United Nations Patron of the Oceans, spent three days this week swimming parts of the dangerous waterway to highlight how the war with Iran threatens the area's habitat and wildlife.

In this handout photo provided by the Lewis Pugh Foundation, British endurance swimmer and UNEP Patron of the Oceans Lewis Pugh dives into the Strait of Hormuz, off the Musandam Peninsula, Oman, on Wednesday, Nov. 18, 2026. Lewis Pugh Foundation via AP

Wearing only swimming trunks, goggles and a cap bearing the U.N. logo, the athlete started from the Musandam Peninsula, on the southern tip of the strait, and ended by rounding the Cape of Hormuz, completing about 9.3 miles in total. Pugh is believed to be the first person to undertake a long-distance swim there since the war started.

The swimmer said that minutes after he entered the water on Monday, he heard two loud explosions that rocked the sea.

"I looked up and I could see that an oil tanker about four kilometers away had been hit," he told The Associated Press after he returned to London. "The explosion was so loud, two booms, and then fighter jets coming in. And at that moment I realized we have to get out of here right now."

Pugh, 56, managed to finish his feat after more stops and starts, including passing another vessel that sent fireballs into the sky after it was attacked.

"Most people, when they think about the Strait of Hormuz, they think of a shipping lane," he said. "But it is also one of the most beautiful places I have ever been … it's one of the treasure troves of the natural world."

"With all these ships being sunk, this area is under severe threat," he added. "It's going to take years, decades for this area to recover."

In this handout photo provided by the Lewis Pugh Foundation, British endurance swimmer and UNEP Patron of the Oceans Lewis Pugh dives into the Strait of Hormuz, off the Musandam Peninsula, Oman, Wednesday, Nov. 18, 2026. Lewis Pugh Foundation via AP

Iran has in recent weeks increased attacks on vessels that it claimed traveled along unauthorized routes in the strait as it seeks to impose its control on the crucial waterway, where a fifth of all oil traded passed through before the U.S. and Israel launched the war on Feb. 28.

Several tankers have also struck sea mines laid by Tehran, in some cases exploding and bursting into flames, among them one that was carrying more than 2 million barrels of oil last month.

Pugh warned of how oil leaking from the dozens of tankers damaged since February could create lasting problems for the region's animals, as well as its coastlines, coral reefs and mangrove forests.

He described seeing large numbers of dolphins following his boat as he sailed in, as well as turtles and ospreys. He also marveled at the hundreds of turtles he saw during a swim along the Omani coast before the war.

"When oil gets in there, when chemical pollution gets in there, it becomes very, very difficult to clean up that type of mess," he said. "It lasts for generations."

Pugh has had plenty of experience facing extreme temperatures and predators, including great white sharks. But swimming in a conflict zone presented entirely new dangers.

Lewis Pugh gestures as he looks at a map of the Strait of Hormuz before he swims in Plymouth Sound, off the coast of Devon, England, Wednesday, Nov. 11, 2026. Alastair Grant/AP Photo

To stay safe, the challenge was done in sections over three days, with a total of about 6½ hours of swimming. The athlete recalled seeing a gas carrier being struck as he returned to the harbor on the second day.

"I'll never ever forget going past that gas carrier, the smell of the chemicals and then the flames, they were literally like fireballs going up into the sky. Around the ship, the water was on fire," Pugh said.

"And to think of the impact which a casualty like this has on nature — it was very, very acute."

Pugh has spent much of the past 40 years swimming in places from Antarctica to the Red Sea and the English Channel to urge more action to protect marine environments from climate change, pollution and loss of biodiversity.

He was the first athlete to swim across the North Pole and complete a long-distance swim in every one of the world's oceans. In 2023, he swam all 315 miles of the Hudson River to highlight the importance of clean rivers.

His foundation says the challenges have helped secure official agreements to protect more than 1.35 million square miles of vulnerable ocean.

Some have dubbed Pugh's blend of epic swimming and political outreach as "Speedo diplomacy."

"Sport opens doors, it creates dialogue, it enables people to start thinking about these important issues," Pugh said.

"My message is very simple," he added. "We've got to stop the war. We've got to open the strait, and we've got to clean up the pollution."

World.title: ICE officers arrest at least 1 passenger boarding flight in Seattle
World.content:
Masked immigration officers detained at least one person on a crowded airport jet bridge in Seattle as people were boarding Saturday, causing what Alaska Airlines called a "distressing" scene for passengers and employees and delaying the Los Angeles-bound flight.

Videos of the incident showed officers dragging away at least one person at Seattle-Tacoma International Airport as a woman screamed that her daughter is being taken and she has a work permit. It was not clear how many people were detained.

Online flight data showed that Alaska Airlines Flight 1306, which had been scheduled to depart at 8:10 a.m., was delayed.

Alaska Airlines said U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement officers gave no advance notice of the enforcement action, which occurred during a busy travel weekend ahead of the Thanksgiving holiday.

"We are concerned by this morning's law enforcement action during the boarding of Alaska Flight 1306," the airline said. "We recognize how distressing this incident has been for affected employees and guests."

It added that the airline is committed to "treating every guest with dignity and respect."

CBS News has reached out to the Department of Homeland Security, the parent agency of ICE, for comment.

Democratic Rep. Adam Smith of Washington said in a statement that "masked ICE agents detained at least one passenger waiting to board an Alaska Airlines flight at Sea-Tac Airport. The masked agents forcibly dragged the individual off the jet bridge, taking them into custody."

The arresting officers wore unmarked jackets and khaki pants. Videos showed them struggling with someone on the ground as passengers surrounded by rolling suitcases looked on.

ICE has stepped up arrests at airports since the summer, especially targeting people who overstayed visas in the past. ICE sources told CBS News in July that the uptick in arrests stems from increased collaboration between ICE and the Transportation Security Administration.

On Thursday, a Princeton University student and Chinese national was detained by ICE at Ronald Reagan National Airport in Washington, D.C., after attending a neuroscience conference, the school and her colleagues said.

Alaska Airlines said it was working with the Port of Seattle, which manages the airport, to see if protocols were followed, and also that it has raised concerns "directly with the appropriate authorities."

The Port of Seattle said in a statement that the arrest was distressing not only for the affected family but for other passengers, and that local authorities would "engage federal officials to understand more about what occurred."

Washington Gov. Bob Ferguson, a Democrat, called the incident "just the latest example of ICE's deeply un-American tactics."

"ICE is completely and totally out of control," Ferguson said in a statement. "Like many Americans, I'm outraged by masked agents, who do not identify themselves, dragging people off jetways as they board a flight, creating chaos in our communities."

Democratic Rep. Pramila Jayapal of Washington said in a social media post that she was "disturbed by the reports of this detention at Sea-Tac," adding that her office was "working to gather more information on the situation."

DHS numbers obtained by CBS News last week found that ICE arrested 491,000 people in fiscal year 2026, a record, including nearly 475,000 administrative arrests, also a record. Administrative arrests are those in which alleged undocumented immigrants are arrested for civil violations rather than criminal charges.

In a "60 Minutes" interview earlier this month following the heavy losses suffered by Republicans in the midterm elections, President Trump appeared to acknowledge that his administration's immigration crackdown may have contributed to his party's poor showing.

"For getting people out, I get very high marks for getting the bad ones out," Mr. Trump told "60 Minutes." "But I get hurt because we also took people that had good jobs, that created one violation, or breaking of the law, and that was that they came into the country illegally. Now, there is a large part of the country that think that they should be put out. And there's a large part of the country that think that they should be allowed to stay if they're good people working in a landscaping company, or working in a hotel, or doing something, right? And in some cases, paying taxes."

Of his deportation policies, the president said: "I think it was too tough. A lot of people would say that it's great, but a lot of people think it's too tough."

World.title: Princeton student detained by ICE at Reagan Airport after conference
World.content:
A Princeton University student was detained by U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement this week at Ronald Reagan National Airport in Washington, D.C., after attending a neuroscience conference, the school and her colleagues said.

Eva Yi Xie, a third-year Ph.D. student, was detained on Thursday night following a presentation she gave at the Society for Neuroscience, her colleague wrote on X.

"News of Eva's detention is distressing for me and many members of the Princeton University community," Rodney Priestley, the dean of the Princeton graduate school, said in a statement. "The University has arranged for Eva to be represented by legal counsel, and we will remain in contact with her legal team, her family, and colleagues to provide support. We hope Eva will soon be able to resume her studies at Princeton."

A Department of Homeland Security spokesperson said in a statement that Xie was taken into custody during a "targeted immigration enforcement operation" at Reagan Airport.

FILE -- Princeton University professor John Hopfield after receiving the Nobel Prize in physics in 2024. Graduate student Eva Xie asks Hopfield to sign a copy of one of his academic papers. Princeton University; Denise Applewhite

Xie was admitted to the United States on a temporary basis on March 16, 2016, according to DHS, which said she is a Chinese national. DHS said Xie had been required to depart the U.S. by Sept. 15, 2016.

"Xie will receive due process and remain in ICE custody pending her removal proceedings," DHS said in a statement. "Xie has NEVER held valid authorization to study in the United States. To be clear, a pending application does not confer legal status in the United States."

Carlos Brody, of the Princeton Neuroscience Institute, wrote on X that Xie sent her lab mates a Slack message for help before she was detained. She's being held in Chantilly, Virginia, according to Brody.

"Her lawyers are working on her release," Brody wrote. "She's a brilliant neuroscientist, mentor, and friend. She went to a conference to present her work, and now she's in a detention center. She should be home."

Xie's attorney, Kerry Doyle, said in a statement that her "arrest and detention is without legal basis."

"They cannot arrest people without a warrant if they are not a flight risk or danger to the community," Doyle said. "She is neither. She's a star rising scientist with permission to be in the US and they grabbed her because she is easy pickings at an airport where TSA and ICE are sharing information and targeting unsuspecting travelers with authorization to be in the US."

World.title: Violence breaks out in Mexico after capture of drug kingpin wanted by FBI
World.content:
Mexico's military announced Saturday that it had captured a drug kingpin on the Federal Bureau of Investigation's Top 10 Most Wanted List. Violence broke out in the state of Sinaloa afterwards, rattling civilians.

Fausto Isidro Meza-Flores, also known as "El Chapo Isidro," is allegedly the leader of the Meza-Flores Transnational Criminal Organization, which the FBI described as a "heavily armed, major drug-trafficking organization" based in Sinaloa.

The cartel is allegedly responsible for the possession, distribution and importation of heroin, methamphetamine, cocaine, fentanyl and marijuana into the U.S., according to the FBI, and has controlled drug production, transportation and distribution throughout Mexico.

Meza-Flores, his second-in-command "Germán" and cartel financial operator "José N" were all taken into custody during a raid in Sinaloa on Friday night, the Mexican National Defense Secretariat said on X.

Elite military agents were able to find the targets and then arrive surreptitiously in the area, the Mexican National Defense Secretariat said. The agents set perimeters around a residence to prevent Meza-Flores from escaping, while also defending the area from reinforcements who could have interrupted the operation.

The arresting agents were attacked with gunfire and explosives, the Mexican National Defense Secretariat said. Seven attackers were killed during the operation. The agents entered the house and captured Meza-Flores, his two lieutenants, and five other suspected criminals. They also recovered drugs, cash, 10 firearms, a grenade launcher and other ammunition and weapons.

Meza-Flores and his lieutenants were flown to Mexico City and placed in custody of the Specialized Prosecutor's Office for Organized Crime. The other five arrestees were taken into custody in Sinaloa, the Mexican National Defense Secretariat said. One of those arrested is a first cousin of Meza-Flores and a logistics operator for the cartel.

Video shared by authorities shows heavily armed men in camouflage marching a man who appeared to be Meza-Flores through a dimly lit house and putting him in the back of a truck.

Vehicles burn on a highway near Los Mochis, Sinaloa, Mexico, on Nov. 20, 2026, following an announcement by the interim government of the arrest of Beltrán-Leyva Cartel leader Fausto Isidro Meza Flores, known as "El Chapo Isidro." Yohari Leon via Facebook/via Reuters.

The Mexican government said in an early Saturday report that intelligence from the Trump administration helped authorities capture him, but provided few details about how the two countries coordinated. U.S. ambassador to Mexico Ronald Johnson said on X that "strategic intelligence sharing" between the U.S. and Mexico "helped make this operation possible."

In a social media post Saturday, U.S. Attorney General Todd Blanche said that Meza-Flores had ben captured "in an operation by the Mexican government supported by a coordinated interagency effort that included" the U.S. Homeland Security Task Force.

Videos and photos from the city of Guasave, Sinaloa, where Meza-Flores was captured, show screaming civilians fleeing gunfire at a baseball game, as well as burnt cars. The Mexican National Defense Secretariat said that four members of the Mexican Army's regular infantry forces "traveling to reinforce security" in the town have been killed.

Meza-Flores was indicted in 2012, then again in 2019. He faces multiple counts of drug-trafficking violations and the use and possession of a firearm. The FBI has described him as armed and dangerous. U.S. authorities had previously offered a reward of up to $5 million for information that led to Meza-Flores' arrest.

The high-profile capture comes as Mexican President Claudia Sheinbaum faces pressure from President Trump to crack down on cartels. Sheinbaum has gone after illegal groups more aggressively than her predecessors, and homicides have dipped significantly in her two years in office.

A member of the Mexican Army stands guard outside the Special Prosecutor's Office for Organized Crime (FEMDO) following the arrest and transfer of cartel leader Fausto Isidro Meza-Flores, 'El Chapo Isidro', in Mexico City, Mexico, on Nov. 21, 2026. Daniel Cardenas/Anadolu via Getty Images

The government has knocked out several cartel kingpins. Chief among them was Mexico's most powerful cartel leader, known as "El Mencho," who was killed in February. Similar to the capture of Meza Flores, the dramatic operation resulted in a burst of violence and burning cars.

Mexican Security Secretary Omar García Harfuch wrote in a post on X Saturday morning that armed forces would remain deployed in the state of Sinaloa to protect civilians.

"These detentions are an important step in pacifying Sinaloa," he said.

World.title: Lock of George Washington's hair sells at auction for $4,000
World.content:
A lock of hair from America's founding father, George Washington, was sold at auction Saturday for $4,000, according to the South Carolina-based auction house Richmond Auctions.

The auction house said the lock of hair was obtained by famed collector John K. Lattimer, a descendant of John Gadsby, who had hosted the first U.S. president's final two birthday celebrations at his City Hotel and Tavern in Alexandria, Virginia, in 1798 and 1799.

A testament — posted with the framed lock of hair — on the auction house's website said that Gadsby, a resident of Alexandria, Virginia, entertained Washington for dinner shortly before his death at Mount Vernon in 1799.

The White House Historical Association said Gadsby leased and operated the City Hotel and Tavern in Alexandria and the Indian Queen in Baltimore. He ended his career operating the Franklin House and the National Hotel in Washington, D.C.

A framed lock of George Washington's hair, obtained by famed collector John K. Lattimer, from a descendant of John Gadsby who had hosted George Washington's final two birthday celebrations at his City Hotel and Tavern in Alexandria, Virginia, in 1798 and 1799, according to Richmond Auctions. Richmond Auctions

Gadsby was believed to have bought and sold enslaved people to work in his hotels, the association said, although records from that time were tenuous.

The granddaughter of Gadsby, Julia Ten Eyck McBlair, said in a 1928 affidavit that he came into possession of Washington's lock of hair "in view of the friendship and association with his last days ..."

She added Gadsby had the lock of hair framed and it hung "under General Washingtons portrait in our home in Washington City, there I have seen it all my life."

The auction house said the hair is framed in a 9-inch-by-2 1/2-inch round gold-gilded wood frame with a glass window. Details on the buyer were not provided by the auction house.

CBS News reached out to Richmond Auctions for more information.

Various artifacts of Washington have sold at auction throughout the years. In July, a letter from Washington requesting to raise the new Continental Army was sold for more than $109,000.

A letter written by Washington, dated Jan. 5, 1780, sold in 2024 for thousands of dollars. Briggs Auction in Pennsylvania said Washington was writing to Col. Stephen Moylan in Connecticut, who headed up the Fourth Continental Light Dragoons.

They were discussing commissions for different officer positions in the regiment.

World.title: Princess Kate reflects on healing in new documentary: "Cancer does change you"
World.content:
Britain's Catherine, Princess of Wales, opens up about finding hope and joy amid uncertainty in a new documentary exploring life since her cancer diagnosis in 2024.

"Heal" follows 44-year-old Catherine as she attempts the Three Peaks Challenge, climbing the highest mountains in Scotland, England and Wales within 24 hours.

The Princess of Wales said at the time she undertook the challenge in support of the Royal Marsden Cancer Charity, an organization connected to the hospital where she received her treatment. She was greeted by her husband Prince William, who is heir to the throne, and their children Princes George and Louis and Princess Charlotte, as well as her parents and brother after completing the climb.

In a trailer released Saturday by Prince William and Catherine's Kensington Palace office, the princess reflects on her cancer journey and speaks to others about their experiences.

Catherine, Princess of Wales, meets a cancer patient during a visit to The Royal Marsden NHS Foundation Trust on Sept. 11, 2026, in London, England. Ian Vogler / WPA Pool / Getty Images

Catherine announced in March 2024 that she had cancer and was undergoing chemotherapy following major abdominal surgery. She did not reveal what type of cancer she was treated for.

Catherine disclosed in January 2025 that she was in remission about 10 months after announcing her diagnosis. At the time, she said in her post on Instagram that she remains focused on recovery: "As anyone who has experienced a cancer diagnosis will know, it takes time to adjust to a new normal."

She has gradually resumed her public duties, visiting India with William earlier this month.

In the trailer, Catherine says cancer changes people profoundly, and "healing is a journey. How to reconnect with the things you once knew, and how to find a sense of hope and joy alongside uncertainty."

She adds that "it's clear we're not meant to carry life's challenges alone" and "often, it is through pain that we realize there's a greater beauty that lies beyond that."

The film will premiere on the BBC in the United Kingdom on Nov. 29, before airing internationally on NBCUniversal in the United States on Nov. 30.

World.title: Trump signs executive order on federal workers' responses to Congress
World.content:
President Trump is directing federal contractors and subcontractors to consult with his administration about inquiries they receive from Congress and to withhold any communications that the White House considers privileged, according to a new executive order issued late Friday.

The companies must also coordinate with the White House and U.S. agencies on "appropriate responses" to any such requests, the order says. If they fail to comply, the White House warns their contracts could be terminated and their future work with the federal government suspended.

The order signed late Friday is the administration's latest effort to resist what are expected to be wide-ranging and aggressive oversight efforts from Democrats when they take over Congress in January. Democrats have made government contracts one of their top investigative targets, noting that federal money has been flowing to companies linked with Mr. Trump's family, particularly at the Pentagon.

It comes as White House officials have already begun taking steps to exert more control over how agencies and officials respond to congressional requests, anticipating there will be a flood of investigations once Democrats take power in January.

On Monday, White House Counsel Will Scharf told U.S. agencies that they must seek approval from his office and the White House's Office of Legislative Affairs before agreeing to appear before Congress. Scharf also suggested in a recent letter to Rep. Robert Garcia, the top Democrat on the House Oversight Committee, that some congressional investigations may amount to "blatant criminality."

Garcia earlier this week sent letters directing members of Mr. Trump's family and top administration officials to preserve documents. Scharf sought to dismiss the requests, noting in a letter to Democratic lawmakers that they are not yet in the majority and cannot compel compliance.

In a fact sheet, the White House framed the new requirements as "protecting executive privileges from congressional overreach," arguing that some congressional leaders have tried to intrude on executive branch privileges by "harassing private companies that contract with the federal government."

Presidents of both parties have long used executive privilege to resist congressional inquiries, but the claims can set up messy, protracted legal fights as parties dispute whether it applies. Executive privilege allows the president to keep information from the courts, Congress and the public to protect the confidentiality of White House deliberations, but the protection is far from absolute.

Friday's executive order applies to all contractors and subcontractors, a universe of tens of thousands of businesses.

World.title: Bayer reaches Roundup settlement that could cost the company billions
World.content:
Bayer reaches Roundup settlement that could cost the company billions

toggle caption i Justin Sullivan/Getty Images North America

The agrochemical and biotech giant Bayer has agreed to pay billions of dollars to people who sued the company alleging the weed-killer Roundup caused their cancer.

On Friday, a judge in Missouri gave final approval to the nationwide settlement that could cost the company up to $7.25 billion in the coming years.

The money will go to thousands of people who have been or will be diagnosed with non-Hodgkin lymphoma — a blood cancer that they claim is linked to glyphosate, which is the main ingredient in Roundup.

Under the settlement in circuit court, people affected could receive anywhere from $10,000 to $165,000 in compensation, depending on whether their work in agriculture or other occupations exposed them to higher levels of glyphosate, the age when they were diagnosed with non-Hodgkin lymphoma and other factors.

Sponsor Message

In a statement , the CEO of Bayer, Bill Anderson, called the settlement a "decisive milestone" that will "mitigate the risks" of pending and future litigation.

The presiding judge, Timothy Boyer, said it was "among the largest in the history of mass tort personal-injury class action settlements."

Earlier this year, the U.S. Supreme Court ruled in favor of Bayer, the German company that now owns Monsanto, finding that it could be shielded from lawsuits filed in state courts over claims that it failed to warn consumers about the cancer-causing effects of glyphosate.

Roundup is the most widely used weed-killer in the world.

The attorney representing the plaintiffs, Christopher Seeger, said in a statement that "Today's final approval order delivers guaranteed compensation to Roundup cancer victims who have waited more than a decade for justice."

The latest settlement comes in addition to a previous one in which Bayer agreed to pay between about $10 billion and $11 billion to settle more than 100,000 claims related to Roundup.

More than a decade ago, the World Health Organization's cancer agency concluded that glyphosate is probably carcinogenic to humans. Prominent scientists in the field of environmental health have echoed those concerns as recently as this year.

But Bayer has steadfastly denied that its product causes cancer.

The Environmental Protection Agency has also concluded it "did not identify risks of concern from glyphosate uses, including for cancer," though the agency is currently conducting a review of the evidence related to human health after facing intense pressure from advocates and some scientists.

Sponsor Message

Concerns about the safety of glyphosate has been an animating issue for supporters of Health Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr and his Make America Healthy Again agenda.

However, the Trump administration has taken steps to support the herbicide-maker, siding with Bayer in the Supreme Court case and issuing an executive order to promote domestic production of glyphosate.

Several years ago, the company removed glyphosate from its U.S. products used in residential settings, although it's still in use in the agricultural industry.

World.title: Storms expected on both coasts threatens Thanksgiving travel
World.content:
Storms expected on both coasts threatens Thanksgiving travel

toggle caption i Joe Raedle/Getty Images North America

Before worrying about the temperature of the turkey, travelers could face a different type of uncertainty next week. This time, it's the weather — and it's affecting both U.S. coasts.

"I know there's a lot of travel for many of you as you head into the Thanksgiving holiday, but I'm going to ask you all to consider not traveling unless it is absolutely essential," said San Francisco Mayor Daniel Lurie on X Friday. He said the city is preparing this weekend for extreme high tides and rain that could hit the area Monday afternoon through Wednesday.

Sponsor Message

Over the past week, cities in California saw mudslides, waterspouts and flooding while Florida also saw coastal flooding and inundated streets. A new set of storms are expected to hit both sides of the country early next week, just as travelers head into the holiday week.

It's already been a wet fall in large swaths of the country, thanks in part to a Super El Niño, a natural climate pattern that shifts weather around the world. Devastating flooding in the Southwest U.S. left multiple people dead and hundreds stranded, and California and the Pacific Northwest have seen high sea level and multiple strong atmospheric rivers.

Atmospheric rivers are here to stay

"Take this weekend: get yourself ready," Lurie, the San Francisco mayor, said after a call with the National Weather Service and the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration.

Rain and snow, in higher elevations, is possible over parts of the northwest and northern California on Saturday, according to the NWS.

The West Coast is forecasted to see an atmospheric river, a narrow band of water vapor pushed by the wind, on Monday. Another is expected for the Pacific Northwest later in the week, according to the Center for Western Weather and Water Extremes. Atmospheric rivers hang over an area and dump precipitation. They can cause months worth of rain in just a few days.

Sponsor Message

The center expects two to four inches of precipitation over northern California and southern Oregon through Wednesday.

Coastal flood advisories are also in effect through Monday morning in the Bay Area, the NWS said. This comes on top of historic high tides, known as King tides.

Travel troubles could persist after Thanksgiving

toggle caption i Joe Raedle/Getty Images North America

A storm that started in Florida Friday will move north to the Mid-Atlantic and into the Northeast by Sunday evening, according to the NWS.

Some of the heaviest rain could be seen on the coast of the Carolinas through Sunday morning. Then, heavy rain is expected to move up the coast, said Dan Hoffman, a meteorologist at the National Weather Service in Baltimore, Md.

Hoffman said during a busy travel week, even with the weather not expected to bring flooding or strong winds, it "doesn't usually take too much to cause things to start to have delays."

As for New England, Andrew Loconto, a meteorologist at the NWS in Norton, Mass., said the storm this weekend is not forecasted to be as big as another storm hitting the region after Thanksgiving. "That could be more impacts for people coming back home," Loconto said, pointing to another highly anticipated day across the U.S. — Black Friday.

World.title: Cartel leader captured in northern Mexico in a bloody firefight that left 11 dead
World.content:
Cartel leader captured in northern Mexico in a bloody firefight that left 11 dead

toggle caption i Claudia Rosel/AP

GUASAVE, Mexico (AP) — Heavy gunfire, helicopters and burning trucks marked Mexico's Sinaloa state Saturday after authorities captured cartel boss Fausto Isidro Meza Flores, known as "El Chapo Isidro," in an operation that left at least 11 people dead.

Meza Flores, one of the FBI's 10 most wanted fugitives, was captured and flown to Mexico City on Saturday after the firefight between Mexican forces and cartel gunmen overnight left residents of the city of Guasave terrorized.

toggle caption i U.S. Department of State via AP

Mexico's Defense Ministry on Saturday afternoon said that seven alleged cartel gunmen and four Mexican soldiers were killed.

The capo climbed the cartel ranks to lead the Beltrán Leyva cartel and later became the leader of his own group, the Meza-Flores Transnational Criminal Organization. The United States had a $5 million reward offer for information leading to his arrest, and he was wanted for trafficking drugs to the U.S. and illegally carrying firearms.

Sponsor Message

Mexico's government said in a report early Saturday that intelligence from the Trump administration helped authorities capture him, but provided few details about how authorities in Mexico and the United States coordinated to detain Meza Flores.

He was also a key ally to "Los Mayos," a faction of the Sinaloa Cartel, which was designated as a foreign terrorist organization by the Trump administration last year. His capture represents a blow to the cartel as it fights with another faction for control of the northern Mexican state.

Authorities in the United States and Mexico celebrated the arrest as a security win. U.S. President Donald Trump has pressured Mexico's government to go after criminal groups.

As a fierce firefight settled into a tense calm Saturday, experts warned that picking off capos could set off another wave of violence in a region already caught up in a power struggle between warring cartel factions.

Mexican forces' move against cartel fuels violenceThe capture of Meza Flores and his No. 2 in the city of Guasave, Sinaloa, set off a wave of violence when a firefight broke out around 7 p.m. on Friday, according to residents of the 290,000-person municipality. Soon, military helicopters and drones were flying overhead, and helicopters opened fire on key locations across the city.

Sponsor Message

Videos show screaming civilians fleeing gunfire at a baseball game, burning cars and businesses, and circling helicopters shooting at people below. Such shows of force by cartels are common following the capture or killing of leaders.

"The fighting was happening all over Guasave," said Alma Camacho, a Guasave resident and local journalist. "It spread throughout the city."

Mexican authorities said that they used "stealth and surprise" to arrest Meza Flores, establishing a security perimeter around the building where he was located. After coming under attack with guns and explosives from suspected cartel operatives, armed forces personnel entered a home and detained him.

Video shared by Mexico's Defense Ministry shows Meza Flores and two others being marched by heavily armed soldiers onto a military aircraft to appear before prosecutors in Mexico City. A total of eight people were detained, according to authorities.

Because of the violence, the Mexican army and National Guard special forces were unable to extract Meza Flores from Guasave until 4 a.m. on Saturday, said a federal official who spoke on condition of anonymity because he wasn't authorized to discuss the case.

"Getting him (Meza Flores) out was extraordinary," the official said, describing an intense response by members of the criminal group who maintained at least "10 roadblocks" with burning vehicles on Guasave's streets.

Terror in SinaloaGuasave resident and firefighter Paola Sánchez said that thousands of people were terrorized late Friday as they took shelter from intense gunfire in grocery stores and other locations.

"Last night, many businesses were burned ... along with cars and trucks," Sánchez told The Associated Press.

She said that the city's firefighters had to take shelter at their station and wait until Saturday morning for orders from their superiors to dispatch the first crews to check whether any businesses or vehicles were still burning.

Sponsor Message

An uneasy calm seemed to settle over the city Saturday. Mexican Security Secretary Omar García Harfuch wrote on X on Saturday morning that armed forces would remain deployed in Sinaloa state to protect civilians. He lamented the deaths of the four soldiers killed in the operation.

Burned-out trucks continued to line the freeway leading into the town, blocking roadways on Saturday.

"The aftermath of last night's war still lingers. Burned cars in the streets, several Oxxo stores completely burned down," Camacho said, referring to a chain of convenience stores in Mexico.

Guasave residents remained "very afraid" because security forces were absent from the streets, Camacho said.

Capture prompts celebration and warningsMeza Flores' detention marks another high-profile capture of a cartel leader as Mexican President Claudia Sheinbaum faces pressure from Trump to crack down on cartels. Sheinbaum has gone after illegal groups more aggressively than her predecessors, and homicides have dipped significantly in her two years in office.

The U.S. and Mexican governments celebrated the capture on Saturday, with the DEA commending Mexican authorities.

"Results like these don't happen overnight. They are built on sustained cooperation and trust. This is what partners can accomplish together," U.S. Ambassador Ronald Johnson said in an X post. "We will continue the hunt."

Mexican Security Secretary García Harfuch called the detention "an important step in pacifying Sinaloa."

Sheinbaum's government has targeted a number of cartel kingpins, including Jalisco New Generation Cartel leader Nemesio Oseguera Cervantes, known as " El Mencho," who was killed by the military in February.

Mexican security analyst David Saucedo said that the capture of Meza Flores marked another case of the governments of Mexico and the U.S. increasingly falling back on a longstanding security strategy that critics warn could fuel more violence in the long run.

The so-called kingpin strategy relies on zeroing in on capos like Meza Flores as a way to combat cartels. But experts say that it often triggers violent power disputes among groups, like the one underway in Sinaloa.

Sponsor Message

"What is evident is this is a product of pressure from the United States," Saucedo said. "What they do is capture high-profile kingpins — the leaders — but they don't dismantle the entire organization. They arrested the No. 1 and No. 2, but the entire network of hit men, street-level drug dealers, businesses and political and police connections remains intact."

World.title: Killer robots: U.N. talks fall short of hopes for legally binding rules
World.content:
Killer robots: U.N. talks fall short of hopes for legally binding rules

toggle caption i Efrem Lukatsky/AP

GENEVA — Diplomats meeting at the United Nations in Geneva have agreed to start discussing options to regulate lethal autonomous weapons, often called "killer robots."

After a week of negotiations that dragged on until the small hours of Saturday morning, a compromise emerged: countries would have two years to suggest regulations that could be legally binding, but could also be optional.

Bleary-eyed negotiators insisted the agreement was better than nothing and showed the U.N.'s disarmament process could still function. But for many humanitarian organizations and many countries, the deal falls far short of what they had hoped for.

Sponsor Message

Before the negotiations got underway, the International Committee of the Red Cross, the guardian of the Geneva Conventions, said it was urgent for legally binding rules to be drafted within a year. That call was backed by the U.N. secretary-general and by Pope Leo.

Their concerns stem from the kind of warfare we are now seeing. In Ukraine, Sudan and Gaza, civilians are being killed by semi-autonomous drones. This year in Sudan, 80% of civilian deaths were caused by drones according to the U.N.

Humans remain, albeit very remotely, in control for now, but humanitarian organizations fear we are on the verge of seeing artificial intelligence-assisted weapons make the decision to kill entirely on their own.

Algorithms making life-and-death decisions

"There is a fundamental ethical concern with having what are essentially these life-and-death decisions determined by programming, determined by an algorithm," said ICRC legal adviser Georgia Hinds. "That's not something that you can fix with better technology. That is a moral red line that we cannot cross."

No one went into the negotiations thinking they would be easy; some of the world's most powerful countries, among them the U.S., Russia and Israel, had already indicated their reluctance to agree to binding regulations.

Sponsor Message

On day one, Russia delayed proceedings by objecting to the meeting's agenda. Then the United States proposed a five-year window to discuss nonbinding, optional guidelines for autonomous weapons.

"They're just kicking the can down the road," said one frustrated delegate. As the clock ticked on and the weekend approached, diplomats scrambled to get some kind of result from negotiations that had been billed as a last chance to regulate weapons whose technology and decision-making capabilities we may not even fully understand.

Finally, at 4:30 a.m. on Saturday morning, they emerged from the negotiating room to announce their compromise: no to a deal within a year, maybe to legally binding rules, or maybe not.

A "nothing burger"

The ICRC immediately said it regretted the move and renewed its appeal for a binding treaty. Other campaigners were less polite, calling the deal "a real disappointment" and a "nothing burger." "I am concerned people will die because of this," added another.

A key worry is that, with two years to talk about possible rules that might only be optional, the technology will race ahead, uncontrolled.

"We're likely to see the systems proliferate," said Anna Hehir, an expert in military AI governance at the Future of Life Institute. "They're not like nuclear weapons in that they're inaccessible. There are autonomous weapons that are easy to purchase or even to create for all kinds of actors: individuals, nonstate actors, criminal groups."

There are also big questions about how our existing rules of war – the Geneva Conventions – can be upheld if those doing the killing are not humans, but machines.

"These rules are the bare minimum that militaries and states have developed and agreed to adhere to," said the ICRC's Hinds. "The commander remains responsible for making sure that the use of force is lawful. The commander remains accountable. You cannot hold a machine accountable for a violation of the law."

Sponsor Message

But in the race to develop new weapons, no country wants to come second. Although most U.N. member states do agree there should be some controls over autonomous weapons, the compromise in Geneva means that, for the next two years at least, weapons that can use artificial intelligence to make life-and-death decisions will remain unregulated.

Meanwhile, weapons technology is developing at pace, while diplomacy is struggling to keep up.

World.title: Federal jury convicts man of starting the deadly 2025 Palisades Fire in Los Angeles
World.content:
Federal jury convicts man of starting the deadly 2025 Palisades Fire in Los Angeles

toggle caption i Etienne Laurent/AP

LOS ANGELES — The man accused of sparking last year's deadly Palisades Fire was found guilty of arson charges Friday after his first federal case earlier this year ended in a mistrial.

Jurors convicted Jonathan Rinderknecht, 30, of lighting a fire on Jan. 1, 2025, that burned undetected deep in root systems before flaring back up Jan. 7, becoming one of the most destructive wildfires in California history. The Palisades Fire killed 12 people as it incinerated entire neighborhoods in Los Angeles and Malibu.

Rinderknecht pleaded not guilty to federal charges of destruction of property by means of fire and arson. The scope of the first charge was narrowed to only include the Jan. 1 blaze, known as the Lachman Fire, and the second addresses the Palisades Fire. He was convicted on both charges.

Sponsor Message

With little apparent reaction, Rinderknecht gave his attorneys hugs before leaving the courtroom. The verdict was delivered on the third day of deliberation.

Bill Essayli, the top federal prosecutor in LA, said the verdict was a "testament of the hard work" his team put into the case. He said he was "intimately familiar" with the strength of the evidence and was happy with the jury that convicted Rinderknecht.

Rinderknecht's attorney Steve Haney said in a statement they were disappointed in the verdict but respected the jury process.

"After a lengthy deliberation, they clearly gave this case a great deal of consideration," Haney said. Regarding an appeal, he said they would review all the options at the right time.

Rinderknecht is set to be sentenced March 17, 2027. Each count carries a mandatory minimum of five years and a maximum of 20 years in federal prison.

Prosecutors continued to pursue the case after Rinderknecht's first jury deadlocked 10 to 2 in favor of acquittal after a two-week trial in June. They dropped a third charge of timber set afire when they filed a new indictment for the retrial. Essayli said he believed the first jury acted improperly and appeared to consider things in their decision that weren't presented as evidence during the trial.

Sponsor Message

Juror says Rinderknecht's own testimony pointed to a guilty verdict

toggle caption i U.S. Attorney's Office/AP

Juror No. 3, who only wanted to be identified by his first name Cameron, said he was the only person who felt Rinderknecht was not guilty at the start of deliberations. Another person was undecided, and the rest of the 10 jurors believed Rinderknecht was guilty.

"It took a lot for me to be convinced otherwise," he said. "After listening to every single point, I do now agree that he's guilty."

Cameron said he initially had concerns about a technical review conducted by a defense expert witness, who argued the government had gotten the origin area of the fire wrong. He said there was a "lack of information" presented to the jury about the technical review.

In the end, it was Rinderknecht's own testimony that was the strongest piece of evidence pointing to a guilty verdict, he said.

"Stating that he was up on the hill, didn't smell a fire, didn't see fireworks … no one else was on the hill that night," Cameron said.

Prosecutors say Rinderknecht had been 'mad at everything'

During the second trial, prosecutors presented a more tightly organized case that presented digital forensic data, expert testimony and Rinderknecht's state of mind in the hours leading up to the fire. They did not focus as much on his resentment toward the rich and powerful to present the crime as arson motivated by "societal revenge" like they previously did.

Prosecutors zeroed in on evidence placing him at the fire's origin area, such as photographs that showed his car parked at the base of a trail leading up to where the fire started and cellphone tower data pointing to his movement on the hill. Fire detection camera images showed the time window the blaze ignited, and experts eliminated any other source of ignition that night, including fireworks.

Sponsor Message

They established that Rinderknecht was acting erratic and angry in the hours leading up to the fire through the testimony of Uber passengers and texts sent to his girlfriend at the time.

"He was mad at everything, and frustrated," said Assistant U.S. Attorney Mark Williams.

After the fire began, Rinderknecht called 911 more than a dozen times as he walked down the hill. Prosecutors presented the video he screen-recorded on his phone while calling. As he was calling, he asked ChatGPT: "Are you at fault if a fire is lit because of your cigarettes?"

These were part of an alibi Rinderknecht was trying to create for himself, prosecutors said.

They also presented extensive testimony on how fire investigators determined the Palisades Fire was a holdover fire from the initial blaze Rinderknecht sparked.

Defense argues fire's origin is unproven

Haney cast doubt on the government's case, saying the fire scene could have been compromised because the area was publicly accessible until the Palisades Fire started Jan. 7.

The defense called their own expert witnesses, including a retired fire investigator for the U.S. Forest Service who argued the fire origin area was different from what the government concluded.

Prosecutors attacked the fire investigator during cross examination and at one point accused him of perjury, alleging he did not disclose all records related to the case. The judge ultimately rejected prosecutors' request to strike his testimony.

Haney argued the government could not conclusively say there was no one else by the fire ignition point that night because of missing cell data records, and pointed to a neighbor's testimony that he saw a group of teenagers running away from the direction of the trailhead.

He told jurors to disregard any evidence related to Rinderknecht's character, such as his angry text messages, because they were "evidence of the man, not evidence of the act."

Sponsor Message

Finally, Haney presented an alternate explanation for what ignited the fire — fireworks. Multiple witnesses, including two neighbors and a local firefighter, all said they heard a loud bang or explosion from the direction of the hill the fire purportedly started on.

In the thousands of images of the evening collected from cameras in the area, none showed fireworks in the sky above the hill where the fire started, prosecutors said.

World.title: Hegseth reportedly moves to restrict defence ties with Canada, but Ottawa sees no change
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

U.S. Secretary of War Pete Hegseth has reportedly issued a classified directive restricting military co-operation between the United States and Canada — something that Canadian government and military officials were not aware of and have seen no evidence it has been put into practice.

The Washington Post reported late Friday that the directive was circulated last week in a secret memorandum. The report cited U.S. officials familiar with the decision.

Three Canadian defence officials speaking on background on Saturday said they were aware of the reports and were looking to substantiate them, as well as seeking clarification because there's been no change at the military operational level between the two countries.

A Republican senator attending the Halifax International Security Forum confirmed the existence of the memo and the restrictions but downplayed their impact, saying they have no effect on operations between the two countries.

"It does limit general flag officer meetings to those that advance [U.S. Department of War] objectives," said Sen. Mike Rounds, who sits on the armed services committee.

U.S. defence officials — uniform and civilian — must seek permission before attending social events or think-tank conferences.

The measures were drafted months ago but only signed recently, Rounds said, adding that it's unfortunate they were leaked.

The intent, however, was to put pressure on Canada.

U.S. Sen. Mike Rounds speaks to reporters in the U.S. Capitol Building on Monday in Washington, D.C. Rounds on Saturday confirmed the existence of Hegseth's memo and the restrictions, but downplayed their impact. (Finn Gomez/Getty Images)

"Look, we really want you to bring up your defence spending," Rounds said, before quickly adding the U.S. delegation at the conference had a chance to be briefed on the latest measures.

"We just had a chance to talk with our Canadian friends, and they indicated and laid out the roadmap that they're using to significantly increase their defence spending."

Democratic Sen. Chris Coons of Delaware says he was irritated by Hegseth's directive and its impact on relations with Canada.

"This is a completely unnecessary insertion of a negative tone," said Coons, who is also in Halifax and sits on the Senate foreign relations committee.

"I'm relieved this has no significant operational impact, but at the end of the day, as we've got our adversaries globally pulling together and working more closely — Iran, North Korea, China, Russia — the United States should be doing nothing to further aggravate some of the distance and division between the United States and Canada."

Defence Minister David McGuinty, who is also at the security forum, said the two countries continue to work "hand-in-glove" on various missions such as stopping the flow of illegal drugs in the Caribbean and on new policy initiatives such as integrated air and missile defence.

"It's the first time we heard of this — just yesterday," McGuinty said, referring to the directive. "It's clear there's some sort of document we haven't seen. I'm not aware of the contents of it."

Minister of National Defence David McGuinty rises during question period in the House of Commons on Parliament Hill in Ottawa on Nov. 3. McGuinty says Canada and the U.S. continue to work 'hand-in-glove' on various military missions and new policy initiatives. (Justin Tang/The Canadian Press)

There was no mention of the directive from the Americans at the security forum dinner Friday night, according to two of the confidential defence sources, one of whom wondered if the congressmen and senators were even aware of it.

CBC News is not identifying the sources because they were not authorized to speak publicly.

In an interview with CBC's Adrienne Arsenault, McGuinty said he has not yet contacted Hegseth over the issue. He said Canadian officials are reaching out to U.S. counterparts on a host of security-related issues.

Asked if he thinks there were certain issues in Canada-U.S. relations that may have precipitated the memo, McGuinty declined to speculate, noting Ottawa has learned to take the often unexpected decisions of the Trump administration in stride.

WATCH | 'Business as usual' between Canada and U.S., McGuinty says: 'Business as usual' between Canada and U.S., McGuinty says following Pentagon restrictions report | Duration closed caption 2:02 In an interview with CBC News chief correspondent Adrienne Arsenault, Defence Minister David McGuinty responded to a Washington Post report that U.S. Secretary of War Pete Hegseth has issued a classified directive restricting military co-operation between the U.S. and Canada. McGuinty declined to speculate on what may have precipitated the memo and said it was 'business as usual' between the two countries.

"There have been curveballs of this kind," McGuinty said of the sudden nature of the directive.

"We've learned to move forward."

The existence of such a directive would only add to mounting tensions between the long-standing allies over trade and defence spending.

Canada, U.S. working on trade deal

The move comes as the Trump administration and the government of Prime Minister Mark Carney inch toward a trade deal that could see some relief in key sectors such as automotive and steel and aluminum.

The military and defence ties between Canada and the U.S. are deep, long-standing and would be difficult to restrict at an operational level without harming the security of the U.S. itself in one fashion or another, said one of the sources.

Cross Country Checkup is asking: Is it OK to start travelling to the United States again? Leave your comment here and we may read it or call you back for this Sunday's show

The two countries co-operate in the defence of North America through NORAD. In Europe, they are founding partners of NATO and work side by side with the other 30 members of the Western alliance. They also work together in the Indo-Pacific in joint military exercises.

A third source said it would also be difficult and counter-productive for Washington to, for example, restrict access to U.S.-made weapons systems and equipment, which Washington has been eager to sell and pressuring Canada to buy.

WATCH | Carney says he's examined risk of U.S. military action in Canada: Carney says he examined 'extreme tail risk' of U.S. military action in Canada | Duration closed caption 8:20 Prime Minister Mark Carney said in an interview with the New York Times that he's studied the risk of a U.S. military attack on Canada. Matina Stevis-Gridneff, the newspaper's Canada bureau chief, said Carney took several seconds — 'a pregnant pause' — before responding as to whether such a scenario had crossed his mind.

Officially, the scope of Hegseth's restrictions is unclear, according to the Washington Post report. Since the memo is classified, the Department of War has not identified which military programs or activities might be affected.

In a statement to CBC News prior to Rounds's comments, the Pentagon's chief spokesperson, Sean Parnell, ruled out restrictions on operational level matters, but was vague on what precise impact the memo would have.

"The Department of War is taking steps to ensure its engagements with Canada advance tangible U.S. defence objectives and ultimately support a reinvigorated defence relationship," Parnell said in a written response.

"DoW is prioritizing opportunities for bilateral cooperation that strengthens the defence of our Homelands and shared hemisphere, while supporting Canada's ability to meet NATO obligations. This guidance does not impact defence intelligence co-operation, our binational NORAD command or our co-operation through NATO."

The response left open questions about bilateral military exercises, training exchanges, defence planning and other forms of co-operation.

But even on that level, Canadian officials say they've seen no evidence thus far of any restrictions and point to the notion that the memo has been in circulation for a week.

WATCH | Pentagon withdraws from Canada-U.S. defence board: Pentagon withdraws from Canada-U.S. defence board | Duration closed caption 2:33 The Pentagon has announced it has paused its participation in a joint Canada-U.S. defence board that's been around since the 1940s, accusing Canada of not making enough progress on its commitments. Canada says it's always ready for constructive discussion on how to strengthen mutual security.

Last spring, the Trump administration paused U.S. participation in the Permanent Joint Board on Defence (PJBD) with Canada.

Halting the activity of the decades-old board, a bilateral advisory group that co-ordinates continental security and recommends defence policy to both governments, was considered largely symbolic because it met infrequently.

Canada has been routinely criticized in Washington over its lacklustre defence spending.

There has been change under Carney, and Canada has now hit the NATO target of spending two per cent of GDP.

Carney, however, has publicly stated he wants to diversify both the country's trading relationship and where it sources its military equipment. He has said it's not good for more than 70 cents of defence equipment dollars to be going to one market — the United States.

World.title: Montreal police arrest 2 ex-officers for alleged assault, criminal harassment, breach of trust
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

The Service de police de la Ville de Montréal (SPVM) announced Saturday in a news release that it arrested two of its own officers in connection with allegations of discriminatory and racist acts by police officers at Station 39.

According to the arrest warrant issued by the Directeur des poursuites criminelles et pénales (DPCP) — which was reviewed by CBC News — the former police officers in question are Vincent Routhier, 24, and Zachary Belzil, 25.

Both face charges of assault and breach of trust. Zachary Belzil also faces one count of criminal harassment.

The arrested officers were released under the promise to appear in court, according to the SPVM.

The two officers had previously been placed on administrative leave, and were among seven who were fired on Nov. 2. Two were dismissed from Station 21 and five from Station 39, according to Montreal police Chief Fady Dagher.

WATCH | Two former Station 39 officers arrested after dismissal : Two former Montreal police officers arrested on assault, harassment and breach of trust charges | Duration closed caption 1:41 Nearly three weeks after their dismissal by the Service de police de la Ville de Montréal (SPVM), the charges laid against two former police officers include: assault, criminal harassment and breach of trust. Both officers were assigned to Station 39 in Montréal-Nord, which has been at the centre of allegations of racist and discriminatory conduct.

The firings were the result of an internal disciplinary investigation that was carried out at the administrative level of the SPVM.

Other related criminal investigations are still being handled by the SPVM's Division des normes professionnelles.

Montreal groups praise arrests

In an email to CBC News, Montreal Mayor Soraya Martinez Ferrada thanked the police officers who "had the courage to defy the code of silence."

"The trust that Montrealers have in their police force is paramount," she said. "The work continues, and justice must take its course."

For Fo Niemi, executive director of the Center for Research-Action on Race Relations in Montreal, the arrests are reassuring.

"It validates everything we had hoped would take place," he said. "The whole country is watching this."

Niemi says the arrests are a step in the right direction towards protecting the public and rebuilding its trust in police.

"If you want to uphold police values and standards you must report the misconduct of others," said Niemi, speaking to police officers. "You must denounce injustice inside, committed by your colleagues."

He says the charges could also help set a precedent for how police officers are held to account going forward.

Alain Babineau, director of racial profiling at the Red Coalition, a Montreal group that works to dismantle systemic racism, said that it's very rare that charges against police officers are brought forward.

He agrees that the arrests are positive, but said that "it's only a beginning."

Babineau says that the practice of street checks facilitates racist and discriminatory behaviour by police. The Red Coalition is calling on the SPVM to end the practice.

"That kind of power has to be put in abeyance," he said.

A spokesperson for the union that represents Montreal police officers, the Fraternité des policiers et policières de Montréal, said only that the organization had taken note of the communications issued by the DPCP.

World.title: Capture of cartel leader in northern Mexico sets off gunfight that leaves 11 dead
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

A burst of violence in Mexico's Sinaloa state after authorities captured cartel boss Fausto Isidro Meza Flores, known as El Chapo Isidro, left at least 11 people dead, authorities said Saturday.

Meza Flores, one of the FBI's 10 most wanted fugitives, was captured and flown to Mexico City on Saturday after a heavy firefight between Mexican forces and cartel gunmen overnight left residents of the city of Guasave terrorized and trucks and businesses burning.

Mexico's defence cabinet on Saturday afternoon said that seven alleged cartel gunmen and four Mexican soldiers were killed.

Meza Flores climbed the cartel ranks to lead the Beltrán Leyva cartel and later became the leader of his own group, the Meza-Flores Transnational Criminal Organization. The United States had a $5 million US reward offer for information leading to his arrest, and he was wanted for trafficking drugs to the U.S. and illegally carrying firearms.

Mexico's government said in a report early Saturday that intelligence from the U.S. helped with the capture of Meza Flores, but provided few details about how authorities in Mexico and the U.S. co-ordinated to detain him.

Meza Flores was also a key ally to Los Mayos, a faction of the Sinaloa Cartel, which was designated as a foreign terrorist organization by the administration of U.S. President Donald Trump last year. His capture represents a blow to the cartel as it fights with another faction for control of the northern Mexican state.

The Trump administration and Mexican authorities both celebrated the arrest as a security win, but experts warn it could set off another wave of violence in a region already ravaged by cartels.

Night of terror after forces moved against cartel

The capture of Meza Flores and his No. 2 in the city of Guasave set off a wave of violence overnight, terrorizing civilians. Calm appeared to set in Saturday morning.

Videos show screaming civilians fleeing gunfire at a baseball game, burning cars and businesses, and circling helicopters shooting at homes below. Such shows of force by cartels are common following the capture or killing of leaders.

Vehicles on fire on a highway near Los Mochis, Sinaloa, on Friday following the announcement of El Chapo Isidro's arrest. (Yohari Leon/Facebook/Reuters)

Guasave resident and firefighter Paola Sánchez said thousands of people were terrorized late Friday night as they took shelter from intense gunfire in grocery stores and other locations.

"Last night, many businesses were burned, including Oxxo [convenience] stores, kiosks and pharmacies, along with cars and trucks," Sánchez told The Associated Press.

The city's firefighters had to take shelter at their station and wait until Saturday morning for orders from their superiors to dispatch the first crews to check whether any businesses or vehicles were still burning, she added.

"Everything looks calm today," she said.

Mexican Security Secretary Omar García Harfuch wrote on X Saturday morning that armed forces would remain deployed in Sinaloa state to protect civilians.

This undated image released by the U.S. Department of State shows Fausto Isidro Meza Flores. (U.S. Department of State/The Associated Press)

U.S. pressure on Mexico to crack down on cartels

Meza Flores's detention marks another high-profile capture of a cartel leader as Mexican President Claudia Sheinbaum faces pressure from U.S. President Donald Trump to crack down on cartels.

Sheinbaum has gone after illegal groups more aggressively than her predecessors, and homicides have dipped significantly in her two years in office.

WATCH | El Mencho's killing briefly caused mayhem in Mexico: Thousands stuck in Mexico as cartel chaos calms | Duration closed caption 7:01 Calm has started to return to Mexico following the killing of the powerful cartel leader known as El Mencho, but travel advisories remain and Canadians are waiting for flights to resume. Meanwhile, Mexico's president said authorities tracked a romantic partner of the drug kingpin to start the operation that left about 30 cartel members and 25 troops dead.

Both the U.S. and Mexican governments celebrated the capture on Saturday, with the U.S. Drug Enforcement Administration (DEA) commending Mexican authorities.

"The capture of El Chapo Isidro delivers a significant blow to a ruthless criminal organization that has used extreme violence to traffic deadly drugs, including fentanyl, a designated weapon of mass destruction, into American communities," the DEA said in a statement.

"This operation underscores the critical importance of intelligence sharing in targeting dangerous cartel leaders."

García Harfuch called the detention "an important step in pacifying Sinaloa."

Firefighters hose down a burning cargo truck on a highway between Guamuchil and Guasave in Mexico's Sinaloa state on Saturday, following overnight violence after Mexican authorities captured Meza Flores in Guasave. (Martin Urista/The Associated Press)

Mexican authorities said they used "stealth and surprise" to capture Meza Flores, establishing a security perimeter around the building where he was located. After coming under attack with guns and explosives from suspected cartel operatives, armed forces personnel entered a home and detained him, they said.

Video shared by authorities shows heavily armed men in camouflage escorting a man who appears to be Meza Flores through a dimly lit house and putting him in the back of a truck.

'Kingpin strategy' causes more violence, experts say

Sheinbaum's government has immobilized a number of cartel kingpins. Chief among them was Nemesio Oseguera Cervantes, known as El Mencho, who was killed in Guadalajara state in February. Similar to the aftermath of the capture of Meza Flores, that dramatic operation resulted in a burst of violence and burning cars.

Members of the Mexican army stand guard outside the Specialized Prosecutor's Office for Organized Crime in Mexico City on Saturday. (Paola Garcia/Reuters)

Mexican security analyst David Saucedo said the capture of Meza Flores marked another instance of the governments of Mexico and the U.S. increasingly falling back on a longstanding security strategy, which critics warn could fuel more violence in the long run.

The so-called "kingpin strategy" relies on taking out top capos as a way to combat cartels. But experts say it often triggers violent power disputes among groups, like the one underway in Sinaloa.

"What is evident is this is a product of pressure from the United States," Saucedo said. "What they do is capture high-profile kingpins — the leaders — but they don't dismantle the entire organization.

"They arrested the No. 1 and No. 2, but the entire network of hit men, street-level drug dealers, businesses and political and police connections remains intact."

World.title: Sunrise on the Reaping may be a prequel, but it's the worst way to start The Hunger Games
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

There is perhaps no worse instalment of The Hunger Games franchise to get started with than the new prequel, Sunrise on the Reaping.

That should be a silly statement on face value. With five movies in the young-adult, Battle Royale-esque series already out — four of them following "girl on fire" Katniss Everdeen's quest to stop the dictatorial Capitol government from pitting randomly selected kids against one another in modern gladiator matches — you'd think the audience is coming in fairly well versed.

So with Sunrise on the Reaping simply moving back and telling the story of how one grizzled character once competed in a blood-soaked tournament of his own, why does The Hunger Games need to hold your hand?

Well, because its creator said that was the goal. According to director Francis Lawrence , making Reaping function as a genuine entry point into the series works for both new and old audiences, independent of their experience with other films — a claim to craft a functional and entertaining midbrow action movie with new faces, but also to make it stand entirely on its own merits.

It's a lofty pair of goals — the first of which Reaping actually more or less meets as a relatively strong entry in the overcrowded, clichéd YA post-apocalyptic canon.

But in confronting the second goal, it ends up either failing outright; or barely passes by crafting one of the more bizarrely morose entries in the "chosen one" narrative field of all time.

WATCH | The Hunger Games: Sunrise on the Reaping trailer:

Instead of introducing the undauntable, constantly thwarted heroine Katniss, we follow the battle-scarred side character of Haymitch Abernathy — whose function has long been to be unhappy — and are told what made him so titillatingly broken when fans first met him.

That might be interesting for those who have followed along from the beginning and are just hungry for more.

But to those without any insight into who eventually triumphs over whom decades after all this unrewarding, unrelenting, unromantic failure, Reaping is something else. Its framing as a painful, almost universally nihilistic and unrelentingly dour backstory for a single character makes it a deeply strange movie when viewed as a standalone feature.

Played in the original Hunger Games by Woody Harrelson as a grizzled, traumatized veteran of the games, Haymitch is here taken on by Joseph Zada. It's 24 years ahead of the events of the first movie, on the eve of something called the Second Quarter Quell.

It is a requisitely arcane term for a pivotal Hunger Games competition, one that those following along know ended in even more bloodshed and tears than is normal — and somehow left an older, meaner Haymitch looking on in fiery-eyed fury when the corrupt, manipulative government presented him with doctored, propagandistic footage of it in the first movie.

For those out of the know, though, this movie could still end in either heroic victory or heroic martyrization.

Those expectations seem even more likely as we go through the typical setup: music video shots of Haymitch telling his girl Lenore (Whitney Peak) in a slightly southern accent that he'll never let her go; Haymitch saving her from his fate by selflessly setting himself up "tribute" for his district — the saddest, rinky-dinkiest, underdoggiest district in the whole state of Panem; and his ironic slow-clapping at the impassive President Snow (Ralph Fiennes) looking down at the moaning and dying young combatants in the arena below.

Ralph Fiennes as President Snow in a still from The Hunger Games: Sunrise on the Reaping. (Lionsgate)

These are all expected and solidly executed moral and narrative markers for the tragic or triumphant formula to work off. They get more narrative juice once the real plot starts, as the mysterious Beetee Latier (Kelvin Harrison Jr.) sneaks out from the arena compound's shadows to present Haymitch with a plan to take the Capitol down from the inside, forgo trying to win the competition, and try to stop the ruling class from exploiting them.
