World.title: Love at first bite: The Paltok bakery that sells out early
World.content:
PALTOK STAPLE. Residents of Barangay Paltok, Quezon City, often flock to Bong & Dynah Bakeshop for their morning pastries.

Residents of Paltok, Quezon City, flock to a yellow-walled corner bakery every day before its freshly baked bread sells out

Carmen Mariano, 65, used to wonder why so little bread remained whenever she passed by the small bakery in her neighborhood in Barangay Paltok, Quezon City.

It’s called Bong & Dynah Bakeshop, but residents have taken to calling it Matias Bakery, a nod to the street where it’s located. The small shop opens at 5 am to serve classic baked goods to early risers, and for the longest time, Carmen thought the bakery simply offered an oddly tiny selection of bread.

“Anong klaseng bakery ba ‘to? (What kind of bakery is this?)” Carmen would often say to herself whenever she laid her eyes on the big glass case situated in front of the store.

It turned out, however, that by the time she would arrive at the bakeshop, most of them had just already been bought by other customers who happened to get there before she did.

Carmen is now a regular at the bakeshop — making the trip for buns, banana cake, and egg pie. Her son also buys pandesal in the morning.

Carmen Mariano on one of her regular visits to Bong & Dynah Bakeshop. All photos by Jade Tan/Rappler

A familiar corner

When Bong & Dynah Bakeshop opens its doors at the crack of dawn, its staff only has a window of one to two hours to enjoy the lull before the morning rush starts. Hordes of customers start pouring in by 6 or 7 am, and by 8 or 9 am, its pandesal is completely sold out.

Spanish bread and pan de coco are among the bakery’s bestsellers, said Dynah Carizal, who owns the shop with her husband Cornellio “Bong” Carizal.

Spanish bread, pan de coco, and pastries at Bong & Dynah Bakeshop.

This is already Dynah’s second bakery. After spending 10 years as a call center agent, she saved up enough to try her hand at a pastry business again with Bong. Now, the shop is a year old and counting.

The space used to house tapsilog, lugaw, pancit, and fried chicken businesses, until it turned itself into a yellow-walled bakery that residents have quickly come to love.

Bong said their immediate goal is to keep serving customers and keep the business afloat.

“Kami, kumbaga, dahan-dahan lang. Basta magsurvive tayo,” he said.

(We’re taking it slowly. We just want to survive.)

More than just survival, Bong & Dynah Bakeshop has now become a familiar stop despite surrounding businesses coming and going. It’s a staple that looks like it’s here to stay, so long as the people of Paltok keep their love for pastries alive.

Tedious task

Dynah said customers often overlook the time needed for dough to rise, which takes about five to six hours to complete. Bong said that a second batch of the famous salt bread could be ready only after the morning demand dies down.

Making bread is a labor of love that takes more than just mixing ingredients and sticking the dough in the oven. This is something baker Genesis Ordano, who has been working at the shop for 16 years, knows full well.

Empty shelves show the sold-out putok/star bread. The shop also offers toasted siopao for P15.

Genesis said getting the mixture right takes work customers rarely see. Production uses two and a half sacks of flour, rising to three when sales are good. Like clockwork, the longtime baker — who attests that nothing about the practice of baking challenges him — can recite the whole process of preparing pandesal off the top of his head.

“Magtitimbang muna ng asukal, tapos lalagyan ng asin at mantika. Tapos hahaluin at paalsahin muna. Tapos puputulin,” he explained.

(You weigh the sugar first, then you add salt and oil. Then, you mix it all and let it rise. Then, you cut the dough up.)

Some bread, however, sometimes goes unsold. Still, nothing goes to waste at Bong & Dynah Bakeshop. Genesis said leftovers become crumbs for pudding and custard, while Bong himself also turns some into toast with butter and sugar.

P50 custard cakes made from leftover bread.

The backbone of the bakery

Bong attests that it’s the workers that keep the bakery alive.

While the bakers keep the pastries flowing, saleswoman Joanne keeps the shop running in her own way. Once she clocks in at 6:30 am, she immediately cleans the racks and sweeps up the entire space. Then, she arranges the trays and sets up the tongs and plastic bags used to pack the bread customers will buy.

Joanne, though, has a more difficult task that onlookers may not usually see.

When the demand at the bakery gets high, the challenge of keeping up with it doesn’t only depend on the bakers. It’s a burden Joanne has to bear, too. Sometimes, customers get upset when certain products sell out, but she gets through it all with patience.

“[Kailangan] habaan talaga ang pasensya. Kahit galit ka na, nakangiti ka rin,” she said.

(You really have to be patient. Even when you’re already angry, you still have to smile.)

But at the end of the day, the famed Paltok bakery turns into a home for its employees, many of whom hail from provinces like Iloilo. It provides workers with food and accommodation, and often celebrates their birthdays with meals at places like Mang Inasal.

Shelves may empty by mid-morning, but keeping the bakery going starts before its doors open.

Beyond the loyal customers who buy out the bakery’s bread every single day, the staff is a big contributor to Bong & Dynah Bakeshop’s success, even though the shop is only a year old. Perhaps Bong and Dynah, then, have found the formula to fulfilling their dream of making the bakery survive. – Rappler.com

Jade Tan is a Rappler intern studying AB Journalism at University of Santo Tomas, Manila.

World.title: [Tambay] Paasa pa rin ang depensa ni VP Sara
World.content:
“There are no accidents.”

Ang linyang iyan ay isa sa mga paborito ng inyong friendly neighborhood tambay. Isa ito sa mga siping sinabi ni Master Oogway, ang pawikang maéstro sa maalamát na pelikulang Kung Fu Panda.

Ang ibig sabihin ng pantas ay laging may dahilan ang báwat pangyayari, at hindi bastá-bastá nangyayari ito. Walang aksidente o walang nagkakataon lang. May paliwanag kaya nagkakilala kayo. May dahilán ang pagsasalubong ng inyong landas. Pinagtatagpo ang lahat ng pangyayari, hindi ito “good timing” lang. Hindi ala-suwérte ang “being in the right place at the right time.”

At noong Biyernes, Nobyembre 19, pumasok sa isip ng inyong tambay na, bagamá’t hindi raw sinasadya, may dahilan kung bakit may sumiklab na visual effects ng naglalagablab na apoy sa broadcast ng impeachment trial ni Vice President Sara Duterte.

Day 44 ng impeachment (panoorin dito mula sa markang 56:16 minute), tóka ni Senator Alan Peter Cayetano ang opening prayer. Nakapikit at nakayuko pa ang senador. Nakatayo sa rostrum at may bukas na Bibliya sa harap niya. Nakikita ng mga manonood na taimtim na nananalangin ang senador. Bago matapos ang dasal, pagkasabi ni Cayetano ng “make it very, very clear whether a conviction is in order or an acquittal,” saglit na sumikláb at nabalot ang screen ng mga nanonood mula sa kaliwa pakanan ng transition effect ng lumagabláb na apoy.

Ang bilis ng pangyayari. Ano ‘yun? Bahagi ba ‘yun ng pa-effect ng dasal ni Cayetano? Pagkakamali lang ba ng admin ng tech na nangangasiwa ng live stream?

Noong hapon ding iyon, humingi ng paumanhín ang Public Relations and Information Bureau ng Senado. Sabi ng PRIB sa kanilang pahayag: “We sincerely apologize for the accidental transition effect that appeared during the live stream of the Senate Impeachment Court proceedings today.” Ang sinisisi: “[an] unexpected technical issue during the broadcast, which we deeply regret.”

Bumuô agad ng kuwénto ang malikót na utak ng inyong tambay. Siguro dahil palígoy-lígoy ‘yung panalangin, pabirông pumasok sa isip ng isang nasa tech booth ng Senado na “singitan ko kaya ng maapoy na pa-effect” ‘yung eksena ni Cayetano? Káso, nagkatotoo ang iniisip niya nang hindi sinadyâng napindot ang transition button.

Ilang beses na ring nangyari sa inyong tambay iyan. Pabirô lang dapat o kaya’y usapang “atin-atin lang ito, ha” kaso naro-wrong send. Naku po, sabit na naman!

Pinagalitan ni presiding judge Senator Chiz Escudero ang Senate PRIB sa nangyari. Sabi ng senador: “The flames are not well-taken and inappropriate in this proceedings.” Iniútos ni Escudero na alisin ang eksena sa talaan ng Senado.

May mananagot kaya sa PRIB kung hilingin ni Senator Alan na disiplináhin ang may sala? Pero wala akong nabasang komento ni Cayetano sa nangyari. Na-let-go na kaya niya? O baka naman may hindi tayo nalalaman?

Looking forward sana sa depensa ni Sara

Ilang beses na binanggít ng tambay ninyo na, “looking forward” itong marinig ang sagot ng depensa ni Vice President Sara Duterte sa mga ibinibintang sa kanya sa gumugulong na pagdinig.

Noong sinabi ng prosekusyon na tapos na silang ihayag ang mga ebidénsiyá ng kanilang articles of impeachment, sabay isinapubliko pa ang pagbawi sa tatlo sa apat, natuwa ako dahil sa wakas maririnig ko na ang panig ng depensa ni VP Sara. Oras na para ang depensa naman ang maglahad ng kanilang ebidénsiyá. Malalaman na natin ang mga arguménto ni Duterte.

Sabi pa nga ng abogado ni VP Sara na si Michael Poa, may paliwanag sila sa mga ipinukól ng prosekusyon. Dagdag ni atorni, ang mga saksi ng depensa ang tutugon.

Ilang linggo na ang lumipas, ngangá pa rin ako.

Inasahan ng publiko ang matinding balik ng depensa sa mga ibinató sa kanila. Parang may nagsabi pa nga, hindi ko lang maalala kung sino, hintayin daw ang pasabog ng panig ni VP Sara.

Pero puro mintís ang mga testigo ng depensa.

Pinakamabigat na sanang saksi itong ipinakilalang anti-money laundering expert na si Rainer dela Fuente, CPA at abogado.

Sa pag-unawà ko bilang isang hamak na tambay, napiling saksi ng depensa si Dela Fuente para tibagin ang nilalaman ng financial analysis na iniharap bilang ebidensya ng prosekusyon sa impeachment court. Ang financial analysis ay nagsasabi diumanó ng hindi maipaliwanag at nakatagong yaman ni VP Sara.

Sa ulat na isinumité sa impeachment court ng saksi ng prosekusyon na nagpakilalang forensic financial analyst at abogadong si Alex Cabrera, sinabi niya na sa kanyang “conservative estimate” mayroong hindi idineklarang yaman si VP Sara na P817.87-million.

Kahit mas maalam sa anti-money laundering si Dela Fuente, tumestigo siya sa tingin niyang pagkukulang ng financial analysis. Ang problema sa opinyon ng testigo ng depensa ay hindi niya nabasa ang buong financial analysis. Sa huli, sinabi ni atorni na ang mga nasabi niya ay sagot lang niya sa mga theoretical na itinanong sa kanya.

Tanggap ng inyong tambay ang sinabing iyan ng testigo.

Ang hindi ko mapapalampas ay nang usisain ang political affiliation ni Dela Fuente. Nasabi kasi niya sa unang bahagi ng testimonya niya na wala siyang political affiliation. Sa katunayan, hindi siya bumoto noong 2019.

Pero parang nabalatan ang testigo nang tinanong siya ni Senator Kiko Pangilinan tungkol sa kanyang malapit na kaibigan at dating law partner mula 2018 hanggang 2021. ‘Yung law partner ni Dela Fuente ay dating counsel ng Duterte Youth. At sinabi rin ni Pangilinan na ang law partner na iyon ay supporter din ni kandidatong Rodrigo Duterte nung halalan ng 2016. Si Dela Fuente, ‘yung law partner, at si Digong ay kapwa mga nagtapos sa San Beda Law.

Sinabi ni Dela Fuente na hindi niya alam na ang law partner niya ay sumuporta kay Tatay Digong. Hindi rin niya alam na abogado ng Duterte Youth kahit magka-partner sila sa law firm.

Sunod na tanong ni Sen Kiko: “Sabi mo hindi ka bumoto since 2019. Sinong binoto mo noong 2016 presidential election?” Hindi na raw niya maalala, sabi ni atorni. Tinanong pa ni Dela Fuente: “Sino po ba ang kandidato noon?”

Tulad na din ng mga naunang testigo, naging makakalimutin na si atorni.

Gusto ko sanang tanungin si atorni: Kung sakaling maalala mong si Tatay Digong pala ang ibinoto mo noong 2016, kahit ’ika mo nga “ang tagal na nun,” wala namang mali doon. Eh, sa iyon ang kandidatong pinaniwalaan mo.

At nasa mga disclosure din lang naman tayo, inaamin ko na pabor ako kay Tatay Digong noong 2016. Ang paniniwala ko kasi ay panahon na para magkaroon ang Pilipinas ng presidente na taga-Mindanao. Kahit hindi ko siya kilala, dahil taga-Mindanao siya, dapat subukan naman natin.

Malay ko bang magkakaganoon tayo? Sorry na po. – Rappler.com

Si Chito de la Vega ay Tambay ng Rappler dalawang beses kada buwan. Kasama rin siya sa mga anchor-host ng programang Balita Kwento Serbisyo ng DZME 1530.

World.title: Trailblazers in the desert: 5 Filipinos make their mark in Dubai
World.content:
Whether topping global essay contests or rising from odd jobs to five-star hotel management, these students and professionals highlight the resilience and talent of the Filipino community in the United Arab Emirates

DUBAI, United Arab Emirates – Five Filipinos, two of them children of overseas Filipino workers (OFWs), are blazing trails in this fast-paced global city.

Three of them — a businesswoman who is the lone Filipino member of a Dubai Chamber of Commerce business group, a high school graduate who earned a degree online to become a hotelier, and a social media specialist working with the Dubai government — all rose from humble beginnings.

The other two, both children of OFWs, are excelling in school. One is a published author — having written a trilogy — with immersion experience at Oxford University and a string of awards to her name; the other placed 11th overall among more than 1,000 competitors at Yale University’s World Scholar’s Cup Tournament of Champions this month.

Published author

Seventeen-year-old Izabella Faye Lebig — deputy head of the student council at Cambridge International School Dubai who boasts a long list of achievements — is a silver awardee in the Queen’s Commonwealth Essay Competition, which drew 25,648 global entries from 54 countries.

She also received a “Very High Commendation (Top 1%)” in the law category at the UK-based John Locke Institute’s 2026 Global Essay Competition, which received more than 100,237 entries from 183 countries, according to the institute.

Moreover, Izabella Faye has won law essay-writing contests at Oxford and Cambridge Universities.

She’s the daughter of Dr. Ben Lebig Jr., a financial analyst at the Dubai office of American multinational energy firm Chevron Corp. He, himself, had come far from being a young boy who had to cross two knee-deep rivers and climb a hill just to get to school in Iloilo.

Izabella Faye Lebig

A published author, Izabella Faye wrote the Alex Hades trilogy, which she described as exploring the “theological side of fantasy… starting off as a fantasy-suspense and morphing into fantasy-action throughout the series.”

“Overall, I consider the Alex Hades trilogy… an experiment and a diary, where readers can see not only the development of the story itself, but also my development as a writer and a kid growing up,” she said.

While considering business, law, or digital marketing as potential career paths, Izabella Faye — who was once featured at the annual Emirates Literature Festival — said writing remains central to her life.

“One [thing] that I know for sure, though, is that writing will always be my thing all throughout; it’s how my mind and soul breathe, and I practically live off it,” she said.

Writing for film is also on her mind.

“One thing I know for absolute certain is I’ve always wanted an opportunity to bring my stories to the big screen, and really getting involved in the production and the making of how it comes to life — it’s something I knew for sure I wanted to take part in even before I started writing,” Izabella Faye said.

Still, she keeps her feet firmly on the ground.

“I aim for the moon, but even if I land among the stars, I’ll feel just as proud. Achievements like these, as my parents always remind me, are just one part of the journey — they are reminders of how far I’ve come, but they’re not the destination,” she said.

Academic achiever

Another OFW child making waves is 17-year-old Ocean Thomas Tayo, who — along with teammates Jillian Denise Pilapil, and Sean Ezekiel Cosmiano — traveled to Yale University in Connecticut for the World Scholar’s Cup Tournament of Champions.

“We were excited. We researched deeper… and met up every now and then for active recall and to try our best to soar high,” said Tayo, a 12th grader at The Philippine School Dubai, which is attended mostly by OFW children.

The team placed 11th overall in the global competition, which featured more than 1,000 participants.

The World Scholar’s Cup is an internationally recognized academic competition where individuals and teams debate, write collaboratively, and answer questions based on an annually updated curriculum. Competitors begin in regional rounds and, after passing a point threshold, qualify for global rounds before advancing to the Tournament of Champions at Yale.

Ocean Thomas Tayo

Earlier, Ocean’s three-member team placed second in the Dubai Global Round, where he also finished third individually out of hundreds of scholars.

“As an Emirati [resident], I feel fulfilled. After hours and days of hard work, it really all paid off after feeling the medals and trophies, but what makes it worth it the most is bringing pride and joy to the UAE,” said Ocean, noting he had “prepared really hard — a bit too hard.”

“During the competition, I was sick the whole time. However, I still conquered and got 13 medals and seven trophies with my team,” Ocean said.

A student-leader, he founded The Pathfinder’s Project at his school, an initiative focused on personal growth, student direction, and leadership development. He was also named champion of the senior category at the Emirates Environmental Group Public Interest School Speaking Contest and won Best Debater in a simulated International Court of Justice competition.

Entrepreneur

A Filipino businesswoman, who once commuted daily from Bulacan to Far Eastern University (FEU) in Diliman during college, has been named a board member of the Printing and Publishing Business Group (PPBG) under the Dubai Chamber of Commerce (DCC).

“I am proud of having become a member of the board because I’m carrying our flag and I am the youngest as well,” said 42-year-old Michico Lopez Ramos in a mix of English and Filipino.

“Most of those sitting on the board are older because of their huge experience in the market, and all are males. Hence, I’m so flattered. I can keep up at that level with them, knowing that I’m the youngest and probably have a lot to learn.”

“I am so honored, and I know I can’t achieve this without my team supporting me,” she added.

Michico Lopez Ramos

Ramos arrived in Dubai in 2004, fresh out of college, and landed a job as a sales representative at a mobile phone and IT shop. Three years later, she ventured into opening her own digital marketing business before launching an events and advertising company in 2021.

Today, she is also co-owner of The Global Stories DXB, an online and print magazine, and the Brilliant Training Institute, which is accredited by Dubai’s Knowledge and Human Development Authority (KHDA).

“My main responsibility as a board member is as sales and marketing director overseeing the group’s brand identity, social media mileage, and online presence, including press releases, website, campaigns, and other marketing collateral,” said Ramos, who holds a degree in information technology and an MBA certification in project management.

Ramos said the DCC emailed to ask if she was interested in the position.

“Of course, it involves voting, and I had to share my experience and profile. It was all God’s plan that I was chosen,” she said.

She plans to use her role to “help amplify our voices as Filipinos in the printing and publishing sector.” So far, she has spearheaded the PPBG’s logo and branding guidelines, LinkedIn and Facebook pages, and online member database, among other initiatives.

The PPBG board also includes elected and founding industry representatives such as Secretary General Hamid Maammer, Lakshmanan Ganapathy of Al Ghurair Printing & Publishing, and Roger Nicodeme of Heidelberg Gulf LLC.

General manager

Ronin Ronald Endozo of Candelaria, Quezon, went to Oman as a high school graduate at just 16 years old in 1994.

“My first three years… were some of the hardest of my life. With limited experience and skills, I struggled to find my footing and moved from one job to another just to get by,” recalled Endozo.

Now 49 years old and recently appointed general manager of a five-star luxury serviced apartment hotel, Endozo worked his share of odd jobs before pulling himself together, pursuing a college degree at 41, and reaping what he sowed.

“I worked as a garage helper, a car washer in public parking areas, a kiosk attendant, a dishwasher in a coffee shop, a catering assistant, a cargo-moving helper, a bakery helper, a meat shop attendant and cutter, and a food server,” Endozo said.

Born and raised in a remote area, Endozo grew up in a small nipa hut with no electricity, with the nearest water source at least half a kilometer away. He has eight siblings, and his father worked as a carpenter in their barangay.

“Even as a young child, I already understood how hard our life was. We considered ourselves lucky if we could eat three times a day, or if we had any viand to go with our rice. I attended elementary school in our barangay, which meant walking more than a kilometer every morning, then walking back home at noon for lunch, because we couldn’t bring packed meals. Our parents often didn’t even know whether there would be anything for us to eat at midday. Many times, our meal was nothing more than rice and salt,” narrated Endozo .

He finished elementary school having had money to buy something during recess “only a handful of times.”

“I never experienced owning a new school bag; most of the time, I used an old hand-me-down one or even a fishing net,” he added.

Ronin Ronald Endozo

Despite these hardships, the Endozo siblings became known at their barangay public school for their strong academic performance.

“That academic excellence became my bridge to continuing my education at a high school in the town proper,” he said.

Endozo earned a scholarship to a private high school in the town proper, though getting there was far from easy. Because his parents couldn’t afford the fare, he had to walk at least three kilometers every day just to reach the main road where he could catch a ride.

He owned only two school uniforms throughout high school. “I never had a textbook of my own and relied entirely on books borrowed from the library,” he shared.

“My daily allowance was always just enough to cover my fare to and from school and a small viand to go with the rice I brought from home. For four years, I lived on mongo soup and pancit habhab as viand.”

After graduating from high school with flying colors, he faced a daunting question: What’s next?

He knew education was his only way out of poverty, yet his family could not afford college. So, he set off for Oman.

“Eventually, I landed my first job in a hotel. From that moment, I never stopped learning. I began setting my sights on the next available position, working hard to be recognized and considered for promotion,” Endozo said.

“Step by step, I rose through the ranks: from waiter to captain, then supervisor, restaurant manager, operations manager, department head, director, and finally general manager.”

He proved to those around him that he deserved every promotion. Competing against professionals of many different nationalities without a college degree or formal background in hospitality, Endozo faced challenges at every turn — yet he prevailed.

Throughout his career, Endozo has worked with some of the world’s most prestigious hotel brands, including InterContinental Hotels, Burj Al Arab, Jumeirah Group, Raffles Hotels, Millennium Hotels, Hilton Worldwide, Citadines, The Ascott, and Fraser Hospitality.

Once he began earning steady money, Endozo started helping his siblings move to Dubai. Eventually, six of them landed good jobs in the city.

“After that, I helped my nephews and nieces, then cousins, then distant relatives, and later even people from our barangay. What started with one person became a chain reaction of helping one another, and today there are more than 120 of us from our family and community working in Dubai,” he said.

Everyone has a story, and Endozo’s shows that poverty and a lack of early resources are not dead ends to reaching your dreams.

“Keep going, keep believing, and never give up,” he said.

Content creator

Michael Banua holds a degree in chemistry, though he eventually realized his real passion lay elsewhere: storytelling— where his true chemistry is.

Today, Banua is recognized as one of the Top 100 Influencers in the Middle East, with a social media community of more than 230,000 followers as @YourKuyaMico, an award-winning, mentor-driven content platform in the UAE.

It all started during the COVID-19 pandemic with just AED 500 to his name after the company where he worked announced it was shutting down.

“Since I couldn’t travel, I started posting old food photos from my gallery. To my surprise, these received great engagement and positive reactions. Soon, brands noticed my work and began sending complimentary meals in exchange for content,” Banua said.

His very first restaurant review featured a small cafeteria in Karama that served him an AED 12 biryani.

“One day, a restaurant near our office asked how much I charged. Without knowing the industry rates, I confidently said AED 150. That became my first paid collaboration and made me realize content creation could actually become a career,” Banua said.

Michael Mico Banua

One of his first major collaborations was with a Dubai bottled drinking water company. The campaign brief arrived at 10 pm, and the content had to be delivered by lunchtime the next day.

“Instead of creating a traditional , I documented my real routine as an OFW — from waking up, preparing for work, commuting on the Metro, spending the day in the office, and ending the day creating food content — while naturally integrating [the bottled water brand] into the story. The campaign stood out because it felt authentic and story-driven rather than promotional,” said Banua.

He landed a follow-up contract with the company, with the campaign appearing on billboards across the UAE — including along Sheikh Zayed Road, the main highway artery — as well as on buses, the Dubai Metro, YouTube ads, cinemas, and other nationwide marketing materials.

That campaign proved to be the turning point in Banua’s career, opening doors to new opportunities — including an invitation from the Dubai Media Office (DMO) to join the #BrandDubai and #DubaiDestinations campaigns promoting the city to the world.

Today, Banua works with leading government entities and brands, including Brand Dubai, Dubai Department of Economy and Tourism, Dubai Culture, Sharjah Tourism, the Department of Culture and Tourism – Abu Dhabi, the Abu Dhabi Sports Council, the General Directorate of Residency and Foreigners Affairs (GDRFA), the Roads and Transport Authority (RTA), Emirates National Oil Company (ENOC), Abu Dhabi National Oil Company (ADNOC), Miral (Yas Island), Majid Al Futtaim, and Big Ticket.

More importantly, Banua has been paying his success forward by educating and mentoring aspiring content creators inspired by his journey.

“I continue to conduct workshops, with my latest initiative focused on helping Filipino content creators better understand the UAE influencer and content creation landscape,” said Banua, who wears barong tagalog to major events, television appearances, speaking engagements, and UAE campaigns — even those unrelated to the Filipino community — “because representing my culture is something I deeply value.”

“At the heart of everything I do is storytelling, mentorship, and proudly representing the Filipino community while inspiring others to pursue their passions and create opportunities for themselves,” he added. – Rappler.com

World.title: COP31 climate summit risks failure as talks go deep into overtime
World.content:
EMPTY. Cameras are set up as talks stretch into overtime at the UN Climate Change Conference (COP31) in Antalya, Turkey, on November 21, 2026.

Negotiators expected a revised draft on November 20. But by the afternoon of November 21, with no new text on the table, hopes for significant changes have faded and frustration is mounting.

ANTALYA, Turkey – The COP31 climate summit will either produce a good deal or no deal at all, the European Union’s top climate official said on Saturday, November 21, as talks stretched deep into overtime.

Negotiators from nearly 200 countries are struggling to bridge divisions over fossil fuels and climate finance, delaying an agreement at the two-week conference that had been scheduled to end on Friday, November 20.

“It’s either going to be a good deal, or it’s going to be no deal,” EU Climate Commissioner Wopke Hoekstra told reporters.

Asked about the chances of no deal emerging, he said, “We will find out.”

The last major breakdown in UN climate talks came in Copenhagen in 2009, when countries failed to adopt the Copenhagen Accord by consensus in a setback for multilateral climate diplomacy.

As workers dismantled catering stands and exhibits at the venue, delegations shuttled between meeting rooms to discuss tactics, while others rested as they awaited a new version of the negotiating text.

Turkey’s COP31 President Murat Kurum met officials from the EU, Australia and Saudi Arabia in an effort to break the deadlock, but acknowledged a deal could prove elusive.

“I call on every country to act responsibly,” he told reporters. “There is no benefit for anyone to ruin this process by getting hung up on words, phrases.”

The biggest sticking points are whether a final agreement should mention the fossil fuels driving global warming and whether it should include support for poorer countries adapting to climate change.

A draft deal published on Thursday, November 19, removed earlier references to ending fossil fuel use. Observers said Saudi Arabia and other major oil and gas producers had opposed the language.

The draft also dropped a proposed $120 billion target for finance to help developing countries adapt to climate change.

Negotiators had expected a revised draft on Friday. But by Saturday afternoon, with no new text on the table, hopes for significant changes had faded and frustration was mounting.

Delays

Recent climate summits have regularly overrun without collapsing, eventually producing agreements.

Isatou Camara, Gambia’s finance negotiator, said some countries appeared to be using delay tactics to pressure others into accepting a weaker outcome.

“This delay strategy, which has been used at previous COPs, could be so at the end when things are put on the table you accept because you are fed up, exhausted, and want to go home,” she said.

This year’s talks have been further complicated by war and rising living costs, which are competing for the attention of policymakers and the public.

The US, the world’s largest historical greenhouse gas emitter, is also absent from the talks for the second year in a row after President Donald Trump ended cooperation on climate policy, calling global warming a hoax.

A UN report last month found the world is on track to exceed 1.5 degrees Celsius (2.7 degrees Fahrenheit) of warming above pre-industrial levels, a threshold governments agreed under the 2015 Paris Agreement to try to avoid breaching.

The draft agreement acknowledges that projected overshoot and calls for faster deployment of technologies that remove greenhouse gases from the atmosphere to help bring temperatures back down.

Some delegations opposed including carbon-removal technologies, arguing that doing so could open the door to continued fossil fuel use.

“The fact there is loads of unfinished business at this COP shows there’s a big problem here,” said Brenda Mwale, Malawi’s loss and damage negotiator. “The question is, are we in a leadership crisis? Was there really a vision for this COP?” – Rappler.com

World.title: At Rappler summit, human rights figures call for solidarity amid AI threats
World.content:
HUMAN RIGHTS. (From left to right) Amnesty International spokesperson Agnes Callamard, Norwegian Nobel Institute director Kristian Berg Harpviken, Norwegian Nobel Committee chairperson Jørgen Watne Frydnes, and Nobel Peace Prize laureate Maria Ressa speak at Rappler’s Social Good Summit on November 21, 2026.

MANILA, Philippines – Global human rights figures came together at Rappler’s Social Good Summit to emphasize the importance of collective action and community in fighting modern crises worsened by the threats of artificial intelligence (AI).

“Resistance matters, resistance can work,” Amnesty International spokesperson Agnes Callamard said on Saturday, November 21, when asked how to convince the public to side with human rights over profit-driven motives to the AI race.

Callamard pointed out that the public is part of a global majority willing to stand up to Big Tech.

“We must get together. Join organizations,” she added. “Collectively, we can fight back and hold the line.”

Callamard recalled how Navi Pillay, the most recent winner of the Nobel Peace Prize, faced a barrage of instant online hate after she was announced the recipient of the award.

The experience was familiar to Callamard, a former UN special rapporteur on extrajudicial executions, and fellow panelist Maria Ressa, both of whom were targets of online harassment during the Duterte administration. The two women have been vocal critics of former president Rodrigo Duterte’s bloody drug war.

“Women were attacked in the Philippines in 2017 at least 10 times more than men. What we did is we took the attacks down. It’s a curse because you feel it, but a blessing because you have the data,” Ressa, who won the Nobel Peace Prize in 2021, said.

“We studied it. We learned how to do it, and we turned it into a system where we can help others,” she added.

The closing panel, moderated by Rappler’s head of community Pia Ranada, discussed how AI has made warfare more efficient.

“If you look around us and we look at the various conflict zones, whether we’re talking about the geographical areas where war is playing out, or a conflict zone such as the struggle over where the reaches of AI are going to be allowed and not, I think we see that there is no lack of actors or individuals with enormous courage and integrity,” Kristian Berg Harpviken, Norwegian Nobel Institute director, said.

“There is no lack of organizations that are fighting back. And in the situation we are now, I think they are just more important than ever,” he added.

Jørgen Watne Frydnes, chairperson of the Norwegian Nobel Committee, said breakthroughs in fighting technology-driven threats can emerge from coalitions that set aside differences.

“What I hear is cooperation, it’s the necessity to cooperate, to lift your own perspective from your regional or local to global. And many of those campaigns that have succeeded, that did receive the Nobel Peace Prize, were campaigns that were able to take away the differences they had between them.

“Even though under our hardships, our trauma, war, terror, we continue, we continue as human beings. And that is a strength which is so inspirational,” Frydnes added.

This year’s Social Good Summit is themed “We, The Humans,” highlighting the importance of human rights, values, and community in the age of artificial intelligence. – Rappler.com

World.title: NU extends UAAP cheerdance reign with 3-peat; UE cops historic silver
World.content:
CHAMPS AGAIN. The NU Pep Squad bags its third straight UAAP Cheerdance crown.

(2nd UPDATE) The untouchable NU Pep Squad rules the UAAP Cheerdance Competition anew for a title three-peat and record-extending 10th championship, while UE wins its first silver medal in 24 years

MANILA, Philippines – The kings and queens of UAAP cheerdance still sit comfortably on their well-earned thrones.

For a record-extending 10th time in UAAP history, the NU Pep Squad is the UAAP Cheerdance Competition champion, adding another title three-peat to its dynastic history on Saturday, November 21, at the packed Mall of Asia Arena.

With its latest golden coup for double-digit titles, the Gab Bajacan-coached squad created a two-championship gap from the league’s long-tied second-placers, the legendary eight-time titlists UST Salinggawi Dance Troupe and UP Pep Squad.

Taking its act from Japan last year to Mexico on Saturday afternoon, NU embodied a tribal, ritualistic spirit, and took the capacity 21,126-strong crowd on an Aztec whirlwind, highlighted by a literal whirlwind toss to kickstart one of its multiple perfect pyramids.

Meanwhile, the UE Pep Squad — perennial middle-of-the-pack performers — finally broke a nine-year podium drought with a unique Chinese martial arts routine, embodying a true Red Warrior spirit for its first silver finish in 24 long years, or since Season 65 in 2002.

The UE Pep Squad barges into the top two with a Chinese-inspired routine.

Completing the top three, the FEU Cheering Squad extended its podium run to eight straight seasons with its third consecutive bronze medal after a deliberately paced Aladdin routine.

“We had such a hard time getting this routine going,” NU head coach Gab Bajacan said in Filipino. “In our practices, we hardly had a complete routine. We were really frustrated because we needed to present our own standard every time we practice, and we couldn’t do it.”

“So when we finished our routine as flawless and as perfect as possible, we were so happy because we never expected to complete our stunts, and we were all so nervous, especially the new ones. We just put our full trust in them, and they finally showed our strong “NU tribe” spirit.”

NU ruled the roost with 693.5 points, while UE earned its historic silver with 664.5 points. FEU completed the podium with 647.5 points, edging fellow contender Adamson with a fourth-best 636.5 points.

The San Marcelino standouts, who wowed the crowd with their extreme motorsports-themed routine, slightly missed the mark as they snapped a two-year podium run that produced back-to-back silver medals.

The FEU Cheering Squad lands on the podium with an ‘Aladdin’ theme.

In its ongoing pursuit of lost glory, UP placed fifth with 596.5 points, while La Salle broke a five-year, seventh-placer run with 565.5 points to land at sixth.

Following an error-filled curtain-raiser routine, UST plummeted to seventh with 537.5 points — its worst finish in 13 years. Meanwhile, Ateneo completed the field with its sixth straight last-place finish, far below UST at 469.5 points. – Rappler.com

World.title: The fellowship of the grind
World.content:
'It was moving to watch, and a little shaming that, in this industry and in this country, working musicians can depend only on each other'

In my first week of college in Manila, I went looking for the nearest, and cheapest, folk house in the University Belt. It was 1978 and the scene was in full bloom. Once my campus paper allowance kicked in, I graduated from the folk houses of Recto and Morayta to Ermita, the mecca, the venues we read about in Jingle Magazine: Kola House, Hobbit House, My Father’s Mustache.

Beer was cold and nobody minded the smoke. The sets ran from the ’60s canon of Bob Dylan, Peter, Paul and Mary, and Simon & Garfunkel, the gritty folk of Neil Young, the two-part harmonies of Seals & Crofts and Loggins & Messina, to the acoustic pop of James Taylor and Jim Croce, the bruised love songs of Jackson Browne, and the country-folk of John Denver.

But the folk house was never just about the music, particularly after the declaration of martial law in 1972. These intimate venues, usually a dim room with one singer and perhaps thirty listeners, became one of the few places where young people could gather, listen to “Blowin’ In The Wind” or “He Was My Brother” and other socially relevant songs, and not look over their shoulders. They provided sanctuary for the weary, the worried, and the dreamers.

Behind the performances was a grind.

Pendong Aban Jr. of Asin got his first gig at Charcoal House on Recto in the early ‘70s with his friend Keith. As Keith and Fred, they played two sets a night for P20 each. Charcoal House, however, was pang-masa, a student hangout; someone told them they were ready for Mabini, where the serious folk houses were.

At their audition at Pension Filipina, they watched God’s Ego, the heavy hitters known for spot-on Crosby, Stills and Nash covers. They realized they were not ready for Mabini yet.

By 1975, Keith and Fred were regulars at Kola House, My Father’s Mustache, Bodega, and Pension Filipina. Aban eventually went solo and did gigs in Japan. Back from a six-month stint, Aban alternated sets with a trio composed of Mike Pillora, Cesar Bañares, and a Manila-born singer with a big, soulful voice, Lolita Carbon. The three were Salt of the Earth, packing rooms with Peter, Paul and Mary covers. Aban’s solo set was eclectic, with covers of David Bowie’s “Space Oddity” and Dylan’s “Masters of War” and “Hurricane.”

Pillora, recalls Aban, invited him to play bass for the group, and that was the beginning of Asin. When “Anak” made Freddie Aguilar, another folk singer, a star, the labels came scouting the folk houses for the next big act, and one of them found the quartet.

A generation of Filipino musicians was made through gigs abroad, bands formed between sets, and countless auditions where competition was tight but friendly.

Chickoy Pura recalled those years at a recent benefit show his contemporaries staged for him at My Brother’s Mustache in Quezon City, perhaps the only remaining venue for folk songs and folk singers today. Folk singers of his time, said Pura, shared experiences, a bond, and sometimes guitars.

“Ang unang tanong sa iyo noong araw, ilan na ba ang pondo mo?” he recalled. A singer’s pondo was his stock of songs. Pura had maybe 15. Come back when you have 30, he was told. His first pay was a sandwich; later, P30 a night.

Today, he said, young players walk into bars with top-of-the-line gear. “Before, we looked for jobs on borrowed guitar sometimes.”

“We’re older now and some of our friends fell by the wayside, but we remember them with much affection and pride… You stop playing, you stop living,” he told the audience.

By the early ’80s, the mass market had drifted back to formula pop; the restless young channelled their restlessness through punk and heavy metal. Still, every eatery, canteen, or food court needed live entertainment, and folk singers came cheapest, although the songs have changed. I once sat through a lunchtime acoustic rendition of “Careless Whisper” in a busy student canteen.

The pioneers, their best years behind them, continue to make their living from shows that are few and far between. Those who landed record deals and delivered hit songs received meager royalties, if they came at all. The road takes its toll on voices and bodies, and many of them are well past retirement age. The medical bills begin to pile up.

What has never left is the fellowship. When one of them falls ill, the others play a benefit, as they always have, before small crowds of loyal, graying fans.

They were there that night for Pura. Lolita Carbon’s voice was powerful as ever, her stage presence still electric. It was also her birthday. The secret of life? “Basta masaya lang lagi dapat,” she told me after her set.

Lito Crisostomo, former lead guitarist for The Blank, Ang Grupong Pendong, and Asin, played Crosby, Stills and Nash classics with Erwin, his partner from their days in the circuit as Fat and Thin. For more than five hours, act after act took the stage: Bobby Mondejar and Friends, Corky and Kiko, Rene Vega, Albert de Pano, Koko Marbella, Pete Velasquez, Ding Laag, and Joel Yu. Special guests were Pido Lalimarmo, founding member of Side A and Artstart who now fronts an all-Steely Dan covers band Black Cows, as well as the Kakoy Legaspi Blues Collective, whose smoldering blues set prompted advertising maverick Vince Pozon to declare “may pag-asa pa sa kabataan.”

An extended jam on James Taylor’s “Steamroller Blues” rounded off the night of music and fellowship. By that time, it was almost 1 am but no one was in a hurry to leave. It was moving to watch, and a little shaming that, in this industry and in this country, working musicians can depend only on each other. The voice, the energy, the spirit, those things the grind could not take from them. – Rappler.com

World.title: Maria Ressa: Understand AI to defend ourselves from ‘predatory’ tech
World.content:
FIGHT BACK. Rappler CEO and Nobel Peace Prize laureate Maria Ressa delivers a speech during the plenary session of the 2026 Social Good Summit titled 'WE, THE HUMANS: Reclaim Our Future,' at BGC, Taguig City, on November 21, 2026.

'For those who are saying they cannot act: Don’t fall into learned helplessness. When you are the target, you are powerful,' Rappler CEO Maria Ressa says of the fight against artificial intelligence

MANILA, Philippines – Understanding artificial intelligence is essential to defending ourselves from the harms of the “predatory, extractive” technology, Rappler chief executive officer and Nobel Peace Prize laureate Maria Ressa said.

During the 2026 Social Good Summit on Saturday, November 21, Ressa warned that AI was built to “hack our biology” as the end goal of Big Tech is profit.

She explained that AI hacked people’s attention, intimacy, and agency, through machine learning in social media, generative chatbots, and agentic AI.

“What have we lost? Sustained attention… our ability to hold complexity, nuances, to move away from identity politics,” Ressa said in her speech, adding that AI is “shifting the evolution of our species.”

“The technology that we’re getting has essentially been predatory and extractive, like mining. How much data have been given, and where has it gone to?”

That defense should be complemented with building own technologies, according to Ressa. (READ: From Duterte to Big Tech: Maria Ressa’s blueprint on fighting back)

This is after Big Tech is “breaking the social contract” by taking and scraping content from news outfits, pushing the journalism industry to already “reaching market failure.”

In 2025, it was found that bots already drove 53% of internet traffic, according to the latest report of cybersecurity firm Imperva.

“For those who are saying they cannot act: Don’t fall into learned helplessness. When you are the target, you are powerful,” she also said.

Ressa also centered on the continued push to protect democracy by establishing facts and truth, in a bid to “reclaiming our future from the machines we built.” (READ: Maria Ressa on AI overreliance: ‘Don’t outsource the nuances’)

“When you don’t have facts and lies spread faster, you cannot actually solve any problem. Not climate change, not rule of law, not child safety. Because if you don’t have facts, you can’t organize. You can’t hold anyone accountable,” she said.

“The chain of facts is what makes a crowd or a mob into ‘we,’ the people. You break that, and there’s no ‘we’ left to reclaim anything.”

Citing the preliminary report of the United Nations Independent International Scientific Panel on AI, Ressa said AI is changing geopolitical powers.

Ressa is a co-chair of the 40-member panel, which assesses opportunities, risks, and impacts of AI.

“A few hold the future in their hands, five or six companies, and in terms of compute power, the US has 75% of the world’s compute power. China has 15%, and the EU (European Union), which has put in place the safety measures we need, has 5%,” she said.

She also said that the AI deployment is “far outstripping the ability of law, of audit, and of oversight.”

On Monday, November 16, California sued OpenAI, accusing the company of developing a dangerous product without adequate safety procedures or oversight after reports that its AI models had independently carried out cyberattacks. Among this cyberattacks was the July hack of the open-source platform Hugging Face.

In September, Australia said an OpenAI agent breached a government health data portal and gained unauthorized access to files.

“Can we stop impunity in tech?” she asked. – Rappler.com

World.title: LTO suspends vlogger’s driver’s license over alleged traffic violations
World.content:
The Land Transportation Office (LTO) ordered the 90-day preventive suspension of vlogger Geo Ong’s driver’s license over alleged traffic violations in Palawan, including riding a motorcycle without a helmet and taking photos while driving. Ong later apologized. The agency also issued a show-cause order directing him to explain the violations. (Photo from LTO)

CALAPAN CITY, Oriental Mindoro — A vlogger faces a 90-day preventive suspension of his driver’s license after the Land Transportation Office (LTO) flagged him for alleged road safety violations in Palawan, including riding a motorcycle without a helmet.

The LTO, under Assistant Secretary Markus Lacanilao, also issued a show-cause order (SCO) directing the vlogger to explain the alleged violations.

According to the LTO Mimaropa (Mindoro Occidental, Mindoro Oriental, Marinduque, Romblon, and Palawan), photos and videos circulating on social media showed the unnamed vlogger riding a motorcycle on a public road without a standard protective helmet. Two passengers riding with him were also seen without helmets.

Article continues after this 

Information gathered by the Inquirer identified the vlogger as Geo Ong, who later apologized in a social media post.

READ: Geo Ong sorry after LTO suspends license over helmet violation

Other motorcycle riders accompanying Ong were likewise seen without helmets, while one photo showed him taking a picture while driving.

The LTO directed Ong to appear before the LTO Palawan District Office on Nov. 24 to submit a sworn comment or explanation regarding the alleged violations.

These include failure to wear the prescribed standard protective motorcycle helmet, carrying more than one back rider or overloading, and reckless driving for taking photos or videos while operating a motorcycle.

Article continues after this 

The agency also ordered him to immediately surrender his driver’s license to the LTO Palawan District Office.

His driver’s license and the motorcycles identified as involved in the incident were also placed under alarm pending the investigation.

Article continues after this 

Lacanilao said social media personalities should act responsibly because their actions could influence their followers, particularly when promoting activities that may compromise public safety.

“As a vlogger, he has a responsibility to be careful about the actions he shows to the public because his followers may imitate them,” Lacanilao said.

He stressed that road safety should not be compromised for the sake of photos or videos intended for social media, adding that drivers must keep their full attention on the road at all times.

World.title: Lipa City pushes for government-run pet cemetery
World.content:
INQUIRER file

LUCENA CITY — The city council of Lipa, Batangas, is pushing for a government-owned and operated pet cemetery to provide deceased companion animals with a proper resting place.

On Nov. 16, the city council adopted a resolution urging Mayor Eric Africa to consider establishing a local government-run Pet Memorial Park and directing concerned city offices to conduct preliminary studies, assessments, and preparations for its eventual operation.

“Companion animals have become an important part of many households, providing companionship, comfort, and emotional support to their owners, who often regard them as members of their families,” the resolution stated.

Article continues after this 

It further noted that humane treatment of animals should not end upon their death but should extend to the proper handling and disposal of their remains in a manner that recognizes their value as companions and respects the feelings of those who cared for them.

Lipa has several privately operated pet crematoriums, but their services are often expensive for many pet owners, particularly those who want to give their deceased animals a dignified farewell.

The issue of pet cremation came following the discovery of dead animals dumped in San Jose del Monte City, Bulacan, on Oct. 30. The remains were reportedly supposed to have been cremated at a privately operated facility in Bacoor City, Cavite.

READ: Bacoor mayor orders probe into pet crematorium

The city council said the absence of a designated and accessible government burial facility for deceased pets could result in the improper disposal of animal remains in vacant lots, open spaces, waterways, roadsides, and other inappropriate locations, potentially posing sanitation, environmental, and public health risks.

Article continues after this 

“There is a need to provide pet owners with a proper and designated place where they may lay their deceased pets to rest, give them a dignified burial, and have a place to visit, remember, and honor the companionship and affection they shared,” the council added.

According to the council, establishing a government-owned and operated pet cemetery would provide an organized, accessible, and properly managed burial facility for companion animals while promoting responsible pet ownership and discouraging the indiscriminate disposal of animal remains. /mcm

World.title: Taal Volcano’s gas emissions rise as earthquakes decline
World.content:
File photo. Time-lapse footage of a minor phreatomagmatic eruption at the Taal Main Crater at 01:45 PM today, 10 April 2026. This event generated a short 200-meter plume as captured by the Main Crater (VTMC) and Daang Kastila (VTDK) Observation Stations on the western and northern rims, respectively, of the Main Crater. Alert Level 1 remains in effect over Taal Volcano. Screengrab: Phivolcs Facebook

LUCENA CITY — Sulfur dioxide emissions from Taal Volcano in Batangas province have increased significantly, the Philippine Institute of Volcanology and Seismology (Phivolcs) reported Sunday, Nov. 22.

In its latest 24-hour monitoring, Phivolcs recorded 567 metric tons (MT) of sulfur dioxide emissions from the volcano, which it classified as a “weak emission.”

The figure marked a sharp increase from the daily average of 215 MT recorded from Nov. 17 to 21.

Article continues after this 

Meanwhile, seismic activity at Taal Volcano has declined, with only three volcanic earthquakes recorded over the past 24 hours, according to the latest Phivolcs bulletin.

READ: Taal Volcano records spike in quakes after days of low activity

The volcano registered 11 volcanic earthquakes on Saturday and 13 the previous day.

Phivolcs also observed no upwelling of hot volcanic fluids in the main crater lake on Taal Volcano Island, which lies in the middle of Taal Lake. No volcanic smog, or vog, was detected during the monitoring period.

Taal Volcano remains under Alert Level 1, indicating low-level volcanic unrest.

Article continues after this 

Phivolcs reiterated its strict prohibition on entry to Taal Volcano Island, particularly the Permanent Danger Zone, including the vicinity of the main crater and the Daang Kastila fissure.

The agency also advised civil aviation authorities to warn pilots against flying close to the volcano due to the possibility of sudden ash emissions. /mcm

World.title: 4 weather systems to drench PH on Sunday
World.content:
.

MANILA, Philippines — The shear line, northeast monsoon, easterlies and intertropical convergence zone (ITCZ) will bring rains and thunderstorms over parts of the country on Sunday, the state weather bureau said.

In its 4 a.m. weather forecast, the Philippine Atmospheric, Geophysical and Astronomical Services Administration (Pagasa) said the shear line will affect the eastern sections of Northern and Central Luzon, while the northeast monsoon, or “amihan,” will prevail over the rest of Northern Luzon.

Pagasa said cloudy skies with scattered rains and isolated thunderstorms will prevail over mainland Cagayan, Isabela, Nueva Vizcaya, Quirino, and Aurora due to the shear line.

Article continues after this 

Similar weather conditions are expected in Caraga, Davao Region, and Southern Leyte due to the ITCZ, as well as in Quezon province due to the easterlies.

READ: PH Weather Updates TodayThe weather bureau warned of possible flash floods or landslides in these areas due to moderate to heavy rains.

The rest of Cagayan Valley and the Cordillera Administrative Region will experience cloudy skies with rains due to the northeast monsoon, with possible flash floods or landslides also expected.

The Ilocos Region, meanwhile, will have partly cloudy to cloudy skies with isolated light rains, with no significant weather-related impacts expected.

Metro Manila and the rest of the country will experience partly cloudy to cloudy skies with isolated rain showers or thunderstorms due to the easterlies, while the rest of Mindanao will experience the same weather conditions due to the ITCZ.

Pagasa cautioned residents against possible flash floods or landslides during severe thunderstorms.

World.title: 3 Inquirer correspondents win big at Bright Leaf awards
World.content:
TRIPLE RECOGNITIONS Three Inquirer correspondents received recognition at the 19th Bright Leaf Agriculture Journalism Awards in Makati City on Thursday. Joanna Rose Aglibot wins Agriculture Story of the Year, Willie Lomibao (left) was inducted into the Bright Leaf Awards Hall of Fame, and Ray Zambrano wins Tobacco Photo of the Year. —CONTRIBUTED PHOTO

Inquirer correspondent Joanna Rose Aglibot took top honors at the 19th Bright Leaf Agriculture Journalism Awards, winning the prize for “Agriculture Story of the Year” for reporting extensively on the struggles of local fishermen amid tensions in the West Philippine Sea.

Aglibot’s three-part special report, “From shore to shoal: Zambales fishers fight to sustain livelihood,” showed how China’s restrictions and harassment in the WPS affected the livelihood not only of fishermen but also traders and buyers in Subic, Zambales.

READ: Inquirer report on PH debt wins CMMA

Article continues after this 

Her entry won over more than 400 submissions. At the awards ceremony held in Makati City on Thursday, Aglibot received a trophy, P100,000 in cash, a MacBook and an all-expenses-paid trip to an Asian destination.

Also at this year’s Bright Leaf, Inquirer photo correspondent Willie Lomibao was inducted into the awards’ Hall of Fame after winning five times (2018, 2019, 2021, 2023 and 2025) in the annual competition by clinching either the “Tobacco Photo of the Year” or the “Agriculture Photo of the Year.”

Lomibao became the 10th journalist to be inducted into the Bright Leaf Awards Hall of Fame since 2010.

Fellow Inquirer photo correspondent Ray Zambrano also won the “Tobacco Photo of the Year” award, his first from Bright Leaf, for his shot of a farmer inspecting tobacco leaves laid out to dry in a barn in Barangay Amamperez, Villasis, Pangasinan.

Both Lomibao and Zambrano also received trophies, cash prizes and trips to an Asian destination.

Article continues after this 

READ: Former DA chief joins ‘Kapatid Angat Lahat’ program

In her speech, Aglibot acknowledged the Zambales fishermen and their families “who have continued to trust us with their stories.”

Article continues after this 

“This recognition belongs as much to them as it does to us,” she said.

“This award comes at a meaningful time as we mark the 10th anniversary of the arbitral ruling (against China’s nine-dash-line claim over the South China Sea).”

“My hope is that our fishermen will finally experience that victory—not just on paper, but through their freedom to return to sea without fear, earn a living, provide for their families, and enjoy the rights that have long been affirmed,” she added.

‘Important platform’

Aglibot thanked the Inquirer for providing an “important platform” for stories that highlight the struggles of fishing communities, as well as the Philippine Center for Investigative Journalism and Internews for supporting the series.

She dedicated her first Bright Leaf Award win to her mother, Juliet; brother, Jonathan Jorge, and her late father Jorge, who was her biggest supporter.

Aglibot, Lomibao and Zambrano also acknowledged the award’s organizer, Philip Morris Philippines, “for bringing the Bright Leaf Awards to life.”

In her opening remarks, Chita Herce, senior director for corporate affairs at Philip Morris Philippines, said this year’s entries brought “new challenges, new perspectives and new stories worth telling.”

“You are the voices behind the stories that matter. You shine a light on the aspirations of our farming, fishing and rural communities,” she said.

Herce noted that through the journalists’ work, “stories that might otherwise go unheard” are able to inspire awareness, action and progress.

“Tonight, we celebrate not only your achievements but also the dedication and purpose behind every story you tell. To your colleagues, families and supporters, thank you for continuing to champion agricultural journalism in the Philippines,” she said.

Agriculture Undersecretary Arrey Perez, the event’s guest speaker, said the future of the sector remained “bright” despite current challenges.

“The problems faced by our farmers are that they don’t have places to store [their produce], they don’t have roads to transport [them], and they don’t have avenues to sell [their products],” he said.

World.title: UN chief Guterres marvels at Ifugao rice terraces
World.content:
NORTHERN EXPOSURE United Nations Secretary General Antonio Guterres is a special guest of Ifugao province, where he spent two days after attending the Asean Summit in Manila. —DOT PHOTOS

United Nations Secretary General António Guterres expressed admiration for the centuries-old rice terraces and local traditions in Ifugao during a two-day visit to the province following his attendance at the 49th Association of Southeast Asian Nations (Asean) Summit in Manila.

According to a statement released by the Department of Tourism-Cordillera Administrative Region (DOT-CAR), Guterres was in Ifugao from Nov. 18 to Nov. 19.

READ: UN chief Guterres visits Ifugao rice terraces after Asean Summit

Article continues after this 

“I just spent some time with a family here in Ifugao and it’s amazing—their culture, traditions, and very strong connection to their land,” Guterres said, as quoted in the DOT-CAR statement.

NORTHERN EXPOSURE United Nations Secretary General Antonio Guterres is a special guest of Ifugao province, where he spent two days after attending the Asean Summit in Manila. —DOT PHOTOS

The UN chief visited the Batad, Bangaan and Hapao rice terraces, as well as the Aguian View Deck, during his trip.

Reflecting on the history of the rice terraces, Guterres compared their age with that of his home country, Portugal.

“When these rice fields were built, my country did not exist yet. It shows the importance of culture and civilization of the Philippines and Asia,” he said.

NORTHERN EXPOSURE United Nations Secretary General Antonio Guterres is a special guest of Ifugao province, where he spent two days after attending the Asean Summit in Manila. —DOT PHOTOS

Guterres was accompanied by Tourism Undersecretary Maria Victoria Jasmin and DOT-CAR Regional Director Jovita Ganongan throughout his visit.

Article continues after this 

The Rice Terraces of the Philippine Cordilleras entered the United Nations Educational, Scientific and Cultural Organization (Unesco) World Heritage List in 1995.

The World Heritage property comprises five rice terrace clusters in Ifugao, recognized for their cultural significance and traditional agricultural practices maintained by generations of local communities. INQ

World.title: Agri losses due to El Niño up further past P10 billion
World.content:
File photo. ‘Very strong’ El Nino is now active in tropical Pacific, says Pagasa. (Photo Courtesy of OMH-Hilongos,Leyte)

The El Niño phenomenon continues to drain the country’s agriculture sector, with losses inching up further past the P10-billion level, according to the Department of Agriculture (DA).

In its bulletin on Friday evening, the DA said the farm sector incurred P10.44 billion in damage, 4.5 percent higher than the P9.99 billion reported by the agency on Nov. 11.

READ: Food stockpiling eyed amid El Niño, other crises

Article continues after this 

In the previous month, the agency already pegged damage and losses at P8.57 billion, from P6.87 billion initially recorded in September.

The prolonged drought impacted the livelihood of 338,066 farmers and fisherfolk across seven of the eight regions in Luzon (Cordillera, Ilocos, Cagayan Valley, Central Luzon, Calabarzon, Mimaropa and Bicol), all four regions in the Visayas (Western Visayas, Negros Island Region, Central Visayas and Eastern Visayas) and five of the six regions in Mindanao (Zamboanga Peninsula, Northern Mindanao, Davao, Soccsksargen and Caraga).

About 311,289 metric tons of local harvests have been damaged, spanning 332,726 hectares of agricultural land.

Corn, rice losses

According to the agency, corn and rice comprised more than 92 percent of the overall losses.

Losses in corn amounted to P5.67 billion, accounting for 54.25 percent of the total. Rice followed with P4.05 billion, equivalent to 38.74 percent.

Article continues after this 

The majority of rice and corn crops that have been damaged are in the vegetative and reproductive stages.

El Niño likewise hit high-value crops (P665.08 million), livestock and poultry (P40.95 million), fisheries and aquatic resources (P20.38 million) and cassava (P5.60 million).

Article continues after this 

DA funding

The DA set aside P18.64 billion worth of interventions to help affected farmers and fisherfolk nationwide, such as P10.82 billion worth of production support that will be distributed through its regional field offices.

About 2.69 million beneficiaries are entitled to financial assistance through the Presidential Assistance for Farmers and Fisherfolk Program.

Affected farm producers may secure funding from the Agricultural Credit Policy Council’s “AgriRecover” program, which earmarked P31.08 million worth of financial assistance for 1,127 borrowers.

Meanwhile, the Philippine Crop Insurance Corp. will provide P703.06 million in indemnification to 77,522 affected farmers.

The DA previously outlined a P61.99-billion action plan to reduce the impact of El Niño on the agriculture sector.

These include P6.2 billion in fuel and fertilizer subsidies under the Unified Package for Livelihoods, Industry, Food and Transport, or Uplift program, as well as cloud seeding operations and measures to curb the spread of red-striped soft scale insects that are affecting sugarcane production.

World.content:
CUSTODY Felicito Guevarra turns himself in at the Santuario de San Antonio Parish outside Forbes Park. —SCREENGRAB FROM NBI FOOTAGE

Martin Romualdez’s co-accused in his P7.44-billion plunder case surrendered last Thursday at a church in a Makati village, according to the National Bureau of Investigation (NBI).
