World.title: Rights Groups Demand Action Against Myanmar Junta After Historic Rohingya Genocide Ruling
World.content:
Rights groups are urging governments to step up diplomatic pressure, impose fresh sanctions and isolate the military regime following Thursday’s landmark International Court of Justice (ICJ) judgment that Myanmar committed genocide against the Rohingya during military operations in 2017.

It was the first time in its 80-year history that the ICJ found a state responsible for committing genocide.

Rights advocates say the historic ruling must now translate into concrete measures to hold the regime accountable, rather than remain a symbolic legal victory.

“This is a big blow for [regime leader] Min Aung Hlaing at a time when he is trying to persuade the world to normalize relations,” Tun Khin, president of the Burmese Rohingya Organisation UK (BROUK), told The Irrawaddy.

The ICJ ordered Myanmar to investigate, prosecute and punish those responsible, and pay reparations, as well as ensure the safe return of Rohingya refugees to Rakhine State.

The ruling is final and cannot be appealed, although the court has no independent enforcement mechanism.

If Myanmar fails to comply with the ruling’s orders, the UN Security Council can act to enforce them, according to Article 94.2 of the UN Charter.

Tun Khin said his organization had called on the UK to organize a meeting of the UN Security Council. Though regime allies Russia and China would likely veto any resolution, they would be forced to explain such a move. London has called for a meeting.

“We hope it will result in new sanctions,” Tun Khin said.

Tun Khin expressed concern that the return of the Rohingya is still impossible due to the policies of both the Myanmar military regime and the ethnic Arakan Army (AA), an anti-regime armed group that controls 14 of Rakhine State’s 17 townships.

Lucky Karim, executive director of the group Refugee Women for Peace and Justice, said that as an initial step following the ICJ ruling, Association of Southeast Asian Nations (ASEAN) member countries should stop engaging with the Myanmar regime.

She noted that this year nine countries have hosted self-appointed president Min Aung Hlaing, who oversaw the 2017 atrocities as military chief. She urged all countries to stop welcoming him. Despite the bilateral engagements, Myanmar regime leaders remain barred from ASEAN’s top-level summits.

“I think the regional states should apply the same rule [as ASEAN] and take a pause for now. Stop hosting him and rolling out the red carpet and engaging him,” Lucky Karim said.

The ICJ decision was welcomed by UN Secretary-General António Guterres, the UN Independent Investigative Mechanism for Myanmar (IIMM), Amnesty International and Human Rights Watch (HRW), along with foreign ministers from the United Kingdom, Australia, Ireland and Turkey, as well as Myanmar’s civilian National Unity Government (NUG).

As immediate actions, London ordered the expulsion of Myanmar’s Defense Attaché from the UK and issued an urgent call for a UN Security Council session to discuss the judgment.

More than 190 local rights groups welcomed the ICJ ruling.

The regime rejected the verdict. Khaing Khaing Soe, a spokesperson for the military-appointed government, said on Friday: “The truth is we were wrongly accused.”

Emphasizing the fact that the verdict was not unanimous, she said, “Not all the judges voted for it, so it’s not a fair judgment.”

The ICJ ruled by nine votes to six that Myanmar had committed genocide against the Rohingya.

Meanwhile, the AA said it would act in the best interests of the state following the landmark ruling.

“We need to wait for the regime’s report to the Court. For example, will the regime deny it, or will they say they can’t pay compensation?” Rakhine politician Pe Than told The Irrawaddy.

Backed by the Organization of Islamic Cooperation (OIC), the Gambia brought the case in 2019, alleging that Myanmar’s atrocities against the Rohingya violated the Genocide Convention. It took seven years to reach a final verdict in the case.

The Myanmar regime has continued to commit war crimes and crimes against humanity across the country since the 2021 coup.

Since seizing power, the regime has killed more than 8,600 civilians and detained over 32,000 people, according to the Assistance Association for Political Prisoners. The group said the regime continues to hold political prisoners, including Aung San Suu Kyi, while millions of young people have fled abroad amid forced conscription, security fears, inflation, widespread crime, job scarcity and escalating conflict.

The NUG reaffirmed its commitment to justice, citizenship, and human rights norms for the Rohingya in a statement Thursday.

It said communities across Myanmar continue to face airstrikes, killings, arbitrary detention, torture and forced displacement, while hospitals, schools, monasteries and churches have also come under attack.

“The pursuit of justice for the Rohingya must be accompanied by action to end the military junta’s continuing violence against civilians throughout Myanmar,” it said.

Tun Khin said the ICJ judgment is good news for everyone in Myanmar. “Now they [the regime] are officially responsible for genocide and facing renewed international pressure instead,” he said.

World.title: U.S. Sanctions Two More Myanmar Regime-Allied Scam Warlords
World.content:
The U.S. Treasury’s Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) sanctioned two more top leaders of the Democratic Karen Benevolent Army (DKBA) on Thursday, accusing them of operating and facilitating cyber-scam centers on the Myanmar-Thailand border.

Commander-in-chief General Saw Shwe Wah and Phaya Thonezu town commander Colonel Saw A One join four other senior leaders of the regime-allied militia on the U.S. sanctions list.

Saw Steel, Saw Sein Win, San Aung and Sai Kyaw Hla were added last November as part of Washington’s crackdown on the multibillion-dollar border scam industry targeting Americans.

Also sanctioned Thursday was Cambodian national Zhao Hui and two of his scam-linked firms.

“Under President Trump’s leadership, Treasury has aggressively targeted overseas scam compounds to protect Americans from fraud,” said Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent. “We will continue to use all available tools to disrupt and dismantle the networks that enable scam compounds to operate.”

Thursday’s order was the U.S. latest action targeting Myanmar individuals in a crackdown on online scam compounds in Southeast Asia that defrauded an estimated $7.2 billion from Americans in 2025 alone.

The sanctions freeze any U.S.-based assets held by targets and make it illegal for Americans to do business or financial transactions with them.

Saw Shwe Wah took over protection of scam operations in DKBA-held Sone See Myaing, Kyauk Khet, Waw Lay, and Phaya Thonezu in December 2025 after replacing the blacklisted Saw Steel as DKBA’s commander-in-chief.

At least seven scam major compounds were under DKBA protection in 2025. However, staged regime raids on KK Park, Shwe Kokko, and Myawaddy in October and November last year forced a mass relocation to the DKBA’s Sone See Myaing headquarters, while others reportedly dispersed inland to villages under the group’s control.

“Shwe Wah has full oversight. The online scams are operating under his protection since he holds the highest position of the group,” a source familiar with DKBA administration told The Irrawaddy.

“Smaller scam sites are now scattered across DKBA territory. Despite their size they still have concrete buildings.”

He confirmed that DKBA-protected scam operations are concentrated in its Sone See Myaing stronghold, though others have relocated to villages in the Mulayit mountain range, roughly 20 km inside the border.

Following last year’s Myawaddy crackdown — widely dismissed as a publicity stunt — scammers reportedly flocked south to the Thai-Myanmar border town of Phaya Thonezu (Three Pagodas Pass) under the command of Colonel Saw A One.

Washington added him to its sanctions list Thursday, claiming he oversaw an expansion of scam operations and buildings.

“Tens of thousands of fraudsters flooded in here during the crackdown over there [in Myawaddy], turning this place into a large scam hub,” a resident of Phaya Thonezu told The Irrawaddy. “Since then, the scam buildings have expanded.”

He added that restrictions on movement make it difficult to determine the exact number of scam compounds and workers, though he confirmed the presence of two major compounds in the town and many more hidden nearby in restricted forest

The U.S. escalated its border scam crackdown in 2025, sanctioning leaders of the regime-allied Karen National Army (formerly the Karen Border Guard Force) including Saw Chit Thu and his two sons.

Washington has since formed the Scam Center Strike Force with Thailand to seize evidence, intercept fleeing scam bosses, and cut off cross-border supplies to compounds.

Jeanine Pirro, who oversees the Strike Force, met with Thai officials in Bangkok this week to discuss strengthening bilateral intelligence sharing, joint operations, and cross-border crackdowns against the scam syndicates.

The Irrawaddy could not reach DKBA headquarters for comment.

World.title: ‘Ungrateful and Two-Faced’: Why a Chinese Analyst Slammed Myanmar’s Junta Chief
World.content:
Following Myanmar regime leader Min Aung Hlaing’s remarks that appeared to blame China for the initial success of Operation 1027, a Chinese commentator responded that the junta was attempting to dodge its own political failures by simply attributing its opponent’s combat effectiveness to external assistance.

In a speech to the junta’s rubber-stamp parliament on Wednesday, Min Aung Hlaing delivered one of his most pointed public comments yet on Operation 1027, the Brotherhood Alliance offensive in 2023-24 that resulted in the seizure of the Myanmar military’s Northeastern Regional Military Command in Lashio and eventually left the regime stripped of control over most of its key trade routes with China in northern Shan State. The offensive brought about one of the most humiliating defeats in the Myanmar military’s modern history.

The regime chief insisted the Myanmar National Democratic Alliance Army (MNDAA), one of the alliance members, did not prevail through its own strength alone. “The MNDAA attacked with superior weapons, technology and manpower, and all their allies were involved,” he said.

“There are some things we aren’t saying simply because it wouldn’t be appropriate. But there was some outside assistance involved,” Min Aung Hlaing said, his voice filled with rage.

Though he stopped short of identifying the country involved, few observers were left in doubt about the target of his remarks. Among Myanmar political watchers and the public alike, the comments were widely interpreted as a thinly veiled swipe at China, which has long been accused by regime loyalists of turning a blind eye to, or tacitly supporting, the Brotherhood Alliance during the northern Shan offensive.

On Friday, the Chinese commentator, who claims to “specialize in Myanmar and Southeast Asia”, made the comments on Chinese social media platform WeChat under the title “The Myanmar Military’s Misunderstanding of China: An Analysis of Min Aung Hlaing’s Unspoken Accusations”.

The commentator, whom The Irrawaddy has learned is knowledgeable about Myanmar affairs and familiar with Naypyitaw, argued that Min Aung Hlaing’s remarks went beyond an assessment of the military’s battlefield defeats.

“He was not explaining his assessment of the enemy; he was assigning blame. He attributed the EAOs’ victory in Operation 1027 to ‘covert support from China,’” the author says.

The commentator also said the Myanmar military has never been on the pro-China end of the country’s political spectrum. From General Aung San, the founder of the Myanmar military, to successive generations of leaders like Than Shwe, Thein Sein and Min Aung Hlaing, all have been full of misunderstandings and suspicions toward China, the author said.

Regarding the junta’s loss in Operation 1027, the author said the Myanmar military failed to look inward for the cause of the collapse of its combat capability after 2021. “The real collapse occurred internally: troops were replenished through forced conscription, military officers’ families enjoyed special privileges, running businesses within the military was rampant, and grassroots morale was shattered. The Myanmar military has failed to rectify these long-accumulated bad habits,” the author pointed out.

“Shoving all the blame onto ‘external assistance’ is the easiest explanation, but also the one that solves absolutely nothing,” the author added.

China mediated a ceasefire between the alliance and the military in January 2024. In April 2025, under Chinese pressure, the MNDAA withdrew from Lashio, allowing the Myanmar military to re-enter the city.

The author says these developments should have encouraged the Myanmar military to rely more on China’s mediation efforts to facilitate negotiations and de-escalation. Instead, the junta leadership interpreted them differently.

“Instead, not only were they ungrateful, but they stubbornly believed: ‘Since the EAOs listen to China and stop fighting when told to, they must also be taking orders from them to attack the Myanmar military; therefore, any military action by the EAOs must be masterminded by China behind the scenes.’”

“If China were truly covertly supporting the EAOs, Lashio would never have been returned. This is the hardest evidence to refute the ‘covert support’ theory, but unfortunately, it is never mentioned in the Myanmar military’s narrative,” the author argues.

The commentator also pointed out that whenever the Myanmar military wants China to pressure ethnic armed groups, it invokes the concept of pauk-phaw, or fraternal, ties. When it needs China to support its economy, open border ports, or buy agricultural products, it repeats the slogan “China-Myanmar Community With a Shared Future.” Yet, the moment domestic governance goes wrong, it immediately shifts the blame to China, the author says.

“This two-faced mentality of simultaneous dependence and suspicion is currently the deepest rift in China-Myanmar relations.”

World.title: Myanmar Regime Rejects ‘Unfair’ Rohingya Genocide Ruling at ICJ
World.content:
NAYPYITAW—A historic ruling by the top UN court that Myanmar committed genocide against its Rohingya minority was “not fair,” the regime’s presidential spokeswoman said Friday.

The International Court of Justice (ICJ) on Thursday laid out searing evidence of Myanmar’s atrocities against the mostly Muslim Rohingya during a 2017 crackdown in Rakhine State.

Myanmar’s security forces killed thousands of Rohingya civilians, committed “widespread sexual violence” against women and “extreme violence” against children, the court’s president said.

Asked about the ICJ decision at a press conference in the capital Naypyitaw, spokeswoman Khaing Khaing Soe called it unfair.

“When we look at the result, not all 15 judges agreed with the decision,” she said, noting the 9-6 vote.

“So this was not a unanimous decision,” she added. “I would say it is not fair.”

Myanmar had always denied genocide, arguing that its actions targeted a military uprising from insurgents after a series of attacks left a dozen security personnel dead.

But the ICJ ruling dismissed Myanmar’s argument that it was carrying out counter-insurgency operations.

“There is no evidence before the court that, in the conduct of the clearance operations, Myanmar distinguished between civilians and alleged (Rohingya) fighters,” the judgment said.

It was the first time in the ICJ’s 80-year history that its judges have determined that a state committed genocide.

Hundreds of thousands of Rohingya were forced to flee to neighbouring Bangladesh during the crackdown, the court said.

Rohingya villages were “systemically destroyed” and replaced with non-Rohingya inhabitants, it said, ruling that the “only reasonable inference” was that Myanmar intended to destroy the population—a key test for genocide.

No enforcement

The court ordered refugees to be given safe passage home and awarded compensation, with specific sums to be determined later.

While the decisions of the ICJ are binding and cannot be appealed, the court has no way of enforcing its verdicts, and it remains to be seen whether Myanmar’s rulers will adhere to the orders.

But the ruling may heap more international pressure on its leader Min Aung Hlaing, who commanded the military during the Rohingya crackdown before ousting the elected government of Aung San Suu Kyi in a 2021 coup.

This year, Min Aung Hlaing was installed as civilian president following deeply restricted elections and is waging a diplomatic campaign for legitimacy.

China, an enduring partner after the coup, raised concerns of judicial overreach after the ICJ ruling.

One of the ICJ’s judges is from China and voted in Myanmar’s favour on all but one count.

The U.S. reacted with caution, stressing the need to avoid “politicization” of the international court.

Despite determining in 2022 that Myanmar committed genocide against the Rohingya, Washington has more recently pushed back on another case before the court, involving accusations by South Africa that U.S. ally Israel perpetrated genocide in Gaza.

World.title: Min Aung Hlaing Lashes Out at Beijing, Scammer Whac-a-Mole Continues in Shan, and More
World.content:
Min Aung Hlaing hints at Chinese hand in resistance’s Operation 1027

Putschist president Min Aung Hlaing is still groping for an explanation for Operation 1027, the humiliating Brotherhood Alliance offensive in 2023-24 that stripped his regime of most of its key trade routes with China in northern Shan State.

In a speech to the junta’s rubber-stamp parliament on Wednesday, Min Aung Hlaing delivered one of his most pointed public comments yet on the offensive.

He insisted the ethnic Chinese Myanmar National Democratic Alliance Army (MNDAA) did not prevail through its own strength alone. “The MNDAA attacked with superior weapons, technology and manpower, and all their allies were involved,” he said.

Then came the interesting part: “There are some things we aren’t saying simply because it wouldn’t be appropriate. But there was some outside assistance involved,” he added.

Though he stopped short of identifying the country, few observers were left in doubt that it was a swipe at China, which has long been accused by regime loyalists of turning a blind eye to, or tacitly supporting, the Brotherhood Alliance.

The comments echoed Min Aung Hlaing’s complaints at the height of Operation 1027, when he publicly alleged that the MNDAA had used Chinese-made drones and advanced technology in attacks on regime positions.

They come after Chinese Special Envoy Deng Xijun delivered a body blow to Naypyitaw by urging “high-level autonomy” for ethnic minorities, a suggestion that flies in the face of the military regime’s centralization doctrine.

Regime chief fingers neighbors for sustaining ‘insurgents’

In the same outburst, Min Aung Hlaing also accused the two neighbors that have made the biggest effort to accommodate his regime—China and Thailand—of sustaining “insurgents” by encouraging trade through border crossings they control.

He started with Kachin Independence Army (KIA) and MNDAA, which now control much of Myanmar’s border with China. “In Kachin, the KIA runs border gates at the Chinese border. In northeastern Myanmar, the MNDAA runs Chinshwehaw gate,” he said.

“Taxation from illegal trade has sustained and financed insurgents,” he complained.

In Kachin, the regime has also lost control over the lucrative rare earth mines, which are now a major source of revenues for the KIA. The situation is not much different in northern Shan, where the regime has lost key border crossings with Yunnan as well as rare earth and other mineral resources.

On the surface, he was only accusing Thailand of directly facilitating trade through resistance-held territory at the Thaw Le Hta crossing in Hpapun, avoiding direct accusations against China except by inference and association.

Chinese Customs figures show a steady increase in cross-border trade through crossings controlled by the MNDAA and its allies. Trade through the Chinshwehaw border crossing alone reached 5.01 billion yuan (about US$700 million) so far this year. The central regime is reduced to heavy-handed efforts to “tax” this trade once goods reach military-controlled areas.

China steps up media ‘outreach’ in Myanmar to shape narrative

China stepped up efforts to shape Myanmar’s information space this week, gathering regime-aligned media figures, officials and commentators in Yangon to promote President Xi Jinping’s four flagship global initiatives.

Speaking at a symposium at the Wyndham Grand Yangon Hotel on Tuesday with over 160 participants, Chinese Ambassador Ma Jia highlighted growing bilateral cooperation in security, governance and people-to-people exchanges. Myanmar is the first country to sign up to all four of Xi’s initiatives, which also include AI.

Ma listed the usual talking points, from law-enforcement cooperation to combat cross-border crimes, including online scam operations, to cultural and media exchanges aimed at strengthening “mutual understanding.” Echoing Chinese President Xi Jinping and Foreign Minister Wang Yi, she called for key projects of the China-Myanmar Economic Corridor (CMEC) to be hurried along.

The event brought together stalwart regime propagandists like Lower House MP Aye Chan, Myanmar Press Council Chairman Dr. Tin Tun Oo, Myanmar Narrative Think Tank chairman Ko Ko, plus figures from regime and regime-aligned media.

Days earlier, Myanmar Foreign Ministry-backed think tank MISIS and state-owned China Media Group gathered academics, media representatives and officials in Yangon to discuss future areas of China-Myanmar cooperation aligned with Beijing’s 15th Five-Year Plan.

The forums follow a similar gathering hosted by Ma in May, when she called on regime-linked media and opinion leaders to tell “beautiful stories” about China.

Chinese-run scam industry lives on in southern Shan

Myanmar’s regime says it arrested 23 Chinese nationals and seized three assault rifles in a raid on an alleged online scam and gambling operation in Laihka Township in southern Shan State on Wednesday.

They were detained at a makeshift compound deep in the forest comprising a workshop, living quarters and a kitchen. A tally compiled from regime media reports suggests some 90 Chinese scammers have been arrested in raids since February in Laihka, which has emerged as a new scam hotspot since 2025.

They take advantage of the lawless environment amid competing territorial claims of local militias as well as the Shan State Progressive Party/Shan State Army (SSPP/SSA), and the Restoration Council of Shan State/Shan State Army (RCSS/SSA).

Even as a docuseries on Myanmar’s scam industry broadcast on Chinese state media last month sold the 2024 crackdown on scam hubs in northern Shan State’s Laukkai as an unmitigated success, the criminal gangs simply scattered across eastern and southern Shan instead. According to the independent Institute for Strategy and Policy–Myanmar, operations have since been identified in at least 17 Shan townships including Tangyan, Tachileik and Muse.

Meanwhile, ASEAN and the U.S., meeting in Manila this week, adopted what was billed as a “partnership work plan” to tackle online scams and thereby increase international pressure on Myanmar’s regime. Regime leader Min Aung Hlaing was not invited to the summit.

Complied by Thurein Lynn

World.title: US Warns Against ‘Politicization’ of ICJ, Studying Myanmar Ruling
World.content:
WASHINGTON—The U.S. State Department reacted with caution to the International Court of Justice’s ruling that Myanmar committed genocide against its Rohingya minority, saying Washington was examining the decision while stressing the need to avoid “politicization” of the body.

Washington’s wary response comes as the United States determined in 2022 that Myanmar committed genocide against the Rohingya people.

But it has more recently pushed back on another case before the top UN court, involving accusations by South Africa that US ally Israel perpetrated genocide in Gaza.

“The proper interpretation of the Genocide Convention is of paramount importance, as is preventing politicization of the ICJ,” said a State Department spokesperson on Thursday.

“We are studying the decision to fully assess its implications,” the official added, referring to the Myanmar ruling.

The US statement comes as the top UN court ordered refugees to be given safe passage home and awarded compensation.

The decision marked the first time in its 80-year history that ICJ judges determined a state committed genocide. It is likely to be viewed as justice for Rohingya victims of Myanmar’s deadly 2017 crackdown on the mostly Muslim minority.

The US official said Thursday: “We express our support for the people of Burma and share the grave concerns over the continued abuses of human rights against Rohingya Muslims and members of other minority groups.”

The official also called for more burden-sharing in the humanitarian response for Rohingya refugees.

For more than one million Rohingya living in the world’s largest refugee camp over the border in Bangladesh, the landmark ruling offered hope for accountability.

World.title: Five Key Points From Historic ICJ Rohingya Genocide Ruling
World.content:
THE HAGUE, Netherlands—The International Court of Justice has ruled that Myanmar committed genocide against its Rohingya minority—the first time the UN top court has determined a state responsible for the world’s worst crime.

Here are the key points from the 191-page ruling, which took nearly three hours to read out in court and is the second-longest in the ICJ’s 80-year history.

Genocide

This was what the hundreds of thousands of Rohingya victims were waiting for: did the atrocities they suffered clear the high bar under international law to be labelled a genocide?

In the end, the ICJ—known for dressing up its rulings in impenetrable legalese—was refreshingly clear.

Myanmar “has committed genocide against the Rohingya group in northern Rakhine State,” said the ruling, which was passed by nine votes to six.

By the same margin, the court found Myanmar had failed in its obligations under the 1948 UN Genocide Convention to prevent the crime.

The ICJ ordered Myanmar to take “immediate and effective steps” to prosecute and punish anyone suspected of genocidal acts.

Myanmar must stop any ongoing acts of genocide and prevent similar violations of the Convention in future.

To prove genocide, judges have to be satisfied not only that genocidal acts have occurred but also there was intention to destroy a given community—a notoriously tricky legal hurdle.

However, the judges ruled that the “only reasonable inference” was that Myanmar intended to destroy “a substantial part” of the Rohingya people.

Safe return

Having concluded that genocide occurred, the court also issued rulings on the consequences for Myanmar—so-called “remedies” in the legal jargon.

It ordered several actions from Myanmar.

The authorities must “allow and facilitate the safe, voluntary and dignified return” of refugees displaced either within Myanmar or abroad.

They must also “return or replace in kind all individual and collective property” that was lost in the violent crackdown.

The Rohingya must also be offered “physical and psychological rehabilitation” for the harms they suffered, the judges ruled.

Reparations

The Rohingya are entitled to “adequate compensation” for the harms caused by the genocide.

The ICJ did not set an amount, saying that would be determined at a later phase.

It gave Myanmar two years to file a report setting out the “amount and modalities” of compensation.

After receiving the report, the ICJ will decide whether Myanmar’s proposal is sufficient.

Investigations

The ICJ is a court that settles disputes between countries, unlike its neighbor the International Criminal Court, which weighs individual responsibility.

However, the ICJ ruling tasks Myanmar with conducting a “prompt” investigation into anyone suspected of committing genocidal acts.

Judges ruled that previous efforts in Myanmar to probe atrocities were insufficient.

“Myanmar has not genuinely investigated or, if warranted, prosecuted its soldiers and commanders and punished them,” the ICJ said.

Scale of killings

The court said that an estimate of at least 10,000 deaths in the crackdown, established by an independent UN fact-finding mission, was “supported by the record.”

“The evidence before the court demonstrates the pervasive and lethal nature of the violence… and establishes that thousands of Rohingya civilians were killed by the Myanmar security forces,” said the ICJ.

The court said there were approximately 815,000 Rohingya in Rakhine State at the time of the crackdown, meaning those killed constituted 1.2 percent of the population.

The majority of the survivors fled to neighboring Bangladesh.

The ICJ also said there were at least 1,834 acts of rape during the 2017 “clearance operations.”

World.title: ICJ Rules Myanmar Committed Genocide Against Rohingya
World.content:
The United Nations’ top court, the International Court of Justice (ICJ), ruled on Thursday that Myanmar committed genocide against the Rohingya during military operations in 2017, in a historic decision.

In the case brought by the Gambia, the ICJ delivered the first ruling in its 80-year history finding a state responsible for committing genocide.

“The Republic of the Union of Myanmar has committed genocide against the Rohingya group in northern Rakhine State, in violation of its obligations under the Convention on the Prevention and Punishment of the Crime of Genocide,” ICJ President Yuji Iwasawa said, delivering the court’s verdict.

Iwasawa said around 10,000 Rohingya were killed during the 2017 “clearance operations,” which also involved widespread sexual violence and violence against children, as the Rohingya fled en masse to Bangladesh.

“Records also contain evidence of intentional targeting of the Rohingya population,” Iwasawa said.

The court found that Myanmar deliberately targeted the approximately 815,000 Rohingya who lived in northern Rakhine before the operation.

Rohingya villages were systematically destroyed and their populations replaced with non-Rohingya inhabitants, the ICJ said, ruling that the only reasonable inference was that Myanmar intended to destroy the population—a key test for genocide.

The ICJ president said Myanmar had failed to investigate, prosecute and punish those responsible for acts punishable under Article III of the Genocide Convention.

The Myanmar military also disseminated and promoted hate speech in a systematic and coordinated way during the 2017 operation, the court said.

The court ordered Myanmar to cease any ongoing violations of its obligations under the Genocide Convention and to “allow and facilitate the safe, voluntary and dignified return” of those who fled the violence to their homes. It also ruled that Myanmar must investigate suspected perpetrators and prosecute and punish those found responsible, and provide compensation. The amount would be determined in future proceedings, it said.

The ruling cannot be appealed. Rather than prosecuting individuals, the verdict determined that Myanmar bears state responsibility for genocide.

As a result of the military operation in Rakhine, over one million Rohingya now live in what is effectively the world’s largest refugee camp over the border in Bangladesh. For some of them, the case offered a glimmer of hope for accountability.

“I want justice,” a 23-year-old Rohingya rape survivor told AFP before the verdict in the cramped shelter where she lives with her family.

“There should be stringent punishment for those who raped women. The ICJ should say something separately about this,” she said, requesting anonymity.

“This is a historic ruling. For the first time, the World Court has found a state responsible for committing genocide—and the man who commanded those operations is now Myanmar’s president,” said Richard Horsey, senior adviser for Asia at the International Crisis Group.

Horsey pointed out that the court lacks the power to enforce the orders contained in its ruling.

“What matters now is whether the governments engaging Naypyitaw are prepared to attach any cost to ignoring it,” he said.

Myanmar should comply with the court’s judgment and end its oppression of the Rohingya, said Maria Elena Vignoli, senior international justice counsel at Human Rights Watch.

“Concerned governments should strongly support the Rohingya and promote justice for atrocities, press Myanmar’s junta to comply with the judgment, and ensure the safe and voluntary return of Rohingya refugees to Myanmar,” she said.

Agnès Callamard, secretary general of Amnesty International, said international governments should not welcome putschist president and former Senior General Min Aung Hlaing, who oversaw a campaign of crimes against humanity and other crimes under international law against the Rohingya.

“Instead, they should stop any transfer of all weapons, security and surveillance equipment, and military and security assistance to Myanmar,” she said.

All other states, including members of the Association of Southeast Asian Nations, must also uphold these obligations under the Genocide Convention and general international law, taking every measure within their power to prevent and punish genocide, Callamard said.

She urged the UN Security Council to impose a global arms embargo and refer the entire situation in Myanmar to the International Criminal Court.

The Myanmar military’s 2017 “clearance operations” in northern Rakhine State forced more than 700,000 Rohingya to flee amid widespread killings, sexual violence and arson attacks, according to UN investigations.

World.title: Trump, Xi and Putin at One Table: What Does It Mean for Central Asia?
World.content:
ASTANA — The unprecedented gathering of the leaders of the United States (U.S.), China and Russia projected an image of great-power diplomacy. The image was striking: Donald Trump, Xi Jinping and Vladimir Putin sitting at the same table in China, the leaders of the world’s three biggest nuclear powers convening in an unprecedented trilateral meeting. The summit in Shenzhen on Nov. 19, held on the sidelines of the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) meetings, carried unmistakable symbolism and inevitably revived comparisons to the Yalta Conference of 1945, when Allied leaders discussed the postwar order.

Trump declared they were “really making history,” while Xi spoke of peace when major powers live in harmony. Yet the summit produced little concrete progress on the conflicts and disagreements that brought the leaders together. The three issued a symbolic declaration reaffirming that nuclear war must never be fought and agreed to pursue dialogue on reducing nuclear risks, but announced no arms-control negotiations or breakthroughs on Ukraine, Iran, trade or other major disputes. The spectacle was historic. Its substance was considerably more modest.

The distinction matters for Central Asia, a region positioned between Russia and China, increasingly connected to global trade routes, and working to maintain relationships with the U.S., Europe and other partners. If the meeting offered a glimpse of a world managed by its biggest powers, did it signal a shift in the international system or simply demonstrate how difficult it remains for them to agree? For Kazakhstan and its neighbors, the answer may lie less in what the three leaders agreed on than in what their meeting reveals about the limits and opportunities of great-power politics.

No new geopolitical bargain

Temur Umarov, a fellow at the Carnegie Russia Eurasia Center whose research focuses on Central Asian foreign and domestic policies and China’s relations with Russia and the region, sees little evidence that the summit represents a fundamental geopolitical shift.

“I don’t think that we’re living in times of major geopolitical shift. I don’t think that this trilateral summit has started a new chapter in the history of global politics,” Umarov said in a comment to The Astana Times.

Rather than a breakthrough, he sees the gathering as largely symbolic, with its limited outcomes reflecting the current state of international relations. He said that the fact that the leaders could agree only on broad, formal principles speaks to how difficult it is to reconcile their competing interests.

The summit was always unlikely to produce a major agreement, Umarov said, given the state of international politics and the differences among the three powers.

But he cautioned against interpreting this uncertainty as necessarily negative for countries caught between competing powers.

“For countries like Kazakhstan or other Central Asian countries, or other regions that are in between these countries that are in rivalry or in confrontation, it doesn’t necessarily mean that it’s a bad period or dark times. It actually provides a lot of ground for maneuver,” Umarov said.

That space, he noted, can open opportunities for deeper cooperation with different partners: provided regional governments can translate the attention they receive into tangible benefits.

Central Asian governments, accustomed to navigating competing interests, have become adept at multilateral diplomacy. The region’s growing international visibility is no accident, Umarov said, as countries seek to turn current geopolitical momentum into something more concrete. The challenge, however, is to convert diplomatic access into economic partnerships, investment, connectivity and political leverage, rather than simply enjoy a moment in the global spotlight.

The danger of being placed on someone else’s map

Ken Moriyasu, a senior fellow at the Hudson Institute focusing on Greater Asia, takes a more cautionary view of what a great-power arrangement could mean for countries across Eurasia. Moriyasu notes that Washington should be careful about institutionalizing a trilateral format with Beijing and Moscow, warning that the U.S. could find itself negotiating from a structurally disadvantaged position.

“I do not believe President Donald Trump went to China to divide the world into spheres of influence with Xi Jinping and Vladimir Putin,” Moriyasu said in a comment to The Astana Times.

He believes Trump was pursuing specific objectives, including nuclear arms reductions, and hoping for a diplomatic breakthrough. But the underlying problem, Moriyasu said, is that China and Russia share a strategic interest in challenging U.S. global leadership, potentially putting Washington in a two-against-one position.

Instead, he advocates elevating the Board of Peace as a diplomatic platform where the U.S. could work with countries that seek greater engagement with Washington while maintaining independence amid great-power competition. He identifies Kazakhstan, Uzbekistan, Azerbaijan, Armenia, Türkiye, Pakistan, Mongolia and Hungary among strategically positioned countries whose interests include preserving their autonomy.

His argument carries a warning for Kazakhstan and the wider region: a world organized around spheres of influence could narrow the space for independent foreign policy. In such a scenario, Kazakhstan could risk being viewed through the prism of Russia’s traditional influence or China’s expanding continental reach, rather than as a sovereign actor pursuing its own priorities.

That is precisely the outcome Astana’s balanced and constructive diplomacy is designed to avoid.

World.title: Almaty Named Among BBC Travel’s 20 Best Places to Visit in 2027
World.content:
ASTANA – Almaty has been named the only Central Asian city among BBC Travel’s 20 best places to visit in 2027, with the British publication highlighting its contemporary art scene, traditional crafts, national cuisine and mountain landscapes.

The annual list also features Burgundy in France, Sardinia in Italy, Alberta in Canada and Christchurch in New Zealand. This year’s selection focuses on destinations where tourism supports cultural heritage preservation, environmental protection and local communities.

BBC Travel recommends exploring Almaty, located at the foothills of the mountains, through its growing cultural scene and connections to Kazakhstan’s traditions.

Among the featured attractions is the Almaty Museum of Arts, which the publication describes as the first major contemporary art museum in Central Asia. Opened in September 2025, its collection includes works by artists from Kazakhstan and other countries in the region.

The publication also highlights Tselinny Center of Contemporary Culture, housed in a former cinema renovated by British architect Asif Khan. The restoration included the preservation of graffiti artwork by prominent artist Yevgeny Sidorkin.

The city’s culinary scene also features in the selection. BBC Travel recommends the Auyl restaurant, located in the Medeu area, for its contemporary interpretation of Kazakh cuisine. Its architecture draws inspiration from the traditional Kazakh yurt, while the interior features carpets and handmade decorations.

Among the dishes highlighted by the publication are horse meat tartare and bone marrow served with flatbread. The restaurant also offers mountain views and can be included in a trip to Medeu and Shymbulak.

World.title: Love, Loneliness and Algorithms: How AI Is Entering Our Personal Lives
World.content:
ASTANA – Artificial intelligence is increasingly becoming a confidant for people navigating loneliness, emotional struggles and complicated relationships. Chatbots offer instant advice, a sympathetic response and a seemingly nonjudgmental space to discuss personal problems. In some cases, they are taking on roles traditionally filled by friends, therapists or relationship counselors.

From analyzing text messages and preparing users for difficult conversations to offering emotional reassurance, AI tools are becoming part of people’s private lives. It can act as a dating coach, help interpret a partner’s messages, offer guidance during a personal crisis or simply serve as a companion available around the clock. However, as the line between digital assistance and emotional intimacy grows less distinct, questions about psychological dependence, accountability and the limits of artificial companionship are becoming harder to ignore.

Humans are inherently social, according to the 2025 report of the World Health Organization’s Commission on Social Connection. Social interaction shapes brain development and mental health throughout life, while strong social connections are essential to overall well-being.

Yet loneliness and social isolation remain widespread. Between 2014 and 2023, one in six people worldwide experienced loneliness, the report found. Social disconnection is associated with increased risks of heart disease, stroke, depression and anxiety, as well as difficulties at school, university and work.

Against this backdrop, AI is increasingly entering a space traditionally occupied by human relationships.

Meta CEO Mark Zuckerberg has also discussed AI’s potential role in addressing people’s need for connection. Speaking on a podcast, he said people want to feel understood, express themselves and avoid loneliness. He suggested that AI could become an additional source of support, particularly for those who do not have access to a therapist.

Zuckerberg also described how users turn to Meta AI to talk through personal problems, prepare for difficult conversations or discuss relationship issues. He said voice-based AI could make these interactions more useful by allowing people to rehearse conversations.

At the same time, Zuckerberg said AI should complement, not replace, human relationships, helping people become more thoughtful and attentive in their interactions with others.

An always-available listener

“Tell me if you want to talk about it. I’m here.”

ChatGPT responds with variations of this reassuring message to users who bring personal problems to the chatbot. It creates an environment that can feel comfortable and safe, where users feel heard and accepted.

Muragul Muratbekova, a software engineer and research associate at the Kazakhstan-British Technical University, said AI has become part of everyday life across almost every field, and she is no exception.

“I often use AI for work, and it definitely helps me automate routine tasks. I also use it in everyday life. For example, when I’m cooking, it’s much easier to ask AI for a recipe. There are millions of recipes online, and you have to spend time choosing one. AI narrows down the options, so you do not have to waste your energy on that,” Muratbekova told The Astana Times.

She also uses AI as a digital wardrobe assistant.

“You can take pictures of all your clothes, tell AI which city you live in, what the weather is like and what your lifestyle looks like. It can then help you put together a capsule wardrobe, suggest what to get rid of and what to buy. Normally, people spend hours browsing the internet and scrolling through pictures to get inspiration. Now you can simply delegate these small decisions to AI,” she said.

Muratbekova noted that she does not necessarily consider AI a friend, but she does see people using it as a kind of psychologist.

“I think it’s partly because life moves so fast. I cannot always wait for my friends to be free, or wait for an appointment with a psychologist. Everything feels urgent, and you want to find a solution right away, whatever the problem is. Maybe we have just become used to getting everything here and now,” she said.

In this sense, AI can act as a first-response tool. It may help ease emotional distress or make a problem feel more manageable in the moment.

However, it does not necessarily offer a lasting solution. There is also a question of whether temporary relief leads to lasting benefits. If interacting with AI encourages people to build real-world connections, it may be helpful. But if it replaces contact with friends, family and other people, the long-term effects could be quite different.

Muratbekova finds AI useful for discussing health concerns, particularly topics that may feel uncomfortable to raise with other people.

“AI is also useful for health-related questions. Of course, it doesn’t replace a doctor, and everyone should understand that. But sometimes you are simply not sure what’s normal and what isn’t. AI chatbots can be particularly helpful with topics you might not feel comfortable discussing with other people,” she said.

Muratbekova does not believe AI will replace professional psychologists. However, she thinks it is more likely to replace jobs that do not require emotional engagement or personal responsibility.

“First, AI does not have empathy. Second, it tells you things you already know, essentially reflecting your own thoughts. Working with a psychologist helps you develop new behavioral strategies and ways of thinking. Psychologists conduct extensive research and preparation to guide their clients. AI, by contrast, tends to follow the direction in which the user leads it,” she said.

AI enters the dating scene

Online dating has quickly become another testing ground for AI.

Some people are skilled at creating attractive profiles and writing witty self-descriptions. For many others, however, putting together a dating profile can be a challenge. AI can make the process easier.

Some users ask ChatGPT to edit their photographs or generate images that look like they came from a professional photo shoot. Some practice conversations with virtual partners, while others let AI handle exchanges with real people in an effort to arrange dates more quickly.

Muratbekova noted that AI can save time in the dating process.

“One of my friends uses ChatGPT to review dating profiles and identify people who might be a good match. The chatbot can even help initiate conversations with potential partners, making the search for a compatible match easier,” she said.

AI can also help people prepare for a date by suggesting venues, activities and conversation topics, or even rehearsing jokes and possible responses.

“Dating has its ups and downs, and you always want someone to share your experiences and concerns with. AI is always available. I think I would turn to it more as an adviser, especially when I’m struggling to understand someone else’s behavior,” Muratbekova said.

ChatGPT can analyze messages users upload, assess each person’s contributions to a conversation, and validate the user’s feelings. It can then offer an interpretation of what happened – one that may closely reflect the user’s own version of events, shaped by the information and perspective they provide in their prompts.

The user is, after all, at the center of the interaction. The AI sees only the information it receives, which means that the other person’s perspective, intentions and feelings may be missing from the analysis.

The risks of artificial intimacy

Ekaterina Talimanchuk, a therapist, noted that AI systems learn about users’ preferences and interests and then mirror them in their responses.

“AI can create the feeling that it understands you completely. That’s why people can become attached to it quite quickly and start turning to it more and more. But we need to remember that AI cannot replace human communication, with all its empathy, disagreements and different points of view,” Talimanchuk told The Astana Times.

She warned that becoming accustomed to constant agreement from AI could make people less tolerant of differences in real-life relationships.

Chatbots can adapt to users’ preferences and respond to almost any request, while partners and friends have their own opinions, ambitions and needs, which do not always align with ours.

Talimanchuk described excessive interaction with AI as a potential “dopamine trap,” warning that avoiding uncomfortable conversations and criticism could make people less prepared to deal with difficulties in real life.

“AI does not frustrate or criticize you, and avoiding uncomfortable situations can make people less mature and resilient. But dealing with difficulties is necessary. It’s an important part of personal development and growth,” she said.

She also emphasized that AI systems can make mistakes and should not be used as a substitute for professional intervention in serious situations.

“Mental health crises, suicidal thoughts, and complex trauma require immediate professional help. An algorithm may offer some support, but it should never become someone’s only source of help. Human contact remains essential to effective therapy,” Talimanchuk said.

Ultimately, she said, no algorithm can replace genuine human interaction.

“No algorithm can replace real human connection – a simple touch, the warmth of a loving gaze, that awkward pause before someone first admits their feelings. Relationships are not always perfect, and they can be difficult. However, we need to build them face to face, not through smartphone screens,” Talimanchuk said.

World.title: Caspian Seals Under Threats as Shrinking Sea Reshapes Their Habitat
World.content:
ASTANA – Falling water levels and shrinking ice cover in the Caspian Sea as well as human activity are putting pressure on the habitats seals depend on to rest and raise their pups. In an interview with The Astana Times, Assel Baimukanova, a researcher at the Institute of Hydrobiology and Ecology, said that protecting the species requires stronger regional cooperation and continued research.

She said changes in the sea are disrupting the animals’ natural habitat, particularly in the northern Caspian, where they rely on islands for resting and winter ice for breeding.

“The health of the Caspian Sea is the health of the Caspian seal. By observing the condition of the seals, we can understand the condition of the sea. And right now, the sea is not doing very well,” said Baimukanova, who has studied Caspian seals for 13 years.

Baimukanova has taken part in more than 30 field expeditions. With her family, she also makes documentary films about the species. Their team has produced nine films about the Caspian seal.

During regular expeditions, she has observed how the sea and the animals’ living conditions have changed over time.

“I first saw the seals in 2013, and I realized that I wanted to stay close to them, study them and work for their protection,” she said.

Shrinking habitat

The Caspian Sea, shared by Kazakhstan, Russia, Azerbaijan, Turkmenistan and Iran, is divided into northern, middle and southern sections. The Northern Caspian plays an important role in the seals’ seasonal cycle, as the animals use its islands and shallow waters as resting areas.

In spring, the seals gather to molt before moving to feeding grounds to build up energy for winter. In fall, they return to the islands to rest until ice forms. The ice is particularly important because Caspian seals give birth and raise their pups on it.

But falling water levels and shrinking water ice are disrupting this seasonal cycle.

“The current period of sea-level decline began in 1995. Since then, the level of the Northern Caspian has fallen by 2.28 meters. This affects coastal areas and gradually changes the islands and shallow waters that provide important habitats for the animals,” Baimukanova said.

Researchers counted approximately 25,000 seals at the Durnev Islands in Komsomolets Bay in the northeastern Caspian during a helicopter survey in April 2009. The count fell to 20,000 in April 2011. Photographs from those years show large groups resting along the shores.

When Kazakh researchers surveyed the same islands in 2016, they found only around 300 seals. By 2019, the number had dropped to 69. By 2021, the Durnev Islands had merged with the mainland and ceased to exist, and seals no longer haul out there.

“The islands where the seals used to gather are disappearing. They need these places to rest, molt and prepare for winter, but there are fewer suitable areas now,” Baimukanova said.

According to a satellite-imagery analysis published by the team in Frontiers in Marine Science in 2026, the northeastern coast of the Caspian Sea in Kazakhstan has been retreating westward. The study covered the area from the mouth of the Ural (Zhaiyk) River to the Buzachi Peninsula, including Kaydak and Komsomolets bays.

“The coastline retreated by an average of around 2.7 kilometers per year until 2020. Between spring 2022 and spring 2023, however, it shifted by 23 kilometers in a single year,” Baimukanova explained.

Over 1995–2023, the coastline moved by an average of 44 kilometers along most of this stretch and by up to 175 kilometers near Kaydak Bay, while the total area of islands shrank more than 15-fold. These changes make it increasingly difficult for researchers to monitor habitats and for seals to find suitable resting places.

Climate change and human activity

Falling sea levels are not the only concern. Climate change is also affecting the availability of ice, which is essential to the reproduction of Caspian seals.

“Where will Caspian seals reproduce if the ice disappears? This is one of the main questions we need to understand,” Baimukanova said.

Human activity is adding to the pressure. The Volga and Ural rivers are major sources of freshwater flowing into the Caspian Sea, but water regulation and withdrawals for economic activities affect how much reaches the sea.

Fishing nets, marine pollution, shipping, tourism and offshore oil and gas activities pose additional risks. Some seals become trapped in abandoned fishing gear, while human activity can disturb their resting areas.

Between 2019 and 2023, scientists examined 395 seal remains and found that 9.4% bore marks of entanglement in fishing nets.

Over five years of fieldwork, researchers also collected more than 36 tons of marine waste, including approximately 17 tons of abandoned fishing nets.

“During one of our visits to a coastal area on the Tyub-Karagan Peninsula in 2013, we recorded around eight tons of rubbish. When we returned five years later, the amount had increased to nine tons. This shows that waste remains a persistent problem along the Caspian coast,” she said.

What research reveals about the seals

Monitoring Caspian seals requires regular fieldwork and multiple research methods. Since 2016, Kazakh scientists have conducted state-commissioned studies, building on earlier research by international teams.

Scientists use drones, aircraft and satellite imagery to count seals, track their distribution and identify changes in their habitats. They also use satellite imagery to identify new islands and resting sites. Researchers also conduct boat-based surveys to monitor conditions in the Caspian Sea.

“Recent aerial counts on island haul-outs in the north-eastern Caspian have raised further concerns about the animals’ numbers and distribution. Researchers counted 59,642 seals on the surveyed islands in spring 2020 and 62,105 in spring 2022. By autumn 2023, the number had fallen to 44,573. These figures refer to seals counted on the surveyed islands, not to the total population of the species,” Baimukanova said.

Researchers also study the seals’ diet and health. Their findings show that Caspian seals feed primarily on small fish, particularly gobies, rather than commercially valuable species.

“Researchers also examine the age of the animals by studying the teeth of dead seals found along the coast. This helps estimate how old they were when they died. In earlier observations, the oldest recorded seals were 50 years old. In more recent research, the oldest recorded animals were 32, while few individuals were found to have reached 20,” she said.

Determining the causes of death remains difficult because researchers need fresh carcasses to conduct detailed laboratory and toxicological examinations. However, available findings point to serious health problems among the animals.

Baimukanova said pollution can weaken the seals’ immune systems, making them more vulnerable to disease. When animals gather in large numbers, infections can also spread more easily.

Efforts to protect the species

Kazakhstan has taken several steps to strengthen the protection of the Caspian seal. The species was included in Kazakhstan’s list of rare and endangered animals in 2020. In 2024, a specially protected natural area dedicated to its conservation was established. Kazakhstan and Russia have also developed a joint action plan, while a seal rehabilitation center is planned within the protected area.

“Further efforts should focus on reducing pollution, preventing illegal fishing and protecting the places where the animals gather. However, the conservation of the Caspian seal cannot be the responsibility of one country alone. Since the Caspian Sea is shared by five states, cooperation among all of them is essential to protecting the species and its habitat,” Baimukanova said.

For researchers, the work also means drawing attention to animals that cannot communicate their problems themselves.

“I think every zoologist considers themselves the voice of the animal they study. The Caspian seal cannot knock on our door and tell us that it is struggling or ask us to improve its living conditions. It cannot speak for itself, so we have to speak for it,” Baimukanova said.

Her words underline a broader point: the fate of the Caspian seal is closely tied to the health of the sea it inhabits. Protecting the species means protecting the ecosystem on which both wildlife and people depend.

World.title: Kazakhstan Secures $1.2 Billion in COP31 Deals in Antalya
World.content:
ASTANA — The world has two years to assess whether countries are doing enough to meet the goals of the Paris Agreement, as governments face growing pressure to turn climate pledges into measurable progress.

The countdown began on Nov. 18 at the UN Climate Conference in Antalya, Türkiye, also known as COP31, which kicked off on Nov. 9. There, countries launched the second Global Stocktake, a review of collective efforts to cut greenhouse gas emissions, adapt to climate change and mobilize financing. The process will conclude in 2028, just two years before a 2030 deadline for global climate targets.

“This is a major moment in the international climate process. And a major opportunity,” said UN Climate Change Executive Secretary Simon Stiell at the high-level on the launch of global stocktake.

The first stocktake, completed in Dubai in 2023, helped establish global goals to triple renewable energy capacity, double the rate of energy efficiency improvements by 2030 and accelerate the transition away from fossil fuels in energy systems.

According to Stiell, nearly 90% of countries have incorporated the outcomes of the first global climate stocktake into their national climate plans.

Concrete projects and investments

For Kazakhstan, the challenge is of translating its own climate ambitions into concrete projects and investments. This effort has to go together with balancing the demands of economic growth, energy security and environmental protection.

In an interview with The Astana Times, Saule Sabiyeva, director of the Climate Policy Department at the Ministry of Ecology and Natural Resources, outlined three priorities emerging from COP31: mobilizing climate finance, strengthening regional cooperation on water security and accelerating the decarbonization of the economy.

Kazakhstan has also signed agreements worth approximately $1.2 billion for renewable energy and gas infrastructure projects at the climate summit in Antalya, as the country seeks to turn its emissions reduction commitments into investments and accelerate its transition to a lower-carbon economy.

According to Sabiyeva, among the projects are a 150-megawatt wind farm in the Turkistan Region and a one gigawatt wind farm in the Kostanai Region. Another agreement provides for the Aqyl Energy project, which aims to introduce 1.35 million smart gas meters with remote data transmission across Kazakhstan’s gasified regions.

The ministry also signed framework agreements on detecting and eliminating methane leaks in gas distribution networks and restoring degraded land in the Almaty Region. Both initiatives envisage cooperation under Article 6 of the Paris Agreement, which provides mechanisms for countries to cooperate on emissions reductions, including through carbon markets

Closing financing gap

One of the major development at COP31 was the presentation of Kazakhstan’s Country Climate Investment Platform (QCIP), designed to bring together government agencies, international financial institutions, climate funds and private investors around a pipeline of priority projects.

Kazakhstan also advances the Qazaqstan Just Energy Transition investment platform (QaJET), developed with support from the European Bank for Reconstruction and Development.

QaJET aims to mobilize approximately $20 billion in investment to help deliver at least 10 gigawatts of new renewable energy capacity by 2035, alongside electricity grid upgrades, energy storage and electrification.

“The next step will be to translate our updated Nationally Determined Contribution [NDC 3.0] into a concrete investment program, identifying the required financial resources, implementation mechanisms and responsible stakeholders,” Sabiyeva explained.

Under its updated NDCs, which Kazakhstan submitted in October 2025, the nation aims to reduce greenhouse gas emissions by 17% below 1990 levels by 2035, with a conditional target of 25% if international support is available. Kazakhstan has also committed to achieving carbon neutrality by 2060.

Meeting those goals will require substantial changes to an energy system that remains heavily dependent on fossil fuels. Coal accounts for nearly 60% of Kazakhstan’s electricity generation, underscoring the challenge of expanding cleaner power while meeting growing electricity demand.

The scale of the financing challenge remains considerable. According to the United Nations Development Programme, Kazakhstan estimates that implementing its updated national climate plan will require $71.8 billion in investment.

“Priority areas include renewable energy development, electricity grid modernization, energy efficiency improvements and methane emissions reduction. We are also advancing the Just Energy Transition platform, QaJET, which aims to facilitate the development of at least 10 gigawatts of renewable energy capacity by 2035,” Sabiyeva said.

Water security and regional cooperation

Alongside emissions reductions, Kazakhstan is seeking stronger regional cooperation to address the growing impact of climate change on Central Asia’s water resources, agriculture and ecosystems.

“For Kazakhstan, climate change is not merely a matter of reducing greenhouse gas emissions. It is also directly linked to water security, food security and ecosystem resilience,” said Sabiyeva.

“This is why cooperation among Central Asian countries is particularly important. We need closer coordination in monitoring glaciers, river flows and water consumption, as well as stronger cooperation on the management of transboundary water resources,” she explained.

The priorities include improving hydrological monitoring, strengthening agricultural resilience, restoring the Northern Aral Sea and protecting the Caspian Sea ecosystem.

At COP31. Kazakhstan also promoted its proposal for an international water organization within the United Nations system, seeking stronger coordination on water-related challenges.

Measurable progress

Sabiyeva also pointed to Kazakhstan’s submission of its second Biennial Transparency Report (BTR) under the Paris Agreement, making it one of the first three countries to complete the latest reporting cycle.

The report, presented during COP31, showed that Kazakhstan’s net greenhouse gas emissions in 2024 were 10.06% below 1990 levels, according to UNDP. The findings provide a benchmark against which future progress toward the country’s climate targets can be measured.

“Kazakhstan has also been recognized as a BTR Champion since COP29 [in Baku]. This leadership provides additional momentum for projects in renewable energy, methane emissions reduction, afforestation, land restoration and the digitalization of environmental monitoring,” she said.

Sabiyeva said Kazakhstan seeks to improve its greenhouse gas monitoring, reporting and verification systems, while expanding cooperation under Article 6 to attract financing for emissions reduction projects.

“At the same time, we emphasized that climate commitments must be accompanied by access to international climate finance, modern technologies and appropriate mechanisms for a just energy transition,” Sabiyeva said.

“Ultimately, COP31 should help Kazakhstan move from climate commitments towards measurable results, supported by investment, technology and stronger international partnerships,” she said.
