World.title: Coles appeals ACCC decision blocking Kalgoorlie supermarket
World.content:
As the crows flies, Australia's largest outback city is 2,290km from Melbourne and 2,618km from Canberra.

But lawyers and bureaucrats on the other side of the country are having a significant say in how Kalgoorlie-Boulder's residents do their weekly grocery shopping.

The Australian Competition Tribunal this week wrapped eight days of hearings in Melbourne's Federal Court, centred on whether Coles should be permitted to open a new supermarket in the historic gold mining city.

To say some of the 30,000-strong population are annoyed at the prospect would be an understatement.

Doug Daws has lived in Kalgoorlie-Boulder his entire life. (ABC Goldfields: Jarrod Lucas)

Kalgoorlie-Boulder's former Deputy Mayor Doug Daws is among them.

"If you want to spend money in Kalgoorlie and create a new supermarket for the people here you have my support," he said.

"Fundamentally, it's appalling that a group of faceless, anonymous people on the other side of Australia get involved in free enterprise here."

Landmark legal challenge

In July, the Australian Competition and Consumer Commission (ACCC) exercised new powers to stop Coles from building a new supermarket and liquor store in the city, located about 600km east of Perth.

Among other factors in its decision, the watchdog cited the potential for Coles's expansion to knock out smaller independent competitors already operating in Kalgoorlie-Boulder.

Coles immediately appealed, in what looms as a test case for Australia's new merger laws.

There are six supermarkets in Kalgoorlie-Boulder, including an existing Coles in the CBD. (ABC News)

In one respect, the case was a David versus Goliath battle.

On one side was Coles, with 860 supermarkets nationwide, fighting to establish a second store in Kalgoorlie-Boulder.

The closest competitor, O'Connor Fresh IGA, is about 2km from the proposed new development and argued there is a "commercially real possibility" it would go out of business.

The closest competitor to the proposed Coles development is the O'Connor Fresh IGA. (ABC Goldfields: Jarrod Lucas)

Competitor flags market exit

ACCC lawyer Declan Roche SC insisted any Coles expansion represented a "substantial lessening of competition" across Kalgoorlie-Boulder.

He said the consumer watchdog assessed competition would be significantly impacted if O'Connor Fresh IGA exited the market, given its operating hours are not regulated like Coles and benefit local shift workers.

"The ACCC's view was it offers consumers a differentiated product in terms of range and service … and a measure of its effectiveness as a competitor is the proportion of Kalgoorlie grocery spend it attracts," Mr Roche told the tribunal.

"Coles' own business case … without getting into the confidential figures … identifies a proportion of Coles' business from the new supermarket will come from the business that's currently being done by O'Connor Fresh IGA."

The O'Connor Fresh IGA is the closest competitor to the site of the proposed Coles supermarket. (ABC Goldfields: Jarrod Lucas)

With six existing supermarkets, Mr Roche described Kalgoorlie-Boulder as a "concentrated market" and backing the ACCC's position was the Kalgoorlie-Boulder Chamber of Commerce and Industry.

"The submission of the chamber of commerce is the expansion is neither necessary nor justified, wouldn't provide any meaningful increase in consumer choice and would over-saturate the market," he said.

O'Connor Fresh IGA's counsel Robert Yezerski SC told the tribunal the market had been impacted by last year's arrival of Tony Galati's Spudshed franchise in a "very material" way, which triggered a "competitive response" from national chains.

"We believe Coles takes more power we because it becomes less constrained by its competitors," he said.

WA businessman Tony Galati at the opening of Kalgoorlie-Boulder's Spudshed supermarket. (ABC Goldfields: Macey Turner)

Future investment uncertain

But the supermarket giant argued the watchdog's intervention would have a "chilling effect" on investment in Kalgoorlie-Boulder.

The warning would be ominous for the City of Kalgoorlie-Boulder, which launched a nationwide marketing blitz in 2021 as part of its ambition to grow the population to 40,000 by the end of the decade.

"Any investor keen to expand its services in a market must weigh up the risk of an incumbent persuading the regulator, that its viability would be threatened if expansion were to occur," Coles's lawyer John Sheahan KC said.

"In many, perhaps most cases, the investor will be unable to make a confident or useful assessment of that risk.

"Given the transaction costs associated … that uncertainty will plausibly and likely have a chilling effect on proposed investments."

An aerial view of the Kalgoorlie CBD. (ABC Goldfields: Jarrod Lucas)

Coles previously operated two stores in Kalgoorlie-Boulder from 1986 to 2021.

Mr Sheahan argued consumers would get the benefits of Coles's national and state-based pricing structure, saying the proposed supermarket was "likely to intensify rather than diminish rivals' incentives to invest in dimensions of competition".

He noted Kalgoorlie-Boulder's growing population of fly-in, fly-out workers as a sign of increasing demand, while pointing to 10 regional locations across Australia with a comparable population.

"All have more supermarkets than Kalgoorlie, and nine of those towns have at least two Woolworths or two Coles," he said.

Case poses 'difficult dilemma'

The hearing delved deep into locals' purchasing habits, including Coles selling more dog food at its Kalgoorlie store than others across the country, while O'Connor Fresh IGA's biggest sellers included barbecue chickens and other takeaway offerings.

Mr Sheahan said Coles's biggest national competitor, Woolworths, is "unlikely to take the opening of a new Coles store lying down" and would likely pursue further investment or additional expansion.

It was also suggested another rival chain, Aldi, was weighing up entering the market.

The proposed site of the Coles supermarket in Somerville is currently bushland, which is surrounded by an industrial area, FIFO camp and childcare centre. (ABC Goldfields: Jarrod Lucas)

"All the consumers in Kalgoorlie are benefited by a new store," Mr Sheahan said.

"It is an odd reaction by the commission [ACCC] to say, 'Fine, just not too close to this store [O'Connor Fresh IGA], because it might make them uncomfortable.'"

Federal Court Justice Michael O'Bryan, the president of the tribunal's three-member panel, said the case posed a "difficult dilemma".

The property developer, M/Group, behind the proposed Amara Estate near Kalgoorlie-Boulder Airport also plans to lease land to Coles for a new supermarket development. (ABC Goldfields: Jarrod Lucas)

"Some consumers may prefer the new supermarket because of location or lower prices or other features," Justice O'Bryan said.

" How do we judge that against the secondary consequences which may appear to be a reduction in competition? "

The tribunal has reserved its decision, and is required to make a final determination within 90 days.

World.title: Remote island's 30,000-hectare carbon forestry project begins
World.content:
On the remote Tiwi Islands in the Northern Territory, a major carbon forestry project is taking shape.

More than 2 million Eucalyptus pellita seedlings have been planted on Melville Island this year across nearly 1,800 hectares, with some of those trees already 4 metres tall.

But this is just the start.

The overall project will see 30,000 hectares planted on the island, which will produce an estimated 12 million cubic metres of high-value wood products, as well as 5 million carbon credits over the life span of the project.

Tiwi Plantations chairman Gibson Farmer Illortaminni said he was excited about this new chapter for forestry on the Tiwis, referring to the seedlings as "his grandchildren".

"From the trees I planted in 1989, we collected seeds from them, so we can grow new trees for the second rotation," he said.

"We've got young Tiwi boys and girls here working on the seedlings and helping trees grow and it makes me proud because these young ones have jobs.

"There's not many jobs on the Tiwi Islands, but there's jobs here in forestry."

Planted as seedlings in early 2026, most of the Eucalyptus pellita trees are already 3 to 4 metres tall. (ABC Rural: Matt Brann)

The long journey to Eucalyptus pellita

The Tiwi Islands have a long and complicated history when it comes to forestry.

In the 1960s, the NT government started forestry trials on Melville Island.

Local sawmills were set up after Cyclone Tracy in 1974 to provide timber to help rebuild Darwin.

Then in the late 1990s, a decision was made by Tiwi people to clear land for plantation forestry.

In 2005, a company called Great Southern bought the project and invested heavily in the establishment of 30,000 hectares of Acacia mangium trees.

But like many other managed investment schemes at the time, Great Southern hit trouble, and fell into receivership in 2009.

Tiwi Islanders watch the first loading of woodchips at Port Melville in 2015. (ABC Rural: Daniel Fitzgerald)

The Tiwi people formed their own forestry company (Tiwi Plantations Corporation) to take over the project, and worked hard to get the trees through to harvest, eventually exporting more than 1 million tonnes of Acacia mangium woodchips.

But by their own admission, the Acacia mangium trees were not the commercial success many had hoped for.

At the start of this year, Tiwi Plantations finalised an $81 million investment with River Capital and the Clean Energy Finance Corporation to create a carbon forestry project, which will involve replanting the full 30,000 hectares with Eucalyptus pellita.

Flying over Melville Island you can see the land that has been prepared for tree planting. (ABC Rural: Matt Brann)

Multiple uses

Tiwi Plantations project manager Chris Oliver said Eucalyptus pellita had a number of benefits.

"Over the decades there's been various trials on the island, but Eucalyptus pellita has shone above the rest," he said.

"It's a good species that grows well in the conditions here, but not only does it have good growth rates, it has great potential for multiple products [once harvested]."

The Eucalyptus pellita's growth rate is much better than the Acacia mangium trees that were previously planted on the Tiwi Islands. (Supplied: Tiwi Plantations)

Mr Oliver said the University of Melbourne was researching the timber's potential for engineered wood products for the construction sector.

"We're not just looking to export everything to customers overseas," he said.

"We're also looking at local production on the island to utilise the resource and put some of this into local housing."

Mr Illortaminii said if some of the timber could be used locally it would be a great outcome.

"This Eucalyptus pellita is a really good wood and very strong," he said.

"They stand up strong in the wind compared to those Acacia mangiums."

Eucalyptus pellita seedlings in the nursery on Melville Island. (ABC Rural: Matt Brann)

Carbon credits 'a game changer'

The project on the Tiwi Islands is not only about timber, it is also understood to be Australia's largest First Nations-led carbon initiative.

Australian carbon credit units (ACCU) from the project are expected to become available from 2027, with the project expected to generate about 5 million ACCUs under the Plantation Forestry (schedule 1) methodology over its lifetime.

A generic ACCU is currently worth about $38, although Indigenous-led projects with co-benefits often attract a premium price.

Mr Oliver said having a revenue stream in the years before harvest was a "game changer" for forestry projects.

"One of the big things about forestry is it requires a lot of investment at the start and it takes a long time to make a return," he said.

"So this project has been developed to produce carbon credits, which helps us to become self-funding.

"Having that revenue stream coming in, in the early stage of the plantation, changes the game completely."

Jobs for Tiwis

The next round of planting is due to start in December, with about 3.8 million seedlings being prepared at the Yapilika Forestry Centre's nursery.

Darnelle Clayton has started a traineeship with the nursery and said she had been learning a lot.

"This is my first month as a trainee and so far I've learnt about planting, how they grow, and how they could be used in the future," she said.

"My mum works here and she kind of inspired me."

Darnelle Clayton is a trainee working at the Yapilika Forestry Centre. (ABC Rural: Matt Brann)

Ms Clayton said she was keen to become a leader at the nursery and inspire others.

She said it would be great to be involved with the project long enough to see the first harvest.

"I'm definitely excited for when [harvest arrives]; I want to see that moment for myself and will feel very proud knowing how much hard work went into it."

Tiwi workers represent about 60 per cent of the current workforce, earning more than $1.4 million in direct wages this year.

Mr Oliver said the island was very busy preparing about 3,800 hectares for planting in 2027.

"We're very buoyant about this project and I think it's going to be a talking point of the Tiwi Islands for the next 30 to 40 years," he said.

World.title: Allegedly stolen car crashes into NT Police housing, 12yo boy among arrests
World.content:
A 12-year-old boy was among four arrested in Tennant Creek overnight, with authorities alleging the group was travelling in a stolen vehicle when it crashed into residential police housing.

In a statement released on Sunday morning, NT Police said it was alerted to "a suspicious vehicle hooning around the Tennant Creek CBD" at around 1am.

"The owner of the vehicle confirmed it was stolen," the statement said.

"Tyre-deflation devices were deployed successfully on Peko Road, with the vehicle continuing into Hilda Street where it crashed into a carport and parked vehicle.

"The building suffered structural damage as a result of the crash."

The ABC understands the allegedly stolen vehicle lost control after the tyres were deflated.

Officers arrested three boys — aged 12, 13 and 15 — and a 21-year-old man over the incident, but charges were yet to be laid.

Police said the alleged offenders received minor injuries in the crash, while the damaged building needed further assessment.

Investigations are continuing, with authorities urging any witnesses with CCTV or dashcam footage to contact police on 131 444 or Crime Stoppers on 1800 333 000.

World.title: Photographer hopes winning dolphin snap inspires conservation efforts
World.content:
Gergo Rugli wants people to feel uplifted and inspired to protect the world's oceans when they see his picture of a pod of dolphins cresting a wave alongside surfers at Sydney's Tamarama Beach.

The photographer, who started his career in Hungary more than 20 years ago before migrating to Australia, has taken out the top prize in the Ocean Photographer of the Year 2026 adventure category.

"This image is very special to me, because I'm fascinated with dolphins … and every time that I see them it just makes me happy. They radiate this freedom and this joy …and I want everyone to feel this," he told the ABC.

"I want to capture the sea life in the best possible light, and make people appreciate it more … because if you love something then you're going to protect it.

"Especially these days with the pollution, plastic pollution, it's unfortunately in danger."

Mr Rugli says his winning entry is very special to him. (Supplied)

The international competition featured submissions ranging from a curious oceanic sunfish staring at a diver in Mexico from Anita Verde, Gentoo penguins at a decrepit whaling station in Antarctica, and a whale shark surrounded by tourist divers in the Maldives.

The annual contest showcases the beauty of the deep blue and the extraordinary encounters that take place in its environmentally fragile ecosystem.

Anita Verde's photograph from Mexico was among the submissions. (Supplied: Ocean Photographer of the Year, Anita Verde)

'They just came'

Growing up near forests, rivers and lakes left an imprint on Mr Rugli. So did time with his grandparents snorkelling around the Mediterranean and watching David Attenborough's documentaries with his grandfather.

Back then, he focused on microphotography, capturing insects and flowers, but on Sydney's beaches his love of the ocean found a home.

His obsession with dolphins took him to Port Stephens, in the NSW Hunter region, where he worked spotting the marine creatures.

"Every time I'm close to the ocean, I'm scanning the horizon and I just automatically in my mind search for the dolphins," he said.

On the day of the winning shot, Mr Rugli was on his daily swim, camera in tow, when he saw "perfect" barrelling waves. He did not expect to see his beloved mammals.

Mr Rugli was out for his daily swim when he took the winning image. (Instagram: @rugligeri)

The swell was six feet, he recalled, making it tricky to get behind the break line.

After almost giving up, he broke through and "they just came", getting his photograph after a "challenging" hour and a half of just "trying to stay alive".

"I started taking photos of the waves and the surfers, and 10 to 15 minutes later a very big pod of dolphins came in, and they started surfing the waves," he said.

"I constantly had to wipe the camera, stay in position and try to figure out where the dolphins would jump through.

"I was very lucky."

A number of Mr Rugli's other photographic works have won accolades. This image had previously come close, but this time "it's a dream come true".

"In 2016, my friend told me, 'Let's go to the Maritime Museum because there's a photo competition there' … I had just started taking ocean photos," Mr Rugli said.

"I couldn't imagine taking such an amazing photo [as the ones] that were exhibited there; and now my image is there as a winning image."

Another submission featured Gentoo penguins at a decrepit whaling station in Antarctica. (Supplied: Ocean Photographer of the Year, Romain Barats)

Ten Australian finalists

Mr Rugli was one of 10 Australians named as finalists in the competition in August, beating more than 15,000 entries from around the world.

Matty Smith, an underwater photographer from Newcastle, won first place in the Fine Arts category with his black-and-white shot of a tawny nurse shark taken in the Maldives.

His photo of a southern elephant seal pup exploring shallow rock pools on Sea Lion Island in the Falkland Islands was also highly commended in the Wildlife category.

Matty Smith's image of seal pups was highly commended in the Wildlife category. (Supplied: Ocean Photographer of the Year, Matty Smith)

Claiming the Ocean Photographer of the Year 2026 title was a striking black-and-white photo of a male seahorse, encountering two juvenile seahorses no larger than grains of rice.

French photographer Julien Anton has been a category winner in previous years of the competition, but it is the first time he's been bestowed the top honour.

Mr Anton captured the prize-winning moment in French Polynesia, with the aim of bringing to light the significance of environmental preservation.

"My hope is that this image can serve as a bridge between science, conservation and a world that deserves to know what is at stake," he said.

Julien Anton's winning entry was taken in French Polynesia. (Supplied: Ocean Photographer of the Year, Matty Smith)

When confronted with the image for the first time, the competition's director, Will Harrison, said the judging panel "fell silent".

"It is an image that demands reflection, pause for thought, and it certainly got that from us," Mr Harrison said.

The winners and finalists of Ocean Photographer of the Year 2026 will be on exhibition at the Australian National Maritime Museum.

World.title: Ambulance volunteers left to fundraise $600,000 for new depot
World.content:
Ambulance volunteers across regional Western Australia are calling on the state government to increase funding, with many questioning why they are responsible for meeting the cost of new ambulances and infrastructure.

WA is one of two Australian jurisdictions, along with the Northern Territory, where St John Ambulance provides ambulance services under contract to the health department.

Volunteers play a critical role, particularly in smaller regional communities where sub-centres are volunteer-run.

Ivan Woodhams is the chair of St John Walpole, about 410 kilometres south of Perth, he said volunteers at the depot have fundraised more than $600,000 to replace its aging headquarters.

Similar stories can be found in sub-centres across the state.

"From here to Kununurra, every sub-centre is under the same expectation to provide everything that they use," Mr Woodhams said.

" The cost of an ambulance service is astronomical ... for the years and jobs that we do, we accumulate very little. "

Ivan Woodhams says the cost of an ambulance service is "astronomical". (ABC Great Southern: Rachel Jennings)

About 20 people volunteer at the sub-centre which services communities around Walpole and Nornalup, both popular tourist destinations.

While efforts to get a new building off the ground have been substantial, Mr Woodhams said costs are rising quicker than they can keep up with.

"We've had significant local donations," he said.

"We're getting towards what we thought was going to be enough, but as the years have progressed, I fear that we'll be well short of the final figure."

He wants the state government to step in and subsidise the cost.

" We have to pay for it and take funds literally out of the hands of locals. "

Kath Broadbent has spent more than 30 years volunteering with the Walpole branch. (ABC Great Southern: Rachel Jennings)

A voice for volunteers

Further inland, Travis Hawkins has been a member of Gnowangerup's sub-centre for a decade.

He is part of a new advocacy group designed to bridge the gap between volunteers and St John's management.

It includes members from across regional WA hoping to identify a sustainable funding model for volunteer centres.

Gnowangerup St John's Travis Hawkins is part of a new group bridging the gap between country centres and St John WA. (ABC Great Southern: Mark Bennett)

While patient transfer fees and other work within the community provide alternative income streams, Mr Hawkins said both volunteers and St John management recognised the need for change.

"The model we currently have is not fit for purpose anymore," he said.

"In some areas the income is not sufficient (to cover costs), while in other areas it's an abundance, that's why we have raised this inequity."

Mr Hawkins said more government support from any level would make funding the sub-centres easier.

Emergency equipment used in ambulances must be replaced every four to 10 years. (ABC Great Southern: Rachel Jennings)

A St John WA spokesperson said investment was prioritised by demand and workforce needs.

"We recognise that the ability of individual communities to fundraise varies, and essential safety and minimum-standard infrastructure should not depend on a community’s fundraising capacity," the spokesperson said.

An ambulance at the St John Walpole depot. (ABC Great Southern: Rachel Jennings)

"Local fundraising can, however, help support local priorities and additional investment.

"We continue to work with communities and government to ensure regional ambulance infrastructure is sustainable, fit for purpose and prioritised according to need."

The state government has been contacted for comment.

World.title: Dawn Fraser fired up for 1956 Melbourne Olympics reunion
World.content:
Amid the reunions and celebrations, Dawn Fraser is drawing some inspiration from the 70th anniversary of the Melbourne Olympics.

Australia's most famous Olympian has come to Melbourne for a lunch on Sunday at the MCG to mark the November 22 opening ceremony date of the 1956 Games.

Fraser is 89 and had to miss a commemorative 1956 Olympics dinner in Melbourne a few weeks ago because of a health issue.

Fraser says she will go from table to table in her wheelchair to meet old friends and make new ones at the lunch, which coincides with the opening ceremony at the MCG 70 years ago.

Asked if she might be there for the 2032 Brisbane Olympics — Fraser was also a key figure at the Sydney 2000 Games — there is a reminder of what made her an all-time sporting great.

TV memories of the 1956 Olympics Watching the 1956 Melbourne Olympic Games was many Australians' first experience of television.

"I would love to be there at '32, to support our athletes," Fraser told AAP.

"I think of my age — I just turned 89 — and, 'Oh well, that's so many years off.' But then when I look at some of the athletes who are coming to this testimonial, some of them are 95, 99.

"Then I'm thinking — excuse the expression — 'Shit! I can do that. If they can do it, I can do it.'"

Likewise, the 19-year-old from a hardscrabble Balmain upbringing had her eyes opened wide at the 1956 Olympics.

Until then, Fraser had only swum against other Australians.

"I never thought about it. [To me, the Olympics] was just another swimming event. But when I won my gold medal, I realised how big it was," Fraser said.

"It wasn't until after I won … competing against so many nations.

"To win a gold medal was something out of this world. You didn't think about it until a month later, that you were the best swimmer in the world."

Fraser won the 100-metre freestyle in Melbourne and was a member of the 4x100 women's freestyle relay team that also claimed gold.

Dawn Fraser (centre) began her Olympic reign in the 100m freestyle in Melbourne. She won her third straight gold in Tokyo in 1964. (Getty Images: Central Press/Hulton Archive)

She went on to become the first of only four swimmers who have won gold in the same individual event at three-successive Olympics. Somewhere in there, she became "Our Dawn".

Two days after the reunion, the Sport Australia Hall Of Fame annual dinner will feature the Dawn Award. It goes to an individual, team or organisation that shows courage, breaks new ground and changes sport for the better.

But as far as Fraser is concerned, she is just one athlete at the reunion.

"I'm an athlete among athletes, and I'm very proud to be among the athletes who I met and competed against in 1956," she said.

Just as the Melbourne Games dramatically changed Fraser's life, it also was a landmark for Australian sport. Only nine years after World War Two, Australia was still an international backwater.

It has been 70 years today since Ron Clarke lit the Olympic cauldron at the MCG to kick off the Games in 1956. (Getty Images)

"Here we were, a small country, having an Olympic event that meant so much to a lot of sportsmen and women in our country … and throughout the world," Fraser said.

"We were holding the biggest sporting event ever in Olympic history.

"It was the start of not only my swimming career but for a lot of other sportsmen and women in Australia — the start of their international careers.

"It was a big stepping stone for all of us because we didn't realise we were competing against the best athletes in the world."

And so to 2032, where Fraser hopes Australia can raise the bar again.

"I want them to make it as successful as all the other Olympic Games — if not a little bit better. It's very hard to do that, but Sydney, I thought the same thing," she said.

"Sydney outshone Melbourne and I'm sure Brisbane will outshine Sydney."

AAP

World.title: 'They are wrong': Defence minister denies US report on AUKUS submarines
World.content:
Defence Minister Richard Marles has rebuffed reports that the AUKUS agreement to supply nuclear-powered submarines to Australia would diminish the US naval force for "many years".

Mr Marles also downplayed US President Donald Trump's threats about US artificial intelligence companies building data centres overseas, as well as ASIO boss Mike Burgess's warning about foreign interference within Australia's AI data centre sector.

A report from the US Congressional Budget Office, released on Friday, said "the US submarine industrial base is currently struggling to meet the Navy's demand for submarines".

"Increasing production further to replace SSNs [nuclear-powered submarines] sold to Australia would increase the challenges that the [US] Navy and the shipyards are facing," the report read.

"The sale of SSNs to Australia would reduce the number of attack submarines available to the navy for many years."

Mr Marles told ABC's Insiders he was not worried about the report and expected many like it over the next decade.

"The reason it doesn't worry me is because AUKUS is very much happening," he said.

He agreed that the production rate of shipbuilding was "definitely a critical part" of Australia getting Virginia class submarines, but denied that the US navy's production rate was flat.

"They're wrong? The US Congressional Office?" Insiders host David Speers asked.

"Yes, they are wrong. The production rate in the United States is absolutely increasing," Mr Marles said.

He said the production rate was one factor, but "sustainment and maintenance" were also important to ensure Australia would receive its first Virginia class nuclear submarine by the early 2030s.

Five years of AUKUS AUKUS has forced the United States to confront its "profoundly lacking" capacity to build and maintain naval submarines, a former top White House official says.

"The very first milestone that we have always been shooting for is the establishment of the Submarine Rotational Force — West this time next year," he said, referring to US and UK nuclear-powered boats having a rotational presence at HMAS Stirling, allowing Australian sailors to deploy on those vessels to get experience with naval nuclear propulsion.

"We're well on track to see that occur."

AI data centre fears

US President Donald Trump has said he will not allow American AI companies to build data centres in foreign countries.

Mr Trump warned there would be "tremendous taxes" for those who do.

The comments come amid an AI data centre boom in Australia, where operators have raised a record sum of at least $35 billion as of September this year.

Richard Marles (right) says it is in the US's own interests for AI data centres to be built in Australia. (ABC News: Simon Winter)

Mr Marles said the government would continue to work with the tech companies themselves and the US government about investment in Australia, adding it was in their own interests.

"If all of that infrastructure is in one place, in other words, if it remains solely in the United States, right there, there's a vulnerability," he said.

"And that's partly why they are looking abroad and why we are of such interest.

"We would like to see that investment in Australia. Of course, you know, it's not at any cost. We need to be doing it on our terms."

Australia this week signed a US-led agreement to identify vulnerable supply chains and protect sensitive AI technology from theft or foreign interference.

Mr Marles said that agreement also encouraged AI data centres to be built overseas.

Mike Burgess is warning of foreign interference in relation to the building of AI data centres. (ABC News: Matt Roberts)

ASIO boss Mike Burgess has also issued a warning about foreign interference, telling 60 Minutes that foreign actors building AI data centres here may try to access sensitive information or critical infrastructure covertly.

Mr Marles says "it is a concern".

"This is the world that we live in, so in a sense it's not new, but the building of data centres creates a new vector, a new avenue for foreign actors to engage in," he said.

"But we are very mindful of our own cybersecurity."

Home Affairs Minister Tony Burke said there was a "national security" interest in Australia housing AI data centres, and referred to Mr Burgess's comments that it came with both opportunity and risk.

"Whenever you get that sort of capability on shore, it also becomes a magnet for people who would want to conduct foreign interference," Mr Burke told News24.

"So we need to make sure that we are alert and that we are being very careful in the ownership structures that happen in Australia for data centres."

World.title: Last sitting week of year turns into one WA government may prefer to forget
World.content:
It was not the ending to the parliamentary year the government would have hoped for.

Instead of switching off for the holidays, it's been forced to defend one of its MPs amid mounting questions about his financial affairs and confusion about where the buck stops with checking politicians’ declarations to parliament.

MP under scrutiny

After extraordinary scenes last week of Labor MPs shielding their colleague Dr Jags Krishnan from media questioning, the backbencher again dominated discussions both inside and outside parliament.

Loading...

The spotlight has been on the business dealings of the Riverton MP and his disclosures to parliament about his debts since it emerged he was being sued in the United States over a million-dollar loan.

On Monday, it was revealed he's facing police scrutiny over a complaint to do with his financial dealings.

"I first learned of the report made to police through a media enquiry yesterday," Mr Krishnan said on Tuesday morning.

Jags Krishnan says police have not contacted him about a complaint relating to his financial affairs. (ABC News: Courtney Withers)

"I have not been contacted by police. I remain committed to resolving these matters."

Despite his assurances, questions continued to mount.

"Is the premier making sure that everyone on his team is upholding the relevant parliamentary standards?" Opposition Leader Basil Zempilas asked outside parliament.

Basil Zempilas has kept the pressure on the government over financial declarations.

Amid repeated questions inside the chamber, Premier Roger Cook kept his responses brief.

"All members of parliament are required to uphold the standards of the parliament and abide by the rules and the obligations," he said.

Roger Cook kept his responses in parliament brief. (ABC News: Keane Bourke)

Who checks declarations?

However, a revelation on Thursday morning about those rules threw a spanner in the works.

Earlier in the week Mr Cook said the accuracy of Mr Krishnan's annual returns, or financial declarations, is "between him and the presiding officers".

In other words, it's the job of the parliament to check that the declarations made by MPs are accurate.

But when questioned by reporters, the presiding officer in the lower house, Stephen Price, said it wasn't up to him to do that.

Parliamentary speaker Stephen Price is the presiding officer in the lower house. (ABC News: Keane Bourke)

"I don't know whose responsibility it is," Mr Price said on Thursday.

"Everyone has the same responsibility to ensure that financial returns are as accurate as required under the appropriate legislation."

System flaw

Mr Zempilas was unimpressed.

"What's the point of these declarations? What are they for? If no one looks into them or no one verifies them, what is the point of them?" he said.

Declarations essentially operate on an honour system, governed by an act that requires members to declare a wide range of personal financial details.

"The obligation is on us to be truthful in our returns," Treasurer Rita Saffioti said.

Rita Saffioti said she supports reviewing the honour system. (ABC News: Keane Bourke )

But unless an MP is hauled before a Procedure and Privileges Committee, how does the public know their disclosures are truthful?

They don't.

Mr Price said the honour system may need to be reviewed — something Ms Saffioti said she supports.

Mr Zempilas leapt on the confusion in Question Time, describing it as a "farcical" lack of accountability.

The ABC does not suggest Dr Krishnan hasn't been truthful in his returns or that he has engaged in criminal conduct.

That's a wrap

Instead of ending the week with clear air to talk about priority areas — like health, jobs and housing — to set the agenda and focus for next year, the government continued to cop heat about an embattled backbencher.

Judging by the faces of several frustrated Labor MPs in the chamber, their last parliamentary sitting week of 2026 did not end on the high note they would have hoped for.

Breaking CultureMoviesCity life ‘Field of dreams’: Scrubland beside a Sydney motorway slated to become city’s next film studio Linda Morris November 22, 2026 — 12:14pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. It’s a semi-cleared swathe of scrubland near the Eastern Creek spaghetti interchange of the M4 Motorway, once marketed as an ideal spot for a tourism caravan park. Now the NSW government hopes it will become the new site of Sydney’s next film studio, boasting six new sound stages and a backlot. The eight hectares of land on Pikes Lane earmarked for Sydney’s next film studio. Sitthixay Ditthavong Arts Minister John Graham has gone so far as to pitch the site as Hollywood’s next “field of dreams”, referring to the 1989 film in which Kevin Costner builds a baseball pitch out of a cornfield. The nominated studio lot lies on eight hectares between the M4 and the Great Western Highway within a designated tourism precinct comprising Sydney Action Park, Sydney Zoo and Sydney Motorsport Park. The Disney film lot at Moore Park is nine studios on 13 hectares but subject of what local producers says is a film production bottleneck.



The Minns government had nominated three Crown land sites near Blacktown – at Bungarribee, Eastern Creek and near Prospect Reservoir – for investors to consider for a “world-class” facility. The nominated site on Pikes Lane sits within the Western Sydney Parklands. It’s offering $100 million fund to the winning consortium who will receive the subsidised lease on this piece of Crown land to build the city’s first new film and television studio in a quarter of a century. The hunt for a private partner to build a second major film studio in Sydney has drawn 16 submissions with three international and local consortia shortlisted – and the winner to be announced in the New Year. The participants shortlisted to move to the next stage bring an incredible depth of experience and reflect the strong appetite internationally for NSW as a screen production location, Graham said.



“Pikes Lane is a field of dreams, a place where the best international productions can film in state-of-the-art facilities, engaging our internationally renowned highly skilled local crew, and enjoy an unbeatable lifestyle for international cast while they’re here,” he said. “A second screen studio will also unlock much-needed production space for our local productions, giving a much-needed boost to keep our internationally acclaimed producers making their productions and employing people here, in NSW.” Arts minister John Graham with producers Jodi Matterson and Josh Pomeranz. Sam Mooy Western Sydney is an area of jobs growth which will benefit from its access near the second airport, due to open this month. Developer led proposals for a film studio on privately held land in Calga near the Central Coast, and at Oran Park appear to have not won support for $100 million investment tied to their purchased lots. The open process appears to have considered and rejected options to build a studio in the railway yards of Eveleigh and Sydney Olympic precinct, understood to have involved remediation of both sites, and in the case of the Olympic Park, legislative amendments.





“A second screen studio will also unlock much needed production space for our local productions, giving a much-needed boost to keep our internationally acclaimed producers making their productions and employing people here, in NSW,” Graham said. World.title: Veteran NSW politician Reverend Fred Nile dies aged 92
World.content:
Updated PoliticsNSWNSW State Parliament Veteran NSW politician Reverend Fred Nile dies aged 92 Jessica McSweeney Updated November 22, 2026 — 11:58am ,first published November 22, 2026 — 9:52am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. NSW’s longest-serving state MP Reverend Fred Nile has died, his family has confirmed. “It is with deep sadness the Nile family announces the passing of Revd the Hon. Frederick John Nile who passed away peacefully on the 21st of November at the age of 92,” a family statement said. The Reverend Fred Nile was the longest serving MP in NSW Parliament. Chris Pearce “Revd Nile is survived by his wife, children, grandchildren and great-grandchildren. Details about a service or memorial will be shared soon.” Nile was a member of the NSW Legislative Council for more than 40 years and was national president of the Christian Democratic Party before leaving politics at the 2023 election.



Best known for his conservative Christian values, Nile was a vocal opponent to same-sex marriage, railed against abortion and wanted to ban same-sex couples from adopting children. The Christian crusader found an unlikely ally in Sydney MP Alex Greenwich before Nile left NSW Parliament, teaming up with the gay MP to support legislation protecting Indigenous culture and heritage. Fred Nile speaking at a protest outside an Oxford Street bathhouse. Anthony Lewis/Fairfax Media Greenwich on Sunday sent a message to Premier Chris Minns requesting a state service to honour Nile’s contribution to NSW. He said he had formed a good working relationship with Nile towards the end of his parliamentary career despite the pair’s opposing views on most progressive issues. “Rev Nile played the ball, not the person,” Greenwich said.



Related Article Opinion

Fred Nile Fred Nile confesses: I’m sorry I prayed for rain on the Mardi Gras parade Peter FitzSimons Columnist and author “His opposition to many of the reforms I delivered came from his faith, and he didn’t engage in the personalised vitriol that comes from many of today’s right-wing politicians.” Nile became well known for praying for rain before Sydney’s yearly Mardi Gras parade, although he apologised for this in an interview with this masthead in 2022. Born in Kings Cross in 1934, Nile was ordained as an evangelical Congregational minister in 1964 and spent most of the 1970s in Christian leadership roles before his election to parliament in 1981. In his inaugural speech, Nile described himself as a pro-child and pro-family campaigner who wanted to stamp out things he identified as moral failings in NSW, including alcohol advertising and drug use.



Transport Minister and fellow upper house MP John Graham said Nile was someone who worked hard to ensure people of faith were respected in public debate. Related Article Obituaries God’s warrior: Fred Nile was never afraid to take up the fight “One of the great things about Fred Nile was over all that time, more than 42 years, you knew exactly where he was coming from, that didn’t change,” Graham said. “In a time when politics can seem pretty chaotic, I think that’s a really good thing and a real tribute to the sort of MP that he was.” Opposition Leader Kellie Sloane described Nile as a man of deep Christian faith with strong convictions.



“While people held different views on the issues he championed, there can be no doubting his commitment to his beliefs and his extraordinary contribution to parliamentary life in NSW,” she said. World.title: God’s warrior: Fred Nile was never afraid to take up the fight
World.content:
NationalObituaries God’s warrior: Fred Nile was never afraid to take up the fight Malcolm Brown November 22, 2026 — 11:47am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Close Share A A A

FRED NILE: 1934 - 2026 Fred Nile came to his prime of life at a time of a tidal wave of change. It was when so many certainties were being challenged, such as the place of women in society, the sanctity of marriage, monarchism, anti-communism, militarism, and the condemnation of abortion, homosexuality and pornography. The challenges represented a tidal wave impossible to suppress. Towards the end of Fred Nile’s life, formal same-sex marriages had been accepted, rights of transsexuals were being protected. For many progressives, all this was positive, wiping away bigotry and making society more just and tolerant. Candidate Fred Nile smiles at the Legislative Assembly Nominations on March 12, 2015. Fairfax But others would have none of it, holding up the Bible as the ultimate arbiter of standards. One of those was Fred Nile, who as a young man responded to preaching in a Congregationalist church in Revesby, south-western Sydney, and began a career that saw him take the lead in the church, community movements, the media and politics.



He was dogged by persecution and ridicule, culminating at one point in having his bust made of papier mache paraded down Oxford Street in the Gay and Lesbian Mardi Gras. But he was respected. Many supported him. Nobody could serve a term of more than 40 years in the NSW parliament if their intrinsic value was not recognised. He became, in several senses, the “Father of the House”. Seminar on prostitution with speakers Fred Nile and Gretel Petiniger, known as “Madam Lash”, at the University of NSW, 1974. Fairfax Frederick John Nile was born on September 15, 1934, in Kings Cross, son of a British migrant and Great War veteran Frederick Nile, who had become a taxi driver, and Marjorie (nee Clark). The elder Nile, described as “hard-drinking and hard-swearing”, was father of Fred, another son James, and daughters Marjorie and Mary. Related Article Updated

NSW State Parliament Veteran NSW politician Reverend Fred Nile dies aged 92 When the younger Fred Nile was young, his parents moved to Mascot, where they bought a grocery business and Nile went to Mascot Public School. Very much in the working-class environment, the younger Nile was briefly a runner for an SP bookie and his brother would continue long-term in the racing industry.



In 1946, Nile went to Cleveland Street Intermediate Commercial High School, and two years later joined the Citizens Military Forces (CMF). He completed his Intermediate Certificate and began work as a junior storeman in the aviation industry, with Paul & Gray Pty Ltd at Mascot. When the family moved to Revesby in 1950, Nile moved to the company’s operation at Bankstown and went through his religious conversion. Nile decided in 1955 to train full-time for the ministry. His boss at Paul & Gray, where Nile had become assistant manager, was reluctant to see him go but said: “We cannot compete with God!” Nile entered the Melbourne Bible Institute, later known as the Victorian College of the Bible, where he spent two years, became Senior Student and obtained a First-Class Diploma. Nile with singer Cliff Richard in 1982. Fairfax He then entered the NSW Congregational Theological College and went on to study at the NSW United Faculty of Theology at the University of Sydney, and the University of New England where he did Philosophy, History and Senior Education. In December 1958, Nile married Elaine Creasly, also a child of the inner city, born in Waterloo, and the next year became as student minister at the Congregational Church in Newcastle, followed by service at Bexley and Brighton-le-Sands. Promoted to major in the CMF, he became father for the first time in 1960 when son Stephen was born, to be followed by a daughter, Sharon, and sons Mark and David.



Nile was ordained at Bexley in 1964, became national director of the Australian Christian Endeavour and led the Australian delegation to the World Christian Endeavour Convention in Belfast. He was appointed assistant director of the Billy Graham Crusade in Sydney Showground in 1968, and in 1970 was appointed a director of the Methodist Mission to the People of New South Wales, led by the Reverend Alan Walker. Nile worked in numerous evangelical positions, edited Christian publications and took a moral stand on issues such as screening of the film O Calcutta. He became principal of a “Jesus Commune” in the city to promulgate a “Jesus Revolution”, involving 20 young men and women who did a one-year course. His campaign led him to the formation of the Australian arm of the Festival of Light. Fred Nile’s papier-mache head on a silver platter during the 1988 Mardi Gras. Fairfax Mary Whitehouse, who founded the festival in Britain to combat what she saw as “Western decadence”, came to Australia in October 1973. The knockers protested vigorously against her and against Nile. Nile refused to back down, and also came into conflict with church people whom he saw as “modernists”, such as the Reverend Ted Noffs and John Spong, whom he said were trying to modify doctrine. In 1974, Nile became full-time director of the Australian Festival of Light, campaigning for “purity, love and family life”. According to Nile, Attorney-General Lionel Murphy laughed at them and said: “You only represent yourself; you people don’t count.” Nile said that instead of the streamlining of divorce as set out in the Murphy’s Family Law Bill, governments should direct their energies to building up family life.



In February, Nile led a Festival of Light demonstration outside the studios of Channel 10, protesting about the television programs The Box and Number 96. He was supported by thousands but also brought ridicule and abuse, and often harsh treatment by an unsympathetic media. In 1974, Nile formed the Family Action Movement, the political arm of the festival. Two years later, he transferred to the newly formed Uniting Church Australia. In 1977, he founded the Call to Australia (Fred Nile) Group, “For God and Family”, to replace the Family Action Movement. The political arena, he said, was where decisions were made, and Christians should be in the thick of it. Nile addresses a rally outside NSW Parliament in 2015. The festival brought out such luminaries as journalist Malcolm Muggeridge and Mother Teresa. It campaigned against the Family Law Act and the repeal of the Summary Offences Act. He attacked school programs aimed at countering “sexism” in schools and advocated the roles of females as “mother-carer” and males as “father-protector”. He entered the media world when he accepted an offer from Ita Buttrose to write a weekly column for The Sunday Telegraph. He also accepted an invitation to host a Sunday night radio talkback program on 2GB, and from there he went to politics, being elected the NSW Legislative assembly in September 1981 with 9.8 per cent of the vote. It was, he said, “God’s will … I don’t want to be seen as a politician but as a Christian citizen in parliament who is also an active ordained minister.”



Nile and his wife, who joined in the Legislative Council in 1988, spoke out about the AIDS epidemic and many other aspects of social life they deemed immoral. The opposition towards Nile became more virulent, including from groups as Sisters of Perpetual Indulgence, who were gay men dressed as nuns. Nile opposed then-premier Neville Wran’s private member’s bill in 1984 to decriminalise homosexual acts. Sacked from 2GB after four years, he soon bounced back to take radio host position on Radio 2CBA. In later years, Fred Nile and independent MP Alex Greenwich formed an unlikely pairing on some issues. Fairfax In parliament, he served and would serve on numerous parliamentary committees, including the NSW Parliamentary Standing Committee on Social Issues, facilitating legislative reforms on adoption laws, drug abuse among youth, rape rates and pornography, domestic violence, youth violence, youth rural suicides, compensation for medically acquired AIDS/HIV victims, juvenile justice, births, deaths and marriage records. The Festival of Light embraced the concept of Aboriginal Reconciliation, and wanted to get rid of certain books from the school curriculum. In October 1990, Nile launched his “Jesus Battalions” in Kings Cross to protest about immorality and introduced privately a Tobacco Advertising Prohibition Bill.



Seeking re-election, Nile said he wanted abortions restricted to certain public hospitals, closure of all private termination clinics, a ban on pornography and casinos, and an immediate stop to public funding of the Gay and Lesbian Mardi Gras. He continued trips abroad to study and give addresses. Call to Australia became the Christian Democratic Party and there were continuing causes to fight, including the pressure on governments to allow same-sex marriage, another being ordination of homosexuals. Nile railed against what he saw as compromises being made by established churches. He disassociated with the United Church because in his view it was drifting from a literal interpretation of the Bible. Fred Nile standing in front of a picture of the Queen at NSW Parliament in 2014. Fairfax He protested about the move to institute safe heroin injection rooms, advocating instead counselling and therapy. He called for the banning of full body covering for Muslims, on the grounds that they might be used by terrorists to conceal weapons, and for a moratorium on Muslim immigration, which offended Muslims totally innocent of radical ideas. He was a frequent target for criticism, but despite all that, he remained in power. When he resigned from the Legislative Council in 2004 to make an unsuccessful tilt at the Senate, he was reappointed. He was re-elected in 2007 for a further term, of eight years.



Widowed in 2011 when Elaine died of cancer, Nile continued his moral crusade, opposing same-sex marriage and same-sex parenthood and vehemently opposed the introduction of “ethics” classes in state schools as an alternative to scripture. He was accepted as part of the system. There were some challenges, including a nasty internal party stoush with MLC Marie Bignold, which he settled, but the jibes he got from MPs were usually friendly ones, such as the occasion when a Labor MP called out during a division when Nile and his wife were the only ones on the other side. Nile said that he was accompanied by angels, to which the MP replied: “Angels don’t vote”. Fred Nile and his second wife Silvana Nero on their wedding day in 2013. James Alcock In an uncomplicated world, there would have been little opposition. The fact that there was so much opposition was a reflection, perhaps, not on him but on the world as it is. Nile at 78 years of age became engaged to a Christian Democratic Party candidate, Silvana Nero, 23 years his junior, in 2013 and remarried. He waxed and waned on retirement and in February 2023, announced his intention to nominate for re-election to the NSW Parliament. But age really was catching up with the old warrior. Nile collapsed the following month at a public morals protest outside Channel 10. He died on November 21, 2026. He is survived by his wife Nero, his children and great-grandchildren. Malcolm Brown

World.title: Bowen faces climate crisis as clock runs down on ‘worst COP ever’
World.content:
EnvironmentClimate changeParis Agreement Bowen faces climate crisis as clock runs down on ‘worst COP ever’ Nick O'Malley November 22, 2026 — 11:41am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Close Share A A A

Global climate talks that should have concluded on Friday remain deadlocked, with negotiators expected to resume discussions on Sunday in Antalya, Turkey, amid questions about the strategy of Climate Change and Energy Minister Chris Bowen in leading the summit. Nations remain at loggerheads over a series of key issues. Small island nations that are vulnerable to climate change, including in the Pacific, insist that any final agreement, known as a cover text, include specific reference to reducing fossil fuel emissions. But that position has been objected to by oil-producing nations led by Saudi Arabia, and supported by Russia and some developing nations. Climate Change Minister Chris Bowen faces a crisis over the coming hours at the COP31 talks in Turkey. Getty Images Some nations in the same bloc have objected to a proposed agreement championed by Bowen to have the world commit to making 35 per cent of its energy use electric by 2035. “Things worth doing, in my experience, don’t come easy,” Bowen said during a press conference at the COP on Saturday. “And I’ll tell you what’s worth doing is electrification. Electrification is the key to transitioning away from fossil fuels.”



Led by France and Panama, representatives from nations including Belgium, Côte d’Ivoire, Finland, Greece, Guatemala, Spain, Sweden and Vanuatu are demanding more ambitious climate action. Related Article Analysis

Paris Agreement ‘Heat records keep shattering’: Time is running out for COP to save us “We cannot [tell] the world we are now getting to 1.5 [degrees of warming] and then do business as if nothing was happening,” said France’s minister for ecological transition, Monique Barbut. There is also disagreement over climate finance, and European Union Climate Commissioner Wopke Hoekstra called demands for increased pledges for finance from developing nations hit by climate disasters “dead in the water” before the talks even began. Finance has long between a contentions issue at climate talks, with developed nations wanting to maintain focus on reducing emissions, and developing nations demanding financial assistance to help them insulate their economies from the impact of warming that they did not cause. The dispute is becoming more complex as the talks continue, with donor nations arguing that some countries that were considered poor when the first climate agreements were made have since become more wealthy and should no longer be receiving support.



A third area of deadlock in the current negotiations is over reference in the cover decision to the use of carbon capture and storage technology. While UN scientific assessments say that any effort to stabilise the climate will need to include removing carbon pollution from the atmosphere when the technology to do so at scale becomes available later in the century, many say that including reference to it now will simply be used as justification not to pursue emission reductions. If the standoff cannot be resolved, UN rules allow for the talks to be suspended until next year. That outcome would be a blow to Bowen, who created the role of president of negotiations at the talks when Australia failed to secure the hosting rights in a standoff with Turkey. Smoke from a wildfire in France in July. France is one of the countries pushing for greater climate action at COP. AFP Though it is not unusual for COP negotiations, which demand consensus agreement between the almost 200 signatories of the Paris Accord, to extend beyond deadline, they have only ever once been suspended without an outcome, when Kyoto Protocol talks collapsed in 2000. By Friday evening in Antalya, frustrated activists had begun to blame Bowen and his Turkish counterpart, Turkish Environment Minister Murat Kurum, for the failure of the COP to command support for ambitious climate action.



“The COP presidents want to tell us this has been a great COP,” said Mohamed Adow, head of the climate group Power Shift Africa at a press conference convened by the Climate Action Network. “Well, I can tell you without any doubt that this has been the worst COP ever.” Dr Bill Hare of Climate Analytics. Others have questioned Bowen’s strategy of allowing nations to insert many ambitious claims in an early draft of the cover decision, and of even insisting that the talks include such a decision in the first place. Leading climate analyst Bill Hare, the director of Climate Analytics – a global non-profit climate science and policy institute – said Bowen made the right call, particularly given the UN’s scientific report published before the COP which said the world was set to miss its 1.5-degree target. “The urgency of the crisis is visible to everyone, and if the COP didn’t do anything visible about the urgency in a political sense, there would be bigger questions about there was any point [in the process] at all,” Hare said.



“I think Bowen is right and correct and courageous to say we need to have a cover decision because it anchors things and provides a focal point for making some decent political signals.” Get to the heart of what’s happening with climate change and the environment.

World.title: There are no easy Tests in the north. The Wallabies’ win over Wales deserves respect
World.content:
Analysis SportRugby UnionWallabies There are no easy Tests in the north. The Wallabies’ win over Wales deserves respect Paul Cully November 22, 2026 — 11:30am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Close Share A A A

1. Wallabies’ big names step up The days of taking Test wins in November for granted are long gone, so the Wallabies’ 29-26 victory over Wales needs to be given proper respect. There were two big factors in the result. First, their bigger names stepped up; second, the tactical plan to stack the bench paid dividends. Len Ikitau was sensational, producing tough carries with some sublime touches on attack. His midfield partnership with Joseph-Aukuso Suaalii was also excellent, with Suaalii delivering his most mature performance in the Wallabies No.13 jersey. Fullback Tom Wright also played brightly, constantly asking questions of the defence. Len Ikitau was one of the Wallabies’ best. Getty As for the bench, they turned a 21-19 deficit with 25 minutes to go into a narrow win. Wales blew a late chance to steal the Test with a forward pass, but the Wallabies were deserved winners.



2. The big bonus from the bench There was plenty riding on Reds halfback Kalani Thomas, and he delivered with an influential 23-minute shift off the bench. Yes, there was a little knock-on from the base of the ruck that prevented a Wallabies try, but Kalani brought some real energy around the ruck while continuing to look for space behind the Welsh defence with his kicking game. Halfback Kalani Thomas played well off the bench. Getty Images Thomas also channelled his inner George Gregan by milking a penalty with a pass straight into a lazy defender, and the resulting three points proved critical. Thomas over Teddy Wilson must have been a close call for the selectors, but Thomas more than vindicated his inclusion. 3. Ireland unrecognisable ahead of Wallabies season-ender



The Wallabies will face Ireland at Twickenham next Saturday morning, AEDT, which gives them a chance of ending the year with a significant scalp. The Irish are now No.2 in the world after beating the Springboks in Dublin, although that performance shows they are a different team than the one that played the Wallabies in Sydney in July. The Springboks don’t spend too many Tests losing the collision battle, but that is what happened in Dublin against the fired-up Irish. Ireland were inaccurate in possession in the second half and could have beaten South Africa by 13-plus with a bit more composure. The speed and aggression in their carries put the Springboks on the back foot, and they looked like a team full of confidence and purpose. A massive challenge awaits. Ireland were too strong for the Springboks. AP Photo/Peter Morrison 4. Springboks looked old and tired How much did the four-Test series against the All Blacks take out of South Africa? They were well off the pace against Ireland in a Test that was supposed to provoke a response after their “the world us against us” messaging this week.



Forget refereeing inconsistencies, the Springboks’ biggest issue is that there is clearly a big gap in quality between their ageing legends and their back-ups. It was evident when the Wallabies beat them in Perth and it was clear again in Dublin, especially when Malcolm Marx departed and the lineout struggled with new hooker Jan-Hendrik Wessels. Related Article Opinion

Wallabies The moment we knew this Test was going to be different for the Wallabies Peter FitzSimons Columnist and author Tellingly, the Test also finished similarly to the loss to France the week before, with experienced centre Jesse Kriel making a handling error under pressure. The Boks are still clearly good enough to win another Rugby World Cup, but the signs of a post-2027 decline are beginning to show. 5. All Blacks are years into their own decline The Wallabies might continue to struggle against the All Blacks, but they are one of the few remaining teams who seem to have a mental block against the Kiwis. England’s record-breaking 37-12 victory against the All Blacks at Twickenham was almost comfortable at times, and the English will be warm favourites to repeat the result when they meet again next weekend.



Is coach Dave Rennie’s position under threat? On the surface, it should be, as his winning rate of 58 per cent this year is well below Scott Robertson’s record. But, NZ Rugby is likely now aware that the challenges facing the game are too big to be fixed by a change of coach. It has not worked in Australia and it would not work in New Zealand. World.title: The moment we knew this Test was going to be different for the Wallabies
World.content:
SportRugby UnionWallabies Opinion The moment we knew this Test was going to be different for the Wallabies Peter FitzSimons Columnist and author November 22, 2026 — 10:14am

November 22, 2026 — 10:14am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Close Share A A A

So much better from the Wallabies! And what a TEST MATCH! It was a game which had everything, starting with a sold-out Cardiff stadium, filled with 73,000 frenzied spectators wanting to see if their team – which beat the All Blacks last week for the first time in 73 years, did they mention? – could go back-to-back against the might of the Southern Hemisphere. Loading It had the 135-kilogram Taniela Tupou, “a back trapped in a forward’s body”, chiming into the backline and taking a ball from fullback Tom Wright otherwise destined for Joseph-Aukuso Suaalii to go over for a big meat-pie and Australia’s first points. It had, minutes later, diminutive backs Max Jorgensen and Len Ikitau pretending to be forwards for the grand occasion, joining a maul to propel hooker Brandon Paenga-Amosa over for a great try of his own.



Australia ahead 12-0! It had endless, deathless charges to the line by both sides, only to be stopped in extremis by derring-do defences which refused to budge. At this point, Wales looked little less fearsome than the side that toppled the All Blacks last week, in no small part because they were missing – in output, if not quantity – about three men. For reasons best known to himself, the Welsh coach Tandy had left out last week’s man of the match, James Botham, grandson of one Ian Botham. Thank goodness, as time and again Wales displayed the oomph to press the Australian line, only to lack that final bit of penetration. Taniela Tupou is mobbed by teammates after scoring the opening try against Wales, Getty Images That is, until right on half-time, when they did score to allow the Wallabies to go into the break with a 12-7 lead, which was at least handy. But it could have been even greater! At one point our outside centre Suaalii gathered the loose ball from 20 metres out, and set off for the far touch line, with fifteen metres start only to be hauled in and mowed down by the Welsh winger Louis Rees-Zammit.



The major worry at this point was we seemed incapable of gathering in their high-ball, either spilling it or – unforgivably – allowing it to bounce from even the bloody kick-off! (Seriously, you blokes. What is going ON??) It was left to “His-name-is-Su” to help restore order in this field, to effortlessly retrieve some high ball of our own, which helped with territory. And a few minutes later, there was gold in them thar hills for the men in green and gold as Jorgensen went over to allow the Wallabies to go to a handsome 19-7 lead early in the second half. Carter Gordon takes on the defence. Getty Images No sooner had Tim Horan said in commentary that “this game is going to open up” than it happened before our very eyes. Wales quickly struck back with two wonderful tries of their own through clever back-line play to lead 21-19 with 25 minutes still left on the clock, mercifully matched soon afterwards by Ikitau going over for a beauty, to see order again restored with the Wallabies ahead 26-21.



“This match could go anywhere,” Horan noted, and wasn’t that the truth! But surely it will go our way? Surely, the team that beat the Springboks this season and very nearly beat Ireland will emerge victorious against a side that must be tired after their sterling efforts last week? Len Ikitau’s try put the Wallabies in front. Getty Images A long-range penalty goal to Carter Gordon to put the Wallabies ahead 29-21 with only minutes on the clock indeed seemed to have iced the game, only for Wales to go over in the corner with a minute to go! Please, Gawd, NO.



Let there be no “Miracle at Cardiff”, after the Wallabies had done so much, come back from so far after a run of defeats to New Zealand, England and Scotland. Related Article Wallabies Aussies hold on to silence Cardiff crowd as Kiss’ men snap losing streak Happily, there was not. Though Wales laboured mightily, and threw everything at us, fierce Australian defence saw the ball spill forward, and the match was over. Australia win, 29-26, their first win on the spring tour, and give us reason for optimism ahead of next year’s World Cup at home. We had some wonderful performances. Skipper Harry Wilson was mighty, as were Tupou, Ikitau and Jorgensen. Suaalii had his best game in some time and at least saw a lot of the ball. But wait, that’s not all! The Wallabies’ win – after both the Springboks and the All Blacks lost, to Ireland and England respectively – means they will face off against Ireland next Saturday morning at Twickenham in the Nations Championship. What is that, some will ask? It is a brand-new international tournament, launched this year, which is a competition between the six leading northern hemisphere nations and their Southern Hemisphere counterparts – pretty much a rugby league “World Cup”, but with real teams, huge crowds, and genuine wonder as to who will win!



If we can beat Ireland – and we can! – we will come fifth. Bring it on. The Wallabies are baaaaaack! News, results and expert analysis from the weekend of sport sent every Friday.

World.title: One dead, one critical in separate stabbings overnight
World.content:
NationalQueenslandQueensland Police One dead, one critical in separate stabbings overnight Cameron Atfield November 22, 2026 — 9:51am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. A young mother is dead and a man is fighting for his life after two separate stabbings in south-east Queensland overnight. A Queensland Police Service spokesperson said officers were called to a home in Slacks Creek about 11.30pm, where they found a 28-year-old woman suffering from a stab wound. Police did not provide street details. First responders began CPR and tactical first aid, the spokesperson said, but the woman died at the scene. Her 34-year-old husband was arrested at the scene and charged with murder. He was due to face Beenleigh Magistrates Court on Monday.



Queensland Police Acting Chief Superintendent Chris Ahearn said the couple’s young children were at home when their mother was stabbed in the chest. Ahearn said the Logan Criminal Investigation Branch was leading the homicide investigation, which was being treated as a domestic violence incident. Acting Chief Superintendent Chris Ahearn. QPS “We can’t begin to imagine what those children must be feeling,” he said. “But there are significant support services that now have been invoked to provide support to those children, and to help them through what is quite simply a tragic set of circumstances.”



In an unrelated incident at inner-city Spring Hill, police responding to reports of a disturbance at the intersection of Berry Street and Wickham Terrace about 8pm found a man with a stab wound to his chest. A Queensland Ambulance Service spokesperson said the man was taken to the Royal Brisbane and Women’s Hospital in a critical condition. There was no information about his age. Investigations into both stabbings were continuing, the police spokesperson said. Separately, the QAS reported that 12 people were assessed at the emergency treatment centre at Surfers Paradise on the opening night of Schoolies Week on the Gold Coast, with four taken to hospital. World.title: One of Australian cricket’s next-gen stars played in an ODI four days ago. Now he needs surgery
World.content:
Exclusive SportCricketAustralian cricket One of Australian cricket’s next-gen stars played in an ODI four days ago. Now he needs surgery Daniel Brettig November 22, 2026 — 12:57pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Close Share A A A

Rising Australian batter Ollie Peake’s summer has been thrown into turmoil by an ankle infection that may require more than one round of surgery. Peake, 20, was on the field for Australia in a one-day international just four days ago and has also been touted as a possible selection for next year’s Test tour of India. Ollie Peake’s immediate playing future is under a cloud. Getty Images However, he has been affected by ankle discomfort related to a previous surgery, and it has now been decided that he needs another procedure to remove metalwork and allow the infection to clear. Peake is definitely out of this week’s Sheffield Shield game against South Australia in Adelaide, and he is also under a heavy cloud for the Melbourne Renegades in the Big Bash League this summer.



His return to play could conceivably be delayed until the back end of the Shield competition in February or March if things do not run smoothly. Editor's pick Australian cricket Marsh seeks sandpaper peace deal, calls on Cummins, bowlers and CA to share responsibility “It’s a disappointing setback for Ollie, particularly after his recent international white-ball duties,” Cricket Victoria head of male cricket Wade Seccombe told this masthead. “On medical advice, he will undergo a procedure on Tuesday to remove metalwork from his ankle, which means he will miss Victoria’s upcoming Sheffield Shield fixture against South Australia. “We’ll consult with Ollie and his medical team after the procedure to assess his recovery timeline and playing availability.”



Peake is considered one of the most promising young cricketers in Australia, and has already travelled on multiple tours for the national side. He was an apprentice on the 2025 tour of Sri Lanka precisely because the national selectors view his game as ideally suited to assignments in South Asia, such as the India Test tour in January and February next year. In ODI cricket, Peake made his debut in Pakistan earlier this year, and made a string of handy scores against Zimbabwe and South Africa at the start of the season – in nine 50-over games for Australia, Peake has made 215 runs at 26.87, with a strike rate of 88.84, and a highest score of 48. Young gun Ollie Peake in action for Australia in June. Getty Images He made similar kinds of contributions early in the domestic season for Victoria, passing 30 at least once in every first-class game, and also making 73 in a one-day cup game against South Australia in Melbourne.



Related Article Ball tampering ‘I didn’t know’: Lehmann adamant he didn’t know about sandpaper plot, reveals how he sank to a ‘dark place’ Other seasoned observers have also noted Peake’s cricket brain being well-developed for one so young. “I remember coming back and saying, ‘I’ve not heard a player talk like that for a while’,” Victorian coach Chris Rogers has said of an early conversation with Peake. “Whether he was 18 or 25, it was impressive to hear his self-awareness, his understanding of his own game, his strengths and weaknesses, and what he was working on. “It had a lot more depth to it than most of the players who come out of the pathway and who probably have only ever tasted success because they’ve been the best players and the challenges haven’t been as hard. It was definitely eye-opening. “I hadn’t had a lot to do with Ollie up until then. But that conversation opened my eyes to just where he’s at and maybe what he’s capable of.”



For now, however, Peake’s immediate future hinges largely on what the surgeon uncovers this week. News, results and expert analysis from the weekend of sport sent every Friday.

World.content:
Breaking CultureMoviesCity life ‘Field of dreams’: Scrubland beside a Sydney motorway slated to become city’s next film studio Linda Morris November 22, 2026 — 12:14pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month.
