It’s a semi-cleared swathe of scrubland near the Eastern Creek spaghetti interchange of the M4 Motorway, once marketed as an ideal spot for a tourism caravan park. Now the NSW government hopes it will become the new site of Sydney’s next film studio, boasting six new sound stages and a backlot. The eight hectares of land on Pikes Lane earmarked for Sydney’s next film studio. Sitthixay Ditthavong Arts Minister John Graham has gone so far as to pitch the site as Hollywood’s next “field of dreams”, referring to the 1989 film in which Kevin Costner builds a baseball pitch out of a cornfield. The nominated studio lot lies on eight hectares between the M4 and the Great Western Highway within a designated tourism precinct comprising Sydney Action Park, Sydney Zoo and Sydney Motorsport Park. The Disney film lot at Moore Park is nine studios on 13 hectares but subject of what local producers says is a film production bottleneck.



The Minns government had nominated three Crown land sites near Blacktown – at Bungarribee, Eastern Creek and near Prospect Reservoir – for investors to consider for a “world-class” facility. The nominated site on Pikes Lane sits within the Western Sydney Parklands. It’s offering $100 million fund to the winning consortium who will receive the subsidised lease on this piece of Crown land to build the city’s first new film and television studio in a quarter of a century. The hunt for a private partner to build a second major film studio in Sydney has drawn 16 submissions with three international and local consortia shortlisted – and the winner to be announced in the New Year. The participants shortlisted to move to the next stage bring an incredible depth of experience and reflect the strong appetite internationally for NSW as a screen production location, Graham said.



“Pikes Lane is a field of dreams, a place where the best international productions can film in state-of-the-art facilities, engaging our internationally renowned highly skilled local crew, and enjoy an unbeatable lifestyle for international cast while they’re here,” he said. “A second screen studio will also unlock much-needed production space for our local productions, giving a much-needed boost to keep our internationally acclaimed producers making their productions and employing people here, in NSW.” Arts minister John Graham with producers Jodi Matterson and Josh Pomeranz. Sam Mooy Western Sydney is an area of jobs growth which will benefit from its access near the second airport, due to open this month. Developer led proposals for a film studio on privately held land in Calga near the Central Coast, and at Oran Park appear to have not won support for $100 million investment tied to their purchased lots. The open process appears to have considered and rejected options to build a studio in the railway yards of Eveleigh and Sydney Olympic precinct, understood to have involved remediation of both sites, and in the case of the Olympic Park, legislative amendments.





“A second screen studio will also unlock much needed production space for our local productions, giving a much-needed boost to keep our internationally acclaimed producers making their productions and employing people here, in NSW,” Graham said. World.title: Veteran NSW politician Reverend Fred Nile dies aged 92
World.content:
Updated PoliticsNSWNSW State Parliament Veteran NSW politician Reverend Fred Nile dies aged 92 Jessica McSweeney Updated November 22, 2026 — 11:58am ,first published November 22, 2026 — 9:52am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. NSW’s longest-serving state MP Reverend Fred Nile has died, his family has confirmed. “It is with deep sadness the Nile family announces the passing of Revd the Hon. Frederick John Nile who passed away peacefully on the 21st of November at the age of 92,” a family statement said. The Reverend Fred Nile was the longest serving MP in NSW Parliament. Chris Pearce “Revd Nile is survived by his wife, children, grandchildren and great-grandchildren. Details about a service or memorial will be shared soon.” Nile was a member of the NSW Legislative Council for more than 40 years and was national president of the Christian Democratic Party before leaving politics at the 2023 election.



Best known for his conservative Christian values, Nile was a vocal opponent to same-sex marriage, railed against abortion and wanted to ban same-sex couples from adopting children. The Christian crusader found an unlikely ally in Sydney MP Alex Greenwich before Nile left NSW Parliament, teaming up with the gay MP to support legislation protecting Indigenous culture and heritage. Fred Nile speaking at a protest outside an Oxford Street bathhouse. Anthony Lewis/Fairfax Media Greenwich on Sunday sent a message to Premier Chris Minns requesting a state service to honour Nile’s contribution to NSW. He said he had formed a good working relationship with Nile towards the end of his parliamentary career despite the pair’s opposing views on most progressive issues. “Rev Nile played the ball, not the person,” Greenwich said.



Related Article Opinion

Fred Nile Fred Nile confesses: I’m sorry I prayed for rain on the Mardi Gras parade Peter FitzSimons Columnist and author “His opposition to many of the reforms I delivered came from his faith, and he didn’t engage in the personalised vitriol that comes from many of today’s right-wing politicians.” Nile became well known for praying for rain before Sydney’s yearly Mardi Gras parade, although he apologised for this in an interview with this masthead in 2022. Born in Kings Cross in 1934, Nile was ordained as an evangelical Congregational minister in 1964 and spent most of the 1970s in Christian leadership roles before his election to parliament in 1981. In his inaugural speech, Nile described himself as a pro-child and pro-family campaigner who wanted to stamp out things he identified as moral failings in NSW, including alcohol advertising and drug use.



Transport Minister and fellow upper house MP John Graham said Nile was someone who worked hard to ensure people of faith were respected in public debate. Related Article Obituaries God’s warrior: Fred Nile was never afraid to take up the fight “One of the great things about Fred Nile was over all that time, more than 42 years, you knew exactly where he was coming from, that didn’t change,” Graham said. “In a time when politics can seem pretty chaotic, I think that’s a really good thing and a real tribute to the sort of MP that he was.” Opposition Leader Kellie Sloane described Nile as a man of deep Christian faith with strong convictions.



“While people held different views on the issues he championed, there can be no doubting his commitment to his beliefs and his extraordinary contribution to parliamentary life in NSW,” she said. World.title: God’s warrior: Fred Nile was never afraid to take up the fight
World.content:
NationalObituaries God’s warrior: Fred Nile was never afraid to take up the fight Malcolm Brown November 22, 2026 — 11:47am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Close Share A A A

FRED NILE: 1934 - 2026 Fred Nile came to his prime of life at a time of a tidal wave of change. It was when so many certainties were being challenged, such as the place of women in society, the sanctity of marriage, monarchism, anti-communism, militarism, and the condemnation of abortion, homosexuality and pornography. The challenges represented a tidal wave impossible to suppress. Towards the end of Fred Nile’s life, formal same-sex marriages had been accepted, rights of transsexuals were being protected. For many progressives, all this was positive, wiping away bigotry and making society more just and tolerant. Candidate Fred Nile smiles at the Legislative Assembly Nominations on March 12, 2015. Fairfax But others would have none of it, holding up the Bible as the ultimate arbiter of standards. One of those was Fred Nile, who as a young man responded to preaching in a Congregationalist church in Revesby, south-western Sydney, and began a career that saw him take the lead in the church, community movements, the media and politics.



He was dogged by persecution and ridicule, culminating at one point in having his bust made of papier mache paraded down Oxford Street in the Gay and Lesbian Mardi Gras. But he was respected. Many supported him. Nobody could serve a term of more than 40 years in the NSW parliament if their intrinsic value was not recognised. He became, in several senses, the “Father of the House”. Seminar on prostitution with speakers Fred Nile and Gretel Petiniger, known as “Madam Lash”, at the University of NSW, 1974. Fairfax Frederick John Nile was born on September 15, 1934, in Kings Cross, son of a British migrant and Great War veteran Frederick Nile, who had become a taxi driver, and Marjorie (nee Clark). The elder Nile, described as “hard-drinking and hard-swearing”, was father of Fred, another son James, and daughters Marjorie and Mary. Related Article Updated

NSW State Parliament Veteran NSW politician Reverend Fred Nile dies aged 92 When the younger Fred Nile was young, his parents moved to Mascot, where they bought a grocery business and Nile went to Mascot Public School. Very much in the working-class environment, the younger Nile was briefly a runner for an SP bookie and his brother would continue long-term in the racing industry.



In 1946, Nile went to Cleveland Street Intermediate Commercial High School, and two years later joined the Citizens Military Forces (CMF). He completed his Intermediate Certificate and began work as a junior storeman in the aviation industry, with Paul & Gray Pty Ltd at Mascot. When the family moved to Revesby in 1950, Nile moved to the company’s operation at Bankstown and went through his religious conversion. Nile decided in 1955 to train full-time for the ministry. His boss at Paul & Gray, where Nile had become assistant manager, was reluctant to see him go but said: “We cannot compete with God!” Nile entered the Melbourne Bible Institute, later known as the Victorian College of the Bible, where he spent two years, became Senior Student and obtained a First-Class Diploma. Nile with singer Cliff Richard in 1982. Fairfax He then entered the NSW Congregational Theological College and went on to study at the NSW United Faculty of Theology at the University of Sydney, and the University of New England where he did Philosophy, History and Senior Education. In December 1958, Nile married Elaine Creasly, also a child of the inner city, born in Waterloo, and the next year became as student minister at the Congregational Church in Newcastle, followed by service at Bexley and Brighton-le-Sands. Promoted to major in the CMF, he became father for the first time in 1960 when son Stephen was born, to be followed by a daughter, Sharon, and sons Mark and David.



Nile was ordained at Bexley in 1964, became national director of the Australian Christian Endeavour and led the Australian delegation to the World Christian Endeavour Convention in Belfast. He was appointed assistant director of the Billy Graham Crusade in Sydney Showground in 1968, and in 1970 was appointed a director of the Methodist Mission to the People of New South Wales, led by the Reverend Alan Walker. Nile worked in numerous evangelical positions, edited Christian publications and took a moral stand on issues such as screening of the film O Calcutta. He became principal of a “Jesus Commune” in the city to promulgate a “Jesus Revolution”, involving 20 young men and women who did a one-year course. His campaign led him to the formation of the Australian arm of the Festival of Light. Fred Nile’s papier-mache head on a silver platter during the 1988 Mardi Gras. Fairfax Mary Whitehouse, who founded the festival in Britain to combat what she saw as “Western decadence”, came to Australia in October 1973. The knockers protested vigorously against her and against Nile. Nile refused to back down, and also came into conflict with church people whom he saw as “modernists”, such as the Reverend Ted Noffs and John Spong, whom he said were trying to modify doctrine. In 1974, Nile became full-time director of the Australian Festival of Light, campaigning for “purity, love and family life”. According to Nile, Attorney-General Lionel Murphy laughed at them and said: “You only represent yourself; you people don’t count.” Nile said that instead of the streamlining of divorce as set out in the Murphy’s Family Law Bill, governments should direct their energies to building up family life.



In February, Nile led a Festival of Light demonstration outside the studios of Channel 10, protesting about the television programs The Box and Number 96. He was supported by thousands but also brought ridicule and abuse, and often harsh treatment by an unsympathetic media. In 1974, Nile formed the Family Action Movement, the political arm of the festival. Two years later, he transferred to the newly formed Uniting Church Australia. In 1977, he founded the Call to Australia (Fred Nile) Group, “For God and Family”, to replace the Family Action Movement. The political arena, he said, was where decisions were made, and Christians should be in the thick of it. Nile addresses a rally outside NSW Parliament in 2015. The festival brought out such luminaries as journalist Malcolm Muggeridge and Mother Teresa. It campaigned against the Family Law Act and the repeal of the Summary Offences Act. He attacked school programs aimed at countering “sexism” in schools and advocated the roles of females as “mother-carer” and males as “father-protector”. He entered the media world when he accepted an offer from Ita Buttrose to write a weekly column for The Sunday Telegraph. He also accepted an invitation to host a Sunday night radio talkback program on 2GB, and from there he went to politics, being elected the NSW Legislative assembly in September 1981 with 9.8 per cent of the vote. It was, he said, “God’s will … I don’t want to be seen as a politician but as a Christian citizen in parliament who is also an active ordained minister.”



Nile and his wife, who joined in the Legislative Council in 1988, spoke out about the AIDS epidemic and many other aspects of social life they deemed immoral. The opposition towards Nile became more virulent, including from groups as Sisters of Perpetual Indulgence, who were gay men dressed as nuns. Nile opposed then-premier Neville Wran’s private member’s bill in 1984 to decriminalise homosexual acts. Sacked from 2GB after four years, he soon bounced back to take radio host position on Radio 2CBA. In later years, Fred Nile and independent MP Alex Greenwich formed an unlikely pairing on some issues. Fairfax In parliament, he served and would serve on numerous parliamentary committees, including the NSW Parliamentary Standing Committee on Social Issues, facilitating legislative reforms on adoption laws, drug abuse among youth, rape rates and pornography, domestic violence, youth violence, youth rural suicides, compensation for medically acquired AIDS/HIV victims, juvenile justice, births, deaths and marriage records. The Festival of Light embraced the concept of Aboriginal Reconciliation, and wanted to get rid of certain books from the school curriculum. In October 1990, Nile launched his “Jesus Battalions” in Kings Cross to protest about immorality and introduced privately a Tobacco Advertising Prohibition Bill.



Seeking re-election, Nile said he wanted abortions restricted to certain public hospitals, closure of all private termination clinics, a ban on pornography and casinos, and an immediate stop to public funding of the Gay and Lesbian Mardi Gras. He continued trips abroad to study and give addresses. Call to Australia became the Christian Democratic Party and there were continuing causes to fight, including the pressure on governments to allow same-sex marriage, another being ordination of homosexuals. Nile railed against what he saw as compromises being made by established churches. He disassociated with the United Church because in his view it was drifting from a literal interpretation of the Bible. Fred Nile standing in front of a picture of the Queen at NSW Parliament in 2014. Fairfax He protested about the move to institute safe heroin injection rooms, advocating instead counselling and therapy. He called for the banning of full body covering for Muslims, on the grounds that they might be used by terrorists to conceal weapons, and for a moratorium on Muslim immigration, which offended Muslims totally innocent of radical ideas. He was a frequent target for criticism, but despite all that, he remained in power. When he resigned from the Legislative Council in 2004 to make an unsuccessful tilt at the Senate, he was reappointed. He was re-elected in 2007 for a further term, of eight years.



Widowed in 2011 when Elaine died of cancer, Nile continued his moral crusade, opposing same-sex marriage and same-sex parenthood and vehemently opposed the introduction of “ethics” classes in state schools as an alternative to scripture. He was accepted as part of the system. There were some challenges, including a nasty internal party stoush with MLC Marie Bignold, which he settled, but the jibes he got from MPs were usually friendly ones, such as the occasion when a Labor MP called out during a division when Nile and his wife were the only ones on the other side. Nile said that he was accompanied by angels, to which the MP replied: “Angels don’t vote”. Fred Nile and his second wife Silvana Nero on their wedding day in 2013. James Alcock In an uncomplicated world, there would have been little opposition. The fact that there was so much opposition was a reflection, perhaps, not on him but on the world as it is. Nile at 78 years of age became engaged to a Christian Democratic Party candidate, Silvana Nero, 23 years his junior, in 2013 and remarried. He waxed and waned on retirement and in February 2023, announced his intention to nominate for re-election to the NSW Parliament. But age really was catching up with the old warrior. Nile collapsed the following month at a public morals protest outside Channel 10. He died on November 21, 2026. He is survived by his wife Nero, his children and great-grandchildren. Malcolm Brown

World.title: Bowen faces climate crisis as clock runs down on ‘worst COP ever’
World.content:
EnvironmentClimate changeParis Agreement Bowen faces climate crisis as clock runs down on ‘worst COP ever’ Nick O'Malley November 22, 2026 — 11:41am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Close Share A A A

Global climate talks that should have concluded on Friday remain deadlocked, with negotiators expected to resume discussions on Sunday in Antalya, Turkey, amid questions about the strategy of Climate Change and Energy Minister Chris Bowen in leading the summit. Nations remain at loggerheads over a series of key issues. Small island nations that are vulnerable to climate change, including in the Pacific, insist that any final agreement, known as a cover text, include specific reference to reducing fossil fuel emissions. But that position has been objected to by oil-producing nations led by Saudi Arabia, and supported by Russia and some developing nations. Climate Change Minister Chris Bowen faces a crisis over the coming hours at the COP31 talks in Turkey. Getty Images Some nations in the same bloc have objected to a proposed agreement championed by Bowen to have the world commit to making 35 per cent of its energy use electric by 2035. “Things worth doing, in my experience, don’t come easy,” Bowen said during a press conference at the COP on Saturday. “And I’ll tell you what’s worth doing is electrification. Electrification is the key to transitioning away from fossil fuels.”



Led by France and Panama, representatives from nations including Belgium, Côte d’Ivoire, Finland, Greece, Guatemala, Spain, Sweden and Vanuatu are demanding more ambitious climate action. Related Article Analysis

Paris Agreement ‘Heat records keep shattering’: Time is running out for COP to save us “We cannot [tell] the world we are now getting to 1.5 [degrees of warming] and then do business as if nothing was happening,” said France’s minister for ecological transition, Monique Barbut. There is also disagreement over climate finance, and European Union Climate Commissioner Wopke Hoekstra called demands for increased pledges for finance from developing nations hit by climate disasters “dead in the water” before the talks even began. Finance has long between a contentions issue at climate talks, with developed nations wanting to maintain focus on reducing emissions, and developing nations demanding financial assistance to help them insulate their economies from the impact of warming that they did not cause. The dispute is becoming more complex as the talks continue, with donor nations arguing that some countries that were considered poor when the first climate agreements were made have since become more wealthy and should no longer be receiving support.



A third area of deadlock in the current negotiations is over reference in the cover decision to the use of carbon capture and storage technology. While UN scientific assessments say that any effort to stabilise the climate will need to include removing carbon pollution from the atmosphere when the technology to do so at scale becomes available later in the century, many say that including reference to it now will simply be used as justification not to pursue emission reductions. If the standoff cannot be resolved, UN rules allow for the talks to be suspended until next year. That outcome would be a blow to Bowen, who created the role of president of negotiations at the talks when Australia failed to secure the hosting rights in a standoff with Turkey. Smoke from a wildfire in France in July. France is one of the countries pushing for greater climate action at COP. AFP Though it is not unusual for COP negotiations, which demand consensus agreement between the almost 200 signatories of the Paris Accord, to extend beyond deadline, they have only ever once been suspended without an outcome, when Kyoto Protocol talks collapsed in 2000. By Friday evening in Antalya, frustrated activists had begun to blame Bowen and his Turkish counterpart, Turkish Environment Minister Murat Kurum, for the failure of the COP to command support for ambitious climate action.



“The COP presidents want to tell us this has been a great COP,” said Mohamed Adow, head of the climate group Power Shift Africa at a press conference convened by the Climate Action Network. “Well, I can tell you without any doubt that this has been the worst COP ever.” Dr Bill Hare of Climate Analytics. Others have questioned Bowen’s strategy of allowing nations to insert many ambitious claims in an early draft of the cover decision, and of even insisting that the talks include such a decision in the first place. Leading climate analyst Bill Hare, the director of Climate Analytics – a global non-profit climate science and policy institute – said Bowen made the right call, particularly given the UN’s scientific report published before the COP which said the world was set to miss its 1.5-degree target. “The urgency of the crisis is visible to everyone, and if the COP didn’t do anything visible about the urgency in a political sense, there would be bigger questions about there was any point [in the process] at all,” Hare said.



“I think Bowen is right and correct and courageous to say we need to have a cover decision because it anchors things and provides a focal point for making some decent political signals.” Get to the heart of what’s happening with climate change and the environment.

World.title: There are no easy Tests in the north. The Wallabies’ win over Wales deserves respect
World.content:
Analysis SportRugby UnionWallabies There are no easy Tests in the north. The Wallabies’ win over Wales deserves respect Paul Cully November 22, 2026 — 11:30am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Close Share A A A

1. Wallabies’ big names step up The days of taking Test wins in November for granted are long gone, so the Wallabies’ 29-26 victory over Wales needs to be given proper respect. There were two big factors in the result. First, their bigger names stepped up; second, the tactical plan to stack the bench paid dividends. Len Ikitau was sensational, producing tough carries with some sublime touches on attack. His midfield partnership with Joseph-Aukuso Suaalii was also excellent, with Suaalii delivering his most mature performance in the Wallabies No.13 jersey. Fullback Tom Wright also played brightly, constantly asking questions of the defence. Len Ikitau was one of the Wallabies’ best. Getty As for the bench, they turned a 21-19 deficit with 25 minutes to go into a narrow win. Wales blew a late chance to steal the Test with a forward pass, but the Wallabies were deserved winners.



2. The big bonus from the bench There was plenty riding on Reds halfback Kalani Thomas, and he delivered with an influential 23-minute shift off the bench. Yes, there was a little knock-on from the base of the ruck that prevented a Wallabies try, but Kalani brought some real energy around the ruck while continuing to look for space behind the Welsh defence with his kicking game. Halfback Kalani Thomas played well off the bench. Getty Images Thomas also channelled his inner George Gregan by milking a penalty with a pass straight into a lazy defender, and the resulting three points proved critical. Thomas over Teddy Wilson must have been a close call for the selectors, but Thomas more than vindicated his inclusion. 3. Ireland unrecognisable ahead of Wallabies season-ender



The Wallabies will face Ireland at Twickenham next Saturday morning, AEDT, which gives them a chance of ending the year with a significant scalp. The Irish are now No.2 in the world after beating the Springboks in Dublin, although that performance shows they are a different team than the one that played the Wallabies in Sydney in July. The Springboks don’t spend too many Tests losing the collision battle, but that is what happened in Dublin against the fired-up Irish. Ireland were inaccurate in possession in the second half and could have beaten South Africa by 13-plus with a bit more composure. The speed and aggression in their carries put the Springboks on the back foot, and they looked like a team full of confidence and purpose. A massive challenge awaits. Ireland were too strong for the Springboks. AP Photo/Peter Morrison 4. Springboks looked old and tired How much did the four-Test series against the All Blacks take out of South Africa? They were well off the pace against Ireland in a Test that was supposed to provoke a response after their “the world us against us” messaging this week.



Forget refereeing inconsistencies, the Springboks’ biggest issue is that there is clearly a big gap in quality between their ageing legends and their back-ups. It was evident when the Wallabies beat them in Perth and it was clear again in Dublin, especially when Malcolm Marx departed and the lineout struggled with new hooker Jan-Hendrik Wessels. Related Article Opinion

Wallabies The moment we knew this Test was going to be different for the Wallabies Peter FitzSimons Columnist and author Tellingly, the Test also finished similarly to the loss to France the week before, with experienced centre Jesse Kriel making a handling error under pressure. The Boks are still clearly good enough to win another Rugby World Cup, but the signs of a post-2027 decline are beginning to show. 5. All Blacks are years into their own decline The Wallabies might continue to struggle against the All Blacks, but they are one of the few remaining teams who seem to have a mental block against the Kiwis. England’s record-breaking 37-12 victory against the All Blacks at Twickenham was almost comfortable at times, and the English will be warm favourites to repeat the result when they meet again next weekend.



Is coach Dave Rennie’s position under threat? On the surface, it should be, as his winning rate of 58 per cent this year is well below Scott Robertson’s record. But, NZ Rugby is likely now aware that the challenges facing the game are too big to be fixed by a change of coach. It has not worked in Australia and it would not work in New Zealand. World.title: The moment we knew this Test was going to be different for the Wallabies
World.content:
SportRugby UnionWallabies Opinion The moment we knew this Test was going to be different for the Wallabies Peter FitzSimons Columnist and author November 22, 2026 — 10:14am

November 22, 2026 — 10:14am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Close Share A A A

So much better from the Wallabies! And what a TEST MATCH! It was a game which had everything, starting with a sold-out Cardiff stadium, filled with 73,000 frenzied spectators wanting to see if their team – which beat the All Blacks last week for the first time in 73 years, did they mention? – could go back-to-back against the might of the Southern Hemisphere. Loading It had the 135-kilogram Taniela Tupou, “a back trapped in a forward’s body”, chiming into the backline and taking a ball from fullback Tom Wright otherwise destined for Joseph-Aukuso Suaalii to go over for a big meat-pie and Australia’s first points. It had, minutes later, diminutive backs Max Jorgensen and Len Ikitau pretending to be forwards for the grand occasion, joining a maul to propel hooker Brandon Paenga-Amosa over for a great try of his own.



Australia ahead 12-0! It had endless, deathless charges to the line by both sides, only to be stopped in extremis by derring-do defences which refused to budge. At this point, Wales looked little less fearsome than the side that toppled the All Blacks last week, in no small part because they were missing – in output, if not quantity – about three men. For reasons best known to himself, the Welsh coach Tandy had left out last week’s man of the match, James Botham, grandson of one Ian Botham. Thank goodness, as time and again Wales displayed the oomph to press the Australian line, only to lack that final bit of penetration. Taniela Tupou is mobbed by teammates after scoring the opening try against Wales, Getty Images That is, until right on half-time, when they did score to allow the Wallabies to go into the break with a 12-7 lead, which was at least handy. But it could have been even greater! At one point our outside centre Suaalii gathered the loose ball from 20 metres out, and set off for the far touch line, with fifteen metres start only to be hauled in and mowed down by the Welsh winger Louis Rees-Zammit.



The major worry at this point was we seemed incapable of gathering in their high-ball, either spilling it or – unforgivably – allowing it to bounce from even the bloody kick-off! (Seriously, you blokes. What is going ON??) It was left to “His-name-is-Su” to help restore order in this field, to effortlessly retrieve some high ball of our own, which helped with territory. And a few minutes later, there was gold in them thar hills for the men in green and gold as Jorgensen went over to allow the Wallabies to go to a handsome 19-7 lead early in the second half. Carter Gordon takes on the defence. Getty Images No sooner had Tim Horan said in commentary that “this game is going to open up” than it happened before our very eyes. Wales quickly struck back with two wonderful tries of their own through clever back-line play to lead 21-19 with 25 minutes still left on the clock, mercifully matched soon afterwards by Ikitau going over for a beauty, to see order again restored with the Wallabies ahead 26-21.



“This match could go anywhere,” Horan noted, and wasn’t that the truth! But surely it will go our way? Surely, the team that beat the Springboks this season and very nearly beat Ireland will emerge victorious against a side that must be tired after their sterling efforts last week? Len Ikitau’s try put the Wallabies in front. Getty Images A long-range penalty goal to Carter Gordon to put the Wallabies ahead 29-21 with only minutes on the clock indeed seemed to have iced the game, only for Wales to go over in the corner with a minute to go! Please, Gawd, NO.



Let there be no “Miracle at Cardiff”, after the Wallabies had done so much, come back from so far after a run of defeats to New Zealand, England and Scotland. Related Article Wallabies Aussies hold on to silence Cardiff crowd as Kiss’ men snap losing streak Happily, there was not. Though Wales laboured mightily, and threw everything at us, fierce Australian defence saw the ball spill forward, and the match was over. Australia win, 29-26, their first win on the spring tour, and give us reason for optimism ahead of next year’s World Cup at home. We had some wonderful performances. Skipper Harry Wilson was mighty, as were Tupou, Ikitau and Jorgensen. Suaalii had his best game in some time and at least saw a lot of the ball. But wait, that’s not all! The Wallabies’ win – after both the Springboks and the All Blacks lost, to Ireland and England respectively – means they will face off against Ireland next Saturday morning at Twickenham in the Nations Championship. What is that, some will ask? It is a brand-new international tournament, launched this year, which is a competition between the six leading northern hemisphere nations and their Southern Hemisphere counterparts – pretty much a rugby league “World Cup”, but with real teams, huge crowds, and genuine wonder as to who will win!



If we can beat Ireland – and we can! – we will come fifth. Bring it on. The Wallabies are baaaaaack! News, results and expert analysis from the weekend of sport sent every Friday.

World.title: Are New Zealanders sick of politics - or sick of politicians?
World.content:
With voter turnout this election on track to be its second lowest in history, and plenty of criticism of negative campaigns, are New Zealanders tuning out of the democratic electoral process?

Now, following an election where National and Labour combined are at historic lows on preliminary results, political reporter Lillian Hanly speaks to experts about some of the cynicism around politics, and whether the 'attention economy' is making it worse.

Audio player for " Negativity in politics? " removed for printing Visit page to play audio: https://www.rnz.co.nz/news/eyJhbGciOiJIUzI1NiJ9._v0.KrRTFtoPsaA8nSDloPZ4KejQJr59ANQpD9ULgGwzaM0/politics/2726771%2Fare-new-zealanders-sick-of-politics-or-sick-of-politicians

During the election campaign, many voters told RNZ they were uncertain about who to vote for - an uncertainty they hadn't felt in the past - or whether to vote at all.

One West Aucklander was so uninspired that he said choosing between the parties was like "picking which shit food to eat".

His final choice? Not to vote for anyone.

Another Aucklander told RNZ during the campaign he wasn't "a big fan" of any of them.

"All of these empty promises, all the time, saying things are going to happen and then they just don't happen."

A key feature of this election was the declining support for both major parties, while minor parties saw a lift.

National and Labour, under Christopher Luxon and Chris Hipkins, consistently polled in the low thirties and even twenties throughout the year.

Preliminary results have them both at 29 percent.

Former chief science advisor Sir Peter Gluckman described the trend as the "hollowing out" of the political middle, something traditional liberal democracies were increasingly grappling with, along with a range of other issues.

Former chief science advisor Sir Peter Gluckman. Supplied / University of Auckland

A global crisis of confidence

Early this year, international relations expert Reuben Steff - now an associate professor at Mendel University, Czech Republic - described New Zealand as being on a path of systemic decline in relation to its living standards, brain drain and economy.

He later told RNZ New Zealand was following the trend of a global crisis of confidence in democracy with increasing dissatisfaction with how it functioned.

He pointed to growing distrust internationally in political institutions, populist sentiment, media distrust, disinformation and declining civic skills.

He described social media algorithms as amplifying outrage, hostility and political division, while shorter attention spans and declining literacy and numeracy were potentially undermining people's capacity to engage with complex issues and informed debate.

He warned of the erosion of the classical liberal centre, rooted in open debate, intellectual humility and the recognition of political adversaries as legitimate opponents

He also warned political opponents were increasingly viewed not simply as being wrong, but as immoral or unwilling to debate in good faith.

Steff said New Zealand was following the same trajectory.

"Citizens are feeling increasingly isolated and alienated. It is not an exaggeration to say that the political system now arguably faces a legitimacy crisis," he told RNZ.

International relations expert Reuben Steff. supplied

The hollowing out of the middle

Gluckman warned the incoming prime minister in 2023 that New Zealand was not immune to the pressures facing liberal democracies internationally, describing them as "cracking".

In New Zealand, he said "our institutions are less trusted, policy debates have often been reduced to personal attacks and citizens feel relatively powerless".

Speaking to RNZ ahead of the election, he said politicians were increasingly claiming to have simple answers to complex problems that had accumulated over decades.

"Citizens are becoming more and more cynical about that," he said.

He also pointed to social media driving demands for short-termism, the lingering effects of the Covid-19 pandemic, economic anxiety and the cost-of-living crisis - which was not unique to New Zealand.

Gluckman pointed to the "hollowing out" of the political middle, saying the MMP system was not designed for the social media age.

"Extreme parties grab more of the attention economy," which worked on single statements which were not nuanced.

"In the end, policy is a complex project over time and with multiple dimensions", which also required agreement and continuity across political parties.

He raised concerns too about the focus shifting towards leaders' personalities, television performances and presentation rather than their policies, and that political debate was increasingly characterised by people defining themselves against opposing parties rather than through their own policy positions.

"There is a tribalism that emerges, there's no doubt about that, and unfortunately, since Twitter appeared with an anonymity and ad hominem attacks becoming easier, we've seen that reflected in political discourse as well."

The attention economy

University of Auckland professor of media and screen studies Neal Curtis described the attention economy as the situation in which information was constantly increasing, so people's capacity to pay attention to it was "ever diminishing."

University of Auckland professor Neal Curtis. Supplied

Curtis said the reason it was an attention economy was because corporations depend on getting customer attention to sell their product.

The rise of the internet and social media had intensified the problem, with social media companies using algorithms designed to maximise engagement and keep people returning to their platforms he said.

Curtis said research had found that scandal and outrage generated particularly high levels of engagement, creating an information environment increasingly dominated by conflict, antagonism and clickbait.

He argued the need for commercial - and publicly funded - media to attract audiences and demonstrate engagement to advertisers and funders created pressure to produce clickbait.

Curtis said (speaking prior to the news of RNZ's deficit blowout) that RNZ wasn't immune from the pressure because it must demonstrate audience engagement to justify its funding.

"Radio New Zealand will damage itself by trying to chase after that kind of [attention], to try and make itself heard in that type of information environment, rather than creating a completely different information environment."

He's concerned about a move away from long-form, deliberate and reflective journalism.

Negative campaigning and political promises

The Listener's political columnist Danyl McLauchlan argued the major parties were losing public confidence because they had become too negative, disconnected from voters and focused on short-term political wins rather than good government.

During the election, he said both major parties had run predominantly negative campaigns.

"They understand New Zealand politics primarily in terms of opposing each other. They define themselves in these negative terms.

"Somewhere along the way they've forgotten to find a way to tell something positive about themselves."

He said voters recognised the disconnect and were moving towards smaller parties.

"The public senses that inauthenticity and that disconnection, and when they see other viable options, they just defect for them."

He also pointed to an "unusual" aspect of this campaign where the major parties didn't have charismatic leaders, while the minor parties did.

"Normally charismatic leadership plays a huge role in politics, and that's not just being mediagenic or who you want to have a beer with.

"It's being able to tell that convincing story about what your party is and what it stands for and what it wants to do."

McLauchlan also warned that political communications had become increasingly focused on announcements rather than delivering results, which was "enormously destructive" to the integrity of the policy process.

Earlier this year, McLauchlan described in the Listener "grid-based politics", in which politicians prioritise announcements - or "announceables" - to dominate media coverage and secure short-term political gains.

He argued the focus on short-term political wins had accumulated over decades, contributing to a dysfunctional political system and economy.

The Listener's political columnist Danyl McLauchlan. Supplied / Te Herenga Waka University Press

The need for long-term thinking

Speaking to RNZ again after the election, Gluckman said the results reinforced his earlier thinking and concerns.

"Quite clearly, the country can't decide on its future direction."

He said the "muddled situation" made it very difficult for the country to make some hard decisions about the long-term direction: on the political economy, on the position of Māori, health, education, and so on.

Those "hard questions" shouldn't be caught in the "pendulum of three-year cycles", he said.

"We do need some long-term thinking desperately in New Zealand."

Veronica Tawhai. Supplied / Huia Publishers

Associate professor at Massey University Veronica Tawhai, an advocate for constitutional transformation, was particularly concerned about the lack of vision from major parties on issues affecting Māori.

She's also concerned at the way Māori increasingly seemed to be considered as any other group in New Zealand, rather than holding a unique position.

According to Tawhai, the major failing from the big parties was a lack of vision and an "extreme lack of policy proposals" that would help Māori achieve equality as citizens, despite experiencing some of the effects of housing and healthcare crises disproportionately.

She said Māori had traditionally been highly politically engaged, but research showed attack-style politics could cause young Māori to switch off.

The concern was that this could move beyond disillusionment and discourage them from participating in politics altogether.

"When elections are based on your antagonism or perceived objections to the other side, you're not projecting a message of where you would want to go, and I think New Zealanders do want have a sense that the country can move forward," said Gluckman.

World.title: Nothing special about Black Friday deals - Westpac
World.content:
Audio player for " Is it time to get my money out of AI? " removed for printing Visit page to play audio: https://www.rnz.co.nz/news/eyJhbGciOiJIUzI1NiJ9._v0.KrRTFtoPsaA8nSDloPZ4KejQJr59ANQpD9ULgGwzaM0/business/2726772%2Fnothing-special-about-black-friday-deals-westpac

Is it time to get my money out of AI? No Stupid Questions with Susan Edmunds Download MP3 12m

If you are holding out for a Black Friday or Cyber Monday special to make your purchases, you may be wasting your time.

Westpac analysis shows you can quite likely bag a bargain through the rest of the year too.

The analysis found it common for 30-40 percent of household appliances to be available discounted all year round and the average size of those discounts is not always larger in the December quarter than any other.

For clothing, about 18 percent of items were discounted every quarter and average discounts were similar through the year. In furnishings, about 36 percent were discounted every quarter.

"Black Friday spending is rising year on year," Westpac product, sustainability and marketing managing director Sarah Hearn said.

"Our card data showed Black Friday spending last year was 48 percent higher than a typical Friday, compared to a 43 percent rise in 2024.

"Appliances were top of the wishlist, with the number of transactions in that spending category tripling on Black Friday. Recreation equipment and shoe purchases were double the normal level.

"There are certainly bargains out there, but our analysis of Stats NZ data shows that bargains come around more often than you might think.

"We encourage shoppers to know what they want to buy and how much they're prepared to spend, then stick to it. If that one last purchase is pushing you too far into debt, take a step back and think about whether you can wait for the next sale to come along."

Westpac financial wellbeing programme manager Warren Ngan Woo said shoppers should keep a sharp eye on whether they were getting a deal or not.

"There's quite a few apps online that can really help guide you on price matching and that sort of thing, but it's also a good opportunity to take a look at your list and, if you need it now, then get it now, but if you need it later on, then that's a good opportunity to just wait and just see what you need.

"You have to do your own market research to some degree to make sure that you're getting a good deal, not just waiting for this Black Friday sale to come around or Cyber Monday."

He said customers shopped Black Friday sales for good deals on Christmas presents, but that could create a feeling of FOMO - Fear Of Missing Out.

"It's important for people to take a moment to pause, just revisit your budget, make sure you're not spending more than you should and then take an opportunity to utilise all the free calculators that are out there.

"The key thing I would like to say is that it's not a bargain, if you don't use that product or service."

Consumer NZ communications and campaigns manager Jessica Walker cautioned buyers against Black Friday sales where the regular or recommended retail price was not clear.

"It's really easy to get misled and purchase something when perhaps you could have got it for a better price at another time of the year," she said.

People should remember that retailers were not obliged to provide refunds if they changed their mind, she said.

"There's going to be promotional language banded about all over the place, bright colours, the stores are going to be really inviting ... the desire to buy something is high, but it's not necessarily the best time to buy."

Walker said this year, people should be particularly wary of scams.

"Scams are always a problem, but right now they seem to have been absolutely supercharged by AI. So if you've got your eye on something online, it's a store maybe you haven't seen before, it's really worth taking a few minutes to just check out that site via another means," she said.

"Don't rely on comments and social media posts. That doesn't necessarily mean that the site is legit."
