World.title: Letterbox port poisoning: Renewed push to solve death of Dave Davan
World.content:
Five years after Northland farmer Dave Davan died from downing a glass of poisoned port, his alleged murderer is still walking free and a $100,000 reward remains unclaimed.

Long-time mate Brett Evans told RNZ he had never given up hope of seeing justice done for the hard-case farmer and his family.

"I just can't let it go. It's the horror of the actual circumstances of his murder," he said.

Evans said Davan became severely ill after drinking a glass of port from a bottle left in his letterbox in remote Herekino, on the Far North's west coast.

He died of organ failure about three weeks later, on 9 December 2021, in Auckland Hospital - after naming the man he believed had murdered him.

Tests of the remaining port showed it had been laced with a restricted, and deadly, weedkiller.

However, police had so far been unable to prove who poisoned the port.

After Davan's funeral, a group of friends put up a $50,000 reward for information leading to a conviction - which Evans had since upped to $100,000.

It was a lot of money but would be worth every cent if it brought a result, he said.

"If there's anything I can do to help solve of the case, I'll do it. Hence the reward really. There's quite a few people contributing to that, not just me, and we've been heartened by the fact that the police haven't ever stopped looking into it."

The poisoned port was left in Dave Davan's letterbox on remote Puhata Road in the Far North. RNZ / Peter de Graaf

Evans said his hopes had been lifted in recent weeks when a new detective was assigned to lead the investigation.

He had already been to Kaitāia to meet him and was hoping new evidence would come to light.

Evans believed it was just a coincidence that the renewed push to solve the crime came as friends and family marked the fifth anniversary of Davan's death.

"But we're pretty happy that there's some action happening again," he said.

"We just want justice for Dave and his family. It's horrible to think of him lying there knowing that he'd been poisoned. He possibly didn't have the ear of the police at the right time and he became too ill and subsequently died. So it's a tragedy really."

Son Conrad Davan previously told RNZ his father, who was 67, found two bottles of port in his letterbox on isolated Puhata Road in November 2021.

He drank the first and, a week or so later, opened the second as he was cooking dinner.

He had barely finished the glass when he fell to the floor and was violently ill.

It took until the following morning before he could drag himself to the phone and call for help.

Conrad said his father was convinced from the outset he had been poisoned.

He had noticed the metal seal on the second bottle was broken but thought little of it at the time.

Also, in a rural area like Herekino, there was nothing unusual about people leaving gifts in their neighbours' letterboxes, often as a thank-you for work on their properties or favours done.

Puhata Road in the Far North. RNZ / Peter de Graaf

Conrad said his father seemed to come right at first but four days later was admitted to Kaitāia Hospital with kidney failure.

As his condition deteriorated, he was admitted first to Whangārei Hospital, then flown to the intensive care unit at Auckland Hospital.

Before he lost consciousness, he was able to tell police and family what he believed had happened.

He had saved the second bottle as evidence.

Conrad described his father as "the best fulla I knew" and a wonderful grandfather to his boy.

Dave's brother, Grant Davan, said whoever killed him knew him well - the port was his favourite brand.

Evans said he got to know Dave in the late 1970s when he landed a job on a farm development in the Far North.

"Dave was the manager and I was his sidekick, and we just became very close mates. He taught me a lot about fencing and farming and all that sort of stuff," he said.

World.title: How world media reacted to All Blacks' loss against England
World.content:
England "made a statement" and "fired a warning" in its win over the All Blacks at Twickenham.

New Zealand was defeated 37-12 and after a loss to Wales last week, the world's media did not go easy.

Some expressed frustration that last week's loss didn't fuel this week's win, others contemplated what the All Blacks' punishment would be.

But most focused on how strong England had been, making them potentially impossible to beat.

The Guardian

The Guardian's analysis piece started off by reminding everyone that last week's loss to Wales was met with heavy criticism that the All Blacks had let down their country, even from coach Dave Rennie.

"What awaits the All Blacks after this? Public humiliation? Exile? A firing squad at dawn?"

New Zealand players after the 3rd England try. England v New Zealand All Blacks, 2026 Nations Championship rugby union test match at Allianz Stadium, London, England on Saturday 21st November 2026. Photo: Matt Impey / Photosport Matt Impey / www.photosport.nz

But the article doesn't encourage a punishment, in fact it criticises Rennie for his own harshness.

"Perhaps it is wise to remember it is only a game, Dave. For what made the very best All Blacks sides so impressive was that they always looked like they were having fun ... This rabble did not look like they were having much fun out there."

Planet Rugby

Planet Rugby gave it's five key takeaways from the game with the first focusing on the "statement" England made.

"England made a statement with a convincing and, at times, exhilarating 37-12 win."

"We are witnessing something very, very special here, an identity being crafted. This England side played with a swagger and a confidence we haven't seen in a white shirt for some time, and it was joyous rugby."

The article also pointed out the game proved "shirt numbers don't matter".

Josh Moorby of New Zealand is tackled. England v New Zealand All Blacks, 2026 Nations Championship rugby union test match at Allianz Stadium, London, England on Saturday 21st November 2026. Photo: Matt Impey / Photosport Matt Impey / www.photosport.nz

"At times you'd have wondered whether the two sides had put on the wrong colour shirts, and nowhere was that clearer than in the way England's forwards ignored the numbers on their backs.

"Ollie Chessum wore 6, but in defence he dropped into the second row and Alex Coles took the blindside edge and then they swapped back when England had the ball."

RugbyPass

"England fired a warning to their rivals ahead of next year's World Cup."

The article started strong in contemplating what this win might mean for the future of both teams.

It also credited some of England's victorious morale to the presence of former captain Lewis Moody, who was diagnosed with Motor Neurone Disease in October 2025.

"The presence of Moody... visibly lifted Maro Itoje's men to set the scene for a five-try rout that registered back-to-back wins against New Zealand for the first time since 2002 and 2003."

The All Blacks' morale on the other hand was cited as lacking an energy many expected after their previous loss.

"The backlash expected after New Zealand's shock defeat to Wales last Saturday never materialised, instead they played like a tired team with the weight of the world on their shoulders."

Wallace Sititi of New Zealand is tackled by Fin Baxter of England. England v New Zealand All Blacks, 2026 Nations Championship rugby union test match at Allianz Stadium, London, England on Saturday 21st November 2026. Photo: Matt Impey / Photosport Matt Impey / www.photosport.nz

ESPN

ESPN led with Lewis Moody's presence during the haka, saying this was an initial sign England was going to be hard to beat.

"For all the talk of the All Blacks channelling the frustration of their defeat to Wales into England, the hosts never let them really throw a punch in anger."

It seemed less about New Zealand's poor performance and more about England's undefeatable power.

"This was one of England's greatest performances, the eventual 25-point margin eclipsing England's previous record triumph over the Kiwis, back in 2012 when they won 38-21."

BBC

The British broadcaster also put the spotlight on England's "revival" which "roared up a gear".

"They dominated the All Blacks from the start.

"Henry Slade crossed for the opening try in the fourth minute and only England's own mistakes prevented them taking a bigger lead than their 19-5 advantage into the break.

"Beauden Barrett marked his 150th Test appearance by rounding off a coast-to-coast Kiwi try to cut England's advantage to 24-12. But his team never really threatened to reel in Steve Borthwick's men."

For New Zealand, who suffered a shock defeat by Wales last weekend, it is a result that suggests a long Test season, which included four Tests against South Africa, may be catching up with them.

World.title: New Zealander Navajo Stirling knocks out Jiří Procházka at UFC Qatar
World.content:
New Zealander Navajo Stirling has staked his claim for a shot at the UFC light heavyweight title after a devastating knockout win over former champion Jiří Procházka at UFC Qatar on Sunday.

The City Kickboxing product landed a vicious right hook at the end of the second round, forcing referee Marc Goddard to step in for the stoppage victory.

Stirling did exactly what he said he would, taking his time before launching an assault at the wild Czech fighter.

The opening exchanges saw both tentative to throw anything too risky, with Stirling finding a home for his low kicks, and Procházka's jab peppering his opponent from afar.

For a moment in the first round it looked as if Stirling had been dropped by an overhand right, but replays showed it was a slip as the two light heavyweights closed in on each other.

The second round was much of the same until Stirling picked his shot perfectly, slipping an attack from Procházka and unleashing a huge right hook to the send his opponent crashing down the canvas.

New Zealand's Navajo Stirlng fights against Jiri Prochazka at UFC Qatar. MAHMUD HAMS

Stirling swarmed him but the Czech was already out, and the referee waved off the fight for a dominant victory for the New Zealander.

It was Stirling's fourth finish in a row, and will be hard to deny him a title shot, even if the New Zealand himself doesn't really want it - at least yet.

Currently champion and teammate Carlos Ulberg won the belt after knocking out Procházka in April.

Stirling has previously said he would wait his turn for the title, and the pair wouldn't need to fight for the belt.

Asked who he wanted next in his post-fight speech, Stirling said anyone ranked above him, and instead, made a bigger case for custom shorts.

In a division desperate for new talent, some honest conversations will need to be had at City Kickboxing over the coming months as the UFC won't want to wait long to give Stirling a title shot.

New Zealand's Dan Hooker reacts after defeating American Brian Ortega. MAHMUD HAMS

Meanwhile, fellow Kiwi Dan Hooker snapped a three-fight losing skid with a win over American Brian Ortega.

Like Stirling, Hooker had great success with leg kicks, finding a home regularly, with Ortega struggling early on to connect with anything.

The American grew into the fight, with both men bloodied in the third round, but it was Hooker who used his reach to his advantage, earning the unanimous decision win.

After the fight, Hooker said he wanted the finish but was equally pleased to have ended his three-fight losing streak.

He called out Max Holloway for the BMF title.

In the card's co-main event, Kevin Vallejos defeated former bantamweight champion Aljamain Sterling by unanimous decision in their featherweight bout.

World.title: Alcaraz digs deep to beat Shelton and reach ATP Finals decider
World.content:
Seven-times grand slam champion Carlos Alcaraz battled back from a set down to beat American Ben Shelton 3-6, 6-3, 7-6 (7-1) in their ATP Finals semifinal to charge into ​Sunday's showcase for the ‌second consecutive year.

Alcaraz, beaten by Shelton in the US Open quarterfinals on the Spaniard's return from a four-month injury break, stretched his winning run to 13 matches after ‌back-to-back titles in Vienna and Paris.

He will face Alexander Zverev, who beat Daniil Medvedev of Russia in the other semifinal.

"I was a ​little bit frustrated at ‌the beginning because I didn't start the match the way I wanted to," said Alcaraz, unbeaten on indoor courts this season.

"Just happy that I came back in the second set playing such great tennis, step by step, ​focused ‌on all my things and ended up playing good tennis. The third set was even closer."

Shelton, making his second consecutive appearance in the ⁠season finale, grabbed an early break to ‌race to a 3-0 lead.

Alcaraz, ‌whose fitness had come under scrutiny after he left the court with heavy ‌strapping on his left leg following Wednesday's win over Medvedev, had his thigh wrapped heavily against Shelton.

He upped his game and ‌started ​moving the American around ⁠more, engaging him in longer rallies. He earned two break points at 4-2 but could not convert either, with Shelton's booming serve getting him out of trouble.

The world number four fired a second-serve ace ⁠on his first set point to move ahead but Alcaraz went 5-3 up in the second before ‌serving out the ‌second set.

The pair traded blows in the third set ​before Alcaraz eased through the tie-break, sealing the win with a return winner.

Zverev beat Daniil Medvedev 7-6 (0), 6-4 in the second semi-final at the elite season-ending event for the year’s top eight players.

In their only meeting this year, Alcaraz beat Zverev in the Australian Open semifinals. The Spaniard also holds a 7-6 edge in career meetings.

"We had a practice before the tournament started. It was unbelievable. We played one set for one and a half hours. So I hope it’s going to be similar tomorrow," Zverev said.

"I hope both of us are going to be at our best and hopefully it’s a really entertaining match for everybody."

Reuters/AP

World.title: England thrash All Blacks after Moody faces haka with team
World.content:
England has roared to a record victory over New Zealand at Twickenham in the Nations Championship, after emotional scenes before the game involving former skipper Lewis Moody, who has Motor Neurone Disease (MND).

The English beat the All Blacks 37-12 to the delight of home fans, inflicting New Zealand's second-straight defeat after last week's loss to Wales.

Moody, who played 71 Tests for England between 2001 and 2011 and was part of the team's 2003 Rugby World Cup win, came onto the ground to a huge ovation and took his place with the team to face the NZ pre-match haka.

After the haka, various England players came to embrace Moody, who announced his MND diagnosis last year.

"Lewis is such an inspirational man, he ⁠was an inspirational player and, given his ‌diagnosis, the players jumped at ‌the opportunity to support him," current England captain Maro Itoje said.

"I think he and his family gave us that ‌extra lift today. He came to spend some time with us yesterday. He presented us our shirts for today's game.

"He addressed us ‌and there's no doubt that his ⁠presence, him joining us for the haka, him spending time with us, gave us an extra lift."

Itoje, though, played down the impact of how England responded to the haka.

"The most important thing is how you start ⁠the game against New Zealand," he said.

"You can do whatever you want. There are teams historically who've done different ‌things, different formations.

"It's ‌important, but the most important thing is how you start ​the game. I wouldn't pay too much attention to whatever anyone does to respond to the haka."

Ben Earl (second from right) scored one of England's five tries in their record win over NZ. (Getty Images: RFU/Steve Bardens)

The English ran in five tries against NZ, but Itoje was determined that his side must keep improving.

After four victories in a row over Fiji, Argentina, Australia and Japan, England were braced for a much sterner test against the All Blacks, who were hurting from a shock loss to Wales.

But ​England demolished NZ, ‌racing into an early lead and ultimately winning at a canter to record back-to-back victories over the All Blacks for the first time since 2003.

"I thought we took a step forward ‌today," Itoje told reporters.

"I thought we took advantage of the opportunity we ⁠had, but … we don't want this to be our ceiling, ‌we don't want this to be as good as it ‌gets for England.

"We want to push, we want to get better. We have an amazing opportunity next week, however the chips fall to do that."

In other matches in the Nations Championship, Ireland beat world champions South Africa 20-17 in Dublin, Scotland overwhelmed Japan 67-5, and Fiji defeated Italy 21-16 in Udine.

South Africa's losing bonus point meant they topped the Southern Hemisphere standings, and will play in next week's final.

Reuters/ABC

World.title: Wallabies snap four-match losing streak with tense win over Wales
World.content:
The Wallabies have snapped a four-match losing run with a tense 29-26 win over Wales in their Nations Championship Test in Cardiff.

The result gives the Wallabies an injection of confidence and relieves some of the pressure on coach Les Kiss, although Wales did its best to deny the visitors in the shadows of full-time.

Wales scored a try through reserve hooker Ryan Elias in the 79th minute of the match, cutting the Wallabies' lead to three points.

Following the re-start, the home side launched an attacking movement from deep inside their 22, knowing it was the final play of the match.

But it came to nothing, allowing the Wallabies to celebrate victory after defeats to All Blacks (twice), England and Scotland.

The Wallabies claimed the James Bevan Trophy after defeating Wales. (Getty Images: Nations Chammpionship/Jan Kruger)

The Wallabies had entered the match low on morale, but their hopes were boosted when they established a 12-0 lead in the first half on the back of tries to Taniela Tupou and Brandon Paenga-Amosa.

But poor discipline proved costly, with the Wallabies giving away nine penalties to four, including seven inside their half.

Taniela Tupou opened the Wallabies' scoring with a first-half try. (Getty Images: Dan Istitene)

From one of those penalties, Wales scored its first converted try via captain Dewi Lake to reduce the Wallabies' lead to 12-7 at the half-time break.

The two sides traded tries early in the second half before Wales hit the front.

Wales hit the lead following Blair Murray's converted try. (Getty Images: Nations Championship/Jan Kruger)

Fullback Blair Murray's converted try gave Wales a 21-19 lead, but the Wallabies struck back with Len Ikitau scoring a five-pointer and Carter Gordon adding the extras in the 65th minute.

Leading 26-21, the Wallabies extended their advantage through Gordon's penalty goal with six minutes remaining in the match.

Wales refused to roll over, however, setting up a grandstand finish with Elias's late five-pointer.

The Wallabies finished third on the Southern Hemisphere standings in the Nations Championship.

They play Ireland at Twickenham next Saturday, AEDT, as part of the Nations Championship's Finals Weekend.

Wales, fifth in the Northern Hemisphere standings, faces Japan on Sunday, AEDT.

South Africa and France will face off in the Nations Championship grand final at Twickenham on Monday, AEDT.

Look back at how the action unfolded in our live blog.

World.title: Lehmann denies knowledge of sandpaper plot despite Bancroft statement
World.content:
Former Australian cricket coach Darren Lehmann has once again denied knowledge of a plan to use sandpaper in the Cape Town Test against South Africa in 2018, revealing the fallout left him in a "dark place".

Speaking on ABC Radio before Australia's T20 against England at the MCG, Lehmann apologised for his role in the team's culture at the time, admitting that the team's attempts to find reverse swing during the tour "went too far".

Lehmann said he had not signed a Non Disclosure Agreement with Cricket Australia and therefore was permitted to talk about the subject freely.

Cummins to retain captaincy with CA board's 'unanimous' support Cricket Australia's board throws its support behind embattled skipper Pat Cummins as the sandpaper furore continues.

"I haven't changed my views from what happened in 2018," he said.

"It was a dark time, and we got a lot of things wrong, but my version still stays the same. It was just a bad time. We all made mistakes."

Lehmann said he could not remember being a part of a conversation where David Warner raised the prospect of using sandpaper on the ball, as Cameron Bancroft detailed in his statement earlier this week.

"I can't remember being present in that conversation," he said.

"But again, it is eight and a half years ago; you'll have to ask those people. That's the issue, I have my version, and that's where I stand."

Darren Lehmann said he felt 'empathy' towards Cameron Bancroft after his statement. (Reuters)

Bancroft's statement mentioned Lehmann speaking to squad member Peter Handscomb via a walkie talkie asking him to tell Bancroft to remove the sandpaper from the field.

However, Lehmann stated that he only knew sandpaper was on the field after seeing vision of Bancroft hiding it on the TV screen.

Lehmann denied intentionally not asking about how the players were tampering with the ball during the 2018 tour.

"With reverse swing, you throw it into the dirt, you rough up one side of the ball, you might pick at it; that's been happening for 100 years, "he said.

"For me, I didn't know, but you're always ball tampering to try and get the reverse swing happening, but you never go to that extent.

"In 2018, it went too far, and I'm [responsible] for that as the coach."

Lehmann hit back at suggestions he did not pay a price for his involvement in the saga as he detailed the mental toll it took at the time.

"People said I didn't lose anything. I actually lost the best job in the world, and I'm sorry for that, and I'm sorry for what happened. That's all I can say to the general public," he said.

"I went to a really dark place. I went to as dark a place as you can think about.

"It took me probably three to four years to actually get back to some sort of normality.

Lehmann described the job of being Australia's coach as 'the best job in the world'. (Getty Images: Ryan Pierse)

"I'm not going back to that dark place. I'm trying to move forward. I'm not going back.

"There's things I remember and not remember. It is eight and a half years ago, it was a traumatic time.

"I don't want to go back to that dark place, and I hope no one does. I feel for everyone and their families."

When asked what he felt towards Bancroft in particular after his statement, Lehmann said "empathy", adding that he felt empathy for all the players and staff involved.

The context you need to understand Bancroft's version of Sandpapergate If you feel like you missed a beat with the Australian cricket's sandpaper scandal and why its back in the news, this breakdown of Cameron Bancroft's article will bring you up to speed.

He also took aim at reporters doorstopping the individuals involved and the general media coverage of the sandpaper saga.

"Some of the things that have been said are just outright hurtful to a lot of people. That's what I care about," he said.

"There's a lot of people being hurt at the moment and I think people have forgotten about that aspect.

"Yes, we made mistakes, we apologise as best we can and you try and move on.

"I'm not going back to that place … but it feels like everyone is pushing everyone to these bad places."

Lehmann denied knowledge of a specific conversation Khawaja detailed in his book in which he claimed a coach told the players to get the ball moving by any means possible.

Lehmann says he trusts Australian bowlers' accounts of the events in 2018 despite having no evidence to back them up. (Getty Images: Cameron Spencer)

"I don't understand that statement as such, because at the end of the day, I didn't get that statement," he said.

"I didn't get that question posed to me, so I can't comment for anyone else."

However, Lehmann admitted the environment surrounding the team at the time was centred around winning at all costs.

"You're always trying to get the ball moving anywhere, in any Test match, whether it's normal or reverse," he said.

"It was an ugly series, that's what I do know. A lot of people suffered and paid the price.

" I just remember how volatile that series was … and we certainly could've handled it better. "

Lehmann also could not recall whether there were any meetings where an individual stood up and voiced their concerns against the use of sandpaper.

"Everyone talks about meetings at the moment; there [were] a whole heap of different meetings," he said.

"There are conversations going on and some people are privy to them and some people are not. I'm not privy to every conversation or meeting.

"So a lot of different conversations happen all the time, different meetings, not altogether, that's how it is."

Lehmann said he had no evidence to back up the fierce denials from Australia's bowling quartet at the time — Pat Cummins, Mitchell Starc, Josh Hazlewood and Nathan Lyon — but said: "I trust the bowlers. Everyone is entitled to their own opinion."

Lehmann confirmed that he would attend Cricket Australia's independent forum for those involved on the 2018 South Africa tour to tell their version of events.

Australian captain Pat Cummins has also stated his intention to attend the forum, as have Usman Khawaja, David Warner and Cameron Bancroft.

World.title: Aussie bowlers no longer in control of public perception of legacies
World.content:
Three days ago — an eon in the context of Australian cricket's most embarrassing and avoidable omnishambles — former Australian wicketkeeper Ian Healy offered a reasonable take on Australia's famed bowling group.

"I would say it taints their personal legacies … I don't think it's going to taint their performance legacies," Healy said. "Personally now, they're not as credible as they once were, unless they change something drastically in the next few days."

Healy's personal stake in this is self-evident: his niece is married to Mitchell Starc. And in a fast-evolving crisis, his qualifiers were understandable, although we will get to Josh Hazlewood's version of drastic intervention later.

Cummins to retain captaincy with CA board's 'unanimous' support Cricket Australia's board throws its support behind embattled skipper Pat Cummins as the sandpaper furore continues.

Healy was right to differentiate between the professional and personal: one need not disparage all the hard work, all the joy, all the winning they have given Australians, by admitting that Australia's bowlers have, in recent times, irreparably damaged their own and Australia's credibility.

The bowlers also surely must concede that the precise and absolute truth of what happened in 2018 no longer matters to most fans. In fact, their carefully-worded prevarications and collective obsession with semantic distinctions project an air of guilt almost comically out of proportion with the original offence.

No matter what they saw or heard, barely anyone believes what they are saying about it.

Even if players have publicly approved of Cricket Australia's "truth forum", the rest of us surely agree it is as likely to establish an agreed and convincing set of facts as it is to locate Jimmy Hoffa.

So, to extend Healy's thought, what is their legacy, exactly?

They can hardly blame us for pondering it now in unflattering light. Because the obsession with the "legacy" of Australia's bowlers predates Usman Khawaja's book.

In the past 12 months, the idea has been fairly rammed down our throats as justification for keeping the gang together for a marathon 12 months of Test engagements against South Africa, New Zealand, India and England. The last hurrah for a golden generation, they said.

The legacy of Australia's veteran group of bowlers remains up in the air amid the recent sandpaper furore. (Getty Images: Cameron Spencer)

It could be argued that the very concept was rendered pointless weeks ago, before Sandpapergate's flare-up, on Australia's disastrous recent tour of South Africa.

It is one of the ironies of the present crisis engulfing the bowlers: it has precluded lengthier analysis of their deep and abject failure in the most recent Cape Town Test.

All the noise coming from within the team, of course, suggested this was a mere setback: South Africa are world champions for a reason, ya know? Geez, I guess we shouldn't have bowled first. Oh well, onward and upward, eh?

Actually, it was proof not just of muddled selection priorities and dwindling returns from old stagers, but a deeper crisis of philosophy and proof that the bowlers, in particular, were not operating in a meritocracy.

Having played out of his skin in the second Test, Scott Boland was dropped for Nathan Lyon, who was in turn out-bowled by Simon Harmer, an off-spinner most Australians had previously thought of as a glorified clubbie.

Nathan Lyon was brutally out-bowled by South Africa's Simon Harner in Australia's most recent Test performance. (AP Photo: Halden Krog)

And Harmer didn't merely take wickets. He publicly called out and dismantled the Australian captain in a manner that should have caused far more alarm than whatever Cummins did or didn't see as a 24-year-old.

To delve into another modern-day obsession — being "aura" — the loss went far deeper than a 2-1 scoreline. Before its present distraction, Australian cricket pretended otherwise, but symbolic damage was done on a scale we will see more clearly in a few years.

Which brings us to Josh Hazlewood. On a very simple level, his claim yesterday that he would "review" his place in the Australian team if Cummins lost the captaincy was an impassioned if artless expression of loyalty and solidarity with the skipper in times of disloyalty.

More so, it smacked of the cart being placed a hell of a long way in front of the horse. It was an expression of entitlement that brought to mind another unflattering scene from a year ago, of an "absolutely filthy" Nathan Lyon sulking away to a sideline TV reporter after being omitted from last December's pink-ball Test. There have been others.

The context you need to understand Bancroft's version of Sandpapergate If you feel like you missed a beat with the Australian cricket's sandpaper scandal and why its back in the news, this breakdown of Cameron Bancroft's article will bring you up to speed.

For a long time now — long before Sandpapergate reared up again — there has been an inescapable sense that Australia's senior players see themselves not as members of a team chosen by an independent selection panel, nor as merely a self-selecting elite within that team, but as the self-appointed bosses of Australian Test cricket.

It is hard to escape the feeling that it is this self-absorbed culture of entitlement and the desire to control its own narrative — much more so than anything that happened in 2018 — that now defines what the public thinks of Australia's bowlers.

And yes, it is true that those who've thrown their weight around like this are, by most definitions, indisputably Australia's best. And it is also true that they have sometimes needed to exercise their collective power for the benefit of others, too, as in their pay negotiations.

But what is the average fan — who, by the time the Perth Test rolls around in nine days, will have been subjected to weeks of a melodrama which is only a paternity test and a few exploding boats away from a Home and Away plot — to make of a 35-year-old multi-millionaire threatening to take his ball and go home if his mate's not in charge?

Australia's bowling 'cartel' has always been inseparable, particularly in the years following the infamous 2018 South Africa tour. (AAP: Dean Lewins)

"The cartel". It has always had a faintly sinister ring to it, don't you think? Some of the behaviour is, frankly, gangsterism, albeit in the territory mined by Martin Scorsese and David Chase — the petty spats over matters of honour and respect, the fragile egos and wounded pride.

In this light, we now see Cameron Bancroft as the hapless 'Spider', egged on and then assassinated. Perhaps we suddenly respect Steve Smith a little more for silently doing all that time for crimes he didn't commit.

Which leaves us with how Australia proceeds in the short-term. Cricket Australia, more to blame for the mess than any player, confirmed on Saturday that Cummins would be retained as captain. It was the most predictable and probably the most sensible course of action based on a sober appraisal of all relevant facts, but it did also have the unfortunate effect of validating Hazlewood's veiled threat.

Even granting the need to extinguish a tabloid bin-fire, and acknowledging the overwhelming good Cummins has done for Australian cricket, there is an irony in this: backing him in as leader guarantees him a higher work and stress load than he would ideally be shouldering at this point of his career. In an ideal world, free of this scandal, honest conversations about succession planning would already be happening.

Hazlewood's defence of Cummins came after Mitchell Starc had also previously whacked down claims of knowing about the plot to ball tamper in 2018. (AP Photo: Halden Krog)

Hazlewood's interjection and the self-conferred gravitas of his Test spot, meanwhile, sit somewhat at odds with the prevailing views of his contemporaries. Only a week ago, players' union boss Paul Marsh admitted there was "decreasing" support among players for the idea of Test cricket as the pinnacle of the sport.

Fans, by extension, are now buffeted by administrators who care too little about Test cricket and a few players who care too much.

In the time since Sandpapergate, Cricket Australia has had six chairmen, four CEOs, three men's head coaches and capped 21 new Test players. That a few mainstays attained an over-mighty status is perhaps natural enough, but it is surely time that senior players are reminded that Test selection is not their birthright.

Australia's next 15 Tests would have been brutally difficult in any context. Against such a draining and unpleasant backdrop, the degree of difficulty for an aging and now embittered group of old hands has only increased.

And that really is the stuff of "legacy" — not just everything in totality, but the aftertaste left by the final few bites.

World.title: Roos head to fourth straight final after booking decider against Melbourne
World.content:
Back in the AFLW grand final for the first time in four years, Melbourne are determined to embrace every bit of the lead-in to a blockbuster decider against two-time defending premiers North Melbourne.

After North beat a gritty Sydney by 32 points to reach a fourth straight decider, Melbourne overcame a stern challenge from Carlton to prevail 10.15 (75) to 6.9 (45) in front of 8,037 fans at Ikon Park on Saturday.

The preliminary final victory under first-year coach Tom Wilson sets up arguably the most hotly-anticipated grand final in years, next Friday night at the same venue.

The Demons and Kangaroos have never faced off in a decider but North only beat Melbourne, then playing under 2022 premiership coach Mick Stinear, by 10 points in last year's preliminary final.

North beat Melbourne by 31 in round seven but Melbourne will feel primed to deny Darren Crocker's Kangaroos an unprecedented three-peat after a high-pressure win in hot conditions.

"I couldn't be more positive and optimistic about what this week looks like," Wilson said.

"We're just going to enjoy every second of it because we worked extremely hard to get here and I don't want the girls to let that go by.

"I want them to sit in it and enjoy what comes with the week because they deserve to."

Midfield double act Olivia Purcell (31 disposals) and Tyla Hanks (20) were particularly influential.

"I'm extremely biased, but they're superstars in my eyes," Wilson said.

Defender Maeve Chaplin (27 disposals, 15 intercepts) was exceptional, skipper Kate Hore (20 disposals) and Megan Fitzsimon kicked two goals apiece while Tayla Harris (nine marks) made her presence felt.

"Really proud of the playing group. The way they went about it today was really professional," Wilson said.

"Difficult conditions, quite hot and Carlton threw a few punches.

"So for us to be able to absorb their throws … just really pleased for the girls and the playing group for the work that they've done."

Carlton skipper Abbie McKay (27 disposals) fought hard with support from Irish livewire Erone Fitzpatrick (two goals), Claudia Whitfort (17 disposals) and Lila Keck (two goals).

Down back, Harriet Cordner and the retiring Gab Pound never gave up as Mathew Buck's Blues suffered a second straight preliminary final exit.

"Disappointed as a group, of course," Buck said.

"But when we get time to reflect post this, it'll be a chance to reflect back on the whole season and be proud of another prelim that we've made it to.

"To fall short is disappointing, and we've got lots of stuff we still need to improve on, but achievement of itself to make it."

Melbourne led by six at quarter-time, then at the start of the second quarter, Carlton jagged two quick goals and took a seven-point lead.

But Melbourne wrested the contest back their way, peppering the goal until Shelley Heath-Barker drilled a terrific finish to restore the Demons' lead.

They wouldn't lose it again.

The Demons led by eight at half-time then seized control with a four-goal third quarter, with Maggie Mahony toe-poking home just before the siren to deliver a 26-point lead at the final change.

Poppy Scholz gave the Blues a lifeline at the start of the final quarter but the Demons romped to victory.

Buck conceded the Blues, who are set to again target GWS defender Cambridge McCormick, were currently five or six goals off the competition's best — North and Melbourne.

"We look forward to hitting the draft again this year and our trade period as well," Buck said.

"Any way we can do it (improve), we'll look to achieve it."

Roos survive Swans scare

North Melbourne is within touching distance of an AFLW premiership "three-peat" after fighting out a 32-point victory over a Chloe Molloy-inspired Sydney in their preliminary final.

Ash Riddell and veteran Emma Kearney were centre stage as the Kangaroos kicked six goals clear in the first half before holding off a brave Swans challenge in the 13.5 (83) to 8.3 (51) triumph at Princes Park on Saturday.

Darren Crocker's all-conquering side is into a fourth consecutive grand final, with the chance to complete the first flag hat-trick in the history of the women's competition.

But there is some concern over ruck Kim Rennie, who spent some time on the turf in the final quarter and eventually hobbled off with what appeared to be a right knee injury.

Riddell (29 disposals) and Eilish Sheerin (22) were outstanding, while superstar Jasmine Garner finished with three goals from 18 disposals despite attention from Swans tagger Tanya Kennedy.

Tahlia Randall and Blaithin Bogue kicked two each for the Kangaroos.

Kearney (15 disposals) was dependable as always on managed minutes in her return from a hamstring injury, and got under her opponents' skin in trademark fashion.

Molloy (three goals) did her best to lift Sydney, sparking a second-quarter fightback, but North had a greater number of contributors across the ground.

Laura Gardner (25 disposals), Zippy Fish (18) and Cynthia Hamilton (two goals) also fought hard for the gallant Swans.

A global Ticketmaster outage caused long queues for frustrated fans outside the ground, but those lucky enough to get in early witnessed a slice of history.

Hamilton opened the scoring for Sydney with the fastest AFLW goal, finishing well on the run just 21 seconds into the contest.

But Garner responded within a minute, and the opening term belonged to North, who led 4.2 to 2.1 at the first break.

Garner added her second early in the second quarter and it opened the floodgates, with the Kangaroos piling on another four consecutive goals.

Molloy breathed life back into the contest with three of Sydney's four goals in a nine-minute burst before half-time.

The Swans' superstar caught both Riddell and Kearney holding the ball, and kicked team-lifting goals against the tide.

The North duo demonstrably disputed the decisions with umpires but were not penalised further for dissent.

Kearney also sparked a melee when she riled her opponents by sarcastically joining in the Swans' celebrations.

Molloy's third major cut what was a 36-point margin back to 18 by half-time, with North leading 9.2 to 6.2 at the main break.

It was one goal apiece in a tight third quarter and the Swans got within a couple of kicks when Maddie Quinn (two goals) kicked the first major of the final term.

But North held firm and Garner kicked the sealer when she snapped her third major with less than four minutes left on the clock.

AAP

World.title: Khawaja and Warner taken off commentary as CA backs Cummins' captaincy
World.content:
Usman Khawaja and David Warner have been removed from Fox Cricket's commentary team as another day of developments in the sandpaper saga saw Cricket Australia back captain Pat Cummins.

Khawaja and Warner will miss Australia's T20 series against England but are expected to return for next month's Test series against New Zealand.

"In light of recent events both Usman and Davey will be rested from our broadcasts over the next few weeks," Fox Sports managing director Steve Crawley said.

The context you need to understand Bancroft's version of Sandpapergate If you feel like you missed a beat with the Australian cricket's sandpaper scandal and why its back in the news, this breakdown of Cameron Bancroft's article will bring you up to speed.

"While we always support all members of our commentary team and welcome a diversity of views which is a feature of our summer of cricket, we also understand the pressure they are under to respond to each and every new comment.

"We think it is increasingly difficult to focus on the game while the situation continues to unfold and think it is unfair on both commentators to put them in that position.

"Our focus remains on providing our viewers with the best broadcast of Australia's summer of cricket. We will continue to monitor the situation.''

Fox's decision to sideline Khawaja and Warner comes as Cricket Australia threw its support behind embattled Test and one-day captain Pat Cummins on Saturday afternoon.

Cummins was unanimously backed by the CA board to continue as captain after meeting with CA chair David Boon and CEO Todd Greenberg on Friday in Sydney, with Cummins saying the meeting "meant a lot" amid the ongoing speculation

Pat Cummins will remain the captain of Australia's men's cricket team amid ongoing speculation. (Getty Images: Gareth Copley)

His captaincy had been questioned following claims by former Test batters Usman Khawaja and Cameron Bancroft that knowledge of the sandpaper plot during the 2018 South Africa tour was widely known.

"Being Australian captain carries with it an awesome responsibility. I have and never will take that lightly," Cummins said in a statement on Saturday.

"David and Todd have a very tough job navigating cricket through all of this, and I commend them for reaching out to me and to many of the players and staff from 2018.

"I support the forum 100 per cent. I will be there. All of the players and staff I have spoken with are very keen to go and have their say. There will be a lot of difficult conversations, but that is what's needed.

"Otherwise, from this point, captaining the Australian team in Perth will be my focus and priority."

Cummins has come under fire for his denials made in a 68-minute press conference on November 13. (Getty Images: Darrian Traynor)

Cummins encountered several reporters at his house this week after Bancroft broke his silence on the sandpaper saga with a 4,500-word statement.

In the statement, Bancroft said he was left feeling "angry, betrayed and alone" by Cummins's lengthy press conference where he denied any knowledge of sandpaper being brought onto the field.

Among the issues discussed in the meeting between Cummins, Boon and Greenberg were Cummins's welfare and the support required for the upcoming home Test series against New Zealand.

"We are absolutely determined to steward Australian cricket through this very difficult time with diligence and patience and to listen and learn," Boon said in the same CA statement.

Cricket Australia chair David Boon (pictured) says CA "unequivocally" rejects suggestions Cummins's integrity has been compromised. (ABC News: Ebony ten Broeke )

"That's what the independent forum we announced this week is about, and the board encourages all players and support staff to tell and discuss their stories there. We will be publishing the terms of reference in due course.

"We've expressed our support to Pat and our concern for everyone impacted by the events of the 2018 tour of South Africa.

"We have learned from that experience and are proud of the team and the culture Pat and other leaders in the team have fostered over the past eight years and unequivocally reject any implication that Pat's integrity has been compromised."

Cummins has been Australia's Test captain since 2021 and is also the captain of the one-day team, having led Australia to the 2023 50-over World Cup title.

World.title: Hazlewood backs Cummins as sandpaper saga continues
World.content:
Josh Hazlewood has thrown his support behind Pat Cummins to remain Australian men's captain following the resurfacing of the ball-tampering scandal.

Speculation about Cummins's future in the role has intensified since Cameron Bancroft alleged the entire Australian cricket team knew about the 2018 sandpaper plot.

Cummins has maintained he and the Australian bowling unit did not know sandpaper was being used on the field during the infamous Test series in South Africa.

He was not Australia's captain at the time.

Cummins spoke at length in a media conference last week and released a statement via his management following Bancroft's allegation on Wednesday night.

Several former international Test players, including retired Australian fast bowler Mitchell Johnson, have publicly questioned whether Cummins could continue as captain.

Speaking to News Corp, Hazlewood, who played alongside Cummins in Cape Town, said he had no knowledge of ball-tampering being used in the series against the Proteas.

Hazlewood said he supported Cummins remaining Australia's captain.

"It feels like it's been a bit of a pile-on the last few days from different people," Hazlewood said.

"I want to back Pat and everything he said in his press conference last week, everything he's done for the last five or six years in particular as captain.

"To get the group where it is now and in a position where something like that [sandpaper] is never going to happen again — I think is just a remarkable job."

Hazlewood said Cummins was an outstanding captain.

"He's a great leader," Hazlewood said.

"If you went around and asked everyone in the team, you'd hear the same response.

"I think if we turned up for the first Test [against New Zealand] and he wasn't the captain and it was someone else, honestly, I don't know how that would go."

Pat Cummins has maintained his stance on the ball-tampering allegations. (Getty Images: Darrian Traynor)

Hazlewood said he might reconsider his position in the Australian squad if Cummins was removed as captain.

Last week, Cummins held a 70-minute media conference in response to Usman Khawaja's ball-tampering allegations, which were published in his memoir, Sabr.

"When he [Khawaja] says we all knew, if by that he means that we knew sandpaper was going out in the field, he's 100 per cent wrong," Cummins told reporters in Sydney.

"I've said that consistently for the last eight years. I did not know that was happening.

"But Usman actually says things that are actually far more serious than that. He says that I and others were architects of a scheme to ball-tamper with sandpaper.

"That's complete and utter nonsense."

Tech.title: Amazon is complaining about NYC Council on shipping labels, too
Tech.content:
is the Verge’s weekend editor. He’s covered the tech industry for over 18 years and knows a thing or two about synths.

Posts from this author will be added to your daily email digest and your homepage feed.

Amazon is leaving no venue unexplored in its fight against the New York City Council and the Delivery Protection Act. The company is now putting labels on shipments claiming that the Council could add up to $5 to any Amazon order. The Delivery Protection Act would effectively ban the sort of third-party arrangements Amazon currently uses to deliver many packages, including small companies and independent contractors. Last-mile delivery firms operating warehouses would need to be licensed by the city and directly employ their workers.

Earlier this week, Amazon started showing notifications in its mobile app and on its website reading “Attention NYC Council could add up to $5 per order.” Now the company is including an almost identical message on shipping labels.

Amazon claims that the bill, if passed, “would likely mean slower and more expensive delivery for millions of customers in New York City,” and has threatened to move its warehouses outside of the city. However, labor unions, Council Speaker Julie Menin, and Mayor Zohran Mamdani have countered that the company is attempting to “threaten New Yorkers and intimidate this City Council” and is acting out of “greed,” pointing to Amazon’s market cap of nearly $3 trillion.

Tech.title: The UN fails to agree on rules regulating ‘killer robots’
Tech.content:
is the Verge’s weekend editor. He’s covered the tech industry for over 18 years and knows a thing or two about synths.

Posts from this author will be added to your daily email digest and your homepage feed.

One of the items on the agenda for UN diplomats meeting in Geneva this week was working towards rules regarding the use of autonomous weapons, or so-called “killer robots.” Eventually, representatives left the meetings agreeing to “start discussing options” after a largely fruitless week of negotiations.

According to NPR:

Before the negotiations got underway, the International Committee of the Red Cross, the guardian of the Geneva Conventions, said it was urgent for legally binding rules to be drafted within a year. That call was backed by the U.N. secretary-general and by Pope Leo.

The compromise reached was that countries would instead have two years to propose regulations. Negotiations between countries on which regulations to adopt and how to enforce them will likely drag on well beyond that. Additionally, room was left for some of those yet-to-be-adopted regulations to remain “optional.”

Humanitarian organizations and some countries see a need to urgently adopt legally binding rules as semi-autonomous weapons and drones have been responsible for a significant number of civilian deaths in conflicts around the globe, including in Ukraine, Gaza, and Sudan.

According to NPR, Russia, Israel, and the US proved to be the primary obstructions:

On day one, Russia delayed proceedings by objecting to the meeting’s agenda. Then the United States proposed a five-year window to discuss nonbinding, optional guidelines for autonomous weapons.

Tech.title: The FBI and USDA were reportedly hacked
Tech.content:
is the Verge’s weekend editor. He’s covered the tech industry for over 18 years and knows a thing or two about synths.

Posts from this author will be added to your daily email digest and your homepage feed.

Friday, it was reported that both the US Department of Agriculture (USDA) and the FBI were hacked. In reporting on the FBI hack, CNN noted that this is the second such attack on the agency in the last few months, this time targeting the National Crime Information Center (NCIC), which federal, state, and local law enforcement use to share information, including warrants and missing persons. President Donald Trump later confirmed the hack in an interview with Fox News. NBC first reported the USDA hack on Friday. According to Reuters:

While the payments ​database is the known extent ​of the intrusion so far, the former ‌officials ⁠warned that the compromised system could provide a backdoor to more sensitive information, including food safety ​data and ​research on ⁠animal-borne illnesses, according to the report.

The breaches come following a week of major outages across several sectors, including at the FAA and NSA, which the government has sought to reassure the public were not the result of a cyberattack.

President Trump suggested that the breach of the FBI might not be an entirely bad thing, telling Fox News that, “Maybe we’ll learn about the voter fraud, all the voter fraud that took place,” and “wouldn’t it be great to learn about Russia, Russia, Russia?” referring to investigations into his ties to Russia.

The FBI suffered a breach, reported in late September, that allegedly compromised personal records of “all FBI employees and applicants.” This was followed by a hack of DHS, reported in October, comprising 40,000 employee records. In the wake of these major outages, the White House national cyber director, Sean Cairncross, stepped down this week.

Update November 21st: Added President Trump’s comments.

Comedy is just part of Roberts’ life, however. In addition to his appearances on Gravity Falls and Comedy Bang! Bang!, he’s also a musician with deep roots in New York City’s queer nightlife scene. He just released his latest record, I Am, on Friday, and it dabbles in ’80s pop, ’90s house, and even dashes of ’00s rave. But while the record sounds made for the dance floor, it actually tackles some pretty heavy subject matter, like mortality, aging, and grief following the loss of his mother.
